-and to some of those four or five-hour runners who get the track and keep it till the end of the session. There are half a dozen men in the House who could save us a good deal of time if they would. But, Sir, when I recall the distinguished appearance of my hon. friend from Graspy as he utters one of those orations-taken largely from the speeches of Lord Palmerston-I am afraid that he will not accept my advice. What I would propose would be this-a change in the rules that would limit speeches to half an hour, unless the unanimous consent of the House were given for an extension of time for The speech of any hon. member. I have sat in other legislative bodies where we had a rule of that kind; and if a man

had really anything to say that required more than that time, he was always given permission; but the rule gave us an excellent opportunity to see that the debate was not carried on simply for the purpose of some man hearing himself speak or preparing material for the next general election. If the House would make a rule that half an hour should be the limit for a speech, we would not need to sit after eleven o'clock at night and we would not need to form a Canadian National Union of Orators.

subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTING. REGULAR ADJOURNMENT AT ELEVEN O'CLOCK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this matter has been brought up as it has been on other occasions in this House, I have always subordinated my view as to the time spent in this chamber to the opinions of members representing constituencies in the far East or the far West. It is possible for myself andmanyother members from Ontario and Quebec constituencies, to go home on Fridays and to get in touch with their businesses. That is a privilege and a very great advantage to those hon. gentlemen; but members from the far West and those from the Maritime Provinces cannot very well do that without losing time in the House. Therefore, I have felt that, whatever my views might be in regard to the time that is spent in this chamber, I should be willing to give way to the opinions of those members who represent constituencies at a distance from Ottawa.
I do not think there is any more time wasted in this House in proportion to the number of its members, the vast extent of this Dominion and the multiplicity of questions that come up, than is wasted in other deliberative assemblies throughout this country. It has become a common practice to refer to long speeches and the length of time wasted in this House, and frequently we see our newspapers writing editorials on the question. This has always struck me as somewhat inconsistent on the part of newspapers when one has only to turn over a page or two in order to see the quantity of space absolutely wasted with "Peter Pal," "Mutt and Jeff" and other stuff of a like nature which is not of any benefit to any person in the Dominion of Canada. Another waste of time that I have seen on the part of newspapers and newspaper editors is a repetition of one day's editorial in the next day's issue. I do not think there is any more time wasted in this chamber than is wasted in county councils or other municipal bodies in proportion to the num-

ber of members in those bodies and the subjects with which they have to deal. We are all fallible; we are all liable to make mistakes and I presume, as long as there is a Parliament for Canada, there will always be a certain amount of time wasted in this as in any other assembly, I do not care what it is.
It has always struck me that some time might be saved in the early part of the session. It is usually two or three weeks before committees get down to work, and I see no reason, and I have never been able to see any, why Parliament should not meet in the mornings in the first few weeks of the session, at least until committees organize and get to work, when, of course, morning sittings would be impossible as members could not be in the chamber and on committees at the same time.
As regards Wednesday evening sittings, it has always seemed to me that the Wednesday evening holiday, which is given to members in the first few weeks or month or so of the session, has been for the benefit of two classes of persons who attend Parliament, those persons who have formed the habit of attending prayer meeting once a week, usually on Wednesday night and who, having formed that habit, of course, want to continue it when they come to Ottawa-and there is very great reason why they should continue it-and those other persons who have got caught in the social whirl in Ottawa and want Wednesday evening to attend to that. I have never been greatly troubled in either direction and, therefore, I have always been willing to attend sessions of Parliament on Wednesday evenings. I can see no earthly reason why Parliament should sit from two to six o'clock on Wednesday and not sit on Wednesday evening, but sit from three to six o'clock on Thursday and from eight to eleven or twelve o'clock the same night. I am absolutely opposed to the Wednesday evening holiday, whether it is for the benefit of those who want to attend prayer meeting that night or for the benefit of those who are caught in the social whirl and want to attend to that. In other words, I think that they might confine all their dances to Saturday evenings and their prayer meetings to Sunday afternoons and evenings.
As regards limiting the evening sitting to eleven o'clock, I do not think it would be advisable to make any hard-and-fast rule in that respect. We have an hour fixed for the meeting of Parliament, but to fix eleven o'clock or any other hour as

the hour at -which the House should and must close at night, -would be inadvisable. Very often you might be in the midst of something of importance, perhaps a matter of getting through some Estimates; the subject might have been pretty well exhausted in debate and just about ready to go through, some progress to be made about eleven o'clock; but some person realizes that there is a rule or an understanding that the House is to adjourn at eleven o'clock, and, availing himself of that, keeps the thing going for a few minutes more until the House automatically rises. The closing hour should be left to the common sense and intelligence of members composing this House, and when, in their wisdom, they think it advisable for the House to sit until half past eleven or eleven o'clock or a quarter to eleven, well and good. We are not schoolboys; we are men of mature age, and common sense will regulate the matter pretty well. There may be some nights when we will exceed the limit and go to one or two o'clock in the morning, without doubt to the regret of every person in the chamber. That sort of thing is not likely to be repeated night after night, and why? Because the common sense of members is opposed to anything of the kind. Therefore, it would be far better to leave the hour of closing to the good judgment of the members composing the House.
Right hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Prime Minister) : The first section of the motion of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), to the effect that the Wednesday afternoon sitting should open at three o'clock commencing with the first of the session, deals with a matter that I think should be regulated pretty much to meet the will of the majority of members, and consequently could best be done after inquiry and report by a committee. The rules of the House are almost invariably amended on report of a committee. It is now some years since such a committee sat, but I would not think it would be wise at the present session to appoint another. We have so many important and special committees now, and so many hon. members are engaged thereon, that, particularly at this period of the session, with the work becoming heavier for each and all of us, we should consider carefully before embarking upon another.
As to the second and more [DOT] important portion of the resolution I have views that I desire to oppose to those of the hon. member who moves it, and I do so with
deference, knowing that his experience is much longer than mine, and that he doubtless has studied the subject more carefully. I, of course, naturally look upon this matter from the standpoint of the Government. He, just as naturally, looks upon it from the standpoint of the Opposition.

subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTING. REGULAR ADJOURNMENT AT ELEVEN O'CLOCK
speechtext:
The hon. member for Maisonneuve has reinforced the argument of the mover of the resolution by a reference to the practice of the British House. I think I can use that reference to show wherein we necessarily differ from that House. The British House does have some general rule whereby it closes at about eleven o'clock, but there is this very great difference: In the British House closure became a fact and a rule away back in the eighties, I think. It became a matter of constant practice through many years and even decades, and growing out of the constant application of closure there evolved what is looked upon as a sort of voluntary closure, agreed upon by the whips of both sides-a practice that never could have become established, and never, indeed, would likely have existed, had it not been for the fact of the closure being constantly applied by the Government, and necessarily applied, to get the public business done. In this House we have voluntary closure at times, but it is very, very rare, and I do not think that with the practice we have now, even though we have a rare resort to closure, we could ever make much progress by agreement between the whips for the shortening of speeches or the shortening of debates. We try that, but we do not succeed; that has been the practice under both Governments. The reason, chiefly, is the one I have just given, that closure in Canada is of much later growth. In England they have had closure all through these years, and consequently there has been time for this practice to grow, a practice that naturally takes root in the closure rule, because the whips on both sides know that unless they succeed voluntarily, then by force majeure the debate comes to an end anyway, because closure is applied. Consequently, they are able to get business done from day to day under the influence of the rule on the one hand, and this practice that has grown out of it on the other.
But there is this further. In Great Britain the closure rule is immediate and almost automatic, that is to say, they can bring discussions to a close almost at any

time, and without notice. In Canada we have a much more considerate closure rule. We can only apply it one day to take effect the next, and then only at one o'clock on the following morning. I think it is well that in these matters we move slowly. While the closure rule remains as it is in this House, it is a matter of actual experience that we can make no sufficient progress if we are going to have an automatic rising of the House at eleven o'clock at night. Of that I have not the least doubt whatever. Why, what progress have we made up to now, Mr. Speaker? Any real business that has been done since the House opened on February 14, this year,-and we have not had any eleven o'clock automatic rising,-has been done mainly after eleven o'clock at night, and much of it well on towards morning. On the whole of this question I am very much in agreement, under present circumstances, with the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). I do not think it is possible to make progress if we have anything like an automatic rising of the House at eleven or any special hour.
While I am on my feet, I call attention to the hours at which the House has risen. Sometimes, but very rarely, have we risen much past eleven o'clock. I have before me the hours from the beginning of the session until now, and eleven would represent about the average. I know the dates on which we rose later, and those are the very dates when we got the work of Parliament done. I would like, indeed, if faster progress could be made. I am not saying this to complain especially. Possibly if I were on the Opposition side I would have another viewpoint, but I am going to try, if I ever get there, to be more reasonable in this regard than I have found the present Opposition. We are met practically every time we attempt to go into Supply with a motion on one subject or another; I will not say of no importance, but I do say that if this House sat 365 days in the year I could guarantee to place in the hands of the Opposition an amendment every day that would be of equal importance to any that they have advanced so far. You can always get a matter, I will not say of no importance, but one that will serve the purpose of creating a discussion and creating press material, and that is what really goes on. So if we intend to make progress from now onwards, it would be fatal, indeed, if we should now come to any decision to rise automatically at eleven o'clock. I would think we would soon be where the

British House is to-day in one regard: we would be sitting the whole year round, for that has become the British practice. Indeed, so great is the effort there to get on with public affairs, that automatic closure is applied constantly, and even then they frequently do not rise for dinner. The House will run right on from six to eight o'clock, certain members going out at certain times. That is how they are able to rise at eleven. If they had our practice in other respects, had our closure, and the rare application of it, the business of the Old Land could not begin to be done if they rose at eleven o'clock or at any set time, though it were hours later than that. Consequently, while I do not feel there is any possibility of the acceptance by the Government of the latter part of his resolution, there is considerable to be said for the first part, and it would appear to me it would be better for that matter to be taken up by a special committee at the beginning of a session.

subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTING. REGULAR ADJOURNMENT AT ELEVEN O'CLOCK
speechtext:
I
find myself in agreement to a certain extent with what the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) has said. The method of conducting the business of this House, and the length of the sittings is of considerable importance to those members whose homes are a long distance from Ottawa. It appears to those of us who are so situated that several changes might be made with considerable advantage to us, at least, and without any great disadvantage, I believe, to members residing nearer to the seat of Government. Take private members' day. I can see no good reason why private members, instead of having Monday and Wednesday, should not have Monday and Friday. I believe it is usually understood between the party whips just what matters are to come up on private members' day, and members who were sufficiently interested in any matter that would come up for discussion might very well remain over the week-end. I do not think that would seriously interfere with the rights of any one.
For once at least, I agree with the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). We do not usually see eye to eye, but I do concur in his views, to a considerable extent, in the matter of Wednesday sittings. He is of the opinion that we might very well sit on Wednesday mornings during the early part of the session. I would go much further and suggest that during the early part of the session we might also sit on

Wednesday night, at least while the debate on the Address was being discussed. After all, no particular question is ever under discussion in that debate; it is usually a rambling repetition from beginning to end; it is practically a re-hash of what has been previously dealt with. In the debate on the Address the same matters come up that have been talked over scores of times before and I think we might very well devote Wednesday nights to a continuation of that dehate until its conclusion. I would not press my point in regard to the Budget debate. But I do think, Mr. Speaker, that we might very well sit on Wednesday nights during the early part of the session, at least until we disposed of the debate on the Address.
I was much interested in the remarks of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken), regarding the length of speeches It struck me forcibly at the time he was speaking that there is very little difference between an hon. member making one long speech on a specific subject, and another hon. gentleman making several possibly shorter speeches on another subject. I have listened, on several occasions, to the hon. member making somewhat lengthy speeches in regard to the Civil Service Commission, and if we took the various periods taken up by him and added them together the result would probably compare favourably with the length of time occupied the other night by an hon. member who spent, I believe, something like five hours of the time of the House discussing a certain subject. Even if the House adjourned at 11 o'clock I am doubtful if it would have shortened the speech of the hon. gentleman very much, for I am convinced that, from his point of view, the subject was far from being exhausted, and had the House adjourned at 11 o'clock, supposing he had the floor then, it might have been possible for him to have started again the next day and to have continued for several hours more. So that in that respect we might not' have been further ahead on that occasion by an early closing.
Members from a distance would suggest an earlier calling of the session. Why not go back to the old practice of calling the session in November and giving a fairly lengthy recess during the Christmas holidays, so that those engaged in the retail business might have sufficient time to wind up their affairs for the year, and also better cope with the Christmas rush? If that were not quite convenient, then I would suggest that we
meet as early in the New Year as possible. Then again, in the matter of Easter holidays, we think it is rather unfair for members who reside in proximity to Ottawa to object to a longer recess at Easter. I understand the objection comes principally from those who are so situated and who can attend to their business over the week-end. Now, we do not very seriously object to their paying particular attention to their business at that time, but we do submit that to those of us who live at a distance from the Capital, a five-day recess is of no use; we should have the privilege of a two weeks' vacation to enable us to attend to our affairs at home. If we calculate strictly the number of days which members have off, we find that in addition to the fifteen days to which members of Parliament are entitled, a great many members can avail themselves of the week-end holiday. If I might make the remark, I observe in the lobbies on Fridays quite a number of coats, canes, etc., hanging around, which disappear shortly after the House opens; and a similar condition prevails on Mondays, when members on their return even have their grips in their hands in order to get into the House before adjournment. Those who can avail themselves of the week-end, in addition to the fifteen days allowed, are to all intents and purposes taking forty-seven days to themselves out of a total of eighty days, if we reckon on a basis of sixteen weeks as the length of the session. Those of us who cannot take advantage of more than the fifteen days think this is scarcely fair.
A point raised by the member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) was that if you did away with this Friday and Monday holiday, if I might. term it a holiday, you would practically prevent business men from becoming members of Parliament. I wonder whether we are to conclude from that remark that there are no business men in the House other than those who are enabled to attend to their business over the weekend. Leaving myself and those employed in the same occupation out of the question, I could mention several business men in this House whose business is just as difficult [DOT] to manage from a distance as that of the average commercial and industrial business man, if not more so. We have such men representing western constituencies. We have a number of professional men who cannot delegate their business to others without very serious loss, and I do not see why it should be any more difficult for an eastern business man to be a member of

Parliament than it is for a western business man, from my hon. friend's point of view.
Now, as to the closure, I do not think I can be accused of taking up more than a fair share of the time of the House, hut to me word "closure" sounds somewhat harsh. I think that other methods just as effective and less objectionable might be devised. For instance, suppose you cease the publication of Hansard. I wonder what effect that would have. I am of opinion that if you cut out the printing of Hansard, it would have considerable effect on the length of debates; and, to use the ordinary expression, it would then be up to the member himself if he wished to have his speech distributed among his constituents. I would still furnish the facilities for him if he wished to have that done; but as to his speech being printed, it would be a matter entirely for him to decide and it would be for him to defray the expense. Again, referring to the question of closing at 11 o'clock, I fully agree with the Prime Minister when he says that so far this session the real business of the House has been conducted after 11 o'clock. I believe I am within the mark when I say that the Opposition have been largely responsible for this fact.
On almost every occasion when a motion has been made to go into Committee of Supply an amendemnt has been moved which, in most instances, has occupied very nearly the whole of the sitting up to eleven o'clock. I am not criticizing this proceeding-it may be absolutely necessary and the submission of such amendments may be quite proper-but nevertheless if we are going to limit the time within' which we shall sit to eleven o'clock, then I think we must be prepared for a similar condition to that in the Old Country where Parliament sits practically all the year round.
In the discussion considerable importance has been attached to the matter of physical endurance, and as to the possibility of the limit of that endurance being reached when members are asked to sit so late. If hon. members occupied their seats all the time there might be some foundation for that argument. I quite agree that if hon. members had to keep their seats during the entire sitting of the House, there might be force in such an argument, but, the actual facts do not support the contention. A casual observation will show that, on the average, not more than one-fifth of the seats of the House can be claimed as occupied

continuously; the attendance of members varies and has even fallen to the point where the Speaker has had on one occasion to adjourn the House for want of a quorum. Very often the attendance will only number some fifty or sixty members-indeed unless the occasion is a special one it is very seldom that more than fifty or sixty members are in their seats. Unfortunately for me I am not a smoker, and I have not as good an excuse to advance for leaving the chamber as some hon. gentlemen employ when they wish to take a little leisure out in the lobby or elsewhere. I do not think, therefore, that any hon. member is suffering very much by reason of the continued occupancy of his chair, and we do not need to worry very much about such a point as that when we are not compelled to remain in the chamber continuously. For these reasons I do not know that I can support the resolution except as to opening the proceedings at three o'clock on Wednesday. I am unable, however, to support the proposition that the latest hour for sittings, unless there be good reason to the contrary, shall be eleven o'clock.

subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTING. REGULAR ADJOURNMENT AT ELEVEN O'CLOCK
speechtext:
If the House will bear with me for a few minutes I think I shall be able to say before the House rises for dinner, all that I wish to say in reply. I regret that the motion has come up at a time when so many hon. members are absent, because, from the conversations 1 have had with many hon. gentlemen on both sides, I am satisfied that the purpose of this motion has a larger degree of sympathy than has been made evident in the discussion to-day. I have already intimated that I have no intention of asking the House to divide upon this motion. If I felt that such a motion would have the effect of prolonging the session, as suggested by the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr.Stevens). I would be among the first to oppose it. However, I do not think it would have that result; I think the effect would be quite the opposite.
I sympathize with the views expressed by hon. members who have been described -I think it was by my hon. friend from Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg)-as the "long distance members." They are in a different position from those hon. gentlemen who come from Montreal and Toronto, and I quite sympathize with them in their attitude. On the other hand I must make this observation-which I hope will not be found to be inaccurate-that in looking around at the empty seats at a late hour

I find that just as many " long distance members " are absent as those who might be described as " short distance members." I do not find that in that respect distance makes very much difference. There is a disposition on the part of members not to submit to the long and continued sittings;
and if you are not going to have 6 p.m. an occasional recess-if you are going to sit on Wednesday nights, and on other nights as well, until eleven o'clock, you may do so nominally but later than that you will not do so in reality because members will not remain; and anybody who wants evidence of that fact can come into this chamber almost any night right after eleven o'clock and he will find that in most cases there is little more than a bare quorum on the Government benches-that is an actual fact.
Now the discussion broadened into one upon the advisability of a general revision of the rules of the House. Much has been said on questions of interest, but I do not think such questions bear directly on the matter at issue here. The Prime Minister, for example, talked about motions to go into Supply and amendments thereto. That is a very interesting subject and I should like to deliver an essay some day on what is the real basis of amendments to Supply in this chamber, but I do not care to do so now. My hon. friend from Maple Creek proposed that Parliament should meet earlier. I agree with that. My hon.. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) proposed to enlarge the closure. Well, that is a large question. Possibly there may be wisdom in that suggestion, but I confined my motion to one or two particular points which seemed to me to be easily within the grasp of the House, and I do not think any sound reason has been advanced against those suggestions. It has been said by the hon. member for Centre Vancouver that there is an unwritten law that on Mondays and Fridays no business of importance shall be transacted. My hon. friend has certainly no warrant for that statement; there is no such unwritten law to my knowledge. There is a convenience at times in not bringing on matters on Monday or Friday afternoon; but there is no written law or no unwritten law on the subject. As the best evidence of that I call attention to the fact that the Prime Minister on Friday last brought forward a motion of great importance, one that he knew was likely to be a matter of contest. Still he brought it forward on Friday; he felt free
to do so and I make no complaint of his taking that course. However, I think there is no such Monday and Friday rule as my hon. friend from Centre Vancouver describes. Now, as I pointed out, if hon. members are not to be allowed an evening off they will probably take it for themselves and the only result will be that we will take up business when the House is largely empty.
There is another thought that I would like to express. Much has been said about the waste of the time of the House. There are 235 members in this chamber-I think I am correct in the statement-men with heads on their shoulders and brains in their heads. They have not been sent here to be indifferent to what is going on, and if we are going to have democratic government, if we are going to have real representation of the people, those men must give expression to their views from time to time. That is not a waste of money and it is not a waste of time-it is simply a feature of the democratic government under which we live. Very much has been said about the waste of time in Parliament which is entirely unwarrantable.
There is only one other thought which I desire to express at the moment, and it relates to a matter as to which I have no personal grievance, and from which I suffer no personal discomfort. Some of the members of the House are not as young as I am. Some that may be as young in years are not as blest with health and strength as I have the happiness to be. There are members of the House on both sides- perhaps to be accurate more on the Government side,-whose condition of health does not permit them to sit here and yet we find them brought to the House at two, three, four or five o'clock in the morning. These men have been dragged out of their sick beds to come here and take part in the discussion or to vote. That, I think, is a thing exceedingly to be regretted, and in my opinion it would be very much in the interest of good government, very much for the comfort and convenience of members as well as in the interest of efficiency, if we had rules which would enable more regard to be paid to the condition of health of these gentlemen. Mr. Speaker, I desire to withdraw the resolution.
Resolution withdrawn.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's) moved:
maintopic: INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY-EXPROPRIATION OF LAND AT LEVIS
speechtext:
For a copy of all correspondence since January 1, 1912, between the Minister of Railways and Canals or any officer of the Department of Railways and Canals at Ottawa, and any officer of the Intercolonial Railway, and between any of such officials and Messrs. G. T. Davie and Son, or any solicitor or agent of the firm, respecting the expropriation of land at Ldvis, Quebec, for the purposes of the Intercolonial Railway.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the transaction referred to in this motion for papers began, as the dates will show, several years ago, but has attracted public notice only recently through an action that has been tried in the courts-one which, indeed, is still before the courts. In August, 1912, the Government of Canada, for the purposes of the Intercolonial Railway, acquired by expropriation a property in the town of Levis in the province of Quebec owned by the firm of George T. Davie and Son and other members of their family. In the course of the transaction they employed the services of a gentleman in the real estate business in Montreal, Mr. D. W. Ogilvie, doing business under the name of D. W. Ogilvie and Company. A little later they brought into their service another gentleman in Montreal, a member of the legal profession, Mr. C. A. Barnard, K.C. These gentlemen were employed to carry on the negotiations with respect to the property. When the transaction as respects the Government was closed and the compensation determined, some difficulty arose between Messrs. Davie, the owners of the property, and Mr. Ogilvie and Mr. Barnard, who had been employed in the negotiations. A dispute having arisen as to the compensation which Messrs. Ogilvie and Barnard should receive for their services, Messrs. Davie effected a settlement with Mr. Barnard to his apparent satisfaction, but in the case of Mr. Ogilvie they were not so fortunate. Mr. Ogilvie objected to the compensation allowed him, whereupon he brought an action in the courts of the province of Quebec against Messrs. Davie. At the first stage of the action Ogilvie failed; Davie was successful. The case was then appealed to the Appeal Court in the province of Quebec and there again Mr. Ogilvie was unsuccessful. The case was

then brought to the Supreme Court of Canada and was dealt with quite recently, judgment being given in favour of Mr. Ogilvie, the judgment of the lower courts set aside and a new trial ordered. That is the way the case now stands in the courts. It is but right to say that in these proceedings the Government was not a party and neither the plaintiff nor the defendant appears tc have had any interest in probing the Government's side of the question, if there was a Government side; so that any information we get in the matter concerning the Government's action comes from what we might call the side lights; we get a glimpse of it occasionally as we look over the proceedings in the courts. Information of that character is necessarily incomplete, and it would not be wise to form a conclusion based upon it. But I think when I state in outline the facts as they appear on the records of the courts the House will agree that it is a case in respect of which we ought to have further information.
It was on August 12, 1912, that the Government acquired the property. On that day the engineer of the Intercolonial railway deposited in the Registry Office of the county of Levis a plan and description of the property in question. I think I am right in stating that in accordance with the law,. upon the plan and description being so deposited, the title to the property became vested in the Crown, subject, of course, to the right of the late owner to receive fair compensation. Now, there are two methods, either of which may in the ordinary way of business be employed to determine the compensation. The Government may themselves, by such method as suits them, fix a valuation on the property and may offer accordingly the price which they are willing to pay. If the late owner -whom I shall speak of now as the owner -is content with that; if he accepts the price so offered, the transaction is ended: But if he is not satisfied with what is offered, or if no offer is made, then the owner has the right to take his case into the Exchequer Court and that court will determine the compensation to be paid. It seems to me rather strange that neither of these ordinary business methods was adopted in this case. The Government do not appear to have made any offer to Messrs. Davie, and Messrs. Davie certainly entered no action in the Exchequer Court. The matter appears to have been allowed to drift along in the expectation that negotiations would in some way bring
about a satisfactory solution. Messrs. Davie seem to have had the notion that they could not go about this thing in a straight, simple, businesslike way-send in their claim and establish it; they seemed to have had the notion that influence-I use the word that is found in the record- was required, and they obtained the services of Mr. Ogilvie because they thought his influence would be useful. Later they thought they needed more influence, so they obtained the services of Mr. Barnard. Let me say at once that Mr. Barnard himself says he was not employed in a professional capacity; he, therefore, was not to be considered as merely making a claim for ordinary legal services-he was employed as negotiator, as he says himself, to get all that he could for the parties. Mr. Barnard, as I have said, was brought into the transaction some time after Mr. Ogilvie became concerned in it; Mr. Ogilvie seemed to have conducted the negotiations at first, and later Mr. Barnard came in. At the beginning there appeared to have been negotiations with Mr. Gutelius and others, officers of the Intercolonial Railway, but after a short time the conclusion seemed to have been reached that the matter could not be settled in that way; that recourse must be had to higher authorities. So it came about that Mr. Gutelius and others dropped out of the matter and the scene was transferred to Ottawa.
Shortly after Messrs. Ogilvie were employed they wrote a letter to Messrs. Davie with regard to the compensation that was expected. On May 7, 1913, Messrs. J. W. Ogilvie and Company wrote this letter to Messrs. George T. Davie and Sons, of Levis, Quebec:
Dear Sirs,-The Intercolonial railway of Canada have sent us a blue-print of your property situated in Dauzon Ward, Ddvis, showing the land they purpose to expropriate lying between the present Intercolonial railway and the King's Highway; the strip of land having a superficial area, according to the plan as prepared by C. A. Bourget, of 36,900 sq. ft. E.M.
In order to take up this matter with the Intercolonial railway, will you kindly write us giving us the best cash price you will accept for the 36,900 sq. ft. of land. On receipt of your letter we will communicate with the proper officials and endeavour to make a sale of the property direct to the Intercolonial railway without expropriation proceedings.
Trusting you will give this matter your early attention, as it is advisable to settle with the railway before expropriation proceedings are -started.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) D. W. Ogilvie & Co. Inc.
Per D. W. Ogilvie.
Here you see that the agent was asking from his principals a definite price for

which they were prepared to dispose of the property. This is the reply of George T. Davie and Son, dated at Levis, May 14, 1913:
Levis, May 14, 1913. Messrs. D. W. Ogilvie & Co.,
11 St. Sacrament Street,
Montreal, Que.
Dear Sirs,-In answer to your letter of May 7, we beg to say that we are asking one dollar and twenty-five cents ($1.25) per foot of our property which has been expropriated by the Intercolonial railway.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) Geo. T. Davie & Son,
Per J. O. A. V.
That communication offering the land at $1.25 per foot appears to have been conveyed, although I do not know how, to the Intercolonial Railway authorities, because at some later stage when Mr. Barnard endeavoured to get $3 per foot for the property, he was told that was ridiculous, as the Government already had the offer of Messrs. Davie and Son to sell at $1.25 per foot. That seems to have been for the moment rather a knock-out blow to the negotiators. They recovered, however, and they represented that when they offered the property for $1.25 per foot, they really meant $1.75, and that the error was merely a clerical one. The negotiations appear to have proceeded for some time on that basis and, in fact, the matter was ultimately settled without reference to the original offer. At one stage Mr. Gutelius was offered the property at $1.75 per foot, and he said that that was too much and he refused to pay it. After.the principals and their representatives made further representations to the Government, they ultimately, as I shall show, effected a settlement in which they got a very much larger price than Davie was willing to sell for. It is important, in view of what occurred subsequently to notice this letter signed by George T. Davie and Son per one of their officials offering the property at $1.25 per foot, when at a later stage the demand was made for a much higher price, and as I stated the representation was made that this letter contained a clerical error. It appears that when the matter came to trial, the gentleman who wrote this letter, under the authority, presumably, of George T. Davie and Son, was no longer in their service. He was, however, available, but he was not called as a witness. I suppose it did not interest either party to the suit to probe that question of the $1.25 per foot. After the matter was all settled, when

there was no longer any question with the Government, but when there was some question between Ogilvie and Barnard regarding their compensation, we obtained through the record, for I have no other source of information, a statement of what Mr. Barnard thought about this mistake. Mr. Barnard, writing to Mr. Ogilvie in connection with the arrangement about their compensation said :
We have succeeded in getting them-
The Davie's.
[DOT]-$1.75 per foot, notwithstanding the fact that they had at one time offered to take $1.25, and I do not possibly see how they can raise any objection to turning over everything over $1.75 per foot.
That is Mr. Barnard's letter to Mr. Ogilvie after the transaction was settled with the Government. Mr. Barnard also wrote to Mr. G. C. Stuart, K.C., of Quebec, one of the counsel in the case, as follows:
As regards the Davie's themselves, they should remember that Ogilvie's services, outside of these $15,586.15-	_
That has reference to a previous portion of the matter which is of no importance here.
-has resulted in their getting in any case 50 cents per foot for their property more than they had at one time been willing to take, which 50 cents amounted on 36,900 to $18,450, so that even if they pay Ogilvie the amount I consider he is entitled to, they are still $18,450 better off than they would have been had they not dealt at all with Ogilvie.
That is Mr. Barnard's statement. Then Mr. Barnard was a witness at the trial and this occurred in his testimony:
I thought therefore, that I ought to point out to Mr. Stuart that as a matter of fact our joint services-
Ogilvie's and Barnard's.
-in any case had resulted in getting $1.75 for the property that Davie's had been willing to take $1.25 for.
Q. That was the fact? A. That was the fact, yes.
The Government, you see, had then been settled with; but while the transaction appears to be carried on on the basis that this $1.25 per foot offer was a mistake, we find Mr. Barnard, in correspondence and in his evidence at the trial, stating and swearing that $1.25 per foot was what the Davie's were really willing to take at that time. The story is too long to burden the House with it all, because I only want to show sufficient ground to make a basis for getting further information. There was

some question of difficulty at an early stage about the area in question. At the beginning there seemed to have been one or two surveys and some misunderstanding arose in that way. At one stage a larger quantity of land was mentioned, and Mr. Campbell, Deputy Minister of Railways, in a letter stated that he thought they had included some land already owned by the Intercolonial. Messrs. Davie and Son, however, had that matter all amicably settled by declaring that the quantity of land was 30,900 feet, and in all their negotiations later on they mentioned that quantity and at the trial they swore that that was the quantity. When the deed was ultimately passed, a larger quantity of land was mentioned; instead of 36,900 feet the deed contained a mention of 63,000 and some odd feet. Mr. Barnard, commenting on that, said that it appeared to him that it was a manoeuvre-I am using his word-

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY-EXPROPRIATION OF LAND AT LEVIS
speechtext:
The hon. member said
69,000; it should be 39,000.

maintopic: INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY-EXPROPRIATION OF LAND AT LEVIS
speechtext:
Yes. The quantity
mentioned in the deed is 38,000 and some odd feet. The "sixty-nine" comes in a more substantial matter of dollars and cents. Mr. Barnard said that he could not quite understand why that change was made. At all events, he said, Davie was not getting any more for 38,000 odd feet than he was going to get for 36,900 feet. He said that this was a manoeuvre to cover up a sum of $5,000 which he was to get in the transaction, and that so far as he was concerned he did not want to be covered up at all. That matter, however, in the end, perhaps did not affect the general question. The main question seemed to be that Davie offered this property to the Government for $1.25 per foot, and in the end the Government paid not only $1.75 per foot, but $5,000 more. Davie allowed Barnard $10,000 for his services. Some may say: "If it suited Mr. Davie to pay to Mr. Barnard a sum of $10,000 for his services, what business is it of ours; we need not care." We need not care if it were absolutely the fact that Davie paid the $10,000; but a more careful examination of the facts shows that what Mr. Davie did was to pay only $5,000, and the other $5,000 to Mr. Barnard was paid by the convenient device of adding that sum to the charge to the Government and making the Government pay it. Mr. Barnard got $10,000, but only $5,000 of it came out of Mr. Davie. The record seems to show very clearly that for a property which the Government were offered for $1.25 per 117
foot, they paid in the end $1.75. Not only that, but they also paid an additional sum of $5,000 under the circumstances I have described.
These are the facts set forth in the proceedings in the court. If it be true that an offer was made in good faith, and Mr. Barnard treats it as a bona fide offer, to sell this property for $1.25 per foot, and if the negotiations were carried on for a long time and finally carried to Ottawa, and negotiators were employed to do that which ought not to have needed negotiators, it seems to be as simple a fact as we can present that the Government paid $18,000 odd more for that property than the owner was willing to take, and that an additional $5,000 went, not to the Davies, but to Mr. Barnard. These facts are only sidelights which come out in the course of the inquiry in the court. Again I say, one only gets a partial view of the situation. I do not want to draw any conclusions from incomplete information of that character. I quite admit that we should reserve our judgment, and I present these facts accordingly. All, I ask is that in view of these facts set forth in the court-I have no other source of information-the House should adopt the resolution, whereby we would get all the papers relating to the subject.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY-EXPROPRIATION OF LAND AT LEVIS
speechtext:
When this motion was placed on the Order Paper I asked one of my officials to get all the facts in connection with the case in order that I might be able to reply to my hon. friend when he moved his resolution in the House. I am sorry to say that up till six o'clock I had not received the information, but since that time I have endeavoured to get what little information I could in order to give it to the House this evening.
Let me say at the outset that there is no reason why all the papers and correspondence in connection with this transaction should not be brought down, and they will be brought down at the earliest possible date. This whole transaction from start to finish took place prior to my being Minister of Railways and Canals and therefore I was not personally siezed of the facts in connection with the case, but in the short time I have had since six o'clock to look into the matter I understand that these are the facts:
On December 15, 1911, the town of Levis advised the railway officials that they proposed to abandon the city stock pens which the Intercolonial had been using

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: until that time. The officials of the railway, after studying various locations for a new stock pen, decided that that site was the best, and that they should try and purchase the property. Accordingly Mr. Brady, the general manager of the railway, on July 2, 1912, recommended to the then Minister of Railways, the late Mr. Cochrane, that the property be purchased, and on August 12, about a month later, the property was expropriated by an Order in Council upon the recommendation of Mr. Cochrane. The matter then stood for about two years. Negotiations in the meantime were carried on between Mr. Gutelius and D. W. Ogilvie and Company, representing G. T. Davie and Sons, Levis. I understand that Mr. Gutelius offered $1.75 per foot, but that was refused. Accordingly, Mr. Gutelius appointed, as was the custom, three valuators, Jos. Gosselin, contractor, Levis, Telesphore Charland, Mayor of Lauzon, and Jos. Edouard Parent, Beaufort, to value the property.
What was the date of their appointment?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
They were appointed on December 30, 1913, on the recommendation of the Postmaster General, dated December 16, 1913, to ascertain whether $1.75 per square foot was a fair and reasonable price. The result was that these arbitrators reported on February 2, 1914, giving a valuation of $3.00 per square foot. On January 30, 1914, D. W. Ogilvie and Company -withdrew the option for the lower price,-I presume that means $1.75,-and on April 4, named the price of $2.75 per square foot. Negotiations were continued with D. W. Ogilvie and Company through their solicitor, Mr. Barnard, and finally on March 15, 1915, Mr. Barnard after an interview offered to accept $69,575 in settlement, the terms being a cash payment of $9,575 with interest thereon, leaving a balance of $60,000, with interest thereon at 4 per cent from date of taking possession, payable when convenient to the Government to do so. Mr. Gutelius in the memorandum signed by him says:
Personally it was my intention to recommend the acceptance of the $1.75, and hoped that the valuators would confirm this as being fair and reasonable. When they raised the price however, to $3.00 per foot and the owners were apparently aware of this figure, it made it more difficult, so that the settlement which was finally affected was to my mind a good business proposition and less than the Exchequer Court would have awarded us, having in mind that our own valuators would endeavour to protect their valuation of $3.00 per foot before the court.

I mention these facts merely to show that Mr. Gutelius as general manager was trying to protect the interests of the railway and the Government by endeavouring to get the property at as low a price as possible, and also to show 'that Mr. Cochrane acted under the advice of his officials, and, I believe, in good faith. I am quite satisfied that if there was anything wrong in any shape or form my predecessor knew nothing whatever about it; nor, I believe, did Mr. Gutelius. On the recommendation of Mr. Cochrane the order was dated October 26, 1915, advising the acceptance of $69,575 for 38,723 feet of land. That was the official Order in Council, and from the information I have received since six o'clock I think it was the understanding that the $60,000 was not to be paid for two years, during which time 4 per cent interest was paid on that amount. The final payment was made, I think, in 1918. Of course, that payment was made after I became minister, but the matter had already been settled, so that I never heard of it until the hon. member placed the motion on the Order Paper. As I have said, however, so far as the Government is concerned, I believe that the transaction was carried out by the officials and by the minister in good faith, and if there have been commissions or anything of that kind they know nothing whatever about them. We are only too pleased to bring the papers down and have the matter thoroughly investigated from start to finish.

There is little I care to add to what has already been said. I am quite aware that the matter must have taken place largely before the minister entered the department, and I have no desire to cast reflections upon any one. But the facts as I have stated them, on the authority of the proceedings in the courts, show the necessity for further investigation. I want to state one or two points in reply to my hon. friend. He says that an Order in Council was passed to pay this sum for 39,000 odd feet.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The quantity is 38,723 feet.

Yes, nearly 39,000
feet. Now, Messrs. Davie, all through the latter part of the negotiations, held, and in the trial distinctly swore, that there were only 36,900 feet. There is no information yet to account for the larger quantity of nearly 39,000 feet mentioned in the deed.

There is a suggestion from Mr. Barnard that there was a manoeuvre to cover up something which he did not want covered up. My hon. friend says that an Order in Council was passed to pay $69,575; but 36,900 feet at $1.75 does not amount to that sum; it gives only $64,575. The facts seem to be that Messrs. Davie and Company offered the property at $1.25 per foot, and though there was some talk of that being a mistake, we have the sworn testimony of Mr. Barnard that it was correct, that Messrs. Davie were getting 50 cents per foot more than they themselves asked for. They were paid, not the sum of $46,125 which they were willing to take, not the $64,000 odd that would be the amount at $1.75 per foot, but the higher price of $69,575. On the surface it does appear that there was something peculiar about the management of this affair. I do not wish to press the matter further, because I admit that the information is incomplete and I would prefer that we reserve judgment until we are in possession of all the papers.	>

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS- REDUCTION IN NUMBER OF EMPLOYEES
speechtext: I desire to refer to a matter which has been dealt with in the public press for the last two or three days, and I should be glad to have an expression of opinion regarding it from the Minister of Railways. I refer to the reduction in the number of working men in the Canadian National shops in the city of Moncton. There is a rumour to the effect that from 600 to 800 men are to be turned out from the C.N.R. shops in that city. Is that report correct, and, if so, is the order only a matter of temporary expediency or is it to be permanent? This is of great importance to the people in that city as well as to the public generally. Will the minister be good enough to make a statement to the House?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Railways and Canals) :
speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS- REDUCTION IN NUMBER OF EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
The hon. member was kind enough to inform me at six o'clock of his intention to bring this matter up on the Orders of the Day. I called up President Hanna at Toronto, and asked him what

the real situation was. Mr. Hanna informs me that owing to a decline in the business of the railways, they could not find work for all the employees in the shops. They therefore offered to keep on all hands and reduce work to half-time. All employees in shops west of Port Arthur accepted. Those on the Government railways as a body refused, and the management could therefore do nothing but lay off temporarily all surplus employees. Just as soon as there is work the men will again be taken on.
CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS- PRICE OFFERED FOR RAILS On the Orders of the Day:
Mr. JOHN C. DOUGLAS (South Cape Breton and Richmond): I desire to draw the attention of the Minister of Railways to a despatch which appears in the Canadian press of yesterday, as well as the newspapers published to-day, which reads as follows:
Roll Rails at Cost for C.N.R. is offer Sydney, N.S., April 9.-In a statement to the Canadian Press today, R. M. Wolvin, president of the Dominion Steel Company, stated that the company had offered to roll rails for the Canadian National Railways at actual cost, but he gave positive denial to a statement appearing in an Ottawa despatch, which reported the offering of a large rail order to the company by the Department of Railways.
In view of the importance of this matter, and the large amount of unemployment that prevails at Sydney and Glace Bay in consequence of the small amount of business being done in connection with coal and steel operations. I desire to ask the minister if he has any statement to make on the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals

On the Order for resuming the adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Mr. Campbell, as amended:
That, in the opinion of this House, work on the Hudson Bay railway should be resumed as soon as financial conditions permit, and that the project be completed with the least possible delay.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand the hon. gentleman who moved the resolution desires to reply.

I was not aware that this matter was coming up to-night. However, as it has been taken up, and as the opportunity is afforded me of replying to some of the statements made during the debate which took place some days ago, I shall take advantage of the occasion to say a few words. May I say, by way of preliminary, that I was somewhat amazed-in fact I was dumbfounded -by the somewhat cold-blooded manner in which the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) when this matter was last brought up, showed his indifference to the pledges and promises of the Government, and of his party generally, in connection with this scheme. Surely the country has come to a sorry state when a responsible Government, such as we presumably have at the present time, can lightly wave aside the solemn pledges which they have made in connection with a matter of national importance such as the construction of the Hudson Bay railway. The only excuse, or at least the chief excuse, which was given by the minister for the absolute disregard by the Government, and by the party which supports them, of the pledges and promises made in connection with this railway, was the fact-or the alleged fact-that the financial condition of the country would not warrant a further vote of money in connection with this road at the present time. Actually, Mr. Speaker, this statement was made despite the fact that money is being spent like water in connection with all other kinds of public undertaking such as shipbuilding, the construction of dry docks, improve-

merits in harbours, the carrying out of the St. Lawrence improvement scheme and various other undertakings. We look at the Estimates this year and we find that sums ranging from two to ten millions, are being spent in various parts of Canada on public works of this nature. Nevertheless we are told that even so small a sum comparatively as $1,700,000 is not available to complete the Hudson Bay project on which $21,000,000 has been already expended.
Two members of the Liberal Opposition, the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) and the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) criticised the project and quoted some evidence given in the past against the scheme. Now, as I have already pointed out, the evidence which they cited is not new; it has been produced in the House from time to time on previous occasions and it has been answered. As the result of various commissions and investigations held from time to time, the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier started the building of this road and intended to carry it to completion but were not allowed to do so. As a result of the elections of 1911 another Government stepped in and went on with the work after further investigation was made. I intimated to the House when this question was last before it that I did not wish to take up the time of the House in giving details as to the evidence in connection with this matter. That evidence is very extensive, in fact, it consists of volumes, and I do not propose to-night to go into it. I would simply refer the two gentlemen in question to the statements of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his Government and I ask them if they repudiate the action of Sir Wilfrid and his Government in 1910 when they began the construction of this railway after having thoroughly investigated the project. I have the same question to ask of hon. gentlemen supporting the Government. Do they repudiate the statements made by Sir Charles Tupper, by the former Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden); by the present Prime Minister, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and others-statements which I quoted in the few remarks I made the other day and which were emphatically in favour of the scheme? I ask hon. gentlemen opposite if they repudiate the statements made by these gentlemen and by the governments which they represented.
The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) during the previous debate told a very gruesome story of the horrible things he had done at various times in the past,
and declared that he was not now playing politics. I would like to ask my hon. friend who is playing politics at the present time? Are those who are asking to have the Government's promises carried out playing politics, or is it those, who propose to set aside one scheme which has been promised, undertaken and nearly completed in order to carry out another scheme which was only put forward in order to win a by-election? I ask him who is playing politics when the Hudson Bay Railway project is set aside, after so much money has been spent on it, in order to construct a dry dock at Esquimalt to fulfil a pledge that was made in order to win a by-election at Victoria not so very long ago? It looks to me as though hon. gentlemen opposite are carrying on the same programme as that which my hon. friend from Oxford declared he had been supporting in the past, although he is now repentant. I would like to ask my hon. friend if he thinks the Estimates in connection with the construction of dry docks, canal improvements, and other matters that are on the Government's programme at the present time, indicate a sincere desire for economy? I propose, Mr. Speaker, when the time comes to bring these questions definitely before the House to ascertain whether the House correctly appreciates the situation- whether we are simply going to have economy in one particular and not in all? If we are going to have economy-something which I very much desire to see brought about as a matter of public policy, then it should be applied everywhere and not simply applied in one particular part of the country.
The hon. member for North Oxford also indulged in certain remarks about something that somebody had told him as to the great amount of dredging that had to be done at Port Nelson. As a matter of fact if the hon. member had cared to obtain reliable information about that particular subject, he could have gone to the Department of Railways and the chief engineer would have told him definitely what the situation was as far as dredging is concerned. He repeated a story that some one had told him, but I may tell him that it will be emphatically denied if he goes to the proper quarter for information. But this hon. gentleman as well as other hon. members have brought down here a lot of hearsay evidence and retailed it as arguments against a scheme which has been thoroughly investigated and pronounced sound and feasible, and the feasibility and practica-

bility of which is not an issue at the present time.
It would seem from the statements made by certain gentlemen that in the case of the Hudson Bay project they contend that this should be a ready-made route. There never was such a situation existing in the Dominion before. The St. Lawrence was not a ready-made route. I have a vivid recollection of taking passage in the steamship Victorian, I think it was fifteen years or so ago and when we were only a few hours' out from Montreal about nine o'clock one morning we ran aground this side of Quebec, and the passengers had to be taken off in small boats and landed at Quebec. In my own case I lost so much time that I had to abandon the voyage. I was told that the Victorian remained aground for some months. If anything like that had happened on the Hudson Bay route the hon. gentleman would have used the incident to condemn the project; yet millions of dollars have been spent on the St. Lawrence route, and although it is not perhaps quite as satisfactory as it should be, we are not condemning the route. But if half as much money were spent on the Hudson Bay route I have no doubt that it would be a certain success. Regarding my hon. friend from Battleford-
North Battleford.

Regarding my hon.
friend from North Battleford, notwithstanding the rather critical tone of his remarks, I think that, generally speaking, I am considerably in accord with the statements made by him. I might interpolate here that in any remarks which I made I was not in any way casting aspersions on my hon. friend. I believe he has honestly investigated this proposition-something that certain other hon. members have not done-but cannot see his way clear to advocate continuance of the project at the present time. He read an article from the Grain Growers' Guide-I have not got it here as I did not know this matter was coming up to-night-written by some one who had been to the Bay, criticizing severely the character of the work that had been done.
9 p.m. I am fully in accord with that criticism, because the scheme appears to have been muddled from start to finish, and to have been so handled, as some think, in order to show that the project will not work out successfully. Although I agree with him that certain of the work already done has been unsatisfactory, owing

perhaps to insufficient investigation in some respects, still I disagree with him in his opinion that the work can well be stopped altogether at the present time until the matter is thoroughly investigated. I say that certain work should go on, and that as to other work for instance, such as that in connection with the terminals, further investigation might.be made.
I made a proposition to the right hon. Prime Minister a short time ago which I think covers the ground. The dump or grade is completed to the bay. I suggested that the rails be laid from the present end of steel for a distance of about forty miles, which would bring the line to the head of navigation on the river. The Government own and operate a stern wheel river steamer at Port Nelson, and if my suggestion were adopted the railway would connect with the steamer and thus complete connection with the bay. The cost would not be excessive, and by this means men and material could be brought into the bay for any investigation or work that may be necessary there. I am told that as soon as connection is made with the bay, commercial fishing will be indulged in. I was also told by a prominent official of the Marine and Fisheries Department that it was the intention of the department-the hon. minister can correct me if I am mistaken-as soon as the railway is completed to the bay to put on one or more steam trawlers for the purpose of investigating the fisheries. I was informed that the department had this in view before the war broke out, but the war forced them to abandon this proposal and it was then decided to allow it to remain in abeyance until connection is made with the bay by means of the railway or otherwise. I received a letter a few days ago from a gentleman interested in iron properties on the east shore of Hudson bay-he is only one of a number who are so interested. He had told me some years ago that he and his colleagues were waiting until the railway was completed in order that they might start work on their properties. Now he wants to know what the prospects are for getting in this year. If this connection could be effected now a great deal of work of an exploratory nature would be undertaken, which will add to the regular traffic resulting from the building of the road.
Now a few words in conclusion with reference to statements made by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals. He stated that the road did not pay. Of course it does not pay. Does anybody in this House

know of any public undertaking with which the hon. minister is concerned that does pay? The day after the debate on this matter recently he read a statement regarding the Canadian National railways, and if ever there was a proposition that did not pay we had a glaring example there. I could name a number of other undertakings with which he is connected that do not pay; for instance, thei Welland canal and the Trent canal in which he takes a great deal of personal interest. As far as the Hudson Bay railway is concerned, it was never intended to pay as a local proposition. The idea was to connect the wheat-fields of the prairies with the Bay, and local traffic was not in the minds of those who undertook the enterprise. But we find a situation has developed in the meantime which shows that the country through which this railway passes is not the wilderness we thought it was, and that there are resources there which, if properly handled, will produce a great deal of local traffic, and it is within the bounds of probability that when the road is completed the local traffic itself will form a substantial part of the operating surplus. The line was to be constructed to Port Nelson and the work was proceeded with at great speed during the war, but when peace came that work was stopped. The road is about two-thirds built, and when operations ceased the road was left practically in a field. It is being operated-not for the 332 miles on which steel, is laid, but only for about 214 miles. It does not go any place in particular, indeed, as I have said, it practically stops nowhere. How could any road under such circumstances be expected to pay? Yet my hon. friend says that because it does not pay we are going to stop work, and go ahead and spend millions and millions of dollars on other public works that we do not expect to get any revenue from whatever.
This matter was brought before certain members of the Cabinet on one occasion by a delegation of members of this House and the statement was then made by one of the ministers that we had to economize, and so far as he was concerned no public works were going to be built that year, although a number of places wished to have public works proceeded with just as the West wished to have the Hudson bay railway completed. I asked him if he had any public works under way, such as post offices or similar buildings which had been left partly constructed without any roof on, and which he proposed to leave in that
way until financial conditions should improve. He said there was no instance of that kind. That would have been an instance analagous to the conditions existing in respect to the Hudson bay railway at the present time.
I might say here, Mr. Speaker-and I have said it before-that if this were a one word of its immediate construction. I would not prefer one request to have the work commenced. Further, if the Hudson Bay railway had been completed for a distance of only one hundred miles or thereabouts, you would not hear one word from me by way of request for an extension of the line at this time. But neither of these conditions applies to the Hudson Bay railway project. The roadbed is practically completed to the bay; the rails are laid three-quarters of the way, about one-half the line is operated, and only a comparatively small expenditure and an inconsiderable amount of work is required in order to put the road in such condition that connection can be made between The Pas and the Bay. In view of these facts, and in order to protect the money that we have invested in the enterprise and to make something out of it; in order to make it a business proposition in a real sense, it is urged that certain work in the way of construction be gone on with.
The Minister of Railways intimated that all expenditure made on railway account was needed for the building of branch lines in the West, and he said that I had appeared before him on several occasions in connection with the building of those branch lines. He speaks very truly; I am as much interested in the building of branch lines in connection with the Canadian National Railway system, as I am in the Hudson Bay railway. But the fact is that the money is not being used for the building of these branch lines in the West. The 1919 programme so far as the building of branch lines is concerned has not yet been carried out. When the minister puts as an alternative to the building of the Hudson Bay railway the completion of these branch lines, he merely attempts to pull wool over our eyes, because, as I say, the branch lines programme is not being carried out. At different times delegations from the West have asked for the construction not only of the Hudson Bay railway but of certain branch lines. The minister has said: We cannot build both; will you take the branch lines or will you take the Hud-

son Bay railway? That is a very unfair proposal? I remember that this question was put specifically to a large delegation from the Melfort district in Saskatchewan, and the reply was: Go ahead with the construction of the Hudson Bay railway if you cannot give us both. It was stated in the resolution on this subject signed by western members that the construction of necessary branch lines should be carried on in addition to the construction of the Hudson Bay railway; that the one should he done and the other not left undone. The question of terminals has been raised. The proposal which I have made is such as would allow for the making of further investigation so far as terminals are concerned. There is a feeling throughout the country, right or wrongly, that the proper terminal has not been chosen. I have been careful to avoid the issue with respect to terminals; I am not prepared to state conclusively whether the proper terminal has been chosen or not. I am not an engineer, though I have my own opinion in the matter, as I have been to both Churchill and Nelson. It is possible that the engineers can make a satisfactory terminal at Nelson; I am not here to say. But apparently there is a feeling that sufficient investigation was not made before the decision with respect to the terminal was arrived at; that a sufficiently careful inquiry was not carried out by experts. My suggestion therefore, as previously outlined, is that the road be completed to the head of navigation on the Nelson, and if there is any doubt in the mind of the Government-and they have not expressed any -with regard to the question whether a proper terminal has been chosen, let the matter be thoroughly investigated by competent harbour experts. If it is then deemed advisable that a change should be made, it can be made without the necessity for any extra work, because the turn would have to be made at a point beyond the end of the construction which I now suggest. I wish in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, to emphasize the fact that the West is paying for this road, not the East, and not Canada as a whole. Preemptions and purchased homesteads have been set aside in the West for the purpose of realizing money in order to build this railway- As I have said, approximately $28,000,000 worth of these lands have already been sold-at least, had been sold up to a year ago; the amount is probably greater by this time. What is the Government doing with this money? It 
is ear-marked, I am told-and this came out in debates in this House-for the construction of the Hudson Bay railway, but instead of going on with the work for which this money was provided the Government have decided to let it stand for the time being, and they do not say how long it will be before the work is resumed.
I contend, therefore, that the case against the completion of the work to the point suggested has not been made out. The question of economy does not enter into the matter. If the Government were carrying out a programme of economy throughout the whole country, not a word would be said by the West so far as the construction of this road is concerned. But when money is being spent lavishly upon other enterprises that do not involve the production of revenue, surely the West is being differentiated against, it is being sacrificed, for interests which appear, for reasons which we can surmise to have a more powerful pressure. Now, I do not know whether it is in order at this stage to withdraw the resolution, owing to the amendment which has been made. But the resolution as amended, is of no benefit, and there would not seem to be any advantage in asking for a vote on it. If I am in order, therefore, I would ask leave to withdraw the resolution.
Motion withdrawn.
