The House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Public Works-chargeable to capital-Marine Department-Government shipbuilding programme-Amount required for the contraction of vessels in accordance with Government programme, $8,330,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This item was before the committee for discussion on Thursday last during the entire afternoon and evening. Shall the item cary?

Dealing with this subject
when it was before the House last week, I pointed out that the minister's statement this year was decidedly different in tone from his statement last year. Then my hon. friend was bold and aggressive. He put all the big strawberries on the top of the basket, but this year he is apologetic and gives a number of reasons why he embarked on this policy. He has evidently begun to realize that in the present financial condition of the country

an expenditure of $70,000,000 which is considered by the ordinary man on the street to have been wasteful and unnecessary, is a very heavy responsibility, and I am very glad to know that he is showing signs of repentance. The minister gave some reasons why we on this side of the House according to his view, have no right to criticize his programme. He said, among other things, that we made no effort to stop him when he was asking for these large votes for this purpose in former years. I think that is true with respect to the vote that he obtained at the inception of the shipbuilding programme in 1918. At that time, in the session of 1917-1918, the war was on, and as everybody knows, ships were being sunk by the submarines. Furthermore, hon. gentlemen on this side of the House were not then acquainted with the facts in regard to the operations of the Imperial Munitions Board. I endeavoured all through the war to keep track of what was going on in the shipping business, but I did not know that in so many of the shipyards in this country ships were being constructed at that time for the Imperial Munitions Board. You are aware, Sir, that the censor was busy at that time and that any news relating to the construction and launching of ships was suppressed. I might say that if I had known in 1918, when my hon. friend came forward and asked for a vote to build these tramp vessels, as a Government venture, that the yards of Canada were all busy building ships for the Munitions Board, on the account of the admiralty, I should have had a great deal of hesitation in allowing him to go forward with his programme without a protest. I took care to enter my protest as soon as the facts were disclosed. The ships built by the Munitions Board were just as good, for the purposes of the war, as the ships built by the Government of Canada. When those ships were finished they were turned over to the British Admiralty, just the same as the ships built by the Canadian Government would also be turned over to the British Government for use in the war. So one ship was just as much use as the other so far as the war was concerned. It was at that stage that my hon. friend stepped in, I think unnecessarily, and asked for the expenditure of what has now grown to be a very large sum of money in connection with this venture.
I also pointed out that it would have been very easy for my hon. friend to retire from this shipbuilding programme at the close of the war. When the war ended,
on November 11,	1918, there were
actually only four keels laid. I have a table here published by the Canada Railway and Marine World which, I believe is a reliable publication, showing the dates. I have no doubt that its information is official, but if there is anything wrong my hon. friend can put me right. The names of the vessels for which keels had been laid were the Voyageur, June 11, 1918, the Pioneer, July 17, 1918, the Warrior, July 17, 1918, the Volunteer, October 1, 1918. None of these ships were launched prior to November 11, 1918, so all that my hon. friend had to do if he wished to discontinue his programme, was to settle with the parties with whom he had made contracts and had not commenced to build, and he could have gone on and finished the four vessels whose keels had been laid. That would have involved a very small outlay comparatively speaking, but my hon. friend did not choose to do that. He went on with his programme, and has attempted to justify it on different occasions since on various grounds. In my former remarks, I challenged the statement of my hon. friend that these ships are necessary in connection with our railway systems. They are only freight vessels. Their speed is about 11 knots, or under. If my hon. friend was projecting a line of fast steamers, and if the country could afford to put the money into them, to connect with our railway system and take passengers across the Atlantic or across the Pacific, that is an enterprise that has often been mentioned in this House and has been favoured by both sides. Of course, it would cost a great deal of money; but that is not what my hon. friend is doing. He is building tramp vessels to compete with private owners. I pointed out to him that the sea is covered with such vessels at the present time. It is estimated that there is now afloat something like 50,000,000 tons of shipping. At the time the war broke out there was only about 40,000,000 tons, so that there is now some 10,000,000 tons more than there was at that time, while trade has decreased enormously since the close of the war. It is therefore easy to see how difficult it will be to make money with freight vessels for some years to come, the shipbuilding programme throughout the world having been overdone. It was unnecessary for my hon. friend to go on with his programme in view of the fact that the war was over, and that he was only building freight vessels that had to compete with ships

built prior to the war for about a quarter of the sum he paid.
I pointed out to my hon. friend that on the Clyde and in other British and European ports, prior to 1914, ships of the same kind as he is building were being built at about $50 per ton deadweight. He admits that the average cost of the vessels he is building is about $192 per ton deadweight, almost four times as much. In these hard times with low freight rates the minister has to compete with vessels that were built at about one-quarter the cost of those he is operating. I have already pointed out that the venture cannot be called a war measure; nor was it necessary, so far as our railway systems are concerned. If there is any freight at all delivered at the coast by our railways, it is easy to find a ship to carry it forward to destination. All that need be done by the owner of the freight or produce is to employ a broker in the big markets of London and New York, and he will find that he can send produce across the ocean at a lower rate than the minister can run his ships and carry it himself. So that government operation of ships is not economic, at the present time at all events, in connection with our railways. The other question was regarding our export trade. I pointed out to my hon. friend that he had not been able to show that he had done anything in the way of expanding our export trade through these vessels. At any rate, our export trade has been going the wrong way ever since these vessels have been operating. I showed that while in 1919 we had a balance of trade in our favour of $150,000,000, in 1920 we had an adverse balance of $150,000,000; so that the balance of trade went the wrong way during the past year to the extent of at least $300,000,000.
But the main difficulty is that these ships must be losing money; they did not pay their way last year. While my hon. friend shows a small earning; he made no proper allowance for depreciation and for the interest on the money that he put into these ships. If he cannot pay at least 5 per cent for depreciation and 5i per cent for interest on the money-for that is what he is paying for it to the public-if he cannot pay 101 per cent on capital, then he is losing money and will end in bankruptcy. Now, he has not done that within four or five million dollars. I have shown you, making the calculation on the capital which my hon. friend says he has put into this venture, that he has come out the wrong

way to the tune of $4,343,619 for the last year. That is not a very good showing. Let me point out, not for the purpose of making the story worse than it is, but in order that we may arrive at the facts, that freights are not nearly as profitable this year as they were last year; in some trades there is not more than 50 per cent this year of last year's output. So that we can easily see that if my hon. friend lost over four million dollars last year he stands to lose a very much larger sum this year. In the face of that we are still going on with the building of ships, knowing that when we get through with them, they will not be worth anything like the money we are paying for them. If I am correct in the statement that in the market they are not worth to-day more than 25 per cent of the amount they cost, the ships we are building now, and for which we propose to vote this money to-night, will be worth, when they are finished, only one-qmarter of what is spent on them; the other three-quarters will virtually have been thrown over the bridge.
According to the statement given to the House a few days ago by the ministers which will be found at page 1331 of Hansard, there are no fewer than sixteen ships now in course of construction. The minister puts the deadweight tonnage of these ships at 114,470 tons, and the average price at $192 per ton. To complete these sixteen vessels will cost the country, according to that statement, $21,978,240. If it be true that these sixteen vessels now being constructed will be worth only 25 per cent of cost when they are finished, we shall, by finishing them, sustain a loss of $16,483,180. That is a very serious matter. We have not the information as to how far this work has been proceeded with. It may be that it is not possible for my hon. friend to stop at the present time. I do not know whether any of these are new contracts or not; that information has not been given to the House. It would be interesting to know what state these contracts are in. I am assuming now that all the money which the minister is asking for is to complete contracts that have already been entered into. I pointed out the other night that, looking over the list of routes on which the minister proposes to put his ships this year, I find that no fewer than three of them are subsidized routes, routes on which the Government are subsidizing ships to compete with those which they purpose operating. That is unbusinesslike. For

example, under the minister's programme, we are going to run a line of ships from Vancouver, through the Pacific ocean, to New Zealand and Australia. We have a line of ships running now from Vancouver to New Zealand and Australia, and we are subsidizing those ships to the tune of $130,000 for the present year, in fact the money was voted a few days ago. But if it be correct-and I think it is- that they call at the same ports-undoubtedly they do in some instances;-then we are giving our competitor an advantage to the extent of $130,000 and that competitor already has the trade. The company that is running the present line has been conducting that service for a number of years. It has worked up business connections and knows all the details. It has fast vessels-better vessels than ours; vessels, according to the blue book which I have on my desk, that run at the rate of sixteen and seventeen knots an hour, while ours only make about eleven knots. These vessels are competing with us for the small trade between Vancouver and those far off ports in Australia and New Zealand. Looking over the returns of the Department of Trade and Commerce I find that the whole trade of last year was very small, that the whole business done between these points would not furnish one cargo for the five large vessels that my hon. friend is proposing to put on the route. I would like to know where he expects to get business for these vessels during the year 1921, remembering all the time that our competitors are on the route and that they have the business at the present time? My hon. friend may have some plan that I do not understand, but it looks to me as if he would be burning expensive coal in sending these vessels on a 6,000 mile trip across the Pacific ocean with very little in them.
In the discussion the other evening my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) dealt with the question of the dry dock at Halifax. This is a question, I think, that is not properly discussable in connection with this shipping venture, but I want to point out, seeing that my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre dealt with it, that he has not studied the question suifi-ciently. He' said that the company that formerly owned the Halifax graving dock had not appealed from the decision of the Exchequer Court and consequently had no right to complain about the amount that was awarded. I understand that is
not the question about wihch they are making complaint. What happened was this: The company were carrying on business in Halifax as a graving dock company for a number of years. Most of the money invested in the enterprise was British capital. It had been invested in this dock a good many years ago, and subsidies were also paid the company. A new company, called the Halifax Shipbuilding Company was started, and what the Government did was to expropriate the property belonging to the old company and hand it over to the new company who have it now,-at least the Halifax Shipyards, Limited have a lease of the dock. The dock was taken from the original company. The Government stepped in and expropriated the property, took it from the old company and gave it to the new concern, without a justification for doing so. That is the camplaint, as I understand it and it is for the Government to explain why they pursued such an arbitrary course.
That, according to my information, is the complaint that has been made by the Halifax Graving Dock Company.
Now considerable has been said in this discussion about the refusal of the Government to give information, not only about the operation of its vessels, but also in regard to the operation of the national railways. The Opposition have repeatedly demanded information, which information has been refused. It should not be necessary for me to undertake to prove the statement, for every member of the House must know it to be the case. I was surprised to hear, however, the Minister of Finance, and also the Minister of Railways, state in the discussion that took place the other day that ample information had been given to the members on this side, and that the. questions the Government refused to answer were trifling questions relating to the salary of a station master or something of that kind. I submit that the questions asked by gentlemen on this side were not trifling questions, but that at the last two sessions of Parliament both the Minister of Marine and the Minister of Railways have constantly refused to answer the most vital and important questions that were submitted to them. Let me give one or two examples. Last session a supporter of the Government, the senior member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Douglas) desired to get some information in regard to the purchase of coal for the use of the Government ships and he asked these questions:

What quantity of coal was consumed by the Canadians Government Merchant Marine in the year 1919? How much of same was Canadian and how much American?
He also asked:
Was this coal purchased by tender and what was the price paid?
Now these were very simple and yet important questions, but the answer the Government gave its own supporter was this:
The Government has no information. These transactions were carried on by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine as an incorporated Company.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I question the truth of the statement that the Government had no information as to the prices they were paying for coal, and that they had no information as to whether the coal had been purchased by tender or not-I simply do not believe it. We expect to get correct information from ministers of the Crown when plain questions of that kind are ask-gd in this House. I submit that there can be no good reason why such questions should not be answered. The transaction was completed, it was not for the year that was to come, it was not even for the current year-it had reference to the year 1919. I can understand that when negotiations are going on, and tenders are being invited, it would not be proper to disclose such matters; but after the transaction is over, after the coal has been purchased and has been burned, and during the following year a member of Parliament asked "What did you pay for your coal?" there should be no secret about it. Our competitor could not get any information from the answers to the questions, unless it was that the Canadian Government were buying coal at better prices than they were themselves, or at a higher rate. In any case these questions should have been answered.
It could not do any possible harm to disclose that kind of information, although the Government has persistently refused to furnish it. About the time this question was asked it was reported in the Halifax papers that the Government had one of their ships there for which they had not provided a cargo and therefore found it necessary to purchase a cargo of coal for the river Plate in order to give the ship something to do, and it was said they purchased about 8,000 tons at a dollar a ton above the market price. Whether that statement be true or not, you can understand, Mr. Chairman, how it makes the public suspicious when the department

refuses to answer such simple and proper questions.
On Thursday of last week I endeavoured to get some information myself with regard to a certain ship called the " Beaver " that had cleared from Halifax for Barbadoes. I asked this question:
How many passengers did this vessel carry on the said trip?
The answer was:
The department has no information.
I also asked:
What is her deadweight tonnage and how many tons of freight did she carry from Halifax on said trip?
The answer was:
The deadweight tonnage of the vessel is 3,972 J tons. The department has no information as to the quantity of freight carried on the voyage referred to.
The department went to the trouble of telling me what the tonnage of the ship was, but they had no information as to the quantity of freight that ship was carrying. That was the very thing I wanted to find out, because I was told the ship sailed from Halifax with so little freight that it was not possible for her to pay her way.
Another example. Last year we were informed that a ship by the name of the "Recruit" was stranded in the St. Lawrence river, and we were assured that the Government would not lose any money because the ship was well insured. I was glad to hear that at the time, and I took occasion during the present session to find out whether the Government really did come out of that transaction without a loss. I put this question on the Order Paper:
Was the steamship Recruit of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine that went aground at Vache Point, St. Lawrence river, rescued and refitted for sea?
That was answered in the affirmative. I also asked:
If so, how much was expended in repairs? and how much was collected from insurance companies?
This is the answer:
The information asked for is information as to operating details under the Canadian National Railway Board, and is not in possession of the Government.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the question as to whether we collected that insurance was a question which there was no reasonable ground for refusing to answer.

186S
In another case I find this question asked by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) :
What are the names of the steamers of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine which entered at the port of Montreal since May, 191S?
That question is answered and the names are given of a large number of steamers. The next question reads:
What are the names of the steamers of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine on which -work was performed by the Hall Engineering Company, of Montreal?
This is the answer:
Information in so far as work performed on Government steamers, no reports are filed at Ottawa as these are matters in connection with operation and under the Board of Management of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine who are responsible for all matters in connection with operation.
My hon. friend has led us to believe on various occasions that he would give us information about construction, but not about operation. These two questions I have quoted are both questions relating to operation. And I would like my hon. friend to explain why he was able to give us the facts in connection with the first question, but was not able to give us the
10 p.m. names of the ships that were repaired by the Hall Engineering Company. I could multiply instances of such refusals, but I will not detain the committee because every hon. member knows that the pages of Hansard are covered with such questions regarding railways and ships where the information desired was persistently refused.
I would like to give a sample of the management of these vessels as disclosed in the answer to a question by my hon. friend from Westmoreland a few days ago. It appears that one of the government steamers by the name of the Laurentian was repaired in the port of St. John. The question is this:
Is the steamship Laurentian owned by the Government?
The answer is: yes.
If so, when was she purchased, from whom and what price was paid?-A. The Laurentian was purchased in April, 1917, from the Canada Steamship Lines, Limited, for $50,000.
Q. Wais said steamer out of repair and tied up at St. John for five months or for any time? If so, for what length of time?-A. Yes, four months.
Q. During the time said steamer was so tied up in St. John, how many of the crew remained aboard?-A. Twenty-two.
This answer goes on to say that the wages of these 22 sailors were paid by the Government during the four or five months that the ship was under repair. That is an extraordinary thing for the department to do. A private owner would never think of doing it. As soon as the ship of a private owner comes into port he discharges his crew and pays them off. He hires another crew when ready to send his ship out again. He does not keep his men on board feeding them and paying them wages for four or five months, but that seems to be the way in which at least one of these government vessels was handled by the department. To'my mind that is a very unbusinesslike proceeding and requires some explanation. In the minister's statement of the other day, I find the following:
There is a further consideration from which as the minister primarily responsible for the programme I derive some comfort, and that is that every contract made, every voucher paid, every letter and telegram exchanged between the department aqd contractors is open for the fullest inspection of any member of the House who desires any further information.
My hon. friend has not produced these papers; he has not given us the pleasure of seeing them. I am glad to hear that they are open for inspection. I am also glad to hear that he derives comfort from anything in connection 'with his programme. I did not think there was very much comfort for anybody else in conection with it; I am quite satisfied there is no comfort in it for the people of this country. It may be quite true that the minister has the vouchers somewhere. But the question is; where is the money? Are we ever going to see it again? I submit it is rather cold comfort to realize that we are spending $70,000,000 on this venture and that there is no prospect of our ever seeing our money again.
Attempts have been made not only by the minister but by other hon. gentlemen on that side to throw responsibility upon the shoulders of hon. gentlemen on this side for the enormous present and prospective losses in conection with the railways as well as with shipping. A few days ago in the course of the railway discussion the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) used this language:
Why are we in this country staggering like weary Titans under this burden? It is because my hon. friend and the hon. gentlemen who led him at that time were in a government that launched railway schemes upon the country fifty years in advance of their time.
My hon. friend from Brantford seems to have forgotten some very recent history in

which he himself figured. I would like to ask him who it was that forced the Canadian Northern railway upon the people of this country by closure? Did we not resist that transaction to the utmost? Did he and his party not enforce the closure rule to put that measure through? Did he not speak and vote in favour of it? The hon. member for Brantford has a very heavy responsibility to answer for in this matter. He has the reputation of being a business man, and I have no doubt that his word goes for much in the councils of his party. He assured the House at the time this matter was up that within from three to five years this project would be a paying venture.' I do not think he would give us that assurance to-day, but he was willing at that time to place an additional burden of from four to five hundred millions on the shoulders of the people in order to take over the Canadian Northern system. Then again, what about the Grand Trunk deal? Who is responsible for the additional four or five hundred millions of dollars of liabilities involved in the purchase of that system? Are members on this side responsible for that? We voted against it; my hon. friend from Brantford and the hon. gentlemen who sit with him voted for it. We were assured that that was going to get us out of our difficulties; that the acquisition of the Grand Trunk would help us in regard to the other lame ducks that the Government had taken over. But it has not turned out that way. If you look at the Estimates you will find that the railway system that requires the largest sum for the current year is the Grand Trunk-something like $89,000,000. In that estimate, I believe, is included the fixed charges on the Grand Trunk Pacific, which, according to the Public Accounts, appear to be a little over $8,000,000. So that if you choose to make us responsible for the Grand Trunk Pacific and take off that $8,000,000, there is still $80,000,000 required for the current year to operate the Grand Trunk system. So the men who insisted on taking over the Grand Trunk have very heavy responsibilities to answer for before the people of this country. We do not know how much of the eight millions is deficit; the estimate does not disclose the fact. It bunches the whole thing together -improvements, betterments, and deficit are lumped in one sum and we are asked to vote the enormous amount of $89,000,000 en bloc to keep the Grand Trunk running for the current year. I submit that my hon. friend should not have blamed us for all these difficulties of which he himself is

guilty. It would be better for that weary Titan from Brantford to manifest a spirit of repentance and to show some contrition for his own mistakes instead of throwing railing accusations at the heads of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. But everybody knows that the Government is responsible for our financial condition both in railways and in connection with merchant ships. They cannot escape the responsibility. Parliament has little responsibility regarding our shipping debt because Parliament had nothing to say with reference to these ship contracts; Parliament was not given an opportunity to discuss them. Hon. gentlemen will remember that at the time of the armistice, November 11, 1918, there were only four keels laid in the ship-building programme, and not a single ship had been launched; but before Parliament met the following February the minister by Order in Council entered into eighteen contracts without competition and without tender. Now can anybody say that members on either side are responsible for these transactions. They were carried out by Order in Council behind closed doors, without Parliament being informed and without our knowing anything whatever about them. Questions were asked when the minister's Estimates came on, and then we discovered that in the interim my hon. friend had entered into these new contracts involving an expenditure of many millions. The trouble is that the war spirit seems to be rampant on the part of the Government. Although the war has been over for two and a half years the Government are carrying on as if the war were still in progress. You know, Mr. Chairman, that description in the New Testament of the Roman centurion who had men under him, and who said: "I say to this man, Go, and he goeth; and to another, Come, and he cometh; and to my servant, Do this, and he doeth it." That is the spirit that seems to pervade the Cabinet. It is the military spirit, the war spirit, and I submit is the reason why members of Parliament were not consulted about these shipping contracts and large expenditures and are not even now consulted. We are told that sixteen ships are in course of construction; but we do not know what stage they are in, nor whether it will be possible to save any of this money or not. We know that if we build a ship to-day for $2,000,000 and launch it tomorrow, she is worth when launched only $500,000; we know that we have thrown away $1,500,000 in the operation. Any shipping man who knows anything about

the shipping business knows that to be the fact. Is it not important that we should know in what stage the shipping programme is? The minister, however, has not told us anything about the matter, and I hope he will not hold us responsible for anything he is doing in connection with it.
Now we come to the question as to what we should do with those ships, my hon. friends on my left always want a constructive policy, and I have no hesitation in giving my views, that if the ships are losing money by our operating them at the present time, we should not continue to operate them, because we have no money to throw away. I am also firmly convinced that it will be better for all concerned if we get rid of them, and put them into the hands of private owners. I read at the time in the London Times, that, within two weeks after the armistice, the British Government announced their policy that the freight vessels that they had purchased and built should be placed on the market and turned over to private owners.
Not bad for a slow little country.

That
was the policy of the British Government and it was the right policy. Private ownership of ships has been successful in Great Britain, which is the greatest shipping country in the world. It has not been necessary for the British Government, in order to maintain their supremacy on the sea, to put the money of the British people into the building of ships. All they have to do is to leave the people alone and the people will do the business themselves better than the Government. My hon. friend should have left the people of Canada alone. The minister would have less to answer for and the country would have been better off if the people had been left alone. He has put the shipping of this country back for a decade by his so-called policy; he has driven shipping enterprise out of the field. Have you heard of any man putting his money into ships in this country since this programme commenced? No man would take the risk. The minister put the prices up so high; he engaged all the shipyards; he inflated prices so that new shipyards were started, and the people who put their money in them are likely to lose it. This policy will be bound to end in putting the shipping business back for a number of years to come in place of assisting it. Some hon. members will say,
"Oh, but we must have ships." Of course we must have ships; we must also have wheat and potatoes and steel; but that is no reason why the Government should begin to plant potatoes or to sow wheat. Or build steel plants. Let the Government stay out of this business; it is far too hazardous a business for the Government to be in. It is not advisable for the Government to be competing with private ownership on the seas without any prospect of reducing freight rates or of being of any advantage to the country. I have pointed out that my hon. friend does not need those vessels for the railways, and that in regard to our export trade, if we have a cargo to send to any part of the world, there are thousands of vessels ready to carry that cargo as cheaply as the Government can carry it. It is, therefore, altogether unnecessary that we should have those ships at all, and the minister will be doing the part of wisdom if he will get rid of them as quickly as possible and put them into private hands. It may be that he will not be able to sell them, at the present time; I do not know whether any one would buy them from him or not. To begin with, he would have to make a heavy loss, and he would require to make terms. He might have to give a number of years to pay for The ships. He would, of course, require to impose conditions that they would engage in Canadian trade, and remain upon the Canadian registry. If the minister had the courage to announce that his policy is to get rid of these vessels and turn them over to private ownership on the best terms he can, I am quite sure that the step would be satisfactory to the business men of this country. And that ultimately we would save a great deal of money. The Government, by engaging in this shipping programme is not doing any good to our trade; it is involving the country in a very large expediture which is likely to become much larger. It is not possible, in my judgment, for the minister to show anything like a profit for several years to come on these vessels. If he is not able to show a profit, to earn his depreciation and interest, he is going into bankruptcy, and we will lose our $70,000,000 in the end. It is far better to make our loss now and to put the ships into the hands of people who will operate them in the interest of Canadian trade. I think I have said enough at the present time, and I hope I have given the minister a few things to think about and to answer.

Perhaps it would be more convenient if I said a few things before the minister replies, and he could deal with them at the same time as with the remarks of the hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair).

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If my hon. friend would allow me, I would prefer to answer the hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough now. I did not think it would be necessary for me to say very much more as regards the Government shipbuilding programme and the operation of the ships, inasmuch as the statement which I presented to the House went into the matter very fully. The hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough is a man who is held in very high esteem in this House and also by everyone who has the pleasure of knowing him. Therefore, I feel it is necessary, on behalf of the Government, to answer some of the salient points that he brought out in his speech. Apparently, the results for 1920 have been rather disappointing to my hon. friend. He has had considerable experience in the shipping business, and from what he knew of the high cost of operation of ships and also the very marked decrease in freights that had taken place, especially during the remaining months of 1920, he no doubt was looking for a very much worse statement than I had the pleasure of presenting to the Houes on behalf of the Government. I think the figures speak for themselves. The result of the operation of the Government shipping by the operating company is, to the mind of the most men, a very creditable showing, and inasmuch as my hon. friend has dealt considerably with the figures of the statement, it is only fair to hon. members and also to the public that I should go more in detail into the figures that I presented to the House a few days ago than I did on that occasion. First of all, I think I made it abundantly clear then-and if not, I will do so now-that the ships made an operating profit. I do not want my hon. friend or ony other hon. friend to get the total profits mixed up with the operating profits of the ships. If < tr railways had made an operating profit instead of having made a loss of $70,000,000, every hon. member of this House would feel in a much better frame of mind that he does now. But the Government ships have made an operating profit on closed voyages, for which profit I take no credit whatever, because the management of the Government

ships is left in the hands of the Canadian Government Merchant jMardne. The management are composed of old, experienced shipping men who have been for many years with the old Allan Line, and I here wish to pay my compliments to the management for the very splendid showing they made under very difficult circumstances during the calendar year 1920. The operating profit on closed voyages, as vouched for by the well-known firm of auditors, Messrs. Marwick, Mitchell and Company, was $1,293,525.55. Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House have distorted, I will not say deliberately, but at all events they have not admitted that the Government ships during the past year made an operating profit. Now all hon. members know that in that operating profit is included the general expenses of operation of the ships, besides $1,000,000 for insurance premiums. If the ships had done nothing more than make the operating profit I have just mentioned, I consider that would be a very good showing, but the operating company have done more than that. On the open voyages a conservative estimate is that the profit applicable to 1920 would amount to $183,000. Therefore, the net operating profit on the Government ships amounted to $1,476,525.55. Will any hon. gentleman that has any knowledge of shipping say that that is not a remarkably good showing that the Government ships made during the year 1920? I know that the public are satisfied, and I know I shall read in the newspapers a little later on that the people of this country are very much gratified at the splendid showing that the Government ships made during the year 1920.

Does
my hon. friend say that the people of this country are satisfied with a showing that did not earn interest on the money that was put into the ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If my hon. friend will wait a moment I am coming to that. First of all, I want to make it clear that the operating profit on the Government ships amounted to $1,476,525.55.
What year was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: Is that a new statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
