It is not the same that you gave to the House the other day. On what

page of Hansard will we find that statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I can tell my hon. friend that in a minute. My hon. friend occupied the time of this committee for four-and-a-half hours the other day, and I hope he will not begrudge me the time necessary to make my statement. I shall guarantee I shall not take longer than forty-five or fifty minutes.

If the minister will allow me, the hon. member for Lunenburg is in an entirely different position from the minister. The minister is here endeavouring to get the House to pass a vote of $8,000,000, and as a representative of the people of Lunenburg I say that I am fully justified in asking any questions that are relevant to the item under discussion. I am not going to allow the minister to tell me that I cannot ask questions. The minister cannot evade my questions by referring to a speech I made the other night, I want to tell the minister he must answer.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before the minister proceeds, it might be well to make the rules quite clear. The hon. member for Lunenburg is entitled to ask any question he sees fit concerning this item, and the minister can of course give any answer which he sees fit, but I must point out that when the minister has the floor, no hon. member can take the floor away from him, even for the purpose of asking a question, until the minister has concluded his remarks.
Unless the minister consents.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Unless the minister
consents, of course.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am sorry the hon. member for Lunenburg did not understand the very plain statement which I made and which appears on the pages of Hansard, but for his information I will gladly repeat the figures. I say that the net operating profit on closed voyages for the calendar year ending 1920 was $1,293,525.55. And to that the net earnings on voyages closed since January applicable to 1920, namely $183,000, and you have a net operating profit for the year of $1,476,525.55, which I think the public of Canada will agree is a very good showing.

The minister is not giving the statement he gave to the House on March 29, as it appears on page 1334 of Hansard. Do the net earnings showh
on page 1334 of Hansard, amounting to $781,460.09, include that $183,000 on closed voyages?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Certainly. My
hon. friend from Lunenburg is taking the net results of the entire statement. I am giving the operating profits first.
You said net profits.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Net operating profits. Now we come to the question of depreciation. A great deal has been said about the cost of the Government ships, and a great deal has also been said, and rightly, about the depreciation of values. Everybody knows that there has been a very sharp decline in the cost of ships, but my hon. friends opposite, in order to show the public that there has been an enormous loss, take off the full depreciation, and take it off about twice over, from the profits for the current year, and say, here is a loss of $20,000,000, sometimes they say $50,000,000. Now these are very unusual times, and after such a long period of war every manufacturer in this country, every wholesaler, and every retailer, has large stocks of raw material and finished goods on hand that have very markedly depreciated in value. Any man who has been in business will know that if a large manufacturer carries a stock of war material estimated at $5,000,000, let us say, and there has been a depreciation in value of say $3,000,000, the manufacturer does not write off that $3,000,000 depreciation for the one year 1920. If business houses did that, they would be insolvent. What do business men do? They recognize the great depreciation in values that has taken place due to the war, and they set aside a reasonable amount for depreciation and spread it over a term of years, and that is precisely what the operating company have done. They have taken off 2 per cent, and just here let me explain a misunderstanding on the part of some hon. gentlemen. That 2 per cent depreciation was not on the full cost of the ships, but on the full cost of the ships as they were turned over to the operating company. Therefore, the depreciation is not 1,135, as some hon. gentlemen made it out to be, but 2 per cent on the full cost of the ships as they were turned over in 1920 to the operating company. The depreciation for last year amounts to $667,665.45. The operating company will reinvest that amount of depreciation, they tell me, probably in Victory Bonds bearing 51 per cent interest, and 51 per cent interest during a period of twenty-five years

will write off the entire cost of the Government fleet. Now, I think that hon. members will agree that that is a sound and conservative way of taking care of depreciation in values of the steel ships bunt by the Government under contracts, most of which were let during the war and the rest in the year 1919 when prices were very much higher than they are now. It js most unfair to the Government and to the operating company to take the full amount of millions of depreciation during the year 1920 and say that there is a loss to the Dominion of Canada on Government ships. Let me point out to hon. gentlemen that when the National Transcontinental railway was built, from Moncton to Winnipeg, at a cost to this country of $200,000,000, there was not one cent of interest paid, and there never will be for a good many years to come. I am not finding any fault with that myself; but what seems peculiar to me is that my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Sinclair), and who has been in the House so long, should earnestly lament the fact that we are not getting full interest on the Government ships. It does not seem to trouble him that no interest was paid in connection with that $200,000,000 spent on that portion of our railroads.
Where does the minister get the $200,000,000 from?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: From the Minister of Railways.
Well, the blue book of the Minister of Railways gives it at $168,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am quite willing to take the corrected figure as given by the hon. member for Pontiac.
What difference does $30,000,000 make?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The principle remains, nevertheless.
The principle is there, but the interest is not.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
So far as depreciation goes, I have had the operating company's figures checked up, and if the earnings keep on as they did in 1919 and 1920, the entire cost of the fleet will be written off in twenty-five years. Let me repeat again, that no business concern in this country would write off depreciation on raw material or finished goods all in one year. Now, when we come to the in-
	-
terest, if the operating company had been able to make earnings enough to pay 5i per cent interest on the cost of the ships as they were turned over to them dur'ing the past year, the amount of that interest would have been $1,828,329.07. I am quite prepared to view the statement in the way my hon. friend would like to have me look at it. What is the loss on interest when we have concluded with the entire statement? It is $1,000,000. That is a fair statement; it is a true and accurate statement, vouched by the company's auditors, the well known firm of Marwick, Mitchell and Company; and it is the only way a statement would be dealt with by any of the banks and business men throughout the country. If it gives any comfort to hon. gentlemen opposite to take off the entire depreciation on the ships at once and say that that is a loss, I have nothing further to say. Let me say, however, that during the last year the operating cost of ships was the highest that the shipping world had ever known. When you take into account the rapidly declining rates of freight and the fact that no shipping company in the world has ever had the same number of ships turned over to them in such a short space of time as this managing company, for them to make an operating profit of $1,476,525.55, to write off for depreciation, outstanding liabilities and incorporation expenses the sum of $695,065.46, and to show 2.35 interest on war cost of ships, is to make what I consider a very good statement, and so do the Government and the people of Canada.
Oh, no, not the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Well, I will come to that in a moment. When the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) was speaking, he said that I made the statement last year in the House that half a million dollars for interest had been paid into the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, and in his usual declamatory style, he brushed that aside and said he did not believe that a cent had been paid into that fund.
I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Well, I will withdraw that statement, but that is the way I understood the hon. member.
You must not understand; read my speech and see what I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
When I get my
summer holidays I shall be glad to read the hon. gentleman's speech. I made inquiry

of the Finance Department to-day and this is the information I received: There was a cheque for $500,000 for the year 1919. The cheque was received by the Finance Department from the National Railways, and was divided thus: $415,358.36 will he found at page 102 of the Public Accounts for 1919-20 and the balance $84,641.64 went into last year 1920-21. There, I think, is clear enough proof; I have indicated where in the Public Accounts the particulars may be found.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I can only inform my hon. friend that the information which I presented to the House last year and which I am giving this year, is information I got from the operating company and which I have no reason to doubt at all. The information I gave last year I repeat again; it covers the full amount of interest on the ships that were in operation in 1919, at the rate of 51 per cent. I come to another very important matter. My hon. friend from Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), said I had given three reasons for the Government entering into a policy of shipbuilding, namely, war, railways, and expansion of export trade. That is quite correct. He then went on to say that he could see no reason for entering upon a shipbuilding policy as a war measure because the first ship not launched until November 1918. That, of course, is quite correct; but I became a member of the Union Government in 1917, and during the very dark months of 1918 the war was at its very height. There was more tonnage sunk then that at any other time during the war, and no minister of the the Crown within the confines of the British Empire could sit down and say he would not enter into shipbuilding, nor would he do this, that or the other thing, because possibly the war might cease at any moment. There was only one policy for the Canadian Government to follow, and the same policy was being followed by the British Empire and all the Allies-that was to strain every nerve and to go ahead with the building of ships as fast as we could as if the war was going to last forever.
Therefore this Government very wisely, and with the unanimous consent of the House, entered upon a policy of shipbuilding, for war purposes only, in April, 1918. Happily the armistice was signed on November 11, but that was no reason for the Government not going ahead, in the early part of 1918, with their plans and their contracts with the various ship builders throughout this country to construct ships under Canadian registry, in view of the very heavy loss of tonnage that was taking place daily.	.

My
hon. friend has omitted to mention the main reason I gave. It was not that the keels were not laid until a certain date; it was that the Munitions Board were building ships and that the Canadian yards were busy with contracts for that board at the time my hon. friend intervened.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend
will also remember that when I announced the Government's policy on April 4, 1918 -I have Hansard here to prove it-I very clearly explained to the House that the Imperial Munitions Board were keeping all the fourteen yards that were building steel ships in Canada busy building ships for the Mother Country under British registry, but that Canada was providing the money to build those ships
Just as a loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
-and I said at
the time the Government thought it the wiser policy-instead of putting up money to build ships under British registry for the Mother Country-which ships would leave this country and be free from Canadian control-to construct ships ourselves inasmuch as we were putting up the money for Great Britain anyway. Then we would be able to build up a mercantile marine of our own under Canadian registry which would remain under our control for all time to come.

We
were simply lending the money.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Of course we
were lending the money. I also said at that time that Canada needed a mercantile marine to co-operate with her large system of railways. Now my hon. friend is a much older man than I am but I cannot follow his reasoning when he says that there is no need of ships in connection with a large system of railways. Well, if my

hon. friend can prevail upon the Canadian Pacific Company to sell their fleet of ships, which is just as large as ours, and if he can impress that company with the fact that they can carry on their transportation in Canada and throughout the world with a railway system only and without ships, -if he can get the Canadian Pacific Company to do that I am willing to recommend it to the Dominion Government.
If my hon. friend can make a profitable business with this venture like the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is doing I would be glad to see him go on, but I do not think he can.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That was not
my hon. friend's statement. My hon. friend stated "In my opinion there is no need for ships for railways.'"
(Guysborough):	Certainly not. _

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: , He further said "No railways should have ships; we can get all the ships that we want."

Quite
true.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have only been Minister of Marine since 1917, and I found ships as scarce as hens teeth. During 1917, 1918 and 1919 we could not get ships at all. My hon. friend also says we have not done anything to expand the export trade of Canada. Very well, I will take the British West Indies about which my hon. friend knows a great deal. When we were building ships an official of the Royal Mail Packet Company that has four ships running to Bermuda, Demerara, and Port of Spain, said "Surely you are not going to run ships down to the West Indies." It was the usual story from private owners. He said "We are taking care of all the trad". What a foolish policy it would be for the Dominion Government to send ships down to the West Indies." I told that gentleman that while we were building ships and owning ships-that is the Government of Canada-we were not operating the vessels, and the routes upon which they would run would be left by the Government to the management. Now what has been the result? Twelve of the Government ships are operating down there and they are hardly able to take care of the trade. Take the South American route. Would the Dominion of Canada have a single ship running to South America if this Government had not built and operated its own ships. Any 
man that is familiar with the transportation to the West Indies knows that the trade of those islands was in the hands of our American friends. The South American trade has also been in their hands. Let me tell my hon. friend what has happened as the result of the ships of the Canadian Government going down there, and in order to save time I will only give the bulk figures. The exports of Canada to the British West Indian Islands-Bermuda, British Guiana and British Honduras-in 1913 amounted to $4,967,312 but in 1920 they had increased to $15,257,014. That is what the Government ships have done in expanding trade between Canada and the British West Indies. Now let us see what the growth in imports has been. In 1913 our imports amounted to $9,864,017 and in 1920 they had grown to $19,863,722. Yet my hon. friend says further that these ships have done nothing to expand the export trade of Canada; and I have only cited to him the figures with respect to the West Indies alone. The hon. gentleman took the trade returns for 1919 and compared them with the returns in 1920, and he discovered from those returns that the exports were some three hundred millions less in 1920 than they were in 1919 but that is not at all surprising. The hon. member knows just as well as I do that the reason for the exports being so much larger in 1919 than they were in 1920 was on account of the need for replenishing the depleted stocks of the world after the war, but now that world-wide depression is being experienced it is not at all to be wondered at that our export trade has decreased. But I can tell my hon. friend that the decrease would be very much more if it had not been for the ships of the Government Merchant Marine.
I want to tell my hon. friend another thing. The Government held a conference with representatives of West Indies in June, 1920. What was the whole problem that had to be solved in order that Canada and the West Indies might draw closer together in the matter of trade arrangements? If the Government had not owned and been able to operate its Merchant Marine I doubt very much whether we would have been able to have successful^ completed, as we have done, the details oi the agreement entered into and which wil. be submitted to this House shortly by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I say that we would not have been able to have concluded that preferential trade agreement with the West Indies if it had not

been for the fact that this country owned its own mechantile fleet. Jamaica, which has never yet granted Canada a preference, is now willing to give us a preference in the best market of all the Islands down there of twenty-five per cent and I repeat again if it had not been for the fact that we were able to give the West Indies the transportation facilities that we are giving them, if we had not been able to provide the passenger accommodation that we have provided-with ships sailing from Halifax in winter and from Montreal in the summer time to the Bahamas, Jamaica and British Honduras-I doubt very much whether we would have been able to have completed, in the successful way in which we did, the preferential agreement entered into between Canada and those Islands.
Now, to hear hon. members opposite one would think that Canada was the only country that had to face the problem of depreciated values of ships. But the Government of Canada has received no credit for not building wooden ships. When the Government launched its shipbuilding programme I was besieged with requests from the Maritime Provinces and from the provinces of Quebec and British Columbia to have included in our programme the construction of wooden ships. As the minister responsible, I advised the Government not to embark on wooden shipbuilding at that time, because when peace came those ships would be of little value to us and would ultimately be an (enormous loss. What were other countries doing in the meantime? Old England was having wooden ships built here, so was Norway and so was France, and while our highest average cost for steel ships was $191.50 per ton, I have seen the contracts placed for wooden ships here and I know the cost ran as high as $200 a ton. Then no one finds fault with the Emergency Fleet programme which our neighbour to the south carried on, but she has millions of tons of wooden ships on her hands and she does not know what to do with something like 536 steel ships. Then turning to the Mother Country, think of the enormous shrinkage in value both on steel and wooden ships that she has had to face. Besides that, England during the war built large national shipbuilding yards, as they were called over there, or, in other words, government yards, and they were building steel ships on a large scale. During the war Australia built just as large a mercantile fleet of steel ships as we did. I have read, as no doubt other hon. members have, what is called the Parliamentary Journal of the Empire, which gives a short synopsis of the debates that take place in the Mother of Parliament and in all the other parliaments of the British Empire. But I have not read a word of criticism in any of those parliaments in respect to the great shrinkage in the value of their ships. I find no fault with hon. gentlemen opposite for criticising the shipbuilding policy of the Government, because one of the duties of the loyal Opposition is to criticise, but inasmuch as this is a national policy I hope that hon. gentlemen opposite will take a national view of the matter and think of what these ships are doing for Canada-of how they are helping our railways and how they are helping to expand our export trade and to advertise the Dominion all over the world. Although the profits are not yet very great, I do not look through the same blue spectacles as does my hon. friend from Antigonish and Guysborough. We will pass through this depression and as long as this Government remains in power our mercantile fleet will continue to be owned by the country and operated by the Canadian Government Mercantile Marine. We are not going to sell these ships to any private interests, for just
11 p.m. so long as we own our Canadian National railways we shall need to operate our mercantile fleet in conjunction with those railways.
Hon. members have even gone so far as to estimate what the loss is going to be on the operation of our merchant marine for 1921. True, they do not know how much cargo is going to be carried, they have not the slightest idea of what the revenue or what the expenses are going to be, but still they sit down and say: Here is our loss for 1920, and here is the loss that we are going to have in 1921. Last year my hon. friends stated that 1920 was going to be a poor year. They said. Wait until you see the end of 1920, and then the people of Canada will realize where they are going to be with your shipbuilding policy. Well, we have finished 1920, and it has been a good year. Everybody thinks so, except the minority of hon. gentlemen opposite. I do not know what 1921 is going to turn out, but in this young country we have got to keep our courage up. Many of us have been through depression in our own business and we have emerged successfully, and I think the country is going to come through this depression all right. It may be that hon. gentlemen will be surprised

next year when they find a profit on the operation of this much-abused merchant marine.
I am not as familiar with the history ot the past as my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark), hut the other day I happened to come across what is known as Crom well's Navigation Act of 1651. I think hon. members will agree that that is far enough hack.

That will he far enough
back. Now come along from year to year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
What was the object of Cromwell's Navigation Act of 1651? No country knows better how to expand her trade than the tight little island of Great Britain, and Cromwell's Navigation Act laid down the principle that imports into the United Kingdom should he in British bottoms only, and that three-fourths of the crew should be British subjects. That is the way England started to secure the supremacy of the seas that she has maintained so well since that time not only with her mercantile fleet but also with her navy. What did Germany do in 1870? She subsidized steel shipbuilding and gave preferential rates over her railroads for cargoes to be carried in German bottoms. Therefore if Canada should lose a few million dollars a year I would conceive it to be good policy for us to have built these ships and to continue to operate them. We hear a lot about Canada being a nation. Show me a nation in the world to-day that is not a maritime nation. It is high time that Canada owned her own mercantile fleet and assumed her place among the maritime nations of the world.
I want to refer to one or two points made by my hon. friend for Guysborough before I sit down. He says that on November 11, 1918, we had only four contracts placed, and that we should have ceased shipbuilding at that time. I do not think he was in the House when I gave the figures the other day, and I will give them again now.

My
hon. friend is a little astray in what I said. I said there were only four keels according to the dates from a return which I got in that journal to which I referred. I am aware that there were a number of contracts, in fact I stated there were eighteen contracts between the date of the armistice and the meeting of Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am quite willing to accept my hon. friend's correction. When

he said that only four keels were laid down I inferred he was under the impression that that was all the Government had done on November 11, 1918.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: If the minister will permit me, I did not make the comparison for the purpose of showing that there was anything wrong _ in that respect with the minister's operations. I did so to show that it was impossible for the minister to make a profit when the ships that he built cost four times as much as the ships built during the war, of which there are millions of tons now afloat. I admit that a ship cannot be built now for the price at which-it could have been built before the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Quite so, and in that respect Canada is in no different position from that of England, United States, Norway, France or any other country. They all have a large amount of tonnage built during the war. Norway had a ship launched at the Vickers shipyard, Montreal, on Saturday last. I know the cost of that ship, but I do not think it is fair to a foreign country that I should here state the price.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Well, I do not
think that I should. I cite the case merely to show that all countries of the _ world placed large orders for. tonnage at just as high prices as Canada paid.- Our friends to the south paid an average price of $215 a ton as compared with our price of $191.50. Canada can compete with the other nations of the world, because other nations have not fleets wholly built in pre-war times. A large proportion of the ships operating on the seven seas to-day were built during the war at high cost, just the same as Canada's were.
Now, there is another thing. The hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) when he was speaking gave figures to show at how much lower prices ships could be built to-day than the prices paid for the Government ships. When I made my statement to the House I said that the same type of ship as our 8,400 ton deadweight would cost to-day in the United Kingdom $130 a ton. My authority for that is this: our naval architect has just returned from England. There he visited all the yards, and I had told him to find out for me exactly what the yards of the United
Kingdom would charge to-day for ships of the type that we are building here. The information that he brings back is that these ships, figuring on the difference in exchange would cost $130 a ton. It is not fair to say that an ordinary tramp ship can be built to-day at a certain price as compared with the cost of the Government ships when it is a fact that the machinery, auxiliary equipment and type of the tramp ship generally are totally different from those of the Government ships. Then, my hon. friend advanced a peculiar argument;
I am not an experienced shipping man but I have never heard it. Shipping men tell me that the speed of a freight ship should not be over lOi or 11 knots an hour. If you have a freight ship with a greater speed than that you burn too much coal and the ship cannot be economically operated. But my hon. friend thinks that Canada's ships are too slow; that freight ships should have a speed of something like thirteen or fourteen knots an hour.

My
hon. friend has entirely mistaken my idea.
I pointed out that the Australian company operating in competition with my- hon. friend was running fast boats and that that would be another circumstance which would make it difficult for him to get the freight. I quite agree that a freight vessel must necessarily have a lower speed than a passenger vessel. I would not favour making the speed of a freight vessel anything like that of a passenger vessel. My hon. friend misunderstood me.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think I did, but of course I will accept the explanation of my hon. friend. But I want to point out to him that more than once in his speech to-night and during his previous speeches he referred to the Government ships as tramp ships-I took note of it at the time-and referred to the slowness of the speed, 10J and 11 knots. That is a proper speed for the ordinary freight ship. So far as the Australian route is concerned, while I have not the details I was told by the management not very long ago that our ships are carrying full cargoes to Australia and New Zeoland and that that is the most profitable route which the Government ships at present operate. My hon. friend also made the point that we subsidize these competing ships. True, we are subsidizing ships running to Australia, to Newfoundland and to the West Indies. But the ships under subsidy by the Department of Trade and Commerce are

freight and passenger ships, whereas the Government ships carry freight only.
Now, I wish to submit the following details of difference in construction and equipment between the Government ships and ordinary British tramp ships:
1.	Increase in accommodation area, and quality also accommodation for 4 passengers with deck saloon and lavatory adjacent.
2.	Additional heavy derricks.
3.	Additional electrical plant.
4.	Total equipment and outfitting, not included in British vessels.
_	5. Sidelights brass in Canadian vessels: cast
' iron in British.
6.	Steam heating in excess to suit Canadian winter ports.
7.	Steering gear: very much in excess of British vessels, being directly connected to rudder head with telemotor control.
8.	Telegraph: largely in excess of British vessels.
9.	Winches: one extro on Canadian vessels.
10.	Navigating position largely in excess of British vessels.
11.. Fittings and equipment throughout in excess of British vessels.
12.	Canadian vessels have cold store and refrigerating engine for ships' provisions. British vessels have only ice box.
13.	Grain trimming and escape hatches in Canadian vessels extra.
14.	Mechanical' operating gear for engine room- skylights and handling lifeboats.
15.	Sundry items throughout vessels, such as teak rails, extra rails and stanchions, canvas work, extra stores, galley and pantry equipment, hospital, galvanizing iron work, upholstery, etc., all additional to equipment in British vessels.
16.	Bronze propeller blades, and bronze spares. Cast iron in British vessels.
17.	Additional covering to boilers.
18.	Ash ejector fitted in addition to ash hoist.
19.	One sanitary pump extra.
20.	Independent in place of attached feed pumps.
21.	Extra metallic packing.
22.	Extra spare gear and outfit.
23.	No trials were held on British vessels owing to war conditions? Ail Canadian vessels perform 6 hours full power trial, with steering and anchor trials.
" I may say also that a number of our vessels are equipped with oil fuel installation in addition to coal fuel." There is, therefore, a long list of differences between a Government ship and an ordinary freighter.
There is another thing that has just occurred to my mind. The hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough Mr. Sinclair) and the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) said that a large number of the Government ships were idle; that they were swinging at their anchors in Halifax harbour. This country has been fortunate; all the Government ships were busy in 1920, and up to this moment they are, so far as my information reaches me, all engaged. The reason that ships are lying

at anchor in Halifax harbour at the present time is because they are in there for their annual overhaul, and when that is done, they are going to enter into the coal trade of Canada. My hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair) says that our small ships are of no use; that they are only yachts. Let us see what size " yachts " they are. Nearly all of those ships are 3,750 tons deadweight, and we have only four that are as small as 2,800 tons. My hon. friend knows that to do trade in Newfoundland and the West Indies where the waters are shallow, you must have vessels of light draft, and we could not send larger vessels than the ones that are plying now either to the West Indies or to Newfoundland. In addition to that, our vast system of railways requires a large number of that exact type of ships to be put into the coal trade.	;
Does my hon. friend intend to put the small ship's into the coal trade?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The operating
company do.
Mr: SINCLAIR (Guysborough) :	They
will be making a mistake.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Possibly. I have never interfered, nor has the Government, with the management. I do not know anything about the operation or the price of their coal. I do not ask them any more questions than I would ask the Canadian Pacific.
Do you not think you should?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: All that I am interested in, as Minister of Marine and Fisheries in this Government, is the net results of the operation of ships at the end of the year. I am not going to cover the debate that took place in this House the other day; but no man could manage ships if the Minister of Marine or any of the other ministers of the Dominion Government were going to ask him where he bought his lubricating oil or coal, or where he bought his butter or cheese. I do not ask a single question at all; they have an absolutely free hand as long as I am Minister of Marine, and as minister and speaking for the Government, I want to say that we are well pleased with the splendid showing made in 1920 and we are very hopeful for the year 1921.

It is considerably past the hour when the House should be closed up if we had carried the pro-

position that was before us to-day, and I do not want to detain the committee unduly at this hour. I am lost in admiration ad the courage and optimism of the minister and I say that unreservedly. He is a splendid type of a Canadian; but even Canadians can be too optimistic, and I really think the minister, just at the moment, is the leader in the class of super-optimistic Canadians. My hon. friend is too optimistic when he assures himself and keeps assuring this committee that the country is behind this shipbuilding policy. I want the minister to listen to what I am going to say on this subject. If there was anything in that statement or as much in it as my hon. friend thinks, I knfiw of no man who would be so loyal to him as the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), but even the Prime Minister the other day used words of very great caution and reserve in regard to this scheme. He said: " It is true the pic. ture is not as rosy as we could wish it might be." I thought I used rather strong language when I spoke of the business as a white elephant, but if there is a fair amount of truth in the representations that have been made by the hon. members for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) and Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), I do not think I used too strong language at all.
There is this further fact which I should like to bring to the minister's mind so as to moderate his optimism as to the people of the country, and it is a point he might be able to clear up. The severest critics in the press of my hon. friend's statement the other day were to be found in newspapers which are about the very strongest supporters of this Government. The Halifax Herald, a newspaper whtch has always been prepared to burn its boats for anything coming from a Conservative ministry or a ministry that might be suspected of any tendency towards Conservatism, offered most uncompromising and severe criticism of the minister's whole scheme, and Halifax is a shipping port where newspapers should know something about this question. I am trying, you see, to get the minister into a reasonable frame of mind on this subject, because if he goes away with the Prime Minister to Great Britain as he is threatening to do, and he keeps in this optimistic frame of mind about shipping, he will be coming back with a string of dreadnoughts in his train. That would be a very serious catastrophe to come over this country at the present time. You come from Halifax to Ottawa, and you have in Ottawa a paper known as the
Journal which has vied with the Halifax Herald in severe animadversions upon my hon. friend's statement. Then you take a trip from Ottawa to Montreal, go back a little in your tracks, and you come to the greatest shipping port in this country, the place where surely my hon. friend's scheme should have enthusiastic support if it gets it anywhere. But here again his journalistic friend, the Gazette, meets him and joins with the Ottawa Journal, with the Halifax Herald, and to some extent with the Prime Minister himself, in taking a gloomy view about the subject upon which my hon. friend is a positive Micawber, who is always sure that something is going to turn up to get him out of his troubles.
I want to give my hon. friend some more reasons why I think his optimism is not entirely well founded. I am going to show him, I think without any fear of contradiction or refutation, that his scheme has already broken down in some of its main features. I want to make very definitely this statement, that the scheme as undertaken by the Canadian Government was not in its inception a war measure atj all. If I need any evidence of that, I find it in the statement which my hon. friend made a few minutes ago. He said that when he embarked upon the scheme, the Imperial Munitions Board was building, I think he said, at fourteen points in Canada, was doing all with Canadian material, Canadian men, and at Canadian shipping points that could be done for the winning of the war. I do not see my hon. friend take any objection to that. Then, I repeat, the first point in his argumentative platform goes out clean from benenth him. It never was a war measure at all, and that has a serious bearing on things we have heard in this debate, not only from my hon. friend the minister, but from this side of the House that this shipbuilding was all right as a war measure, but should have been stopped at the asmistice. It never was a necessary war measure as undertaken by the Canadian Government. The work never should have been taken out of the hands of the Imperial Munitions Board. We had our hands very full during the war, and the Government had my whole-hearted support at that time for anything in reason, but as my hon. friend admitted the other day, I never gave any countenance whatsoever to his taking up this business of shipbuilding.
Well now, if it was not a war measure, what was it? What was at the back of my hon. friend's head when he undertook this? It was nothing that was in any way dis-

creditable to him, neither was it discreditable to my hon. friend from Maisonneuve and my hon. friend from North Cape Breton that they agreed with him. What is discreditable to them, I think, is the way they leave the minister in the lurch to-day. It is especially wrong on the part of a Highland Scotchman, who should always be prepared to die in the last ditch for any cause to which he has given his adherence. But I leave them out of consideration. What was in my hon. friend's head was that if there was to be shipbuilding in Canada, it was a useful industry for the Government to support. That was really what was in his head, and he was an extremely skilful man in setting about it. I do not want to use the words offensively, but when he arranged to burglarize the public purse, he took the precautionary measure of enlisting some of those who ought to be detectives and making them receivers. That is what happened at various points in this country. He got them into the scheme with him,- it is no use going behind the bush in this business-and so he had this put before us as a great scheme for building up the shipbuilding industry in Canada. That was what was in my hon. friend's mind. He had all the anxiety about the war that any member of the Cabinet had, and their anxieties were great, but his anxiety was not that ships were not being built fast enough in Canada for the war, because he knew the Munitions Board were building them fast enough, faster and better than he could build them, and he ought to have known-and this is where I must blame him, kind as he has been to me in his language, and I appreciate his courtesy and kindness-he ought to have known, I say, that he would have got out of his difficulties much sooner if he had left the business in the hands of those who were experienced in this kind of work.
I have not heard any pointed reference to the steel end of this shipbuilding project. What is the position of the steel end of it? The minister says now that we ought to have projected a war that was going to last forever. Well, that is a long way to look forward to, a very long way. Indeed, it is more than the mind can grasp, and it must be clear, I think, to the minister that if we were to look forward to a war lasting forever, we need not have troubled about these matters any further because we should have all gone down in the sweep. There would not have been a government to take the place of the one that is disappearing

on the other side, and all our troubles would have been settled in oblivion.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If my hon. friend will allow me, I did not say the war was going to go on forever, but I said the Government ought to go ahead with its plans for helping win the war as if the war was going to go on, which is a different thing.

That only shows that the minister was careful as a prophet, but very careless as to policy, because if the war was not going to go on forever, it has become fatal for him to go on with his policy forever. While the war has gone, the policy is with us. I do not think the minister is helping himself by his correction.
This was what was in the minds of those implementing this project. What otherwise was the meaning of a contract for five years, and that is a considerable portion of forever, with the Dominion Iron and Steel Company? I think I am right in saying that a contract was entered into with that company for 250,000 tons of steel plate. I do not know precisely what is the condition of that contract now, but it is confidently stated in many quarters that only 40,000 of the 250,000 tons have been delivered, and that that part of the project is closed down at the present moment. I do not think it is going at all-if I am wrong, the minister will correct me-and the Government is being pursued, naturally, by the company for some compensation for their losses under this very formidable contract which has broken down. I do not want to press this point very much further. I am only concerned that the main features of this scheme should be before this committee before we vote $8,330,000. It is somewhat alarming, Mr. Chairman, to reflect that this vote, which now looks so small to us, is one-fifth of the total expenditure of Canada in 1896, when the late Liberal Government came into power-one-fifth of the total money that was running the whole Dominion for federal purposes. We cannot lightly pass this vote until we are sure the committee knows what it is doing, and that the country also knows what are the main features of this scheme. I take it that at the present moment-and I am very anxious to have the minister's attention, because I want to know, and the committee will want to know, exactly what the state of his mind is before he gets his money-the position of the Government is that construction on this programme will cease this year, that

this is the last money that the minister expects to ask for, for the construction of ships under the Dominion programme. Well, I am sorry to say that brings us to this position, that the second plank of my hon. friend's augmentative platform goes out from beneath him, because for the moment this great industry of shipbuilding, this building up of industry along the line of shipbuilding, has disappeared from the Government's programme. The programme, my hon. friend said in his first statement to the House, will terminate so far as the Marine Department is concerned this year, so that the second plank in his platform, I repeat, goes out from beneath him. I wish I could be as sure of the Government as I am of the Marine Department. I will tell my hon. friend why I have doubts on that subject. Just before the statement which I have quoted from memory occurs this other statement:
Regarding the question of a subsidy as an aid to stimulate steel shipbuilding in Canada, the Government has this matter still under consideration, and it may be that an announcement in that connection will be made by the hon. the Minister of Finance when he brings down his budget.
Now I must say that that statement fills me with very considerable alarm. I had hoped that we should get away from our duties here by the end of May or early in June, but if, after we have got the shipping vote all on one side, we are to have a system of shipping subsidies for an industry which is as manifestly difficult to carry on as the shipping industry at the present moment, then I apprehend that the discussion of the Budget will be neither brief nor smooth. I will not say any more about it at the present time than just that, because, if we are to be asked, on top of the minister's statement about the surplus ships that are in the hands of the government of every nation in the world, to invest Canadian money in more shipbuilding, then we are certainly to be asked to take a course which is unbusinesslike and which would lead to certain loss and certain national disaster in the immediate future. I issue that word of warning in the hope that it may reach the ears and eyes of the Minister of Finance and that he will not fulfil the veiled prophecy which is contained in that portion of my hon. friend's speech.
Now, in connection with the building of industries, my hon. friend has repeated an argument to-night for the continuance of this scheme which he used in the year 1919, and which he used last year; that is, as to
the employment of workmen. At first sight, and if we did not go below the surface of the matter, it would naturally appeal to any one of us in these difficult times. But I want to point out to the Government that the employment of public money to give work to any portion of our inhabitants in an unprofitable enterprise only aggravates the difficulty which it sets out to relieve, because you can get money only in two ways. If you raise it by taxes, then you take the money from the pockets of the taxpayer to put it into an unprofitable enterprise; if it remained in the pockets of the taxpayers, it would either go into the development of their own business or to swell the money in the hands of our banks, and would be loaned out to promote profitable business. If, on the other hand, instead of raising it by taxes, you raise it, as is not too seldom the case, by borrowing, then, in addition to the economic evils which I have just pointed out, you have the further economic loss of having to pay interest on the money you borrow; and when, as is frequently the case, we borrow from a foreign country, there is the added evil that for the sake of relief to a few workmen at a few points in the country, we pay interest to foreign people. Capital comes into the country in the shape of goods made abroad, and we make business for the foreign country from which we borrow and employ workmen in that country only to score a loss and put our own workmen out of work in our own country. So that no policy is more reprehensible, no policy in the long run is more economically unsound, than the policy of embarking on unprofitable or unremunerative work.for the simple object of giving temporary and local relief to a handful of our own people.
Now it was not a war policy; the minister has proved that. It was not a necessary war policy; it was simply a continuation of a war policy which was being as well, or better done, and with vastly less risk to the people, by the Imperial Munitions Board. It . clearly was not a good way of building up Canadian industry, because my hon. friend assumes the committee that we are giving it up this year as a Government enterprise. I have pointed out its futility and folly as a cure for unemployment, and their remains the consideration that it is the necessary complement to the Government system of railways. Well, I should like to know exactly where my hon. friend stands under this head. We are left now with the ships on our hands. I do not wish to use language of recrim-

ination. My object is not a party object; it is to serve the country in this matter and help the people and the Government, if they will be helped, out of their difficulties. But I should like to know if I am right in interviewing my hon. friend's mind when I infer from what he has said that he still thinks it is a good thing for the Government to go on operating these ships. A diametrically opposite policy has been suggested by my hon. friend from Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair), who says he would sell the ships. Well, I do not know whether I would recommend that policy at the moment, for the minister is in the unfortunate position of having missed his mark. He said himself that he could have sold them last year; but las year was 1920, and this is 1921, and I doubt very much whether there is anything in the suggestion of the hon. member for Guys-borough, for the simple reason that it is highly (problematical as to (whether he could sell the ships except at a loss that must be regarded as absolutely ruinous.
With regard to the alternative of going on operating these ships, though of a sanguine temperament, I still fail for the moment, I am sorry to say, to share the minister's optimism. It seems to me to be a very doubtful course of national policy to add to railroads, which show a deficit of $70,000,000 this year, a fleet of ships which, at their end of this transportation system, I very much fear may show a deficit in the years that lie immediately in front of us. I hope not. As a good Canadian, I hope I am wrong; but that is how it looks to me. I believe that my hon. friend, even if we allow his figures to be all right tonight, will have a different showing to make next year; and if there were any way of disposing of these ships at a reasonable loss, I would seriously ask him to consider the recommendation of my hon. friend from Guysborough.
For the rest, I should not like to sit down without a constructive word, and I must repeat what I have said to my hon. friend from the beginning of this business. He has referred to-night in complimentary terms to Britain's history in regard to shipping. He spoke of what was done at the time of Cromwell. Well, the spirit that runs British ships was manifest then; but to bring British shipping to where it is to-day, in addition to that spirit, there has been a policy, and that is the policy not want to press this point; I am almost tired of hearing my own voice pressing it in this House, I have had so much to

say upon it. I do want to say, however, that this Government will have to decide whether they want a high tariff policy or a shipping policy, because they will not get both. I repeat that prophecy with the utmost confidence, and I do so for the purpose of urging my hon. friend to bring this consideration before the Cabinet. What is the sense of building railroads to carry the surplus of our crops to the edge of the ocean, and building ships for the avowed purpose of carrying those crops, and then putting up a high tariff wall as an obstacle in the way of goods either going out or coming in? You may have the one policy, or the other to pursue both is an act of economic folly. , If we are to have a tariff wall as high as Hainan's gallows then do not let us fool ourselves about having a successful merchant marine, because we shall not have it.
I have tried to review the minister's policy in as few words as I could compress it into. I have charged that his policy was not a war policy undertaken, for the war. It was taken out of the hands of those who were doing it as well'as he has done it, and better. It has failed as a shipbuilding industry in the hands of the Government; it is a doubtful scheme as regards operation; and I do not think it will be made a success until the country alters its fiscal policy.
I just have one word more to say, and that is that if the minister goes to Britain we shall have to know a good deal about naval policy before that time. I would recommend to him that when he goes to that country to study shipping at first hand, he should meet the shipping men of the Old Land and they will tell him how shipping has been made a success there. He will only find one opinion amongst people who have anything to do with ships in Britain as to what has been the cause of the success of British shipping. He will only find one opinion, as indeed there only can be one opinion; and to continue with this shipping policy at the same time that we follow the fiscal policy that has been followed in this country, from Confederation up to the present moment, is an act of economic folly which can only end in national loss and disaster.

I do not profess to be a sailing man, and I do not profess to know a great deal about the mercantile marine, but I do think there has been considerable criticism from some of our friends across the way, especially those that come from the maritime districts. My

good friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) lives at a good distance from the sea now, and I am afraid that he has forgotten some of the opinions that he brought over with him from the Old Land when he first came across.
My memory is my strong point.

My hon. friend was then more of a maritime man that he appears to be at present. The hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has delivered a long address tonight as did the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), the other day, eonveying the idea that the shipbuilding policy with which the minister has allied himself is one that is going to lead to great disaster in this country. The minister is well able to look after himself as has been proved on many previous occasions. However, I shall say a few words with regard to some of the points raised and I shall, in reply to what has been stated by one or two gentlemen opposite, place on record a few of the press criticisms which have been said to be of a very unkind nature; I think it was the hon. member for Red Deer who made that observation. Some of the newspapers, however, have not criticised the minister in any such way, and if the comments come from papers that are usually unfriendly to the minister and the Government I think perhaps they will have quite as much effect as if they were from papers that have supported the Government, even if those comments are not, in some instances, as favourable as they might be. I shall read first the opinion of the Sydney Post:
Canada's experience with its state-owned merchant marine has been more encouraging than with its Government-controlled railway system. In cost of construction and operation, in freights earned, and in successful business management Mr. Ballantyne was able to demonstrate by a comparative statement that Canada's merchant marine has made a record which suffers nothing by comparison of that of any other country.
That is fairly strong and it comes from a maritime quarter, the Sydney Post of March 31. I hope the hon. member for Lunenburg will take notice of that fact.
Thank you, I have.

I now come to the Winnipeg Tribune. It is published in a city a fairly long distance from .the sea, but not so very far from the Great Lakes where shipping is considerable of a factor.
The Winnipeg Tribune of March 31 contains the following:
"The showing made by the Canadian merchant marine is not by any means bad when the circumstances of trade during the past year are taken into account, and when its position is compared with merchant marine of other countries."
"The merchant marine as it exists, however, forms a great and powerful weapon in the hands of the Government of Canada for the development of overseas trade. It is capable of being used, and should be used both to stimulate trade where it may be profitable to the country as a whole, and to correct some of the unfortunate tendencies of our trade as it at present exists."
I think that is favourable comment coming from the Winnipeg Tribune. Now, let me quote from the Vancouver Province of March 30:
"Happily the Minister of Marine does not share all the experience of the Minister of Railways. He does not report a deficit."
The Government purchase of ships was not intended as a direct financial investment. It was one way of providing employment for returned soldiers for the period or readjustment after the war. In this province, and doubtless elsewhere preference was given to returned men in these works. The industry gave regular and well paid employment at a time when it was gretly needed."	
"Nevertheless the Canadian merchant fleet seems to have been kept busy, and it is now possible to establish several Canadian steamship services which might otherwise have to wait.
Next, I will give a quotation from the Hamilton Spectator of April 2:
It is true that the shipbuilding programme was not completed in time to be of practical service in the campaign; but the Government can hardly be blamed for not foreseeing the exact date of the termination of hostilities.
Now the Toronto Mail and Empire of March 31:
The statement presented by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries respecting the operation of the national merchant fleet for 1920 is very gratifying. It is the more pleasing because in the latter part of the year shipping conditions on the ocean were much depressed. The United States shipping Board had to lay up hundreds of -vessels, and suffered heavy operating losses. British owners had to lay up ships. Rates fell from one-third to two-thirds of what they were in January, 1920. Competition for cargoes was keen by the tramp freighters, and new routes were projected by many of the important old lines. It might have been expected that the Canadian Government fleet, being a new comer on the ocean, would have been at a large disadvantage in breaking into transatlantic cargo carrying, but though the number of ships in operation increased during the year to 47, with a tonnage of 250,000, cargoes were found for nearly all voyages. Hon. Mr. Ballantyne was able to report an operating surplus of $1,293,000. After depreciation, incorporation charges, and liabilities, the net surplus was $781,460

which was 2.35 per cent on the capital cost of the ships. Last year was really the first fair test of the merchant marine, because in 1919 only a few round voyages had been completed by about a dozen ships. When rates had sunk so low that even thousands of British vessels were laid up, the making of an operating profit was a triumph of management. There are sixteen vessels still to be delivered, nearly all of them large vessels. Hon. Mr. Ballantyne complains that the Canadian manufacturers have only given half-hearted support to the government vessels. They have not gone after export business, as they should, and have been too content to do their importing of overseas materials through United States channels. The rapid .extension of routes on which the government freighters ply offers to Canadian business men exceptional sea transportation, and as costs of production come down, and a surplus productive capacity is built up, more energy in developing overseas business should be expected. The government ships are giving the service, at any rate, and if they can continue to pay their way, making some return on their capital cost, the country will have reason to congratulate itself on the experiment. Few countries have attempted national operation of merchant vessels with any success.
I have only read a few of the large number of extracts that I have here.

No. I have read
several, and if my hon. friend wants more they can certainly be handed to him.
You had better read them.

I am not going to
kill time, as my hon. friend might expect.

than I have this session.

I did not say my
hon. friend had killed time. Do not run away with that idea before it is imputed to you. I said I did not want to quote them for that purpose, and although I have these extracts I do not propose to read them at the behest of my hon. friend.
I want to devote one or two moments to the arguments put forward by my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark). He has several grievous faults to find with the shipbuilding policy of Canada as a policy. It is open to criticism probably, and I would expect my hon. friend, who studies all matters of economics, to have some criticism on so large a subject as the shipbuilding policy of Canada. Now as the Vancouver Province article -which I have just read pointed out, shipbuilding was undertaken for several reasons, one of which was to carry freight in co-operation with our railways. And I take issue with my hon. friend from Red Deer and other gentlemen op-

posite who criticize that as not being the part of good policy. The Canadian Pacific railway has made excellent progress along that line. It finds that it is necessary to have freighters on both oceans, and has operated them successfully for a long time in conjunction with its railway system. I admit that it requires very strong backing to do that, but if the Canadian National railways are to be a success they must be able to compete in all matters with the Canadian Pacific railway, and they cannot do that too soon. I can quite understand ' that shipping men do not like that any better than the Canadian Pacific Railway does, but the Government having, partly perhaps from choice, but largely from compulsion, taken over about 20,000 miles of railway, we are now obliged to run those railways to the best possible advantage, and I submit that it is economically a sound policy to have boats on the oceans east and west and also on the lakes, if necessary, to co-operate with our railways and to make our carrying charges as low as possible so as to compete with any other transportation company in that respect.
I think transportation is a national policy. I thought to have ships upon the waters, would appeal to my hon. friend from Red Deer, because though I know he is pessimistic with regard to many things that are made in Canada, if I recall correctly he did not think that Canada was only able to build ships of a small character and for the carrying trade, but in that celebrated debate on the Naval issue my hon. friend even went so far as to strain his free trade opinions in favour 12 m. of building dreadnoughts in Canada. I do not want to misconstrue him. I was in the House when that speech was made, and I was shocked that a gentleman who as a rule was so consistent on free trade could have broken through even to the extent of proposing that we should build battleships, but I believe the hon. gentleman did advocate that policy on that occasion. If I have misinterpreted him I shall be glad to be corrected.

If my hon.
friend will permit me, I do not want to interrupt him, but he is always so fair to me that I know he wants to be told exactly where I am in that matter. Of course, I supported Canada building her own ships for defence. If she was to have a navy at all, I preferred to have it made in Canada. If I may say so, I think my hon. friend has come to my view in that respect. It was

a question of defence, and even so old an authority on economics as Adam Smith states that defence is the first duty of a country. But when it comes to a question of building ships for profit, my hon. friend is dealing with another question altogether. I believe in having good stout locks upon my house for my own security, but it does not follow that I want to embark in the business of a locksmith and lose money in making and selling locks.

Mr. Chairman, I
did not think the hon. gentleman was going to explain his shipbuilding policy and give his reasons for going back on free trade to the extent of supporting a shipbuilding policy for Canada. I thought he would have had uttered only two or three words to tell me whether I was minsinterpreting him or not. I do not like to have a free trade speech thrust in the middle of a protectionist speech because it rather spoils the thread of my argument. The hon. gentleman says that I have come to his line of policy. Not at all. I am backing the building of ships that we can build in Canada to advantage,-these merchant marine ships,-but I am not asking that we should build dreadnoughts, for they are the last word in shipbuilding, and even yet Canada is not prepared in any shape or form to build those big battleships. I do not think my hon. friend accuses me of being unduly peaceful, but I say that at the present time I do not think Canada is called upon to embark on a battleship enterprise. Therefore, I am not in line with his policy on that occasion.
Now, if the manufacturers of Canada, as is stated by the minister-and I am afraid there is some truth in it-have not taken full advantage of his policy, it must be remembered that at the present time export trade presents very serious difficulties, as everybody knows who is in the business. If you sell your goods to-day to foreign countries it is questionable if you can get paid for them, and if you do get paid it is in a depreciated currency or in goods that you are not in need of. Therefore I say it was a most unfortunate time for the minister to embark on this policy. But that is not his fault, and the blame should not be on him. The policy is all right, but it was embarked upon about four years too late. The minister was not in office at that time or I believe that the policy would not have been undertaken too late-I mean too late to get the best financial results, not too late to be of general advantage to the
Dominion in point of trade. I myself waited on the then Minister of Marine four or five years ago and begged him to embark on the building of some ships. That was away back in the second year of the war, when it became evident that we were going to lose a large amount of British shipping through the activities of the German submarines. I tried to convince him that it was the psychological moment to undertake a shipbiulding programme. At that time ships could have been built at half the price that they cost later, and, further, during the war they would have paid for themselves if they made two or three successful voyages, so high was the cost of transportation at that time. Therefore I say to my hon. friend from Red Deer that this is a sound commercial policy providing we are getting good value for the money spent.
The question arises whether or not the best of bargains has been made. I do not think any hon. gentleman has said that the minister did not make the best bargain possible at the time the contracts were let, and while it is easy to figure out now that you have lost money on those contracts, where is there a private firm to-day is not more or less in the same position? I know of small businesses in our town that have had to wipe out nearly half their capital this last year because they were caught when the war ended with a vast amount of material on hand which went down to twenty-five per cent of its original value. I am connected with several enterprises that have had to make very serious reductions in the value of the goods on hand -and it would strike the Government the same as it would strike private individuals. Before the war ended the farmers were getting very high prices for their produce, but if they carried their stock recently they had to write off a large proportion of the value and if they sold they had to sell at a straight loss. Therefore, the minister having in good faith placed contracts for the building of these vessels, is carrying out his part of the contract as an honest man should. Every business man must stand by his business engagements whether they are going to be a loss to him or not. So I say to the hon. member for Red Deer that the policy is all right; the only question is whether the thing is being done at the right time and to the best advantage. If the hon. member knew that proper consideration had not been given to the matter and that fair advantage had not been taken of the oppor-

I did not
question the "right" of the Government. The Government is almighty in the country while it is governing. I questioned the wisdom of the Government's action. I join with my hon. friend in defending the rights of the Government, but I should be sorry to join with him in every thing he thinks wise.

All wisdom, I admit, does not dwell under my cranium, nor does it under that of my hon. friend. Perhaps a little error creeps into both now and again, but there is more error in my hon. friend's cranium, I think, than there is in mine on this question of relief work. He says he questions the wisdom of the Government. Well, both in the Old Land and in this land works of practically no utility have been undertaken for the sake of furnishing employment to workmen. This policy has been followed in order that these men might feel that they were not dependent on the contributions of their fellowmen; in order that they might maintain their dignity and be in a position to say with truth: We are earning our living. So when my hon. friend says that that is not good policy I answer him by saying that the Government was justified in its expenditure which resulted in furnishing employment to returned soldiers and others who would otherwise have been out of a job-justified even if the ships could have been built at twenty-five or fifty per cent less. I believe that my good friend here, the member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) who has every sympathy for the soldiers, will express the view that it is a sound policy to help returned men, even , if at a disadvantage otherwise.
If it is good policy, why does not the Government continue it? Why is the Government finishing its contracts and why has it cancelled its contract for plates?

The minister had a certain programme, and that programme is finished at a certain time. All programmes, no matter how long they are, and all speeches on great questions, must some time come to an end-because they are finished.

The unemployment is still there.
[Mr. Cockshutt.)

Perhaps so, but it
may he relieved in another direction. Why should we keep on building ships if we have enough? Let us build something else that we need more. What about highways? That is a good thing on which to spend money and the proper time to undertake work of that kind is when the workingmen of the country need it. I stand by that as sound policy. It is a sympathetic policy. I will not say it is a charitable policy, because when you furnish work to a man who is willing to work, -I do not think you are giving him charity; you are simply making it possible for him to obtain his daily bread in an honest and satisfactory way and to hold his head up and say: I am a man among men. I am surprised that the hon. member for Red Deer should object when the Government say they undertook this policy partly to furnish work for the unemployed. As is pointed out by the Vancouver paper, this policy was a great benefit to a large"number of returned men in that city.
Now, as to the value of the ships we have, I do not profess to know as much about that phase of the subject as the member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) does. But I am afraid he is disposed to write off somewhat more on these ships than he would if he was the owner of them. I do not know the hon. gentleman's pedigree, but I rather think there must he some Scotch in him. As a matter of ordinary business the whole amount should not be written off in one year; it should be spread over a term of years. No business man would say: Well, this is a pessimistic morning; I will take an inventory of my stock and down comes everything to seventy-five per cent below what it cost. Where would the assets of this country be if we applied that principle all round? What can you sell to-day at one hundred cents on the dollar? I.challenge my hon. friend to pick out of the daily market reports in the newspapers ten companies whose stock is to-day selling even at par or anything near par. Canadian Pacific stock, which was selling two or three years ago as high as 285, has come down to as low as 115. If that is possible in the case of a great and powerful enterprise managed to the last degree of efficiency, is it likely that the Government, embarking on a new policy in difficult times, could foresee that shipping was going to come down with such a sudden bump ? I say, therefore, that business men throughout the country will not be disposed to criticise the minister because he keeps the book value of his ships abcve

the market price. I say that in spite of the contention of the hon. member for Guysborough, who, I believe, paid some attention to me a few moments ago when I was not in the House. I repeat that the proper way to make these reductions is by a- certain amount each year, according as the business will stand it. It is unreasonable for the hon. member for Lunenburg or the hon. member for Guysborough to suggest that the whole thing be cut down in one fell swoop; if they were shareholders in a company, they would not advise such a course as that. Why ask the Government to get pessimistic all of a sudden? I admire the optimism of the hon. Minister of Marine. It is quite true, as the member for Red Deer has said, that it is an optimism that is not, perhaps, given to everybody. Some men are always pessimistic and some are always optimistic; I try to be a little of each. I know that we all want a little bracing in these times. It appears to. me that it comes like a tonic from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to hear him, in answer to wails that come from the other side, wails all down the line about the tremendous loss in ships and to Canadian trade, say: "Well, I see brightness ahead; I see a future for our ships; I see that this is going to be a commercial success some day, and in connection with our railways, is going to be a paying policy for the Dominion of Canada." I really think when the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) sleeps over this situation, he will conclude that he went a little too far in his depression tonight as regards a policy that is really commendable. I do not like to see him get into a pessimistic mood. I know it is very hard for him to refrain from that when he sees protection romping around, but I hope he will not give way to it too much. As I do not want him to become too pessimistic, I will give him as a bracer, a definition of pessimism that I heard the other day. A man is a pessimist who considers it is necessary to wear both a belt and braces. I suggest to my hon. friend that he does not get too pessimistic as to require bracing up to that extent. .
I rose to make these few remarks only because I think the minister has been perhaps unduly pressed on this subject, and he is too good matured, he does not want to use too many hard words, so I do not believe he will object to my putting in a few thrusts to my hon. friends opposite to show them that I, as a business man, believe the minister has done his utmost

to make the affairs of this country successful and prosperous. He began the work at the very top notch, and while that was unfortunate, it was not his fault. He was urged to do it on every hand, and many to-day would have him continue it. I believe even the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux) who made that severe attack on the minister the other day, would be willing to let the item pass, if the minister would say: "I will spend a few million dollars in the constituency of Gaspe in building ships." Do not be too pessimistic about the success of the shipping policy of the minister in connection with the railways. While I admit that deficits of the kind that we have had on the railways cause a shudder to run down our spine, so to speak, we believe that, with our railways and our ships being operated in conjunction with each other, this country will be pulled out of the mire by a board that may be finally brought to give its best attention to the development of these great enterprises. If we boost up our shipping and boost up our railways as we should, if we show the loyalty that is in us towards these enterprises and do not criticise and knock and pound and try to drive into the earth our property, there will be a vast difference m the atmosphere in a very short time. That is the spirit which I commend to the attention to some of my hon. friends opposite; I suggest that they lend a friendly hand and try to get a traffic for our property both on water and on land, and I think in due course they will see the sun smiling just as the Minister of Marine says.
