Parliament passed an Act empowering the Government to lend money to the extent of
120,000,000 to shipyards. Has any shipyard taken advantage of this, and is the Government giving any encouragement, by subsidies or in any other way, to shipyards?

The hon. member for Red Deer seems to. be quite familiar with the matter. The Government took
40.000	tons on account of the contract for
250.000	tons. The demand was very brisk last year from all parts of the world and was greater than we were able to supply. speechtext:
If my memory
serves me aright, the Port Arthur Shipbuilding Company, the Collingwood Shipbuilding Company, the Canadian Vickers, the Three Rivers concern and the Halifax concern were asked, but we got firm bids only from the Port Arthur Shipbuilding Company and the Collingwood Shipbuilding Company.
Has the Government any report on the cost of work due to the inefficiency of the class of help now employed in Toronto?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. We have one of our own men there, and the reports coming into the department from day to day go to show that the work is being done efficiently.
How much is being paid on these contracts, first, to the Dominion Shipbuilding Company or the liquidators, and secondly, to the Collingwood Shipbuilding Company?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member would go on with any other questions he may have to ask, while the deputy is looking that up.

What arrangement
have the Government made with the liquidators relative to the material on hand with the Dominion Shipbuilding Company?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
When the Government 'first commenced to let contracts they took the precaution of getting a surety bond from each shipbuilder for 10 per cent of the value of the contract. In addition, we took a lien on all the material that might be in the yard. In case of the failure of a firm, such as the Toronto firm, for instance, we can collect the value of the surety bond, and in addition all the material on the works belongs to the Dominion Government.
In reply to my hon. friend's previous question, the total contract price amounted to $630,000 for each ship, and the amount paid to the company before they went into liquidation amounted to $409,500. The Collingwood Shipbuilding Company are now completing ships on the basis of cost, plus 15 per cent. They are being paid as the work progresses, on the voucher of our man on the work.

Is the Government
in possession of information relative to steel prices? Is the Government paying the liquidator the 1921 or the 1919 prices for the steel on hand?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There was a large quantity of steel plate in the yards; I saw it when I was there last fall. The contract for that steel was made before the company went into liquidation, and the Government are standing by it.
That will be the 1919 price?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am not sure.
Would the minister mind repeating what he said with reference to depreciation and a sinking fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The operating
company have allowed 2 per cent depreciation on the cost of the ships. That amount of depreciation will be re-invested each year, yielding 5i per cent interest. Therefore, with the 2 per cent depreciation and the interest in the course of 25 years, providing the company's earnings are kept up, there will be enough to write off the entire cost of the fleet.

If we got this $8,000,000 working in that same direction it might work off some of the liabilities of the country. The minister is really borrowing money to put into a sinking fund. I do not see how he can borrow money, pay interest on it, and at the same time use it as a sinking fund to reduce his obligations. If he had a surplus invested, and had not borrowed the money in the first place, there would be some reason in his argument, but to borrow money and place it in a sinking fund and say that you are going to wipe off the liability with that is not a very sound argument I am afraid.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is the usual way in a business concern, so far as my judgment goes. The operating company are in a very strong liquid position. I referred to that in my first statement, and therefore did not want to refer to it again this evening.
They owe one hundred cents on the dollar.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Their current assets show a very nice surplus over current liabilities. They do not owe a bank anything, so they are in a very good liquid position. The only way to write off the excessive cost of the ships is to spread it over a period of years, and I do not think 25 years is too long. I have had their figures checked, and they will be able to do that provided their earnings can be kepi; up. I wish to say to my hon. friend, who understands these things so very well, that there are very few operating companies, if any, that are called upon to make their operating expenses provide for depreciation, as in the present case, and then be expected to earn 5\ per cent on the war cost of the vessels. We are taking it up with the operating company now, and it seems to me we ought to modify that rate of interest, but we have not done so.

Modifying the interest charge would only be a bookkeeping transaction in any event. The people of Canada are called upon to furnish the money; they have to pay the interest on the debt of Canada. So unless the minister pays the interest on the full amount that he borrowed from the treasury for this company, over which he claims to have no control, it does not matter whether he makes a bookkeeping entry at 3J per cent or at 7 per cent, which is the rate, I believe, the Government are paying now. The country is losing the difference. For the minister to say that he can borrow money to create a sinking fund is surely not good business. If the minister had his fleet paid for, if he had sold stock and paid for his fleet in that way, and the fleet was earning profits so that the minister was able to lay aside a surplus, there might be some force in his argument; but to say that with borrowed money he can create a sinking fund to write off depreciation, I am afraid, is not sound business.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We are not borrowing money to create a sinking fund. If my hon. friend and I had been going to build that fleet, we would have had to borrow the money from some bank or issue securities. Having done so, we would then provide a depreciation fund just the same as this company is doing. It appears quite the usual thing to me.
Is there not a charge against the Marine Department or against this shipping company? Do they nor agree to pay interest annually amounting to so much?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: Have they paid it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: But not for 1920?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, they have not earned 5J per cent on the capital cost of the ships, only 2.35 per cent.
Therefore, you have no money to put into a sinking fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Oh yes, we have.

If you pay your interest you have no money to put into a sinking fund. You are probably $1,000,000 short, and therefore, you have nothing to put into a sinking fund, so it is useless to talk about a singing fund that is going to relieve the situation. You are not paying your interest.
It is only a matter of bookkeeping.

Yes, but the difficulty is it is very expensive bookkeeping for the Canadian people. If the minister was doing the bookkeeping for himself, he might go ou and spend his money and I would not criticise him at all, but in this case it is the money of the Canadian people. I do not like his statement that he has a sinking fund that is going to take care of something when, as a matter of fact, it is not because he has not paid his interest. He has made a loss on operation for the last year and therefore has nothing to place to sinking fund and cannot possibly pay for the ships in twenty-five years or twenty-five hundred years.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is a surplus of current assets over current liabilities which will enable the company to set aside the amount of depreciation their statement shows.

Is there a sufficient
amount of current assets to pay interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, and more.

The minister says he has set aside $667,000 for depreciation. I understood him to say that 2 per cent this year, and a corresponding amount during the next twenty-five years, would wipe out the $70,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The company have taken 2 per cent of the value of the ships turned over during the past year, and that 2 per cent amounts to $667,665.46. They will re-invest that at 51 per cent, and the annual interest on the 2 per cent year after year for twenty-five years will accumulate sufficient to write off the cost of the fleet.
The minister says that with this $667,000 odd he is going to pay- off the $70,000,000 in twenty years.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, but depreciation every year.
How much will you pay off in twenty-five years?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The actuaries
have figured it out. I have had one ship taken at a valuation of a million dollars to make sure that their figures would be right, because I am careful not to put anything but correct information before the House. They have taken a ship valued at a million dollars. Two per cent of that will be $20,000; re-invest that $20,000 at 51 per cent, and write off 2 per cent every 
year; then keep on investing with compound interest on top of compound interest, and in twenty-five years it will equal $1,000,000.

The minister says that he has put this $667,000 in the sinking fund, and after doing that he has no money left. Consequently he owes the Finance Department interest_ on the money invested in these ships in 1920, which is $50,000,000. How can any business man put money to rest when he has not paid interest?
It cannot be done.

It is absolutely impossible. The minister owes interest, not only for 1920, but also for 1919. If I understood him correctly about an hour ago, when he was making his third speech this evening, he told us that the amount of $500,000 which he paid to the Finance Department in 1919, was all the money he owed that department for interest on money advanced by the Government up to December 31, 1919. Am I correct? Very good. Then if the minister will be good enough to turn to page 1331 of Hansard, he will find that he made the statement that at December 31, 1919, he had twenty-four vessels of a tonnage of 129,000 tons. If the minister will take his pencil and make a calculation he will see that at $192 per ton these twenty-four ships cost $24,768,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, but bear this in mind-

I catch your point; let me go on and, if I am wrong, you can correct me. Interest at 5i per cent on $24,768,000 is $1,362,000. If I apprehend what the minister was about to say, it is that all this money was not advanced during the year 1919. Is that what he was going to say? Yes; exactly, the minister nods his head. The minister will not forget that part of that money was advanced in 1918, so that one off-set the other. For instance, he was paying out for the work during the progress of construction, from May or June, 1918, to December 31, 1919, so that he not only owes interest in 1919, but also has not paid interest for 1918. Taking what was advanced in 1918 and what was advanced in 1919, the two years' interest would amount to one year's interest on the total cost of the ships.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I admit quite
frankly that during the progress of the construction of the ships, while moneys were being advanced, the country lost interest; but it is not fair to charge interest

to the operating company until the ships are turned over.

It is as broad as it is long.
Some one is losing that interest, whether it is chargeable to capital account or not. The country, in addition to paying $192 per ton from the time the contract is let or the keel is laid, loses that interest, and it makes no difference, so far as the people are concerned, whether the interest comes out of operating account or not. It must be paid, and consequently the minister owes, in addition to the $2,740,000 interest for 1920 which he admits-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Of course, I cannot tell, without looking it up, what the advances have been. I could not give any idea what the interest would amount to, because I would need to find out how the advances were made and the length of time, and then figure the interest. I do not know what it would be.

I agree that it is impossible to tell exactly what the interest is; but it is a fair assumption that he owes the 1920 interest, whether it is $2,700,000 or not, I do not know; it a question of degree.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext:
Does that include also the
interest that would be due on progress payments on the ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
That would be another

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know.

Neither do I; but it would
be somewhere around there. Taking the minister's own figures, the interest due for 1920 would be in the neighbourhood of $2,000,000. Although the Canadian Government Merchant Marine paid into the trasury $500,000 for 1919, there is still owing some interest for 1919 and 1918, either by the merchant marine or by the Marine Department.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is drawing
a very fine line.

When the minister says
that he is putting aside some $667,000, and is making a good showing, I think it is quite fair to say that he has not done so well, because he owes about $2,500,000 or $3,000,000 interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That would not
be fair. I am quite willing to leave it fo my experienced friend, the hon. member
for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). This company is operating the ships and we have to put them on a strictly business basis. We could not charge them interest during the progress of construction of the ships, because that would not be fair. I say that the Government of Canada would have to take care of that interest, but it must not come into this statement at all; it has no relevancy to this statement.

I agree with the minister in the statement that until the ships are handed over to the Government Marine, that company should not pay interest; but that does not effect the position of the people of Canada. Somebody certainly lost that interest. If it is not added to the capital cost of the ships, and I presume from what the minister said it is not, then instead of having expended $50,000,000 on capital account, as the statement shows, we will expend more, or else he owes the Finance Department a certain amount of money for interest which has been added to the capital account.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It was not the
policy of the Government-my hon. friend will allow me to make this explanation- when I was a harbour commissioner for the port of Montreal to pay the interest on the capital expenditure of many millions of dollars while the development was going on, or until the work was finished and it was put in a position to pay its own way. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's will quite readily remember that, and without taking up the time of the committee I could name a port in Canada where millions of dollars have been spent and no interest was received during the construction and none has been received since.
But, these works were in a different position.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are national works.

They are to this extent,- that the minister is coming here and telling us that he has made a profit on this business. It may be a good policy in the case of the harbour works in Montreal, where all they get is a certain amount of revenue and which works are not expected to pay just like ships pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They pay their interest.

If they pay their interest so much the better, but this is a different policy altogether. Harbour works are an

entirely different thing from the Government launching into a shipbuilding programme. However, I do not want to get diverted from my speech. I will answer the remarks of the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) by saying that if it is good business for the Government to go into the ship operating business, it would be equally good policy for the Government to build trawlers in these yards and send them out to Prince Rupert, Lunenburg, Halifax and Canso and operate those same trawlers. The Government has just as much right to engage in the fishing industry as they have to engage in the shipping business. The Government may just as well engage in the refining of sugar or engage in the buying of Canadian wheat. Seeing that practicaly half a crop remains in Western Canada unsold, why not go into the wheat buying business in order to help the farmers. Why not buy all the wheat in the western grain elevators and everywhere else, for that would he carrying out the same principle? Why not buy agricultural implements, and I say this with the greatest possible respect for my hon. friend (Mr. Cockshutt).

The hon. member for Lunenburg is a shipping man. He has a knowledge of the Atlantic ring and the position that Canada and Canadian shippers found themselves in with regard to the transAtlantic trade. Will he say it is not good business for the Canadian Government to place themselves in the position of building and owning ships so that they can open up trade routes for the benefit of Canada and Canadian shipping?
Not on regularly established trade routes.

My hon. friend must know that if there is no freight to be carried no ships are required. The ships to which I have alluded have always carried freight if there was any freight to be carried. Now as to the trade with Brazil, I find these figures on page 6 of the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce: Brazil -1914, $267,858; 1918, $974,368. That was before there were any ships belonging to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. In 1919, and this would be for the year ending March 31-and of course before the minister had very many ships-the trade had increased to $4,000,000; but in 1920 when the minister had opened this particular route, as the hon. member for St. John calls it, the exports to Brazil had dropped to $2,703,000. So you see the minister's steamers are not doing very much to open up trade routes to Brazil and, as I said a moment ago, sailing ships from St. John and Halifax have been carrying the products of Canada to Brazil for the last one hundred and fifty years and there was never any complaint. Now the minister's ships are doing the business which these sailing ships were formerly doing. Vessels representing an investment of millions have been tied up because the Government has embarked on this scheme-that is where the whole trouble lies. I could read the shipments from Canada to other countries. I could make a comparison between shipments in 1914 and shipments in 1918 and 1920. There has been an increase on account of the increased cost of the goods. My hon. friend knows the cost of merchandise is perhaps two hundred per cent greater than it was in 1914 and yet the minister says

we are doing more business because these ships are on the ocean. Why there is nothing in the statement when you analyze it and learn exactly what it means. I repeat that these ships are not opening up trade routes, they are going around looking for freight. They are carrying products to New York, they are loading cargoes in Portland, Baltimore, or somewhere else to carry across the ocean, and so on.
Now to get back to the question of the interest account, because I want this thing straightened out, I say that the minister cannot very well claim that because he had $667,000 at rest for the first year and has not paid his interest for 1918, or 1919, or 1920, he has any surplus, or any money, at rest. The very first thing he must do is to pay interest on the charges before he talks of putting money to rest account. In estimating this interest I take the cost of those steamers which were put in operation up to December 31, 1919, at $192 a ton. I think I am safe in saying that that figure applies to the whole sixty-three ships, and that the cost is on the average $192 a ton. In figuring at $192 a ton for the 1919 ships and the 1920 ships the minister is far too conservative. I think he will find that instead of costing $192 they averaged $202 a ton because they represented the heaviest contracts.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I might inform
the hon. member that the lowest price was $167.50, other contracts were let at $180, and the highest price paid was $215 a ton. It has been very carefully figured out that on the entire programme the average will be $191.50.
Mr. DUFP': That is exactly what I am saying, but I am trying to show that the first ships constructed by the minister cost $215 a ton.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: He paid $215 for some.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: For one or two.
And the ships that are being built now are being constructed for a lesser price titan any of the others.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Some are, some are not.
I mean you did not contract for any ships for $167.50 in 1918 or 1919.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The lowest price we paid in 1919 was $180 a ton for the ships built by the Coughlan Shipbuilding
Company of Vancouver, and one by Wallace at $167.50.
Consequently that figure of $167.50 brought down the average.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That might be, b.ut when the 63 ships are finished the cost to the country will be $191.50.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That does not
come under the Department of Marine and Fisheries at all. If my hon. friend will direct that question to the Minister of Finance he will be able to give him the information required. It is money the Government of Canada loaned to that shipbuilding company through the Finance Department.
Do I understand the minister to say that the Finance Department made the contract with these people?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

Now, the Toronto shipyards. I understand the minister to say that the contract he made with these people is on a cost plus basis. What money had the Government already advanced to the shipyard before the new arrangement was made? And what difficulty, if any, arose with the workmen in the yard?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
$409,000 was the amount paid. We have not had any difficulty with the men in the yards at Toronto. More skilled and unskilled workmen have been offering their services than are really needed. When the war was on that yard paid the highest wages of any shipbuilding yard in Canada, 90 cents an hour. When we came to let this contract on a cost plus basis, naturally I knew that the
1 a.m. Collingwood Shipbuilding Company were not interested in

what wages would be paid, because the higher the wages the greater would be the amount of cost plus they would get from the Government; therefore, the maximum scale of wages was fixed at 75 cents which was the current wage in Toronto at the time.
I understood there was a strike and that the men would not accept the wages the Government offered.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: A few men of the Trades and Labour Council may have struck, but the yard had more men than they really needed.

I understand that the number of men who were previously employed in the yard had some disagreement with the Government about wages, and therefore struck for better treatment. Will the minister explain what happened?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: A few of the old men who were employed by the Toronto Shipbuilding Company at ninety cents an hour for an eight-hour day were not satisfied to take a drop to seventy-five cents an hour, and they left.
Is the minister aware of the fact that the men now employed by the company in the place of those skilled men are not capable shipwrights?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I know that assertion has been made, but the Collingwood Shipbuilding Company have demonstrated fully to the Government that they have one of the best equipped yards in the Dominion and that their workmen are thoroughly skilled. Besides that, the Marine Department have got their own man there, and I can assure the hon. member that the work is being done just as efficiently as in any yard in Canada.
How much money was paid to the Vancouver shipbuilding companies, and how much are the vessels under construction likely to cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We were able to make a much more advantageous arrangement at Prince Rupert than we were at Toronto, and the Wallace Shipbuilding Company are completing those ships for eight per cent over labour and any material they have to buy. I do not know exactly what the ships are going to cost, but I should say it will be a little bit less than the original contract, because that was one of the highest contracts for that type of ship that the
fMr. Ballantyne.]
Government let; it was during' the war and the price was $198 a ton.
Has the minister any information in regard to the work done on the Canadian Inventor?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: None.
Has he received any complaint about the shaft being short after the ship was launched and taken over by the Government? And had the Government to spend a large amount of money to put in a new shaft?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have not any
knowledge.
Of course, I can understand that it is impossible for the minister to give the information which the committee should have before they pass this item. It seems to me there should be somebody here-*

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is my hon. friend referring to something he heard when out at Vancouver?	-
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know whether this ship that my hon. friend has in mind was built by the Coughlan Shipbuilding Company or not. My deputy tells me that the Canadian Inventor was built by the Coughlan Shipbuilding Company. There was something wrong with the tail shaft and the Government inspector made them take it out and put it back without any extra cost to the Government.
I have another complaint with regard to the Canadian Inventor. Perhaps there is nothing in it.
There is nothing in any of them.

The hon. gentleman does
not know anything about the subject.
It is just like your speech.
I should like the hon. member for Muskoka to be courteous.
It is just like your speech; there is nothing in it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: (Mr. A. Thompson) : Order.

I was going to ask a question; now I will read the whole article. It has to do with the treatment accorded to the crew of the Canadian Inventor. It
says:

This reads as follows:
"S.S. Canadian Inventor, at sea.
"We read with pride of the work proposed-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member, but I may say that I have seen that article.
But the hon. member for Muskoka has not heard it.
I am quite willing to give to it the value that usually attaches to my hon. friend's remarks.

Did the hon. member put a question? If he did I would like him to repeat it. The item continues:
"S.S. Canadian Inventor,
At Sea.
"We read with pride of the work proposed and already accomplished by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine Service in opening up various trades between the United Kingdom, Australia, India and the Orient. Prouder still were we when we read that the ships of the service were built in Canada and manned by Canadians; in fact, our pride soared so high that we overlooked many of the essentials which go to perfect the whole system.
What is the hon. gentleman reading from,-Robinson Crusoe?
Read it over again.

I will do so for the benefit of the senior member for St. John (Mr. Elkin) who evidently did not hear my reading of the article so far. It is from the Vancouver World and is dated March 8, It reads as follows:
Seamen on Canadian Ship in Complaint
Crew of C.G.M.M. Inventor Say Treatment Shameful-Were Rationed
Vancouver, March 8.-The Vancouver World says:
Complaning that the treatment accorded them after their ship had put to sea was far from that represented in the ship's articles and appealing to the public for an investigation to "give them a square deal," ten members of the crew of the C.G.M.M. freighters Canadian Inventor, which reached Calcutta on Monday, have addressed a communication to the World. This reads as follows :
"S.S. Canadian Inventor At Sea.
"We read with pride of the work proposed and already accomplished by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine Service in opening up various trades between the United Kingdom,
Australia, India and the Orient. Prouder still were we when we read that the ships of the service were built in Canada and manned by Canadians; in fact, our pride soared so high that we overlooked many of the essentials which go to perfect the whole system.
"One, if not the most essential, is the crews of these ships which have started out to do so much. This is the fact we wish to draw to the public notice, the inhuman treatment handed out to us, the indispensable pieces of machinery which go to make up the perfect machine. We say indispensable, and so we'are, although the government does not classify us as such.
"All returned men and experienced seamen welcomed the service as a means of employment and ready to take advantage of the opening offered rather than throw themselves on the already overburdened list of unemployed.
Louder, louder.
Mr. Chairman, I wish you would try to keep order.
I rise to a point of order. The hon. member is reading his speech.

The hon. member is reading a quotation from a newspaper, the name of which he has given. He is, therefore, perfectly in order.
"At the time of signing deep sea articles, which were read out to us before we gave our signatures, the conditions seemed up to the standard of other services, and while alongside the government wharf, during the time we were loading, conditions seemed as represented. But as soon as we got to sea conditions changed and from then on have gone from bad to worse, until things have come to such a state that one would hardly imagine that we were human beings at all.
"On mustering before the commanding officer of the ship to request sufficient food to feed healthy men, the chief stewart was called and we were informed by him that we were on rations, nothing of which was ever read out of the articles. Even these meager rations ran out two weeks before we reached our first port of call, and we have had emergency rations ever since. We all put up with 'bully beef' and hard tack, some of us for over three years whilst overseas, realizing the necessity of it, but there is no reason for such conditions to exist today.
"The three meals put together each day would not make one square meal for a healthy man. Then, added to the lack of food, was the condition of the weather-not one real fine day ever since we left port. For days snow, ice, rain, sleet and heavy seas washing fore and aft, breaking up the deck cargo, which had to be re-lashed every time, drenching us to the skin day after day ; not so much as a hot dnink when we came below.
"Another thing, in watches, we are on duty day and night, and in all weathers there is a period of fifteen hours without a meal. Take, for instance, the 4 to 8 watch, considered the best, going on watch at 4 p.m., relieved for supper for half an hour at 5 p.m. ; then relieved again by the next watch at 8 p.m.; turn into a nic( bed consisting of a straw pillow and mattresses and one pair of blankets ; called at 3.30 a.m. to

This is an editorial from the Montreal Gazette of Saturday, April 9, headed "The Merchant Marine:"
The debatable point in connection with Canada's merchant marine is that of policy. When the construction of ships was undertaken by the Government in the spring- of 1918 there was no dissent in Parliament, the action being generally approved as a war measure. At that time the sea tonnage of the world was being decimated by German submarines, resulting in a serious shortage of ships, and it was as necessary to the successful prosecution of the war to provide means of transportation overseas as to raise reinforcements for the army. Cost of construction was a secondary consideration. The cry was for ships and more ships ; and to avert the disaster threatened by the enemy submarines the United States engaged in an extensive shipbuilding programme and Canada in as large a one as her resources permitted. There can, therefore, be no profitable discussion as to the wisdom of the policy in the circumstances of its inception, and controversy should be confined to the sole question of the prudence of retaining the ships and operating them through a Government agency at the charge of the Canadian people.
Upon this point there is a division of opinion. Many persons, unconnected with the shipping business, are convinced that a Government service cannot profitably compete with private companies on the sea more than on the land; while there are others who from national priide, or a less worthy motive, are captivated by the idea of Canadian ships flying the Canadian flag, ploughing the seven seas, and carrying Canadian commerce to the four corners of the earth. There is a patriotic sentiment aroused by the picture which the Minister of Marine has not neglected to evoke. But business is business; and it is very dubious whether the taxpayers will long applaud an appeal to patriotic pride that involves dipping their hands deep into their pockets for no practical purpose. The Canadian mercantile marine could probably have been sold, both the completed and uncompleted vessels, a year and a half or two years ago at cost price; to-day they would scarcely realize 40 per cent of cost, and it is very far from certain that a reaction upward to price will occur before the ships have run their course and1 been scrapped. The Government, however, resolved to engage in the shipping trade for reasons which had no relation whatever to the purpose of the original policy, and were wholly an afterthought. Those reasons, as stated by Mon. Mr. Ballantyne, were the desirability of linking a steamship service with the national railway, and the means supplied by the ships of opening up new trade routes and expanding Canada's foreign commerce. The Canadian Pacific had an ocean fleet as an adjunct to its land, and why not the Government? And so, superimposed upop the National railway deficit, we have the deficit of the Canadian Mercantile Marine to be met out of the taxes upon the people.
It is pertinent to point out the fundamental difference between rail and water transportation. In the case of the former the road bed is restricted, while in the case of the latter it is as wide as the ocean. There can be no monopoly of business in respect of ships. Vessels of any and all countries can ply their trade in the ports of the world; there is no such thing as right of way, but free and open competition, and ever the ship comes to seek the cargo. If the National Railway requires ships to carry its over-seas traffic, the ships can be had for the asking without the expenditure of a single dollar on capital account. If the ocean-borne traffic is unprofitable the ship owners bear the loss, and the Canadian taxpayer escapes. The fact that Governments cannot successfully compete on even terms with private enterprise remains as a cardinal objection to the maintenance of the Canadian mercantile marine, and if it is contended that the National Railway requires to be supplemented with a steamship service, the rejoinder is that this service can be secured without price to the people and with equal advantage to the railway by arrangement with privately owned steamship companies.
The Canadian marine venture has already involved the loss of many millions of capital in consequence of the drop in the value of ships, and involved the loss "of at least $2,000,000 on operating account in 1920, under the most favourable statement of accounts. It is most desirable that Canada's foreign trade should be enlarged, that new markets should be sought, that ships carrying Canadian products should reach countries not hitherto tapped, but $2,000.000 in the way of subsidies to steamship lines, over and above earnings, will go a long way towards this end, while at the same time removing the risks of heavy loss to the taxpayers now incurred. The Minister of Marine is firmly convinced of the prudence and advantage of the mercantile marine, and he is an experienced business man. But 'the Minister of Railways is also convinced that the National Railway is a fine proposition. It may be so; but unfortunately for the Canadian people these

convictions 'have loaded uipon them an enormous debt and an enormous deficit; have strained the credit of Canada ; have necessitated very-heavy taxation; and hold out no hope of amelioration for many years while the fatuous policy of Government ownership is persisted in.

(Translation). Mr. Chairman, I willingly abide by your decision. While a programme of ship-building during the war was commendable, subsequent developments dictate a modified policy. In June, 1914, the world tonnage totalled 49,000,000 tons; in June, 1920, it has risen to 57,300,000 tons, and, in addition, at the end of September this year there were 7,565,000 tons under construction. Tonnage at present exceeds requirements, and in expectation of rate reduction and shrinkage in earnings, construction abroad has already been arrested, and empty tonnage is now laid up in many ports. There is no ground for the belief that this condition will quickly pass. The United States recently failed to secure bids for standard ships ; Japan has cancelled orders for 100,000,000 tons in his own shipyards, and Norway is cancelling orders in Great Britain.

These factors constitute, in my opinion, a danger signal that Canada might well heed and stop all further new construction.
Mr. Chairman, such was in the month of December last, the opinion of the president of the Bank of Montreal who, as I said a moment ago, reflects the sentiments of the financiers of the metropolis, and of Quebec and the whole country as well.
We have read-I have for my part-the reports of several other banks issued since then and in no other report from a bank or a financial institution supposed .to be reputable or of any importance have I found a single word of commendation or approval concerning the new policy of the Government Merchant Marine. On the contrary, the president and the directors of the Bank of Montreal, who are the friends of the Minister of Marine, are giving him in the words to which I have just called the attention of this House the most solemn warning that could be given to a public man and to a good friend, by saying:	"Sir, stop; you have done enough;
that might have been all very well during the war; we could have needed it in the beginning, but there is a time when we must stop; otherwise, whatever good we might have expected from that policy will be set to naught by the deficits which will pile up in the future." Such is the substance of opinion uttered by the president of the Bank of Montreal and the directors of that financial institution.
What is happening to-day in this House? In contradiction to that warning, we see the hon. minister asking for eight million and a few odd hundred thousand dollars to go on with the programme initiated two or three years ago, when some necessity may have then existed. Now that necessity has vanished; nevertheless, the minister comes and tells us:	"Vote that sum of money; I
need it and I need it at once."
The hon. minister told us a moment ago: "We shall pass this item and we will be at it the night through."
Mr. Chairman, for my part, if we were to remain here the whole night, I am willing to do so, but I don't intend to let the item pass before I have the opportunity of entering my protest on behalf of the constituents I am representing in this House, and of the party to which I have the honour to belong.

pects are not very good now." I am amazed when I see the hon. minister and his friends offering reasons which do not hold, and are quite conflicting. Minister of Marine has stated to-day, with a view to show the soundness of the Government that this policy, is there any mention of how many returned soldiers have been put to work in the shipyards? speechtext: Mr. Rinfret.

I have so much to say about the question under consideration that I am perfectly willing to bow to your ruling. I would express the wish that the Chair would pay a little attention to what

I say; I think that would be very proper even at this late hour.
Now, the Minister of Marine has said that this policy has been endorsed by the people. I was endeavouring to show that the Government had given the people no chance whatever to endorse this policy, when I was called to order. I do not regret the incident, because this discussion has brought to this side of the House a member who usually sits on the other side, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) -and he seems to enjoy it. While it is two o'clock in Ottawa it is only around ten o'clock in Prince Rupert and probably that is why- the hon. gentleman is so cheerful.
Coming hack to this item, I share the view of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) that this was not altogether a war measure. The minister made that very plain to-night when he said that while he laid down his policy as to building steel ships as if the war was going to last forever, he was more cautious when it came to wooden ships. In another part of his speech he said that at the conclusion of the war we would not have known what to do with the wooden ships and he boasted that he had been clever enough to prevent this country from spending any money on this class of ships. I would say that if he had been a little more cautious, possibly he would also have refrained from engaging this country in such an extensive steel shipbuilding programme. It will be seen that although my hon. friend was at that time under the impression that the war might last quite long and that it was imperative that shipbuilding must go on, he was exercising some discretion as to the quality and character of the ships. I repeat that had he been as cautious with regard to steel as he was with regard to wood, we would be better off to-day.
I may add that I do not share the minister's optimism as to the outcome of this venture. Possibly it is because we on this side have been unsuccessful in obtaining information, although we have made a great effort to obtain it. The minister himself has said to-night that he does not know much about this venture, and that he does not care to know anything about it. He said he was not going to inquire from the management where they bought their coal, butter, milk and so on. I do not feel that way at all, Mr. Chairman. I think we should know from the management not only where they get their coal, but where they get the deficit which we have to face to-day.
120i
My hon. friend admits that other countries have a surplus of ships, and he says that is an excuse for our being in the same position. But the trouble is that other countries have been engaged in shipbuilding for some time while this country seems to have chosen as the time to build the very time when it was imperative not to do so. That is an altogether different situation. As to the surplus which my hon. friend claims, I think he should give his secret to the hon. Minister of Railways. But if we get back to good book-keeping I do not think the hon. minsiter can claim any surplus. It has been shown that the best claim he can make is a return of some two per cent on the capital investment. We know that the Government borrowed money from the Canadian people at the rate of five and one-half per cent and that the securities for these loans are exempt from taxation to the extent of one billion three hundred and some millions. The Government, therefore, in investing a portion of that money in their shipbuilding programme and obtaining a return of some two per cent-which is much disputed, but that is their own figure-are not only using money on which they are paying five and one-half per cent interest, but are using the amount of the income tax return as well. So that the claiming of a surplus under these circumstances indicates a very great degree of optimism. I am inclined to repeat something I heard my good friend from Waterloo say the other day in Montreal: that if the minister can claim a surplus in the face of all the facts relating to his shipbuilding programme, he is entitled to open a sunshine factory with cucumbers as his raw material.
The member for Brantford (Mr. Coek-shutt) has endeavoured to give us some opinions of the press which, he says, show that the people are very appreciative indeed of this policy of the Government. When he started out he gave us the impression that he was going to quote Liberal newspapers which were emphatically in support of this policy, but he confined himself to a few Tory newspapers which were trying very hard indeed to find the least bit of common-sense in it. He started out with the Sydney Post, which could not say anything better in support of my hon. friend's policy than that it was less disastrous than the railway policy. It did not say the policy was a good one, but expressed the view that it was not as bad as another policy which was worse. Then he quoted the Winnipeg Tribune, which simply said that the policy was not

too bad when compared with that of other countries. Again the policy itself was not endorsed; the view was expressed that the condition here was no worse than somewhere else. He then went to the Vancouver Province, another Tory paper, which said not that the policy was right, but that it had a redeeming feature; it gave employment to returned soldiers. So with the Hamilton Spectator, which never dreamed of being a Liberal journal, and so with the Mail and Empire, which has just absorbed another Toronto paper and is also a good, strong Tory journal. So that the Liberal press opinions put forward by the hon. member for Brantford amount to the views of a few Tory papers, not endorsing the policy, but stating in one case that it is not as bad as something else, and in another that it is less disastrous than the railway policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. member knows that La Presse is the largest newspaper in Canada, having a circulation like 140,000 copies a day. Would he mind quoting what La Presse has to say editorially on this subject?

I have read recently the editorial columns of La Presse, and its expressions of opinion with regard to the railway and shipping problems indicate to me that it is perplexed as to what attitude to take.
Now, I wish to quote the words of the president of the Royal bank, Sir Herbert Holt, with regard to this matter. He says:
Government control has practically disappeared during- the year just past-wheat, paper and sugar being the commodities to be treed from regulation. Government ownership of transportation systems has developed. Without any advantage to the public in efficiency or rates, the operation of our national railways during the last twelve months has resulted in a loss which will probably more than absorb the amounts collected on Excess Profits and Income Taxes for the year 1919. Unless Government methods of operation are more efficient in this country than they have been in others tax payers in Canada may find the maintenance of their railroads and fleet more expensive than pension charges and other legacies of the war combined.
Order.

If the hon. gentleman
wishes to rise to a point of order. I will listen to him with great pleasure. I see there is nothing of the kind.
Mention has been made of the Montreal Gazette during this debate; but for some reason or another, perhaps because the House was not in a listening mood, no

quotation from the Montreal Gazette has been placed on Hansard, so far as I know. I have in my hand an editorial which is not very long and which is interesting, and I will crave the indulgence of the House and that of the minister in particular while I read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am in no hurry, and I may say that we on this side of the House are in no hurry at all, so that the hon. member can take just as long as he likes.

I am very glad to hear that. I think we cannot be accused of delaying the debate. What we would like to do would be to delay the shipbuilding, but it is unfortunately too late to do that. This article is headed:	"The Canadian
Marine," and it is from the Montreal Gazette of December 9, 1920:
The building and operating of ships is precarious business for governments to engage in,
more so than the construction and management of railways, because in the case of the latter there can at least be some permanence of rates. The war gave immense impetus to the shipbuilding industry, both from the urgent demand for ships to transport men and supplies and by reason of the large losses caused by submarines. Cost of construction doubled and trebled, and more than one government felt it necessary to supplement private yards with public plants. Now, the inevitable has happened.
As we predicted.
There is a glut of ships. The tonnage of the world at nearly 60,000,000 tons is much the largest of record, and this at a time when the foreign commerce of many countries has been checked by depreciation of currency and the contraction of credit. Freight rates are falling. So expeditiously and easily can ships be sent over every sea to every port that water transportation costs conform quickly to the law of supply and demand, and there seems bound to be considerable loss in the future in the in-rentory value and operating results of vessels built at the peak of prices.
Canada had developed a considerable shipbuilding industry, the principal customer of which h-a,s been the Government The Government will in a few months possess a mercantile navy of 63 vessels, quite a formidable fleet, constructed in Canada, and having an aggregate tonnage of 386,140 tons.
I would commend this to the attention of the minister, but I am sorry that he is not in his place.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He is here.

I apologize to my good friend; I never like to speak when he is out of my sight; but I will read a little louder so that the sound of my voice will reach where he sits now:

The policy of procuring ships was a war policy, and it is very doubtful whether in other circumstances it would have been entered upon; so that while there was ready and adequate justification for the creation of a fleet, it is by no means certain that it should be continued as a Government activity, much less enlarged in number. Last year the nineteen Canadian Government vessels then afloat made an operating profit of $1,056,767 from completed voyages, and a further profit of $350,000 was estimated from open voyages, making a total profit of $1,406,000 on operating account.
Hear, hear.

Here again I may interject that these are the figures given by the Government, and for many reasons and particularly for the reason that we are not given any information, I personally take no responsibility whatever for what I am reading. I continue quoting from the Gazette, and I hope my hon. friends have not missed a word, because I am quite ready to start over again if anything has failed to reach their understanding. The Gazette says:
Interest on capital and depreciation must, however, be provided for, and the failure so to do is a notable omission in the annual report of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited.
I am waiting for the applause of bon. gentlemen opposite.
There is nothing of much note yet.

The money invested in the ships costs Canada 5J per cent, and depreciation in the case of ships is a serious item, so that when all the charges are taken into account the fleet will be found to have entailed loss.
Just what we are claiming to-night.
The retention of the fleet in Government control is a purely business problem The ships are linked up closely with the National Railway System, and the report of the directors contains the statement that the fleet of the Merchant marine forms a most important ally to the National System of railways, and enables the railway to obtain large through shipments of freight to Atlantic and Pacific ports which would be lost to the National System if it were not for the steamship connections of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine Limited.
The last paragraph is a quotation from the Government report made by the Gazette. The Gazette goes on:
We are somewhat sceptical of this statement for the reason ships may be chartered without the expense of capital investment, and that chartered ships can be operated quite as economically as Government-owned vessels. The directors, cognizant of the change in conditions, warn the public that the Government marine is not to be regarded as a money-making proposition, in these words:-
"Having regard to the fact that all of your company's vessels have been built since the war began, the cost of construction has been much higher than prevailed before hostilities, so that the interest, depreciation and insurance expenses on your vessels are much higher than obtains on those of your competitors whose fleets, even after taking into consideration their new tonnage would not nearly equal per ton dead weight the cost of the fleet of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine Limited. Your vessels will also be competing on some trades against vessels carrying foreign crews. It will be seen, therefore, that while a satisfactory business is being done

The Government is speaking, of course.

and much new trade developed, large profits should not be looked for."
Then the Gazette continues:
The considerations counselling a cessation of new building are that the ships are unprofitable, and that they serve no purpose not equally to be secured by charter of by alliance with private steamship companies. The United States Government, very prudently we think, has terminated its war policy of public ownership and operation, and is disposing of its fleet, and in matters of business the Americans are shrewd. There is, indeed, something inspiring in the existence of a fleet of Government ships sailing the seven seas, and extending the commerce of Canada to the four corners of the earth, always provided the sentiment does not involve heavy cost and heavy taxation, for it should be remembered that the loss on the fleet falls on the pockets of the Canadian people.
I could quote from other pa*pers, but I think this puts the case very clearly. I regret that the Government has adopted with regard to the national railways and the merchant marine the policy of not giving information to the House. The reason given by the Government for this policy is that it would not be good business to disclose to the competitors of the Government system its administrative methods, but is it not extraordinary to hear that given as a reason, Mr. Chairman, when we remember that the competitor to the state-owned railways and the Government merchant marine is the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, whose brilliant and effective methods of administration have brought that company to such a brilliant success? However, as the Government persists in not giving information to the House, either on the railways or the merchant marine, I think that we on this side of the House are perfectly justified in trying to get the information and discussing the items before the committee to the extreme limit. As far as I am concerned, I wish to place myself on record as being absolutely opposed to the Government's policy. I think the Government should be censured for ever having embarked upon this shipbuilding pro-

gramme, and not only should it be stopped immediately as regards the building of new ships, but the Government should dispose of its present fleet at the earliest opportunity.
How much does the minister expect to have to spend to complete the contracts in Toronto that are let on this cost plus 15 per cent basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not expect it will cost more than $180 per ton, because labour costs are down, but I do not want to make any positive statement.
What will be the total still to be expended?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The original contract price was $630,000 per ship, and there has been paid $409,500. I could only give an estimate of the balance. It would cost, I should suppose, about $230,000 to $250,000 to finish each ship.
When the ships are completed, does the minister think he could get as much for them in the market as he will have to spend to complete them?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is not the Government's policy to dispose of its ships.

The people of this country are more interested in where this money is going than in the Government's policy. Would it not be good business for the minister to cancel these orders? What is the purpose of expending this money on a cost plus 15 per cent basis when the minister apparently has no control over the company in the matter of expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: One of the principle reasons why the Government went on with the building of these ships-there are many reasons but I shall not detain the committee to give them-was that there was a large number of men out of work in the city of Toronto, and although the Government knew they could not get the same efficiency out of men in the depth of winter, with these boats all exposed, we went on with the work to give bread and butter to our returned men, who were clamouring for employment.
Were the men who were getting the 15 per cent plus, which would amount to something over $60,000 particularly hungry?

I am not speaking of him, because like my hon. friend from Pontiac, he possesses plenty. I was speak-

Under those circumstances would it not have been better to distribute the money to these unemployed rather than give it to the contractors on a cost plus basis? Who is this firm that is getting this $60,000 for overseeing the work?

Shipbuilding Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: As I said in the earlier part of the night, we have only two ship companies in Canada that failed, one at Prince Rupert, and the other at Toronto. The company at Prince Rupert received 8 per cent and the other company 15 per cent.	.
Why do you pay one contractor 15 per cent and another 8 per cent? It seems to me that 8 per cent is high enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I differ from my hon. friend there. I may say that the Wallace Shipbuilding Company, after they agreed to finish the ships at 8 per cent, sent a man here for the purpose of getting out of the arrangement, because they thought there was an immense amount of material yet to be purchased, and they were figuring a large sum to be spent on material as well as labour. Had they known that such a small amount of material was to be purchased they would not have quoted 8 per cent. Fifteen per cent was the best price we could get in eastern Canada.

If I understand the situation, the contractor gets 8 per cent on everything he buys, on every cent of wages he pays out, and on every bit of material he provides. All he does is to oversee the work. Now, on one contract in Toronto where the minister says there is $221,000 yet to be spent, the contractor would get $30,000 for overseeing the building of that

ship. It seems to me that my hon. friend is mistaken when he says that that is not a goodly sum Jto pay out. If the answers he gave me with regard to the Prince Rupert contract are correct, the amounts due on these two contracts total something like a million or a million and a quarter, and 8 per cent on that, it seems to me, is quite a respectable sum. The minister thinks that 8 per cent is rather small. When one looks over the Auditor General's report for the last four or five years and sees the exorbitant prices which the Government has paid to certain shipyards in the country to build destroyers and other boats, it will be obvious why the minister says that this is not a large percentage; but in my opinion, and in the opinion of people who know something about these contracts, 8 per cent over and above the cost of everything that goes into the building of ships, as well as labour, is a fairly good commission for shipbuilders to get.

I have listened all night and into the morning with great patience to the discussion of these Estimates. I have listened on many occasions to the member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) and the member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) discussing, from a theoretical point of view, the issues that are before the House to-night.
This morning.
This morning, rather; and even at 2.45 a.m. I am persuaded that it is still possible for me to tell those hon. members a few things.
What are they?

Be patient and you will hear them. It is quite apparent to everyone on both sides of the House that hon. members opposite have been greatly disappointed by the showing that has been made by the minister. Throughout the length and breadth of the country, newspapers favourable to the Opposition have led the people to believe that they were to expect another financial spectacle such as we had in connection with the Government railways, and ever since the Minister of Marine submitted his report to the House, we have seen the bitter disappointment on the faces of members of the Opposition. They have come here expecting something that they could turn to advantage, and being disappointed, they are trying to bolster up a weak case. The hon. member for Lunenburg and the member for Pontiac- I want them to mark this-refuse to accept
the minister's word when he says that after the armistice this work was carried on, to a great extent, to give employment to returned soldiers. I quite understand that the member for Lunenburg and the member for Pontiac had no sympathy with that undertaking.

That is what I said.
Order.
Take it back.
I do not think that the expression is out of order. The hon. member for Muskoka does not, I suppose, intend to cast any reflection on any hon. members.
Order.

I do not wish to dispute your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but the statement was quite plain, and perhaps you did not catch it. What was said was undoubtedly a reflection on the members to whom it had reference.
I would ask the hon. member for Muskoka to withdraw any remark that casts a reflection on hon. members.

Go to it; come on.
We challenge you to do it.
On another occasion.
Do it now; come on.
You dare not do it.
It takes better stuff than the hon. member for Lunenburg to tell me that I dare not do it.
I must ask the hon. member for Muskoka and other hon. members to keep their temper. I trust no reflections will be cast on any hon. member; I do not do it myself.
I have not the least intention of reflecting on anyone, but if the hon. member's record in the House constitutes a reflection on himself it is no fault of mine.

Order, order.
Mr. Chairman, I must object to this interruption. If hon. members have any questions to ask me, let them do so.

I am speaking to the point of order. In doing so, I am speaking in French, as is my right. If the hon. gentleman cannot understand me, while it is no reflection on him, it is his fault, and he cannot deprive me of the privilege of addressing the House in the language I am using.

(Translation.) My argument, Mr. Chairman, is as follows: An hon. member claims that other members of the House have no sympathy for the soldiers, the president of the committee cannot rule that this is not derogatory to their honour.
I believe, on the contrary, that the president, must take the view that when a member accuses another of not having had any sympathy for our soldiers, he has made a serious charge, which he should retract.

After
the decision of the Chair has been given it cannot be criticized. Therefore I would ask the hon. member for Muskoka to proceed with his speech, but he must be good enough to refrain from indulging in any personal reflections and thus render less difficult the duty of the Chair.

It is a great pleasure Mr. Chairman, for me to submit to your ruling. I have been a member of this House four years and I have never intentionally transgressed any of its rules. I have always, to the best of my ability, extended courtesy to every hon. member but, Mr. ["The Chairman.]
Chairman, there are limits beyond which courtesy cannot be extended. There are times when patience ceases to be a virtue; and at three o'clock in the morning we have had rehashing of old articles and a recourse to old tactics which amounts to nothing more or less than obstruction. The time has come when we should have a show-down, and if any hon. members want their record to be placed on Hansard I am quite prepared to take up the challenge and see that that is done no matter who may be hurt.
All right go ahead and put it on record.

Having said that, I
want to congratulate the Minister of Marine on the broad-minded policy that he conceived and laid before the people of this country. I want to congratulate him on the success which has characterized that policy up to the present hour, and I have not the least doubt that for that policy the future holds prospects equally as bright. Some hon. gentlemen opposite have a very short memory. I ask the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) what would have happened had the war gone on for another eight or ten months? We know that the enemy would have won the war, because the destruction of merchant vessels was so far outrunning the building of tonnage that we would not have kept pace with it. Does any hon. member here to-night deny that? If he does he had better go and consult the records. I tell hon. gentlemen that had the destruction continued for another eight months at the rate it was progressing, the British Empire, and its Allies, would have lost the war on that very ground alone. Are we to condemn the Government of Canada for taking the necessary precautions to try and supply the deficiency in ships caused by the destruction of tonnage that was going on and in order to help us to win the war? Without ships we could not have moved a man and could not have moved a pound of freight. If hon. members opposite do not know that, they had better delve a little into the history of the last five years and ascertain the facts for themselves. If we had lost the war what would have happened? Would hon. members have been here to-night quibbling over the expenditure of a few millions of money spent in pursuing a policy that was imperatively necessary. It is a travesty on parliamentary procedure that we should be kept here until three o'clock in the morning dehat-

ing about the expenditure of a few mil- and when you push your commerce into the lions of dollars upon the construction of seven seas of the world you will not spend a merchant marine that was intended to time until three o'clock in the morning
play an important part in helping to win the war. It is a travesty on our intelli-, gence and our patriotism. Let hon. gentlemen search history a little if they will and what will they find? How has England kept up her balance of trade for the last thirty, forty or fifty years? By pushing her merchant marine and her commerce into unknown lands. Let my hon, friends take up the exports of Great Britain to the United States, to Germany or to any of the other countries that are under protection and what will they find? That during the years I have mentioned those exports were diminishing and her balance of trade was only kept up by opening up fresh avenues of trade with South America and other unprotected countries. What would she have done if she had not had a merchant marine available for that purpose? Are we so short-sighted that we cannot see beyond the present hour? Is it to be thought that our merchant marine has no more prospective value to Canada, and that it ought to be scrapped? Do people think that the trade to be derived in future by pushing into foreign markets is of no value to Canada? I advise hon. gentlemen opposite who indulge in such criticism to study the trade 'statistics, and ascertain what has already been done in that line and what the prospects are for the, future. Let them enlarge their vision and let them conceive of Canada as a nation. Let them conceive of the Canadian people as a nation equal to any on the face of God's earth. How are we going to achieve that trade expension which we all hope to see if we have not the means of carrying our products to the seven seas of the world? Mr. Chairman, I have listened for days-not only during the present session but in former years-to the utterances of the member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) and the member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) and I have gone out of the House wondering whether we are children or whether we are men. I say to hon. members-and I do not very often take up the time of the House-for God's sake broaden your vision, get a true conception of the nation and its status, lift your eyes above the horizon of Canada-yes, above the horizon of the British Empire-and . look at these questions from a broad national standpoint and see if Canadians cannot take their place as one of the great nations in the world. When you do that,
worrying about whether we have a return of two and a half or three per cent interest on your money. For Heaven's sake, is there nothing bigger or brighter in a nation's outlook, or in a nation's ideal, to discuss than to be quibbling over a few dollars? Was it dollars that made the British Empire? Was it dollars that saved the world in the great struggle from which we emerged in 1918, or was it patriotism? Was it the ideals that men cherished or was it mere quibbling over petty issues? What are you going to pin your faith to if you lack ideals, or lack belief in the nation's future? To me it is inconceivable that we should be kept here until this late hour of the morning squabbling over the petty issue as to whether we have got two and a half per cent or five per cent return on our money, when the great issue is before us of what we are going to do to build up our country. What are we standing here for to-night-for a nation within the British Empire, or for that small parochial colonialism that we hear so much about from the hon. member for Lunenburg that is bound up, I was going to say within the four walls of a ship.
Do you stand for the Canadian Government Merchant Marine?

Sure I do. I stand for anything that is going to make Canada a nation. You cannot make Canada a nation without a merchant marine. You may lose a few million dollars, but is it not worth something to carry the commerce of Canada to the four corners of the earth? Are you going to measure that in dollars and cents? I say, Mr. Chairman, for God's sake-
Order.
-let us forget this parochialism, let us get down to business, let us conceive of Canada as a nation, and let us deal with our national affairs accordingly.
Shall the item carry?

order, but if we ever wanted any evidence to prove the necessity of the motion made by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's this afternoon for an adjournment of the House at a reasonable hour, we have it before us to-night. Such business is usually treated by hon. gentlemen in a serious and considerate manner, but although this is one of the largest individual items very little, if any, consideration is being given to it by my hon. friends opposite. vessels until he is able to show that interest and all fixed charges have been paid. My hon. friend gives reasons why he embarked on this shipbuilding industry, the main reason being to provide work for returned soldiers. That was a most worthy motive. But if that was so, I would like to know what the minister thinks of the recent dismissal of seven or eight hundred men from the Canadian National Railway shops at Moncton, the majority of whom are returned soldiers. Surely the same broad sympathy should be extended to those men and others elsewhere, although there has been a deficit in the operation of the Canadian Government rail-3 a.m. ways. In referring to the shipbuilding industry, a moment ago my hon. friend said that we on this side of the House hoped that we will have another "financial spectacle" as we had in respect to the government railways. It is a "financial spectacle," Mr. Chairman, and it behooves all hon. gentlemen, I care not on which side of your Chair they sit, to try and work out the best arrangement possible to meet present conditions. That cannot be done while we are indulging in threats and challenges such as have been thrown across the floor of the House tonight. I can readily understand that my hon. friend can argue that it would be unreasonable to sell these vessels at the present time and go out of the shipping business, but so far as I am concerned-and I do not profess to be an expert in these matters -1 can foresee that we are going to have in this shipbuilding industry, if we can dignify it by that name, another failure next year, and that that failure will be repeated year after year, piling deficit upon deficit, just the same as is happening now in the operation of our Canadian National railways.
We had that before us when my hon. friend embarked on this-I was going to say tragedy; when he embarked on this undertaking. We had the example of the Canadian Government Railways with a deficit year after year, yet my hon. friend saw fit to hand out this dole of fifteen per cent over and above cost to the ship-building concerns in Montreal and elsewhere-and he comes back here and tells us he did it because he hoped to give employment to returned soldiers. If that is so, did he assume any responsibility as to the wages these men should receive? I would like to see the country relieved from the terrible burden which has been imposed upon

it, and I suggest that if my hon. friend consulted and accepted the advice of reliable business men, he would be doing the country a service. He knows such men, many of them, in the city of Montreal; he knows their business capacity and qualifications, and their counsel might be of value. We launched out into this undertaking without proper thought, without proper study, without proper consideration. We have lost money, but to many people to-day a few millions is as nothing; we have come to think in large amounts. I say that we should get back to normal. We should cease thinking in terms of hundreds of millions and get back to a little horse-sense, if I may use the term. Let us not go on drifting until it is too late. I say to my hon. friends opposite that I am serious in this matter; I do not desire to talk politics.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen do not seem to understand the conscientious expression of opinion without reference to politics. That attitude on their part is easily explained, because with the exception of the minister himself not one gentleman opposite has paid the slightest attention to the item that has been before the committee for consideration since yesterday afternoon. My hon. friends opposite should realize that they have as much responsibility as any other hon. member of this House in the matter of seeing that the Minister of Marine is granted only sufficient money properly to carry on the business of the country with due regard to the country's interests and not with a view to continuing the extravagance which has been going on during the past two years.

I find at page 31, on
the last line of the annual report of the Department of Railways and Canals of Canada, for the fiscal year dating April 1 to March 31, 1920, the following words:
"Controlled Companies"
"Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited".
(Translation) :	I would like the hon.

(Translation.) I would now like to know who are the shareholders of the company and who is its president?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Government,
I think.

(Translation.) Who

speechtext: The King.
(Translation.) Where is the head office of the company?

(Translation.)
