I am happy to learn that His Majesty the King is president of the company and that the public are the shareholders. I see that not only do we own the shares, but that we have all the responsibility and deficits as well.
I would now like to know from the hon. minister-I also read on page 31, the following :	.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. We are not on the Railway Estimates and I cannot see how my hon. friend is in order on the Ship-building vote in reading the names of all these subsidiary railway companies.

(Translation.) This is to show what relation the three paragraphs have to one another. I read at the head of page 31: "Constituent and subsidiary companies comprised in the Canadian Northern Railway system." I wished to enumerate the constituent companies. Further on, I read:	Subsidiary companies,
which is another class of companies, and still further on, under the caption "Controlled companies," we have "The Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited." I thought I was entitled to enumerate the various companies making up the entity or class termed "Constituent companies," as well as others which make up the other class known as "Subsidiary companies," and also that which is designated under the name "Controlled Company." I should like to know in virtue of what this company has been classed under that designation. I think the question I have put to the minister is quite in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: (Translation.) I understood the point of order was decided by the very fact that the hon. gentleman had put his question, but I take it now that he has not yet got an answer from the minister.

(Translation.) What I wish to know is just this: I spoke of "Constituent Companies," and under the caption "Subsidiary Companies," I mentioned "The Canadian National Telegraph Co.", "The Great North-Western Telegraph Co. of Canada." and several other companies, and under the last caption "Controlled companies," I mentioned "The Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited." I should like to know under the authority of what Order in Council, of what Act, or other enactment, that company "The Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited," was placed under the control of the "Canadian Northern Railway System."
Has the minister a copy of the contract with the Collingwood Shipbuilding Company of the cost plus basis?

There is a point of
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I understand the
hon. member has a perfect right to ask under what Order in Council or what law or what Statute this Company was placed under the direction of the Canadian National Railways Company; but the Chair is helpless; the Chair cannot oblige the minister to give an answer unless he so desires.
With your permission, I will translate.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is not necessary.

I see at the end of
page 31, controlling company, Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited. I would like to know by what Order in Council or law, or if there is no Order in Council or law, by what Act or deed the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited, came under the control of the Canadian National Railways system?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Government
own all of the stock, as my hon. friend well knows. I am quite prepared to stand for loss of time. I can quite understand what the hon. gentleman is at. What he wants to do is to kill time; it is not information he wants.
Mr. CASGRAIN. We are serious.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: So am I, but the night is young. I am afraid I cannot agree with the hon. gentleman about his seriousness, but I will try to be a little more serious than he is and tell him that the Government own this company and the company was created by Order in Council, as he well knows.

(Translation.) That makes it clear to me that the company has been constituted under the Order in Council which has just been quoted to me, but that does not tell me by what authority that company has been placed under the control of the Canadian Railway system.

Possibly I may be permitted, at this stage of the debate, to protest against the minister's assertion that we are not serious. This was supposed to be private members' day, and his item came on only at the last moment or around midnight and naturally found a House not so well filled as it might have been. There is only a handful of members on both sides of the House; but we are endeavouring, not only myself, but my friends, the hon.

member for Lunenburg ('Mr. Duff), the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) and the hon. member for Charlevoix-Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain), to get information. It is very hard to get it; but we intend to stay here until we do so, and we are very serious and, in fact, more serious than the minister thinks.

(Translation.) If you allow me, Mr. Chairman, I will put my question to the Minister of Marine in a different way: Has the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited, been put under the control of the Canadian Northern system under the last law passed in 1919 concerning the administration of the Canadian National Railway system?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

(Translation.) Since I cannot obtain an answer from the Minister of Marine, I will ask the House to take note of my remarks. I have a right to an answer to the question, which I have put at least three or four times.
The hon. Minister of Marine, said something a moment ago which might seem true, but it was not quite the truth. I must say that I am as serious as the Minister of Marine can be. I am asking for information, and he refuses to give it. If there be an Order in Council as he claims, he must know it and should tell us; if it be under the law passed in 1919 that the Canadian Northern System, Limited, and all the subsidiary companies were put under the control of the Canadian Northern Railway system, he must know it and should tell us. I represent a constituency of 20,000 voters, who sent me here not only to represent them, but to represent Canada as a whole. When we are asked to vote a sum of eight million and some odd hundred thousand dollars, it is not a matter to be disposed of in an instant. The hon. member for Mus-koka (Mr. McGibbon), put the question a moment ago, What is the use of haggling so long over a matter of a few millions? Mr. Chairman, the people's representatives have the right to know how this money is spent. We have here before us a company organized as a company with limited responsibility; it is not known when it was organized; we are told the King is its president and the Government controls the shares. I ask the Minister of Marine, who is in possession of all the information, to tell us what its exact situation is, and he refuses to answer me. I ask the Chair to request the minister to give me an answer
and I am told that the Chair cannot force him to answer. Again I put the question and again I receive no answer, but I am sure that when I go back to my constituency next summer, and tell the electors what has been the conduct of the minister this evening, he can rest assured that the verdict rendered will*not uphold him.
A moment ago, in the course of my remarks, I put the following question to the minister:	How many returned soldiers
have been employed in the various yards in Canada? I had no better success; the minister did not deign to answer.
Mr. Chairman, I asked a moment ago how many returned soldiers had been employed in the various yards of the Canadian Marine. I received no answer. This is the fourth time that we put pertinent questions to the minister, and he says, You are not serious. Mr. Chairman, if we were not serious we would not sit here tonight, the hon. members for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), for Montcalm (Mr. Seguin), for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill), for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), and myself; and our venerated leader this evening, the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) would not be in his seat, being content, notwithstanding his advanced age and all the years of labour which he spent in the service of his country, to remain among us at this hour of the night to lend his help to His Majesty's loyal Opposition.
Our opposition is loyal, we simply ask the Government, whose claim is that the object of this policy is to help the returned soldiers and to prevent the unemployed from starving with hunger, to tell us, at least, how many of those people have been employed in the ship building yards. I do not think the assertion made by the minister is correct. I would not say it is false, as this would be inconsistent with parliamentary etiquette; but we all know what happened, of recent date, in the province of Quebec.
Aided by the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), the hon. Minister of Marine introduced, in the dying hours of last year's session, a bill enabling the Government to dispose, by Order in Council, of Estimates amounting to about $20,000,000. Now, it was hardly a fortnight after that law had been adopted, when two companies supposed to share in that sum were bankrupt; I mean the Three Rivers Shipyard and the National Shipbuilding, such are the industries favoured by the Government and by the Minister.

Glancmg at the ministerial benches, I find that the hon. minister himself has gone out; perhaps he is disgusted with his work. It is about time he should be, having swallowed the millions granted in the preceding years. I am told that I am making obstruction, that I will not understand, that I have no reascSi to take such steps as I am taking to-night. Mr. Chairman, when we are asked to vote this amount right away, I cannot do otherwise than take the position I have taken, and I am surprised that the minister should lack courtesy and loyalty to the extent of not listening to us and of leaving the chamber, because he is afraid that were I to speak at any greater length, I might perhaps make more punctures in his management of the merchant marine for which millions are voted by this House. Mr. Chairman, there is another point to which I would call the attention of the committee and of the country. I asked the minister, a moment ago, some information as to a certain Order in Council and also as to the several resolutions, actions or other nefarious decrees of the Government concerning the management of the marine. I have got no answer, as I said a moment ago I caught, on their flight, some expressions and phrases uttered by the minister while delivering the great speeches of which he has somewhat the monopoly and explaining the management of his great company as he would have done to a small board of directors or to a small and very poor municipal counil. He said: That information, I have it, not because the merchant mai'ine is managed neither by the Marine Department or by myself, but by a company, and all I have to do is to depend upon them and to ask them the results and the remittance of the money.
Money was voted to the minister in that way and he would now have us vote an item of $8,000,000. I, for one, shall refuse to vote it, because that sum will be managed and spent not by the minister himself, but by the company called the Canadian Merchant Marine, under the control of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, the doings of which it will be impossible to supervise and the extravagant expenses of which it will be impossible to control. Should those in charge of that company take a fancy to send ships to any part of the world, where there is no traffic, we could not prevent it, and the hon. minister would tell us next year: "With the eight millions I have completed the

building of a few ships, but I have rereceived a report showing that I have less revenue than last year."
Were we sure that this was the last amount we would be called upon to vote for the merchant marine, and would the Minister give us the information which we now ask, perhaps we might reconsider the decision we are taking to-night to oppose that item; but under the present circumstances we cannot change our attitude with respect to that matter. I may be charged with having said too much, but when such a heavy expense is being dealt with, no one could even say enough. The position we have taken is perfectly justified by the very fact that the Government will not give the information we would like to get. Therefore, I hope that my hon. friends will help me in this contest. I have probably held the attention of this House during too long a time, but I think I owed it to myself and to my electors to say what I have said. I shall now take my seat, reserving the right to begin again later, on the occasion of some other items which will be submitted to us, and I hope my hon. friends will continue the debate which I have opened.

Has the contract with
the Collingwood Company any fair-wage clause in it?
Has the Minister of Marine gone to the Senate?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Minister of Marine has been in the House a very long time. He has gone out for a very short while, and will be back in a few minutes. I understand that in the contract itself a scale of wages was fixed.	.

Has the minister a copy
of the contract? Trouble was reported there.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is not a copy of
the contract here.
Is there one in the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Certainly.
The Minister of Marine was charging us a minute ago with not being serious, but I think he has been carried away by his own seriousness. I hope he will be back in the House to reply to our questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He will be here shortly.

A good deal has been said about the contract for the employment of labour in Toronto. The minister now tells us he has not such a contract; but after considerable effon the part of the members of the Opposition, we were able to find out that there was some kind of contract on the basis of 15 per cent plus on some $460,000 odd. It would appear that the Government are not very serious in their professions of interest in the labour men, at least not so serious as they are in their attempt to provide fat sums to certain gentlemen who, I presume, are friends of theirs - in the contracting business. With regard to this money which the ministry proposes to vote to-night, the statement that has been given to us is, to say the least, the most preposterous thing ever presented to Parliament. The Government come down and propose a vote of $8,300,000 to finish their shipbuilding programme, and the minister mis-states his position; he attempts to bring in a statement showing that he has made an earning when, as a matter of fact, he has incurred a loss. He tried to show the committee that he was placing a sum of money in a rest fund that was to be used for depreciation on his ships. I will not say he was trying to mislead the committee.
You might just as well.

But he gave a statement that was misleading. He stated that he had earned a surplus and had some money to provide for a sinking fund, whereas, as a matter of fact, he had not earned interest on his investment, and therefore had no money to loan. His scheme was all right, but the only thing was that he had no money. So that it is not only bad bookkeeping but it is misleading to say that he has provided a sinking fund to take care of depreciation. Now, the shipping people claim that they should have at least 5 per cent for ordinary depreciation, and my hon. friend has not even provided that amount. He has not earned a total of 5 per cent on the whole operation. He has not actually earned interest, and therefore no amount for the 2 per cent he allows for depreciation, which, -according to the shipping people, should be 5 per cent. The people of this country have reached the point where they are very much concerned over the extravagance of the Government. The Government apparently have lost touch entirely with the country; they do not seem to appreciate what is in the minds
of the people. The people are being taxed to just about their limit of endurance. The Government have devised every possible scheme to tax them, and they are unable to bear any further burdens. Yet the Government are asking for $589,000,000 this year, and unless you are going to borrow, which means bankruptcy, you will have to tax the people for that. The minister said it would probably cost $460,000 to complete these two ships, and he would not say that they would bring that money on the market when completed. The people have no money to squander on these official extravagances. It is all right for the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon), to talk of a few millions here or there; but if I mistake not, his desk mate to-night, the member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) advocated the other night that the Government should go full steam ahead as they did in the United States. Well, so far as this Government's expenditures have been concerned, they have been going full steam ahead for the last five years. They opened the throttle wide and threw away the steering gear, and have gone the limit in every possible kind of expenditure. They have no regard for the people's money; they are simply hanging on as long as possible. I do not know what their hope is; I do not believe they have any, but they will hang on as long as they can, and continue to squander money. Yet the ministers do not think it necessary for them to give information to the committee. The member for Muskoka said we were obstructing. I have not been on my feet as long to-night as he was, in all the time I have spoken. I have been trying to get information, and every time I got up to speak, some one else wanted to follow up the line of argument he had in his mind, and until now I have not been able to state my views on the shipping question. I think the Government will acknowledge that their shipping programme was a mistaken one, and that it was wrong for them to continue it last year. Had they taken the advice of the Opposition, and disposed of the ships, they would have been in a much happier mood than they are to-day. It is not the business of the Government to own ships and chase around the world looking for cargo. That is for private enterprise, and the Government will find that out. The minister was unfair to the committee in pointing out the advantage of his ships to the export and import trade of Canada. He said that in 1914 we had imported from the West Indies $9,000,000 worth of goods, and

in 1920 $19,000,000 worth. In 1914,1 might point out, we imported from France about $3,600,000 worth of various commodities, and in 1920, something like $61,000,000, almost twenty times as much, and I do not think that the Canadian Marchant Marine carried a dollar's worth of these goods. There is also an item in regard to Greece; this has increased sixteen thousand per cent, but it is not due to the Canadian Merchant Marine. And there is an item for Italy, which is equally as laige. There is an item for Italy and it is equally as large. Of course these are exports from Canada, and it will be argued by hon. gentlemen opposite that the Government do not need to provide ships in which to send these goods over to those countries because the Government paid for the goods themselves-they loaned money to the Canadian manufacturers to furnish these goods to Italy, Greece and Roumania. Having provided the goods they do not need to provide the ships. But our trade has increased with a number of countries that our ships do not visit. The percentage under the heading of "other foreign countries" has increased by seven hundred per cent. That is a greater percentage than the minister was able to mention when he spoke of the merchant marine doing such great work for our export and import service.
The minister disclaims all responsibility for the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. He does not interfere with the management in any way, and he does not scrutinize the expenditure, but if there are any deficiencies the people must provide the taxes. We know that he furnishes the money but that is all we do know. But that is not good enough for the Canadian tax-payer. He is being forced to the wall by reason of having to pay heavy taxes, which have become an enormous burden on the country. My hon. friend tells us that he has been building ships in order to provide employment; and in the next breath he tells us that he is paying some person fifteen per cent on the wages of those men. There is something wrong about that; no man has the right to collect fifteen per cent from the labouring men of this country. That is not good business and there must be something wrong when such a system can obtain. The Government should wake up and take notice in regard to all these matters because if they do not the time is coming when Canada will be in serious difficulties. In fact the Government have got the country into difficulties as it is, and the situation is growing worse all the time.

The Government have embarked on a policy of public ownership but for what reason I do not know. Just think of their coming to the House and asking for $8,000,000 in the present case, and then telling us that they have absolutely no control over the expenditure of this money. It is a most absurd position to take, and the people of the country are wondering where it is going to end. They are thinking seriously upon this whole problem. When the minister states we are talking lightly about these matters he is misstating the facts. When hon. members opposite accuse me of wanting to obstruct I have no hesitation whatever in saying that I would be too delighted to obstruct this item until it was withdrawn. If my physical endurance would permit it I would stay here for a week opposing it and hon. members opposite might call it obstruction as much as they liked. I would do that willingly if it would save $8,000,000 for the Canadian people, money which they can ill-afford at this juncture to squander. It is an insane policy to spend money without any objective or without any policy in view, and it is, to say the least, a lamentable condition of affairs for the Canadian people. The Government have no hope of doing any better. They have not the courage to face the situation and take their loss. They admit no responsibility to the country, but they go on taxing the people, and the Minister of Finance is turning grey in his attempts to find money to pay for these extravagances. We have been here now almost two months, and the Minister of Finance is not yet able to say 4 a.m. when he expects- to be able to present his Budget. The Minister of Marine told us to-night that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine is managed by the Canadian National Railways. Yesterday evening the Prime Minister proposed solemnly and as if he meant it the appointment of a committee to look into the affairs of the Canadian National Railways, of which this merchant marine is a branch, and yet the Minister of Marine to-night asks for a vote of $8,300,000. Apparently he has no regard for the committee which the Prime Minister appointed only a few hours ago. It does not look as if the Government were serious or took the Prime Minister seriously. The minister tells us the same old story, that he has no knowledge of the affairs of this undertaking which seems to be an outlet to squander the savings of the people, for apparently the irresponsible directorate in charge may decide what to spend without

any restriction whatever. That condition of affairs would not be permitted if hon. members opposite had the courage to consult the electorate. We are being asked to spend money to help the working man- of which some gentlemen will take 15 per cent-in order that we may provide an export business, for which we must pay the manufacturer in advance, and then in turn we put a tariff wall around the country to exclude imports. But under our system we do not need to exchange goods! We are furnishing the goods, the money and the ships, and, not satisfied with that, we are subsidizing other ships to compete with our own merchant marine. We are going on the assumption that as long as we turn out paper dollars we can bring about prosperity. That is a policy for school children, for this Government, but it is not a policy that will be tolerated by the Canadian people when they have an opportunity to express their views at the polls. I hope the minister will seriously consider the withholding of this item until he can bring it before the committee which his leader named this evening.

I was going to suggest that we rise and report progress on account of the absence of the minister, but as he has just returned I am satisfied to go ahead with the business. I have a few questions to ask him. What time in 1918 were the first ships put into commission on the trade route to the West Indies?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Canadian Voyageur was launched in November, 1918, and the Canadian Pioneer in December, 1918, They were sent to Quebec to be finished o!f owing to the St. Lawrence freezing up between Montreal and Quebec. They went from there to Halifax, and the Canadian Voyageur was the first one to sail some time in February.
I want to get the date in 1918 when your ships started trading with the West Indies.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think the Canadian Voyageur went to the West Indies on her first trip but I am not certain.
Could the minister state the value of the trade with the West Indies at that time?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The exports or imports?
Both.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: To all the West Indian Islands, in 1918, $9,653,761; in 1920, $15,257,014.
Will the Minister give us the tonnage for those periods?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. The Trade and Commerce Department, from whom I got these figures, could not tell me what the tonnage was.

It is difficult for us to know just whether our trade is increasing or decreasing if we cannot have the tonnage. This afternoon the figures given were for 1913 and 1920, I think. I would like very much to have the figures for the tonnage, as dollar comparisons may be very misleading on account of violent fluctuations. How many of the Government ships are on the Great Lakes at present?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: None.
How many could be transferred to the Great Lakes?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Well, that would be a matter for the company to decide, but we have a few 2,800 ton and a few 3,750 ton ships that could operate on the Lakes. We have twenty-five ships of canal draft size.
Twenty-five ships that could be transferred to the Great Lakes?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
No subsidies are paid on the Great Lakes, I believe?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

It seems to me that it would be very good business for the Government to transfer a number of these ships to the Great Lakes. I made this suggestion a year ago, and I believe that the minister promised sympathetic consideration, or something to that effect. In the face of the scarcity of shipping on the ocean and the tremendous fall in ocean freights, I would like to ask why a number of these boats have not been transferred to the Great Lakes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The ships were occupied elsewhere running to Newfoundland and the British West Indies, and some across to European ports. I think I promised my hon. friend last year that I would bring the matter to the attention of the management; I shall be very glad to do so again. I do not know whether the opera-



tion of these ships on the Lakes would be profitable or not, neither can I say now whether or not there is sufficient freight offering there. My hon. friend will understand that I do not follow the details of the operation of the ships.

I am at a loss to understand the position taken by the Government. Is the Dominion to provide seventy or eighty millions of dollars and take care of a continuous loss possibly for years and yet have nothing to say as to the expenditure of those moneys? Are we quite helpless and absolutely in the hands of this shipping company?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. When we first turned the ships over to the operating company I told them to use their judgment in putting the ships on the routes that they thought would pay best, but that one thing we did not want them to lose sight of was the national interest. There may be some very good reason, with which I am not familiar, why they did not put some of these ships on the lakes. Not later than to-morrow, or when I can get away from the House, I will telephone down and let my hon. friend have the answer speedily.
Then my hon. friend cannot say why they have not been put on the lakes?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
ifas the Government made inquiry into the possible profitable employment of those boats on the Great Lakes?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is only reasonable to suppose that the operating company would see that the ships were put on the routes where there was the best chance of making money. They have even gone further than that and put them on routes where they were taking a chance. The absence of our vessels from the lakes would signify, I should think, that the trade there would be unremunerative. But I do not want to make a positive statement; I will have the manager communicated with to-morrow and let my hon. friend have his answer. The answer of the minister suggest another question.
Have any of the directors of this company any interest in outside shipping companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There again I do not want to make a positive statement. I 
have known for many years the gentlemen who are directors of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine and if they had any connection with the Canada Steamship Lines, I think I would know it. So far as I know, they have not.

While the Canada
Steamships are the big noise on the lakes, they are not the whole thing, there are many other smaller companies, some of more or less importance. It does seem to me that the Government have been a little lax in their duty in connection with an expenditure of this size,, especially when it has been made with the idea, as has been stated, of assisting the Government railroads. Now, I think there is a field on the Great Lakes where our railroads can be helped tremendously.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They may be.

I do not think there is any doubt about it. I think the Government should have made inquiries with a view to finding out just in what fields these ships could best serve the railroads; for assistance to the railroads was the one strong argument used by the Government to-day in favour of their construction. Is the minister aware that there are companies on the Geat Lakes that are making handsome profits, paying good dividends on capital, but whose capital is, according to the best information that can be obtained, at least four-fifths water?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. member will understand that I have no knowledge of private companies operating on the Great lakes.

This is public knowledge, as the Canada Steamships, Limited, a few days ago issued a report which appeared in the press showing that they made handsome profits this last year on the Great lakes. It would seem as though it would be wisdom on the part of the Government to keep well informed in that respect. .The point has been raised in this House of the control of transportation rates on our lakes and it has met with considerable opposition. Some members of the Government have suggested, probably not publicly, but privately, that there might be some way of controlling the cost of transportation on the Great lakes, and I was wondering if this was one of the means which they had in mind, because it would be a very effective way of controlling it to some extent. But we have on the Great lakes today, even if the minister would take for

granted a hypothetical case and assume, according to the figures of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) that his ships have cost him five times more than they are worth now, a field of employment whereby he could make full interest on the total cost of his ships.
. Mr. BALLANTYNE: My hon. friend does not want to make an exaggerated statement. He is not a gentleman of that type, and I do not want him to think ships could be bought at one-fifth the price paid by the Government.

I am not saying that; I am saying " even if you take the figures as a hypothetical case." I am not saying what ships could be built for now, whether it is twice or five times less. I have shown to the minister that if we take the actual figures that are being paid for freight on the Great lakes now, he could go into competition on the Great lakes and earn full interest and something to spare on the total investment of his ship. That should surely be good business and worth trying.
Before I go further, I want to show to the minister the actual figures being charged on wheat, which is one of the chief products shipped across the Great lakes and one of the most profitable kinds of business carried on, on the Great lakes. These are actual figures of one company which does a great deal of the shipping on the lakes. I should like the committee to bear in mind that the shipment of grain across the lakes in the month of September is very small, because it is about that time the grain commences to move from the prairies. Even in the month of September, 1919, the rate from Fort William to bay ports was three cents; in 1920 in the same month, it was 4i cents, or an increase of 50 per cent. In October, the grain starts to move freely and in October, 1919, the rate was 3 cents, and in October, 1920, from 5 to 51 cents, or an increase of almost 100 per cent. The same figures apply to November of 1919, and 1920, from Fort William to bay ports. From Fort William to Montreal in September, 1919, the rate was 11 cents; in September, 1920, from 131 to 14 cents; in October 1919, 11 cents and in October, 1920, 151 cents; in November, 1919, 11 cents and in November, 1920, 151 cents. All these rates show a tremendous increase, all the way from 33 per cent to almost 100 per cent over the rates in 1919. This shows that there is a field of most profitable employment for almost the entire merchant marine. As the minister admits that he was not
aware of the profitable field, I thought I would quote these rates so that he need not be in doubt as to possibilities of doing a profitable business on the Great lakes. How many ships were fitted with a view to lake trade?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Twenty.
Yet none of these ships have been employed in that business, and this is most remarkable because a large number of those ships were built right on the lake ports from Port Arthur to Toronto.
Ten of them tied up in Halifax.

Instead of ships plying on the lakes where they were built and where there is plenty of profitable work for them to do, they have been taken off to ocean routes and, as the statement has been made, chasing around the world looking for business. Have any of these ships been used in the coal trade?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not yet, but quite a few of them are at the port of Halifax now being overhauled, and it is the intention of the company to put them into the coal trade as soon as navigation opens.

Are they being rebuilt
so as to be suitable for the coal trade?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
They do not require rebuilding for the coal or grain trade?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Not so far as I
know.
I am glad to know that, because there is a way out for the minister to serve a very useful purpose to this country, by immediately getting those ships into commission on the Great lakes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We will look into that matter with pleasure.

There are now some
40,000,000 bushels of grain in store at the head of the lakes. Some of this is being loaded now; in fact, by this time some of it is probably on its way, and I do not think the Government need worry very much about looking into the matter. The business is there and will always be there, because production in western Canada is going to increase. The boats could serve a useful purpose, not only in carrying grain, but in breaking down some huge combines on the lakes which affect not only the West, but very materially the East. Some are

under the impression that lake rates are not of much interest to the people of eastern Canada; but, to use a popular expression, it gets them both ways, just the same as it does those who live west of the Great lakes. Thus, these boats can serve a useful purpose there and at the same time find very profitable employment.
When you consider the profits that companies can make there with their capitalization such as it is, I am sure you will agree that there is room for improvement. I should just like to mention one or two combines they could break up right away. There is the insurance combine in particular. A few years ago, before the Grain Commission in Winnipeg, a miller stated that they could secure lake insurance at 50 per cent of the price they then had to pay if they could get shipping to carry their goods without having to take insurance from those who had control of the boat space on the lakes. Apart from the saving in dollars and cents, you could put a crimp as it were, in this combine business. Hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of produce goes to waste in these lake ports simply because the shipping companies do not have to take it unless they like; there is no control over them one way or the other. They have held up shipments of grain for days, even when the Grain Board had control of the trade, and they would not supply boats unless their price was met. The breaking up of this combine would be of tremendous value to the country, not only in a direct material way, but in its moral effect in bringing concerns of this kind to their senses. The only conditions at present under which you can do business with them are beyond human endurance.
I do not wish to detain the minister any longer this morning. I thank him for his courtesy, I hope he will take into consideration some of the suggestions I have made, and should we come back here again next year, I hope his answer will be a little different. I hope he will give us more than a promise to take the question into consideration, for really these promises do not get us very far.

speakeroldname: Mr. P. A. SEGUIN (L'Assomption and Montcalm) :

speechtext:
We have sat for quite a long time and do not seem to be getting much further forward. I do not know that any good purpose is being served by continuing the sitting. The cause of its continuance has not been on this side of the House; the policy is that of the Government. There has been a suggestion 

I am not quite sure that it has not

come from the minister-that there has been a want of seriousness on this side. I cannot admit that for a moment. I have listened to the whole debate, I myself having occupied eighteen minutes of the committee's time just before midnight. I have heard all that has been said, and if there has been a want of seriousness, which I would not dispute, it has not been on this side. We do not consider eight and a quarter millions of the people's money a matter for jest, and it was not from this side of the House that a mock presentation of a bouquet was made to the Chairman of Committees. I have not heard a speech from this side of the House that was not seriously directed to some item in the Minister's programme with a view to getting information. There have been three contributions to the debate from the other side since the minister retired from the debate, which he has done for some hours, with the single exception of his replying to the member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg), in his usual courteous manner. So far as speeches are concerned, the contributions from the other side have been three; although there have been numerous other contribution in the way of the opening and closing of desks; and the entertainment has also been added to in a way I have not seen in my experience in this House, in the shape of a midnight lunch. That happened on the other side, however. The seriousness is here; the frivolity is with the people who treat lightly the country's money. The three speeches to which I have referred have not helped the minister's position. My hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt), made a speech in which the one attempt at serious argument was the contention that this money spent for the benefit of returned men was a good thing. I had given economic reasons why I did not think it was a good way to cure unemployment by creating more. As a matter of fact, the contention of my hon. friend falls to the ground in this particular, that unemployment is rifer in this country at the present time than since I came to Canada twenty years ago. So that the very object of the minister has fallen down, as well as other planks in my hon. friend's argument. But it cannot be the opinion of hon. gentlemen opposite that it was done entirely to afford employment to the unemployed, because my hon. friend from Mus-koka had a vision of these ships sailing the seven seas. If it were not so late, I should like to know from the minister what 
disposition has been made of all the ships he has finished at the present time. So far as we are concerned, every minute of this debate has been useful. In the very last words which the minister uttered to the committee, he told us that a number of these ships are in Halifax harbour being overhauled. That is not what the Halifax Herald says about them.
It says they are tied up in that port because they have nothing to do. In previous remarks upon this question I pointed out, that from the columns of the Montreal Star I had learned that some of these ships were coasting up and down Norway, or Scandinavia, and even going to Germany to try and get cargoes. I would like to know exactly where the ships are at the present moment? However, what I want to point out to the committee is that we have two contradictory statements made as to what the ships have actually done, and what they are doing at the present moment. On the one hand we have it asserted that they are doing good business because they are going to promote Canada's trade in all the seven seas, and on the other, that at any rate they have done some good in providing work for the unemployed. As I said when the hon. member for Brantford was speaking, if that was their object it is a pity to have stopped such a programme when my hon. friend considers it so attractive. If the object was to employ the unemployed, then there never was so much need for shipbuilding and road building. If this Government believes in spending public money for this purpose why not raise another Victory Loan and go ahead and spend money?
We of the Opposition, we who are opposing the Government of whatever creed, have no monopoly of the view that this business has fallen down. The ships were built at a loss, they were built in an unprofitable way, and they were built at too high a price. I asked my hon. friend the other day, would he say now, as he said a year ago, that he could sell these ships at a profit. Could he sell them at all?
Not one.

My hon. friend is asleep apparently and I repeat the question-could he sell the ships at all? Then if he could not I reiterate that they are a white elephant on his hands. Now that is the condition of the ships. With regard to their helping out the railroad policy, what my hon. friends opposite, from the minister down to the back bencher, have to

prove is that two deficits make a surplus. We have a defiicit of seventy millions on the National Railways and we, who are not serious forsooth, are to be told that if you only add losing ships to losing railroads the thing will be all right. Well, those of us who live another year will see. Those ships that are in Halifax harbour being overhauled are not earning much money for this year. The ships that are coasting up and down Norway are not earning much money. I am very much afraid they are not earning money because everybody who knows anything at all about ships knows that it is a very difficult thing for shipping to earn money anywhere at the present moment. I admit that quite frankly and seemingly my hon. friend from Skeena (Mr. Peck) agrees with me.
No, I ask why do you blame the Government then?

Why I should blame the Government for going into an unprofitable business against my own warning? When my hon. friend and his friends knew or were told, that this was an unprofitable business and went into it and come forward with a story such as we have heard about these ships, is my hon. friend so lacking in his grasp of public authority as to seriously press the question why the Government should be blamed, if one of the Government enterprises is undertaken against the knowledge of those who know something about shipping, and against warnings in the press of this country? In many quarters from the very beginning, especially in the capital city of the country, in the "Citizen" newspaper which every hon. gentleman could have read. From the beginning of the enterprise, every move in this shipping policy has been pointed out when it was wrong and condemned. That is why I blame the Government, and I ask my hon. friend if he does not think there is good ground for it?
Are the Government supporters alone to blame in that respect? What about hon. gentlemen opposite who supported that programme?
My hon. friend has an excellent opportunity of settling accounts with other members of the House for himself.
I am asking you the question.

A child can baffle a philosopher, and really I am not
prepared to tell my hon. friend at just this moment to apportion the blame. These of course are to blame that defended the policy. But that does not rest at my door, and after all is said and done the Government of the day is responsible for the policy of the day; and I have not known it as a common policy for a Government, when it is being met by solid facts and solid arguments, to ask a person using those arguments and producing those facts to apportion the blame between the minister and other members of the House. That is the business of my hon. friend from Haldi-mand, (Mr. Lalor) not mine. I do not want to delay these proceedings. I have occupied ten minutes in addition to eighteen -that is twenty-eight minutes of the time of the House, I have taken up. I do not feel that I have wasted a moment. I have spoken in what I conceive to be the best interest of this country, just as every word that I have ever uttered was uttered from that point of view and that point of view alone. I would call the attention of my hon. friend from Skeena to the fact that when I qrst uttered these words I was sitting behind the Government as he himself is sitting still. I was sitting behind the Government, and I was one of the few men-if he wants a confession-who were disappointed that by proceedings like these the Union Party was smashed to slivers. When I next blamed this policy, and pointed out the evils of it, I had moved to the crossbenches because I would not make myself responsible for this shipbuilding business. My hon. friend, therefore, has no ground when he asks me why I blame the Government in this matter. The summary of the matter is this: It is an unprofitable enterprise, and despite all I have heard about it being a popular policy from end to end of the country it will not requre many such detailed debates as we have had in the last two days on these Estimates to change any popularity that is left into very great unpopularity. I do not believe quite that my hon. friend is so sure of the popularity of this scheme. I do not see how he can be so sure of it because if it is not popular in the Government press in Halifax and Montreal then I can assure him it is not popular with the farmers of the prairies. Neither is it popular with the working men of Toronto who have had deputations up here revealing the very inwardness of the business. That popularity has not been a thing that has been absolutely evident in the by-elections that have taken place all

over the country. Neither does the confidence of the ministry in their own popularity become evident when they keep byelections back as far as they can by straining the law to the last point. I warn my hon. friend that he is living in a fool's paradise in regard to the popularity of the scheme. This night's debate, so far as this side of the House is concerned, has been fully justified because, up to the last moment, whenever the minister intervene he gave us information which has thrown more light on the scheme and that is what the country wants. It is an unprofitable scheme, it is next door to a bankrupt scheme, and I am afraid that the minister will find that it is a poor backing for an adminis-traton which is rapdly approachng the same position politically as this scheme has arrived at economically.
Now so far as I am concerned I should like, if I have any influence with my hon. friends on this side, to suggest that we have made our protest, we have ventilated this thing pretty well considering the number present, and so far as I am concerned T really doubt whether there is any wisdom in going any further. The minister is looking worried, he has already retired for an hour and we do not want to overwork him. I think therefore the vote had better be passed. Eight million three hundred thousand dollars.	_

It is a large amount
to swallow.

It is needed,
is it not, for the finishing of certain contracts? The finishing of contracts is something that, after all, we are just as sensitive about as any one on the other side of the House. But that fact furnishes the final condemnation of the scheme at the present moment. For, here is a scheme of shipbuilding on the part of the Government for certain purposes, nearly every one of which has been knocked on the head. You have a number of ships already built which are idle, and here is an order for $8,300,000 to build some more. To do what? To get cargoes where those already built cannot get them. If my hon. friend could 5 a.m. sell the ships I would stand the big loss on them, because it will be some years before they do anything for this country, especially if the policy of the Government is not changed on other matters.

The hon. member for
Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) referred to-
(Mr. M. Clark.)
night to the fact that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) questioned the wisdom of the project, but the hon. member for Brantford must surely have himself questioned the wisdom of it when he referred to it as he did. He said the policy itself was all right, but he was not certain that the time of putting it into operation was all right.

It was too
late.

What is the good of advocating a policy if you do not put it into effect at the proper time? It is good policy to sow wheat in my part of the country, but not unless you know when to sow it. I might just as well say that it is good policy for me to sow wheat in January as that it is good policy to go into shipping without knowing the proper time for doing so. I think his argument is just as illogical as he would like the House to believe our argument is.
Then he said that the farmers themselves know all about the fall in prices. I would like to tell the hon. member for Brantford that the farmers do know all about the fall in prices, but they also know something about the advance in prices, particularly of agricultural implements, in connection with which the hon. member's name is very prominent. I had occasion to purchase some implements before leaving home to attend the session here, and the manager of the company through which I did the business told me that there was only one agricultural implement and they handled practically all lines-that had not gone up in price. These advances run from 10 to 20 per cent. The hon. member for Brantford may be glad to have this information, especially as the Cochshutt Manufacturing Company make more than one line of agricultural implements.	*

It is
an extraordinary situation that the twenty-one hon. members sitting on the other side of the House seem to have no arguments to put up against the able speeches that are made from this side of the House. Apparently no one is able to answer the arraignment of the Government just delivered by my hon. friend from Red Deer. It strikes me that my hon. friend from St. John, a distinguished member of the Government, ought to be able to defend it, if it is capable of defence.
He is a dumb philosopher.

And
my hon. friend from Colchester (Mr. McCurdy)-can he say nothing in defence of the Government? If this policy is right why is it that no supporter of the Government can demonstrate it? We are open to argument, but we are determined to do everything in our power to prevent the passing of this $8,000,000, because we are fully convinced that it is an extravagant and useless expenditure at the present time. We have shown that these ships are only worth 25 per cent of the money put into them. Twenty-five per cent of $8,000,000 is $2,000,000, so that we are throwing away $6,000,000. We are told that this is to help the unemployed. It strikes me that there is no more extravagant way of employing idle men than in building ships, for you pay a very small amount for labour and a very large amount for material. Labour is not a great part in the construction of a ship. Besides, if you employ labour in one part of the country you are equally bound to employ it in other parts. In the town where I live there is a shipyard, but the Government have not recently let any contracts there, although there are a great many idle men in the locality. Why do we not get the use of some of this money in New Glasgow instead of its being all spent in Toronto, Port Arthur and other places west of Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend know that we placed a million dollars' worth of contracts at New Glasgow and $8,000,000 at Halifax.
Not millions.

I did
not know that $8,000,000 was to be expended in Halifax.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Quite a large part of it.

How many ships are
being built in Halifax under this programme?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There are two yet.

Does
my hon. friend pretend to say that he is going to spend $4,000,000 on one ship?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

(Guysborough):	If
he is, the condition is much worse that we thought it was. My hon. friend must be mistaken when he says that this money is to be expended in Halifax.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: A portion of it.

Well,
if my hon. friend is to find work for the returned soldiers, how is it that he is placing contracts in a few places like Toronto and Halifax, and making no provision for the returned soldiers in other places in Canada? My hon. friend stated the other day that he had sixteen ships under construction and only two of them are being built in Halifax, so that there must be fourteen somewhere else. He has not told us where the fourteen are being built. He also told us that the total tonnage of the sixteen vessels amounted to 114,470 and that the average cost of building is $192 per deadweight ton. That means that my hon. friend is asking for $8,000,000 to complete a shipbuilding contract involving $21,978,000 worth of work. My hon. friend has not given the explanation of this; it looks to me as if he would be coming back later for a large sum in order to complete his programme. He has not told us, either, how much work has been done on the ships that are now in course of construction. He stated this morning that the ships that were in Halifax harbour were there for repairs. Well, that is an illuminating statement. The newspaper that supports the Government in Halifax and has done so from its inception until very recently has been criticizing the Government severely on its shipbuilding programme. From his window the editor can see in the harbour ten or twelve ships lying at anchor.
Fifteen on Saturday.

Fifteen on Saturday, my hon. friend says; that is the spectacle witnessed by the editor of the "Halifax Herald." Consequently he came out and informed the country of the condition of things. Well, if as the Minister says these ships are under repair there must have been something wrong with their construction in the first place, because they are comparatively new ships. If there are fifteen in the harbour at once and all for repair, it will take a long time to have the repairs made, because only one ship can go on the slip at a time. This is the manner in which we are getting light on this question.
On page 9 of the 53rd annual report of the Minister's Department I find the following :
The following is an approximate comparison of the cost of wages and hoard per month between a British, an American, a Canadian, and a Japanese steam merchant ship of similar tonnage and dimensions; cost of the British

ship for wages and board per month $3,645 09, of the American $6,711.10, of the Canadian $2,303.50 and of the Japanese $1,124.50.
The pay of the master of the Canadian ship was $250 per month, that of the. master of the Japanese ship $100 per month; able seamen on the Canadian ship received $16.20 per month, on the Japanese ship $9 per month.
My hon. friend, then, who is spending millions of money for the purpose of giving employment to men in certain parts of Canada, pays his sailors $16.20 a month, about fifty cents a day. The classification of the Civil Service, page 5, gives the compensation of an ablebodied seaman on the Great lakes and on the coastal waters as $55, $60, $65, and $25 for subsistence in addition. But on the deep sea waters of the Atlantic, and, I suppose, of the Pacific, my hon. friend expects his sailors to work for $16.20 a month, while the master gets $250-as much as fifteen sailors. His ships ought to make money if he is paying his sailors at that low rate.
My hon. friend informs us that there is a sinking fund to provide for the capital expenditure and also for the depreciation, and that at the rate at which he is accumulating amounts in this sinking fund he expects to discharge the debt in twenty-five years. But my hon. friend appears to have made no provision for keeping the ships afloat during that twenty-five years, and to provide for necessary repairs. He tells us that ten or fifteen ships that are at Halifax are there for repairs. It takes a great deal of money to make repairs in these times; the machinery of the ships will depreciate year after year and will have to be renewed; the boilers will have to be renewed every ten years anyway even if the best care is taken of them. The minister cannot repair his ships and renew his machinery and boilers twice during the twenty-five year period without some money, and so far as I can learn, he has not made any provision for repairing his ships or renewing boilers and machinery. How does the minister propose to deal with the question? How does he propose to get the money to put in new boilers? Will he take the money out of the sinking fund? If he does, his sinking fund will be very largely reduced. If he could get along without any repairs for twenty-five years; if his boilers would last for twenty-five years, his theory might work out. But twenty years is regarded as the life of an ordinary tramp vessel; if it lives for twenty-five years, all the better, but it is apparently necessary that the minister's ships should last for twenty-five years to work

out the sinking calculation the minister has made. How does the minister expect to keep his ships afloat during those twenty-five years? I do not see that he has made any provision for that important eventuality.
I pointed out, when I was speaking before, that freight rates have become very much less during the last few months. During the first six or seven months of 1920 rates were high and ship-owners made a good deal of money. The slump came the last of August or the first of September. As everybody knows who knows anything about ships, it is usual to have contracts two or three months ahead, so that most of 1920 must have been carried on under pretty good contracts at fairly high rates. Then the slump came and rates dropped to about one-half. I am familiar with some of the trades; but if any hon. gentleman will go into the library or reading room and take the "Journal of Commerce" of New York or the "New York Herald" and look over the fixtures of vessels last September or August and look over the same fixtures for the same routes at the present time, he will find a very large difference in the rates that are paid. If my hon. friend, on my calculation, lost $4,000,000 last year, how much is he going to lose this year? We are in dead earnest about this matter, because we feel that we represent the people of Canada; that there is at stake, not only this $8,000,000, but probably $10,000,000 or $12,000,000 more to be wasted in connection with these ships during the current year. We cannot afford to spend this money; the people of Canada have enormous burdens to shoulder; indeed, the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) represented the Canadian people as a weary Titan carrying an enormous load. It would be a great mistake for us to permit the Government to do anything we could prevent, in order to increase that load by some $12,000,000 for the coming year. That is the reason why we are fighting this question inch by inch; and if ever we were in earnest in cur lives, we are in earnest now, if possible to get some concession from the minister, to draw from him some promise that he will look into the matter and that if it costs more to finish those ships than to leave them alone, he will not spend the money for the present year. If any of these ships are just about commenced-and I do not know whether they are or not, because the minister has not told us-if the keel

is laid and a few thousand dollars spent, we should not think of throwing away another million to complete the ship when we know that when it is completed, it will not be worth in the market more than 25 per cent of the money put into it. That is the way the matter strikes us, and it ought to strike hon. gentlemen opposite in the same way. I see a number of business gentlemen opposite me. Do they want to waste $8,000,000 or, perhaps $12,000,000, during the current year? I am sure they do not. If not, let them take charge of their minister, and endeavour to do something with him. They alone can do it. We cannot do it on this side; it is like throwing pearls in the wrong direction for us to make speeches on this side attempting to influence the minister; but hon. gentlemen opposite can influence him if they try, if this venture strikes them as it strikes us on this side, as a losing game, a blunder, that should not be committed by the Government of this country.

Just in case anybody thinks nobody on the Government side is going to talk, I should like to say a few words. My good friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) seemed to resent a question that I asked him in all good humour. The hon. gentleman is such a master of eloquence, and we all respect him so much and listen to him with so much interest that I am sorry he resented the question I asked.
I did not resent the question at all.

The hon. gentleman cannot have any more good humour than I have. As I understood the hon. gentleman to be bewailing the decline of freight rates throughout the world, I simply asked why the Government should be blamed for this decline in freights and why that should not be considered in the loss of profits. It is a very god thing that we have continued this debate, because I am quite sure hon. members opposite are entirely sincere; I do not believe they mean to obstruct. When you look across the House at those earnest and sincere countenances, you can see that they do not mean to obstruct. Therefore, is it not very much better that thirty or forty of us should sacrifice our time until this hour of the morning, or if you like during all the forenoon in order to get this item through? This shows that not only we on the Government side, but hon. gentlemen opposite are sincere in this matter,
and we want to get the item through. What is the use of carrying on this debate for days? Let us get the item through, and 1 am sure we can if we go on.
I am not going to carry on the discussion in defence of the policy of the Minister, because we do not need to do that. It is very easy to tear things down, but it i3 very hard to build them up. I am quite sure that the minister's policy is going to win out, and I am prepared to stand hehind it.
I do not care what gibes are thrown at me about my not crossing the floor of the House. I am as good a free trader as the hon. member for Red Deer, absolutely, and if I had a little square constituency down in Alberta, I might talk a whole lot of free trade and nothing else, but I am a practical politician. I am going to fight for free trade where we can get it, but I challenge my hon. friend from Red Deer to say if he can get it from the official Opposition in this House. Take the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), or the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, (Mr. Fielding), or the hon. member for Quebec East, (Mr. Lapointe) or the hon. member for Beauce, (Mr. Be-land)-all these hon. gentlemen have made high protectionist speeches in this House. I look in vain for free traders on the other side of the House.
Here we are.
I know you are there, but there is no free trader there.
Here is one.

If any hon. gentlemen can show me where we can get genuine free trade or a policy that will work towards free trade I will be with him, but in the meantime you have to show me. I always listen to my hon. friend from Red Deer with the utmost respect, and I challenge him to say whether he has any more sympathy than I have with the speeches from the official Opposition.
We are all together on this item.
In the meantime let us get on with this item. We are all good humoured and want to get it through. I know hon. gentlemen opposite want to get it through and adjourn the House.

I just want
to say that if I have earned any portion of the respect of my hon. friend from

Skeena by anything I have done in this country, then indeed it is one of the highest rewards that has come to me, and a far better reward than could come to me in any other form. So far from holding any resentment, I replied to him with the utmost earnestness. He might have mistaken that for temper, but it was not so. I was very anxious to get my point of view into the mind of my hon. friend. It was simply earnestness, not ill-temper. How could I be ill-tempered with so genial a gentleman as the hon. member for Skeena? Let us leave that.
My hon. friend has joined me at one point. I did say a few minutes ago that I did not see much use in continuing this discussion, but I have rather changed my mind since because of the very practical and sensible speech of my hon. friend from Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair). The more we go into this thing the worse it seems to get. Every time the minister speaks or tells us anything it appears to make his case worse. I do hope we shall have a ministerial reply to' the last speech of my hon. friend from Antigonish and Guysborough. He has made a calculation-he knows something about shipping-and he fears that $8,000,000 is not going to finish the contracts of the minister. He has made a calculation by which he has demonstrated to this committee that there are good grounds for fearing $21,000,000 will be needed yet. That is a practical point which the minister is bound to take up, even at this late hour of this sitting. If this $8,000,000 is only a portion, and we shall have to find $21,000,000, I think that is good ground for not getting the item through in a hurry.
My hon. friend from Skeena has issued a challenge to me. I am very proud of him as a confessed adherent of the doctrine of free exchange. He is consistent in believing in a shipbuilding programme, and no doubt if he pegs away at the minister he may get him on a fiscal policy that will make their ships pay. I want, however, to appeal to my hon. friend's imagination-
I do not think it is the strongest thing about him. He is the sort of man I would like to have with me if I was going to fight tigers-but I would like him to project himself in imagination to the harbour of Halifax, and to suppose that by some modern invention an inhabitant from the planet Mars had also come to Halifax harbour to see what was going on there. He would naturally ask my hon. friend from
[Mr. M. Clark. 1
Skeena some questions. He would know he had come from close to the Minister of Marine and would naturally suppose he was well up on the shipbuilding programme. " Well," the man from Mars would say to my hon. friend, " what are those fifteen ships doing over there?" " Oh," says my hon. friend from Skeena, " they are being overhauled." " Is there nothing for them to do on the sea?" "Not for the moment; cargoes are very hard to get." Then they would look around the harbour and see two new ships that were being built. This intelligent inhabitant of Mars would naturally say: "Well, I cannot understand why you should be building two more ships when the finances of the country are strained to the utmost, and you have no cargoes for the fifteen ships that are here." What would my hon. friend from Skeena say if he had it put to him in that way? Does he not see that it is an immensely practical proposition that my hon. friend from Guysborough puts up when he says: We had better cut that loss if there is any suspicion of our being drawn into an expenditure of $21,000,000. But there is another side to this question of hurrying the item through. What would the inhabitant of Mars say to the hon. member from Skeena when he explained that we were building more ships, at the cost of millions of money, when we had dozens of them that we had the greatest difficulty in finding cargoes for now? He would say: " I would like to take the next aeroplane back to Mars." So far as I am concerned, I am content from that point of view. My hon. friend has not convinced my reason about the wisdom of getting the item through, but when reason fails to appeal to the majority, then we must succumb to majority rule. So that I join with my hon. friend in wishing that the item may go through as soon as possible. It is getting on to breakfast time now.
Mr. D'ANJOU: (Translation.) I should be recreant to my duty if I did not join those eloquent gentlemen who preceded me, in objecting most strongly to this item of more than $8,000,000 that is asked by the Minister of Marine. Besides the minister, two other hon. gentlemen from the other side contributed to this debate. The first stated that the discussion was nothing but ridiculous, as it was only a question of a few million dollars. Hon. gentlemen have heard so much about millions during the war and are now so familiar with large figures that they are ready to vote any

amount that may be asked by the Government. However, when they were in the Opposition they proved to be very sharp obstructionists; they used to discuss items of $500 for hours; but now that His Majesty's loyal Opposition objects with good reason to this item, they take occasion of that to ridicule the stand we are taking to defend the rights of the people. Hon. gentlemen are doomed to be disappointed, and when they come before the people they shall have to give a strict account of the moneys they have spent in useless and disastrous undertakings.
It may be argued that this discussion is of no avail since the Government, having a majority in this House, can have the money voted whenever they like. But we on this side of the House are satisfied that we have fulfilled our duty in representing properly not only our own constituents, but the whole people of Canada, who shall have to pay exorbitant taxes to meet the enormous expenditure involved in the construction of ships in this country.
According to the experts, at any rate, it is established that this policy was disastrous and it is time for the Government to stop such foolish expenditures of no benefit to the country. Unrest is rampant in the country and not only the people's representatives but the people themselves beg the present Government to economize. Take for instance the Department of Agriculture, whose credits should be very large; the estimates for Agriculture amount to only $4,502,000 and still the Government come and ask for 8 millions to spend on the mercantile marine. However, it seems to me that the interests of the country would be better served should the Government drop their disastrous shipbuilding policy and transfer those 8 millions to the Department of Agriculture so as to encourage our farming community. For my part, and during the last two sessions, I have had occasion to ask the minister to establish an experimental farm in Rimouski county and, on every occasion, the minister told me that my request was a most reasonable one but that it could not be granted until the country's finances were in better shape. The minister said a moment ago that he was ready to spend the night here in order to put through the vote for 8 millions for his shipbuilding industry, but nevertheless, he refuses to extend the necessary explanations or give all the information that the people's representatives in this House may expect from him.
The hon. members who spoke before me have given the opinion of various newspapers regarding the shipbuilding industry in this country. Extracts were read from liberal newspapers, papers in sympathy with the Government, unionist newspapers. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I shall read an extract from a newspaper which is rather giving its support to the agrarian members in this House: the Ottawa Citizen:
Too Many Ships.
While our government is taking much credit to itself for its extensive and costly shipbuilding program, which goes on apace, there is developing a world situation in tonnage which is becoming of serious import to all maritime nations. This relates to the glut of tonnage from which the European and American continent is suffering. Writing in the New York Evening Post, Mr. Allan Nevins calls attention to the fact that the United States shipping board has tied up seven steel vessels since the end of September and now announces that eight more, all large ships, have been withdrawn. A noted American authority on maritime affairs is quoted to the effect that hardly half the worldfs available ocean tonnage is being employed at this time and that a general fall in shipping securities in the United States and Britain marks the general situation. Companies here and abroad have resorted- to special devices to keep their tonnage moving. Five lines plying from Liverpool to Oriental ports-the Cunard, Ellerman, Moss and others-have, offered rebates to shippers who will promise to restrict themselves to their vessels. Steamships agents in New York and other American ports are making vigorous efforts to obtain parcel freight in default of full cargo shipments. A fortnight ago the American shipping board announced that American lines carrying freight to the four chief ports of Germany, Holland, Belgium and France would be allowed to fix their own rates. This means a price-cutting war in competition with European lines.
The chief causes for tile present situation are given as too much tonnage and a heavy decline in freight shipping. According to Lloyd's Register the world had, in June, 1911, a gross tonnage of about 45 1-2 million tons of shipping. In June of this year it had almost 54 million tons. In addition to this there is building some seven or eight million more tons. In the United States the shipping boa*-d has attempted in vain to sell some of the 1,000 steel ships under its control to private parties but the knowledge that the world is in for a protracted spell of sharp competition and of freight rates that spell disaster to lines lacking in efficiency and very heavy capital has proved too strong for the board to do business.
Mr. Chairman, after the evidence offered by the most important newspapers representing public opinion in this country, after the opinion given by experts in shipbuilding, it seems to me that the honourable the Minister of Marine should open his eyes and that, not only should not we report

progress, but this item should be struck out of the estimates for the mercantile marine and granted to the Department of Agriculture. The Government ,/should strive to economize where economies may be accomplished. When the development of Agriculture is at stake, or when those industries which may contribute to develop or increase the richness of our country are at stake, I have no objection to the Government spending all the money they think proper to spend.
