For my part, I feel sure that the members of the Opposition are now doing their duty towards their constituents and towards the country at large when they oppose with the greatest energy this item of 8 millions which the Minister of Marine asks the House to vote.

I do not want to detain the House, but I must congratulate the member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg), and the member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), for supporting the Opposition in their attitude to this item. We object to the Merchant Marine, and falling in line with the member for Red Deer, have endeavoured to show that even during the war the minister discriminated in his treatment between steel ships and wooden ships. But even if, as the minister claims, this were a war policy, I contend that it is all the more reason why it should now be discontinued. The Government was supposed to be elected for war purposes, but they do not realize that the war is over. We object to this policy on the further ground that it is another form of Government ownership. This Government has been experimenting with railway ownership, and their experiment has proved disastrous. It is well known that Government ownership in the United States has also proved a great failure, and instead of experimenting further and trying their great administrative powers in this matter, the Government should abandon the policy of public ownership in both railways and ships. The funniest part of the whole debate is the claim of the Minister of Marine that he has a surplus in the operations of his ships, and his figures show an elasticity of bookkeeping which is perfectly astounding. The investment in this great venture is about $50,000,000. The Minister says he has obtained, or rather the management has obtained-because he confesses that he knows nothing about the subject himself-a surplus of over $780,000, something like 2.35 per cent on the initial investment of $50,000,000. The Government is carrying loans on which it is paying 5i per cent, besides 
exempting these loans from the income tax. So that it will be seen that the minister cannot show any better statement than a return at 2 per cent on capital. We know that the capital cost of the ships has been shrinking a good deal since they were built. These ships cost $192 per ton deadweight, and it is now claimed that they could be well replaced by ships costing $130 per ton. It is clear, therefore, that we have lost the enormous sum of $62 per ton on the value of the ships, and this represents, both on ships now in commission and on those to be finished, a total deficit of something like $20,000,000. Of course, the minister and his supporters say that we do not need to worry about millions; the war has been won and we must provide employment for returned soldiers, and it does not matter at all if it costs one million or twenty million dollars; we can well afford it. I agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), that the worst way to deal with the problem of the returned soldier is to have such expensive contracts as ship-building for the sole purpose of providing a little temporary work. There are dozens of ways in which we could help the soldiers to equal advantage and with more profit to the country, and this ship-building policy is a poor excuse for providing employment. We have quoted in this House extracts from the press, Tory, Liberal and Independent, and we have also quoted reports of the Bank of Montreal, the Royal Bank, and, in fact, nearly every bank except possibly the Bank of Commerce, all adverse to this scheme of ship-building as well as the policy of the Government ownership of railways. The people have to provide the deficits, and while it is all right for the ministers to say that it is only a matter of a few millions, the people want to know where this money is to come from. We know that in a few weeks' time the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) will have to come before the House and advise that some means of taxation be adopted to make up these deficits; and it is a serious responsibility for hon. members to make light of the matter and pass it off with any trivial remark that it is only a few million dollars, or words to that effect. The people have been labouring heavily under the taxation of the Minister of Finance of last year, and that hon. gentleman is now at work to find some other means of taxation. When the people have to dig down into their flat purses to find a few dollars and give them to the Government it

is outrageous to hear the minister say: Oh, that is all right; give us all your earnings so that we may experiment in Government ownership.
I wish to read the following short paragraphs from a clipping from the "Journal of Commerce," a New York paper, dated October 26, 1920:-
The present cost of operation of modern vessels is from three to five times greater than during the ten-year period prior to 1914, while freight rates are only from two to three times higher at the present time. Building programmes are being curtailed and it is reasonable to believe that freight rates cannot be kept below the actual cost of operation, and unless some international rate war should spring up as a result of the paternal legislation enacted by the last Congress and which the president, with apparent wisdom, has so far declined to enforce, it would seem reasonable to believe that freight rates are not likely to go lower, and with stabilization of the general situation may work higher.
In this connection, it is well for shippers to bear in mind that at this time two years ago the rate on one commodity, for instance, cotton, from New Orleans to Genoa was about $8 per 100 pounds, while to-day the rate is from $1.25 to $1.50 per 100 pounds, or just one-fifth of the rate two years ago, and only about double what the rate was in 1913, although the cost of wages, coal, port charges, etc., have trebled and Quadrupled during the same period.
I could go on reading, Mr. Chairman, but I would not utter one sentence which I felt was not useful and necessary for the carrying on of the business of the country. The United States, with their tremendous export trade, had an over-supply of ships. In Canada, though, we continue to build ships, even in the face of the present situation. It would be better for
6	a.m. Canada to buy ships from the United States at the present time than to continue to build them in this country. But we should do neither, because we do not need the ships. Not only should we censure the Government for entering upon this policy; we should stop building ships and try. to dispose of the ones we have at the earliest possible moment.

the committee at what yards the sixteen ships to be completed are under construction?

I cannot tell the

What are the names of
the builders of the ships not yet finished?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

I do
not wish to put my word against that of the minister, but I stated that, according to the minister, there were sixteen ships under construction and that on the basis of a total tonnage of 114,470, at a rate per ton as given by the minister, the cost would reach $21,978,240. If the minister would tell us now how much money he has expended on the ships we would be able to check these figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I gave them to
the House when I made my first statement. Of the amount of $8,000,000 required to complete the programme $4,665,496.10 is a re-vote from last year.
Is there no way in which the minister can cancel these orders and dispose of the unfinished ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The ships will be entirely finished by July next and it would be quite impossible to cancel the orders now.	[DOT]

According to the twentyeighth report of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1920, the total value of goods of Canadian origin exported in the field covered by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine was $30,000,000. We have apparently spent $1.50 for every dollar's worth of goods we exported; yet the in-

creasing of our export trade was one of the principal reasons why the Government went into the ship-building business. To a country that had any knowledge of the economics of export and import, of production and manufacture, my hon. friend's appeal would not be a very sound one. To attempt to build ships to promote export trade is surely building your house on the sand. Hon. gentlemen opposite criticise us on this side for not offering constructive criticism. Well, it is not exactly the business of an Opposition to provide the Government with policies; when the Government find they have no policy, it is time for them to resign.
Taunts have come from the Government side against members of the Opposition for their war records. I have no apology to make for my war record nor for that of my constituents. From the little village of Portage du Fort, in the county of Pontiac, with a population of 360 souls, we had 37 volunteers before conscription came into effect, and after conscription came into effect there was only one man conscripted, and he was neither French nor Irish, but of my hon. friend's nationality, and that is not saying anything against his nationality.
Who has control of these ships before they are launched?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Government, under the Department of Marine.

I understand that five of these ships are being constructed at inland ports, and that they will be finished in July. I would suggest that if the minister has control over these boats construction be rushed as rapidly as possible, and that these ships be retained on the lakes where they would be absolutely sure to find employment. If he has not control, I would urge that he suggest to the company that the ships be retained on the lakes.

I wish to read an item from the Halifax Herald, one of the papers supporting the Government:
The announcement in parliament that the deficit on the government owned and operated railways amounts to something like seventy millions of dollars, is not only startling, but really alarming. In placing the figures at seventy millions it is stated the Minister of Railways was "breaking the news gently," and by that it would occasion no surprise if the actual deficit ran up to over a hundred millions.
But while public attention is focussed on this enormous and really staggering deficit of the railway system, a note o<f alarm is being sounded from other quarters. There are rumors

to the effect that the railway system is not the only utility that is losing money.
For instance, there is the Canadian Merchant Marine. This gigantic enterprise must have cost the people o<f Canada a huge sum of money. To-day it is costing a huge sum of money. How many millions of dollars went into this enterprise, we do not know. How many millions of dollars are being sipent annually iby this same enterprise we do not know.
We think it would be well for the Parliament of Canada to take this matter in hand.
Are the millions of money being spent wisely? That is the question the people would like to have answered.
Are all those ships earning their keep? That is another question the people would like to have answered.
There are about ten of those fine ships in Halifax harbour at the present time, anchored in the stream. Some of them have been there for quite a length of time, and there does not appear to be any hope of their leaving their anchorage at an early date.
The maintenance of a steamer of any size costs money. The maintenance of the ten steamers of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine service cannot cost under one thousand dollars a day for each ship, or, at the inside calculation, ten thousand dollars a day. These ships are fully manned. The officers and members of the crew are sustained at the Government's expense and they are paid out of Government money.
Why are those ships lying idle in Halifax harbour?
If there are ten of those ships lying idle in Halifax harbour how many are there lying idle in other harbours?
Would it be a fair estimate to place the loss occasioned by the maintenance of those idle ships of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine service at $50,000 a day?
Why maintain all those ships if there is nothing for them to do?
Why use them to crowd out privately owned ships on routes of trade which private capital and enterprise have taken years to build up?
Why should the Government enter into competition with its own people?
There are many millions of dollars invested in those steamers. But the first cost is only a bagatelle in comparison to the cost of maintenance and if Canada is not careful, if Parliament does not put on the brakes, does not find out the reasons why, there is a possibility of the country getting another shock of equal if not greater proportions than that served up by the Minister of Railways last week.
The taxpayer of Canada should keep both eyes on the Canadian Merchant Marine.
If Parliament does not put on the brakes, it says. Well, we are putting them on now.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Westinghouse brakes.

No, the Opposition brakes.
I would advise the taxpayers to keep their eyes on the Minister of Marine.
The minister persists in going ahead with this fQolish and insane scheme in the face of advice from practically all the papers supporting the Government, with the excep-

tion of a few clippings which my hon. friend gathered and handed back to the member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt). I do not believe fifty per cent of the members of the Government are honestly in favour of this enterprise, but they must support the proposition because their majority is getting narrow and they cannot afford to go against the Government.
We had a majority of thirty-eight the last time.
The time is coming fast when you will be glad to have a majority of three, and if I can help to bring that time any nearer, I am prepared to stay here.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Next week?

Well, the sooner the better. Now I am sure that if the minister consulted any schoolboy he would be advised not to squander this $8,000,000 of. the people's money on this insane project. I think we had better call a halt and save the people from disaster.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, since I have addressed this House, only a few moments ago, I have noticed with some astonishment, mingled with anxiety and even fear, I might say, that the Minister of Marine is left alone to pull himself out the best he can, in the discussion of an item in his budget, and which places him at the mercy not only of the Opposition, but also of that of his own Government friends. I am sorry to see that those who supported him in the past years, In the launching of his new policy of a Canadian merchant marine, abandon him entirely to-day. We have now been sitting all evening, even part of the night,-dawn is now breaking-and the only person, the only member on the right, the only minister who has spoken in the defence or helped in the triumph of the Meighen Government policy, was the hon. Minister of Marine. Three ministers sat in the House this evening: the Minister of Customs, the Minister of Public Works, and the Minister of the Interior. Yet not one came to his rescue. Why? I perceive the reason, Mr. Chairman, in the remark which was made by the Prime Minister himself, when he expressed doubts and fears on the future results of the colossal enterprise of the Minister of Marine. The item of eight million and some odd hundred thousand dollars,-which we have been debating for many hours, is not one which should be voted without giving it much thought; I
have already given my reasons why we should strongly oppose it. All my hon. friends who spoke before and after me are of the same opinion. When we consider the item which the Government wishes to have adopted, to-day, by this House and its eagerness to spend not in the interest of the Department of Marine but in the interest of a company called "The Government Merchant Marine, Limited", there is food for thought and we wonder what the Government is doing in other spheres. The Government must devote itself to the public welfare and supervise every thing where its activities find an opening, for instance: wharves and public works in the different provinces, and where they already exist, they must be kept in good condition of repair by the Government; it is its duty to look to these things. Some of these come under the Department of Marine, others are controlled by the Public Works Department.
In my own county there are some wharves which up to the present time were lighted at the expense of the Marine Department. The cost was about $1,000 per year. There was one at Cap a l'Aigle, one at Murray Bay and another at St. Irenee. What is happening to-day? Some time ago, I received a letter informing me that it was the intention of the Department of Marine, of the hon. minister himself and of his deputy minister, to cancel the subsidy which had been granted up to then for the lighting of these wharfs. What will happen when the steamboats of the "Canada Steamship Company" come down at night to this part of the county, to Murray Bay, Cap a l'Aigle and St. Irenee, when they will travel up and down the river; there will be no more lights on the wharves to accommodate travellers, the steamboats and even in some cases not only the boats of the "Canada Steamship Company" but also the Government's own boats. Last night, we were asked to allow the vote on this item of eight million and some odd hundred thousand dollars to go through, and this morning they still insist in having it shoved through; yet we are refused a grant of a few thousand dollars for these wharves. I called upon the deputy minister, Mr. Johnston, and pointed out to him that this was a disastrous policy which would occasion serious inconvenience, many disadvantages and even loss of life. The deputy minister, who that day was a busy man, did not pay much attention to me "Come in some other time, I am too busy at present".



If last night and this morning, we have strongly protested, as we are now doing, it is because the Government, through its representation: the minister, the deputy minister and those who have the care of the commonwealth, are not doing their duty. It is our right to demand from the Government that they look after the commonwealth as they should do. When the Government through its employees and its ministers refuse to do so, it is but just that the members of Parliament should assert the right of those they represent and refuse to pass the items which the Government to-day are pressing them to do. They do not bother about items of two, three, four or five thousand dollars, but they attach much importance to those running into millions, they are easier to shove through, the trick being done, the Government's supporter, those who sell paint for instance, obtain contracts and get rich.
Yesterday afternoon I brought before the House a resolution which came within the province of the Minister of Marine. I was asking for the establishment of a steamship service between Murray Bay, in the county of Charlevoix, and Tadoussac, in the county of Saguenay. You will allow me to say a few words in French on this matter, because this pertains as much to the Marine Department as to the Post Office Department or the Trade and Commerce Department. Nearly two years ago the Minister of Marine himself gave me permission to use the steamer Champlain which, up to that time, had been running between the north and south shores, between Murray Bay and Tadoussac, with calls at Cap a l'Aigle, Saint Fidele, Saint Simeon and Baie Ste. Catherine.
During the winter season 1919-1920 the service given by this steamer was a most satisfactory one. Now, what happened last spring? Friends of the Government offered to buy this steamer-the St. Lawrence Gulf Shipping Company, if I am not mistaken, represented by a man called Charles Barnard of whom our venerable friend, the member for Shelburne and Queen's, has had occasion to speak last night. I do not want to blame the right hon. Minister of Justice, but this Mr. Barnard happens to be his brother-in-law. I leave the conclusions to those wishing to draw them.
Since that time there has been no steamer service between those places. What happened? As I said yesterday afternoon there is nothing but a small boat going across from Baie Ste. Catherine to Tadous-

sac with the result that, during the spring, fall and winter months the traffic is four, five or six days late and that the mail can be carried1 only every second or third day and even only once a week.
Last year, when I criticised the Estimates of the Marine Department, I told the minister that, instead of spending considerable sums-he was then asking for twenty millions-he should not spend all of the amount voted, but save a small part for the constituents I have the honour to represent, a sum of two or three hundred thousand dollars, or grant them a subsidy of three, four or five thousand dollars to permit the establishment of a service between Murray Bay and Tadoussac. Nothing resulted from my request because the Marine Department have much more to do than look after the people of Charlevoix and Saguenay counties. They are busy doing big business. They deal extensively with the Dominion Steel, they carry law suits with this company before the Court of Exchequer; and also with the Nova Scotia Steel Company and the British Empire Steel Co. of which the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries was one of the directors until recently when he resigned to resume his duties as Deputy Minister, so as to give more time to the Canadian Mercantile Marine which was brought forth by the minister and himself. I have but one more thing to add; I have said it several times in the course of this debate, but I would rather say it over again, because the hon. members sitting to your right, Mr. Chairman, iare rather boneheaded. Although we tell them that they simply usurp power, that they hold no mandate to keep up this railway policy and to make the people swallow this policy of a mercantile marine which they are boosting to-day, they refuse to listen. The day will come, which is not far off, when after telling them: "Keep your hands off the public treasury," the electors of the Dominion will tell them in their turn what we, the members on the left side, are telling them to-day: "Leave the merchant marine alone, because this is not a good policy for the people of this country."-"Govern-mind your own business."
How many Government ships have been built and launched in the Port Arthur shipyards?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Six.
In what years were they launched?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: What time of year were they launched?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know the month, nor the day, nor the hour.
I am not quibbling on such minute information. I want to know approximately, within a month, the time of year these ships were launched.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will look up the information.
While the deputy is looking up that information, does not the minister think that as leading the House at this moment, as well as being minister in charge of estimates, he might report progress?
No chance; carry on.

My hon. friend from Renfrew is not leading the House, and I was not appealing to him. It might be well for the minister to consider that if one sitting of the House runs into the other it might become necessary to carry this vote by closure.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend think that is fair after the very plain obstructionist policy that has prevailed on the part of members
7	a.m. on the other side since somewhere about midnight? There has been a most deliberate attempt to delay the business of this country; yet the request is now made, at two minutes past seven in the morning, that the committee rise and report progress. All I can say is, certainly not.

I am not saying anything unfair, I am appealing to my hon. friend to think of his responsibility as leader of the House. Nor can I quite admit, having had considerable experience in Parliament, that the policy of the Opposition has been such as to deserve the characterization the minister has applied to it. The last time I was on my feet I pointed out that the minister never intervened without giving fresh facts upon which further appeals to him could be made as to what his policy really meant: I held out the olive branch to my hon. friend in more ways than one during the night and I thought it was no harm to ask the minister whether he had considered that.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I appreciate the courtesy which the hon. member always
evidences in this House. I have no reference to the hon. member or to those associated with him. But the official Opposition planned this obstruction and put it into effect. Is it fair, therefore, to call upon the Government to ask the committee to rise?
By what authority does the minister say that the Opposition planned obstruction tactics and carried them through.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: According to the evidence to-night.

The evidence as given by the hon. member for Red Deer is that no obstruction was offered. In fact, my hon. friends sitting to our left have taken a more emphatic stand if possible in regard to this item than the members of the official Opposition. No obstruction tactics were arranged or organized. The suggestion made by the hon. member for Red Deer is a proper one, and I again appeal to the minister to consider the course which he is taking. I have no apology to offer for my attitude. I have remained here this morning and I would remain much longer if I thought that the effect would be to prevent the wasteful expenditure of the people's money. The minister may have a very acute and definite knowledge concerning the transactions of his department but hon. gentlemen on this side have not that information, and the only way we can get it is by interrogating the minister when his Estimates are before the House. The minister, guardian of the treasury so far as his department is concerned, asks the people for $70,000,000 which he has virtually handed over without consulting the people to a company they know nothing about. I repeat, Sir, that the conclusions of the hon. member for Red Deer, who is an hon. member of considerable experience, are absolutely right, and I would feel that I was not doing my duty to my constituents, to Parliament or to the people if I did not utter the strongest protest of which I am capable against the procedure which has been adopted by the Government.
Is the minister in a position to answer my question?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Ships were
lounched ready to go to sea, on July 17, 1919, August 6, 1919, October 4, 1920, October 29, 1919, October 15, 1920, and November 17, 1919.
May I ask if these boats left the head of the lakes with cargoes or part cargoes?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know if that comes under the operation of ships.

Has
the Merchant Marine made any report to the Minister this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: None other than that which I presented to the House in my statement. Their annual report will be issued shortly.

I think we should have the advantage of that report before us before We are asked to vote this money. I am surprised my hon. friend undertook to charge the Opposition with obstruction. He has brought this upon himself by stating the other day that we had not opposed the passing of items for the construction of ships, and that consequently we had committed ourselves to the Government programme. We are now endeavouring to make our objections as plain as we can. It is not from this side of the House alone that opposition is coming. There is no newspaper in this country that has been so loyal to the present party as the Halifax Herald, and we have had extracts from that paper read to-night showing that the Herald is arousing the whole people of Nova Scotia on this question. The Ottawa Journal and the Montreal Gazette take the same view as the Halifax Herald of the Government's policy. You could not name three more loyal papers to the Liberal and Conservative party than these three, yet they are all protesting against the expending of this money.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: When the report of the Merchant Marine does come down, it will be an exact duplicate of the figures I have presented to this House already. I can say further that the annual report of the Board of Directors will not contain nearly such extensive information as I have given to the House.

The minister has told us that the amount placed to rest for depreciation is $667,665.46. On the same page you will find that between that amount and the depreciation reserve shown on the consolidated balance sheet there is a difference of $148,175.86.
Mr. BALLANTYNE.: That is the amount of depreciation carried over from last year and added to this.
There is no such amount in the 1919 statement as $148,000. I have looked for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I said that this amount of $150,000 was carried over from last year and added to this year's depreciation.	.

Then it should have appeared in last year's statement but it does not. It does not speak of $148,000, but of $1,056,767.38.
I admit that the minister is in an awkward position, and if he has not the information it is only fair that he should report progress. He said the other day that he was willing to give all information, and there is absolutely no reason why this item should be forced through. We are not trying to block the estimates, but we want to get information in view of the promise given by the minister on March 29, that he would inform the House on these matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the hon. member will read Hansard he will see that I offered to give every bit of information possible regarding contracts placed for steel ships between the Department of Marine and the shipbuilders. I am prepared to do that.

The minister should be
prepared to give information with regard to all of the operations of the Marine. There is an item of $148,000 in regard tc which we want to know something.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What is before the committee is the 1921 statement. The only item here that is taken from the 1919 figures is the item I have just given of $150, 994.46. I have given frankly and freely all the information I have.
I can quite understand that the minister feels we are pressing him too hard.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not at all.
The minister need not deny it. At the same time, we are not blocking his estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: You are.

That is not quite fair. In
the operating account you have an item for depreciation of $667,000, and in the same column you have an item for something like $880,000 for depreciation. The public will think there is something wrong, and someone has to prove where the differences come in.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Are you not satisfied to take the certificate of such a well known concern as Marwick, Mitchell and Company? If you are not going to accept the operating company's figures, audited by their own auditor, and this reputable firm, the Government cannot possibly do more.

The minister is a business
man; he has done business on a larger scale probably than any other man in this House, and he knows how far auditors can go and what information they can obtain. If he will read their statement, he will see that they add a qualifying clause that the information they get is according to the books of the company. They cannot possibly tell what the true facts are.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have seen hundreds of statements of various companies during my time. If an auditor comes to audit your business he has to get the information from you, and he must therefore say that his statement is based on information that is given to him. That is as far as any auditor can go.

That is what I say; it is
impossible for Marwick to be absolutely sure that these accounts are correct. Marwick does not know whether the outstanding liabilities are $22,000 or $222,000, and it a well known fact' that that item is not correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: How do you know it is not correct? My hon. friend must not suppose that the auditors can go to the Government Marine and make a cursory examination of the books. A firm like Marwick goes closely into these questions. The whole statement falls to the ground if we are to take the position my hon. friend is taking.

The minister does not know
whether this is really a profit or not, and I think I am right in saying that no shipping man in the world would make up a statement and say that the Government made money since the first of January on their ships. I do not believe there is a steamer in the world that has made any profits since the first of January, or at all events since September 1, last. And yet, in order to make a good showing, the company puts words into the mouth of the minister and makes him say that he made a profit of $183,000. There is no question that that cannot be correct, and this is another reason why the minister should furnish the Committee with information. The company estimated some $513,000 as profits they expected on unclosed voyages in 1919 and 1920, and the minister expects us to pass this item without any information. If there is one business in the world in connection with which the management cannot predict any sure profits it is the shipping business, and the minister of Customs (Mr. Wigmore) who is present must know that this business is the most precarious in the world. When a ship leaves port, although the owner may know what his expenses are going to be and what the cargo is, nevertheless he can never figure on what his profit will be. He can only tell when his crew are paid off. It is a shame that the Minister should be placed in such a position-to be made to father a statement of that kind, because any man who reads it must know that there is something wrong. There is no justification for figuring a profit of $350,000 on voyages which were not closed.
The minister told us on two occasions that these ships were built so as to increase Canada's export trade, but early this morning, finding that his previous statements would not hold water, he explained the presence of fifteen
8	a.m. ships in Halifax harbour by saying that they are going to be used in the coal trade. Well, they may as well be used in the carrying of coal as lie at anchor in Halifax harbour or take goods to foreign countries at-a loss. But the ministers's argument that his ships were built to increase export trade falls to the ground when he now says that he is going to use practically thirty-three per cent of his ships in the coal trade. Then, there is the curious fact that these ships were built on the Great lakes and subsequently taken elsewhere, although the minister in reply to the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) practically expressed his willingness this morning to place some of them on the Lakes. Surely that shows bad management somewhere.
Another statement made by the minister in regard to the operation of these ships is rather interesting-and this is a point on which I have not touched before. On page' 1331 of Hansard, in his statement of March 29th, the minister said:
With regard to the costs of operation, it will be found that a comparison of Canadian Government wage costs with like costs of operating similar ships by Great Britain, the United States, Japan, Norway and Prance, is as follows :	-
The monthly wage cost of a Canadian Government merchant marine ship of 8,100 tons

deadweight which carries a crew of 41, including 2 hoys, is $3,7'05. Published figures from an authentic source-(bulletin issued Iby Dow, Jones & Co., of New York), show the monthly wage cost of foreign ships of similar tonnage as being, for British ships $3,924 ; American, $5,3115; Norwegian, $3,378; and Japanese, $2,869.
But I find that quite a different statement in this regard appears in the report of the minister's department. It says:
The following is an approximate comparison of the cost of wages and board per month between a British, an American, a Canadian, and a Japanese steam merchant ship of similar tonnage and dimensions; cost of the British ship for wages and board per month $3,645.09, of the American $6,711.10, of the Canadian $2,3I0,3.50, and of the Japanese $1,124.50.
Now, Sir, I would like the minister to explain the discrepancy which exists between the figures given in these two statements. .

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The explanation
is that the figures given in the departmental report are a year old, whereas the statement I presented to the House, gave the figures up to date.

I notice also that in the departmental report it is stated that the pay of the master of the Canadian ship was $250 per month, and that of the master on a Japanese ship $100 per month, and that able seamen on the Canadian ship receive $16.20 per month, and on the Japanese ship $9 per month. Am I to understand that on the Government ships able seamen received last year only $16.20 per month?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am informed that my hon. friend is quoting from the parliamentary report, and that that is a ship of Canadian register operated by a Japanese crew.
It does not read that way. It says that an able seaman on a Canadian ship received $16.20 per month.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Those figures do not apply to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine at all but to a Japanese crew on a ship of Canadian register.
I should like to know who are the managers and directors of this merchant marine?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The maneger is Mr. R. B. Teakle, for many years with the Allan Line. The directors are Mr. Hanna, Mr. Mitchell, Colonel Cantley, Mr. E. R. Wood, Mr. Barnhill, and Mr. Reilly, of Winnipeg.

Mr. Teakle of Montreal may know something about shipping but none of the others do. I think the directors should be competent shipping men, and one
should be located at Halifax and another at Vancouver.

I would again point out to the minister where we have arrived in this matter, and make another appeal to him, such as I made an hour and a half ago. We have arrived at the position where reason does not prevail, where two sets of grown legislators have resorted to a policy, for some hours at least, of pure force or endurance. The vote before us is upon a policy which is very unpopular in the country. There is no difference on the Opposition side of the House in regard to the subject, and I venture to say that if we had an honest expression of opinion we should find very grave doubts among hon. gentlemen opposite as to the wisdom of this policy. As has been pointed out, three of the leading ministerial papers are opposed to this policy, the Halifax Herald, the Montreal Gazette and the Ottawa Joui-nal. I am pointing these things out in order to induce, if possible, a reflective frame of mind in my hon. friend. My hon. friends to my right cannot be moved; I have appealed to them. They at any rate are sure of defeat, and for this reason, that the Government has the machinery in its own hands by which this impasse can be brought to an end along proper and reasonable lines provided in the legislation of the country. If the Minister cannot get his vote without it, he can get it by the closure, as long as he has a majority behind him. Under these circumstances, what is the use of persisting?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot understand the reasoning of my hon. friend. Surely he can remember that the serious business of the House ceased at midnight when the member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) read a voluminous article in regard to certain ill-treatment which had been meted out to' some seamen on one of the ships. I asked him if he would be good enough not to read the article, as we had all seen it. Not only did he read it, but he deliberately started in again and read it over.

In response
to an invitation.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Since midnight we have listened to nothing but newspaper re-

ports from the Montreal Gazette, the Halifax Herald, and other papers. I could read reports from newspapers all over the country commending the Government Merchant Marine, but I have too much compassion on the committee to do that. My hon. friend from Red Deer attaches too much importance to what any newspaper says about the Government shipbuilding policy. If he thinks that the press of the country is opposed to that policy, the first time he is in the library let him read the newspapers and he will see that the majority of them are very much in favour of our shipbuilding programme.
Name some newspapers.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will not take up the time of the House doing so. Now, questions have been discussed all night and this morning which have been dealt with before, and as leader of the Government at the moment I will say frankly and freely that, in view of the systematic blocking of our estimates since midnight, I certainly will not, at a quarter to nine, agree to report progress.
I desire to correct the minister. He said that since twelve o'clock we have done nothing but quote newspaper reports.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I leave out the
hon. member.
Order.

Previously to twelve o'clock I did not say one word. The minister, I will admit, always answered me courteously, and I think he will admit that I never gave him any reason for making a statement of that kind in reference to myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My remarks had no reference to the Agrarian party, which is so well represented in this House today.

It would be ungracious of me not to acknowledge the generosity rf my hon. friend's afterthought. But that is only an illustration of the effect which the strenuousness of this sitting has had upon his intellect. The minister is not fit to go on with the game he is playing.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Do not be alarmed; I am all right.

I think my hon. friend is exhausted, and I would have to take with more than a grain of salt any figures
which he might give, unless they were well audited by someone else.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am perfectly sober.

I do not want to take issue with my hon. friend the minister, or to entreat him to report progress, but I will not permit his statement to go unchallenged, that there had been systematic blocking of the Estimates since twelve o'clock. The minister has occupied more time than any other member of the committee. The hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) in reading a second time the newspaper article referred to, was only courteously complying with a request from the other side. Now, the minister said he did not quote articles which he could have given by the dozen in commendation of his programme. Well, he had newspaper clippings before him and he deliberately gave them to another hon. gentleman to make use of, and in order that they might be read he had to request a member who had the floor to sit down. I challenge him to deny that statement. It is no use his raising his hands in holy horror and shedding crocodile tears on the misuse of time in this Chamber.
I have taken up a few minutes, and I can inform the hon. gentleman that I am prepared to stay here till three o'clock this afternoon or twelve o'clock to-night and see that the people's interests are safeguarded before this item passes.
Louder.

I will speak just as loud or as quietly as I want to. Now, we on this side will not permit the statement to go unchallenged that we have in any way blocked the Estimates. We have only exercised our right in asking for information which the minister should give us.

I did not say a word before twelve o'clock last night, and when I did criticise the Government, I did so mildly. When I read from a newspaper, the extract was very short and it was from a newspaper which, although condemning the Government in this case, usually supports it. I am glad the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid), who is the senior officer in this undertaking, is now in charge of the Estimates. We were told that the Canadian Pacific Railway had ships, and we were asked whether any person would say that they could be sold. The Canadian Pacific Railway ships, I am informed, are not of the kind that we are spending money on.

They are passenger liners running on established routes, while our ships are tramp vessels running all over the country looking for cargo. We were told also that the Canadian National Railway Company could not get along without ships. Well, the Canadian Pacific Railway got along very well without ships. I know that the Great Northern, one of the best railways in the United States, ventured on the shipping business, and went out of it because it was not profitable. But the Canadian Pacific Railway are organized and equipped to take care of international trade to a larger extent than any other organization in the world. I am quite sure the Minister of Railways will not claim that the Canadian Merchant Marine has been an acquisition to the earning power of the Canadian National Railways. It is a mistaken idea that you can assist the National Railways by carrying cargo from South Africa to South America or from Texas to Liverpool. Now, the Government must not try to evade responsibility in this matter by placing it in the hands of an irresponsible body. They have taken a course that will naturally create a great deal of opposition. The Prime Minister, about twenty-four hours ago, appointed a committee to look into the whole question of railways and shipping, and a very few hours after that the Minister of Marine came down with his Estimates and wanted to put this very large sum of money through for his shipbuilding programme. He insisted that he had a programme; that he was going on with it; that nothing would induce him to part with these ships. Well, if any one was unreasonable, it was the Minister of Marine. I hope, therefore, that when the Minister of Railways comes to pass his estimates he will be more generous in the matter of giving information; and that now that he is in the Chamber, he will by furnishing all the information possible, refrain from obstructing the estimates of the Minister of Marine. I do not hesitate to say that I should be glad to obstruct this item if by so doing I could prevent its being passed. I am quite willing to take the responsibility of obstructing in this case; I only wish I could obstruct more successfully than it seems to be in the power of the Opposition to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I think it is hardly fair for the hon. member to say that the Government ships are not bringing traffic to the railways. Last summer I discussed the matter with Mr. Phillips, our agent in London, and he mentioned the fact that our

ships collected a cargo in South Africa, I think it was, for Canada.
What products come from South Africa to Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It was a port in Africa or some other foreign country that Mr. Phillips mentioned. In any case, he said that there was a full cargo from that country to Canada. When our vessels go to England or to ports in foreign countries in that part of the world, they do bring return cargoes, and consequently our railways get the benefit.
Are these cargoes supposed to be shipped to ports where our own railroads will get the traffic?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: If it is a cargo that we can collect for Canada, our railway gets the benefit of it when it is landed.
But in the case of Canadian Pacific freights, would they go to our roads, or to the Canadian Pacific Railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: They work together in order to get a cargo for the vessel. If the Canadian Pacific would ship their freight by our vessel, we would get that advantage; otherwise they might have to send it on one of their own ships or on a tramp vessel at a later date.
If they gave you their freight to take care of, you would hand it over to them at a port where they would secure the railway haulage?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: If our agent could get' a full cargo at some point, say in South Africa, our vessel would take it. If the Canadian Pacific agent had a part cargo, we might take it and let them receive it at this end. Now, a number of these smaller ships could be used between Sydney and Montreal in the carrying of coal.

I have pointed out that it is the experience of the manager of the Dominion Coal Company that small ships did not pay in the coal trade and that they found it wiser to use larger ships with big hatches for operation between Nova Scotia and Montreal. If my hon. friend has any large ships, I would advise him to use them in that coal trade, unless he wants to lose money on the business. There may be use for the small ships somewhere, but evidently that is not the place to put them.

As one of the members who earlier in the night made a few quota-

tions, I wish to say that I have no apology to make for doing so. The Minister of Marine, of course, would not enjoy my reading of the editorial from the Montreal Gazette. I quoted also from the report of the Royal Bank. Any objection on the part of the Minister of Marine to these quotations would be not because of their length, but because they expressed distinct disapproval of his policy. The Minister said some time ago that the Opposition had planned this obstruction. Now, I have noticed that the Minister of Marine always brings up his estimates when they are least expected. Last year, when he was quite aware that a number of members from Quebec were objecting to estimates for the Canadian Navy, he made a point of bringing those estimates down on Saturday evening, when many hon. members from Quebec would be away. But it happened that we were not away; the discussion proceeded forced until midnight, and the Minister was obliged to bring his estimates up on another day. On the present occasion, the minister comes down with his estimates on Monday, private members' day, and at a time when quite a number of members were attending in Montreal the funeral of a former member of the late Laurier administration. It was wholly improper that the minister, about half-past eleven at night, and on such an occasion should ask the committee to consider an important item respecting the merchant marine. Yet the minister wonders why his estimates are not well received and why we raise objection. If he would give notice in the ordinary way that the estimates of the merchant marine would be taken up tomorrow or on a day named, possibly he would not be subjected to this particular treatment. This is a very important item, calling for the expenditure of $8,000,000. I think the point made by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) is a very strong one-that next year the minister will come down and ask for more millions in connection with his ship-building policy.
This item is a large one compared with some of the other items of the different departments. For the Justice Department, which is a very important department, we find the Government is well satisfied with an item of $2,181,000, as will be seen by reference to pages 11, 12 and 13 of the Estimates. For the Agricultural Department, page 24 of the Estimates, all that is asked is $4,500,000, plus another $1,000,000 authorized by statute. For the carrying on of this important service, which we cannot do without, the Government is satisfied with $5,500,000. But they ask us to vote $8,000,000 for the Merchant Marine, which service results in annual deficits, and we do not know when it will end. I think this comparison is very edifying, and we might refer to the Immigration Department, page 25 of the Estimates. That department is satisfied with $1,500,000, and possibly a few hundred thousand more, to carry on the work of the department. It is absolutely out of place that the Government should ask us to vote $8,000,000 for this fantastic Merchant Marine with which we are loaded. The Department of Health is a most important department, dealing with medicine, hospitals, quarantine stations and so on; but the Government is well satisfied with $700,000 for that department. On page 50 of the Estimates we find that the Government is only asking $2,465,000 for the Lighthouse and Coast Service. This service is not intended for ships which are empty, which the Government did not know where to send or what to put into, but this is a very important service for the general steamship trade of the country. I will not say the amount is not large enough, but, when compared with other items, it seems very reasonable. But by comparison the amount asked for the Merchant Marine is much too large. The amounts asked for by the Fisheries Department, the Labour Department, the Dominion Lands Department, or any other department are smaller than the amount asked for by the Merchant Marine. I think it is unfair that the Minister of Marine should refuse the Committee to rise.
I join with the hon. members on the other side of the House in greeting the Right Hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has just taken his seat. He is a sensible gentleman, and I feel quite sure that when we put our case before him he will advise his colleagues to rise and report progress. I think he will agree that it is utterly improper to ask us to vote this amount this morning. This is Private Members' day, the item is important, and the attendance in the House is very slim. I appeal to the good sense and the prolonged experience of the Right Hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) as to whether we are not right in asking the Committee to rise. We are entitled to more information, and it is not at all unreasonable to ask that this item should stand over for further discussion. When we try to speak from our own knowledge and experience in such matters

we are jeered at and referred to as members who did not know much about the question. When we cite quotations from papers supporting the Government, or from reports of presidents of great financial institutions, we are charged with obstruction and an endeavour to kill time. I think the hon. minister has failed to appreciate the earnest desire of members on this side of the House to obtain information, and perform their duties as representatives of the people. The hon. Minister of Marine argued that the Merchant Marine was a war measure and that when he started shipbuilding he had done it as if he thought the war was going to last forever; he said this was a very proper thing and we could take no chances. He said that while other nations were building wooden ships he would not follow their example, because the ships would be of no use after the war, and we would be loaded with them. My hon. friend had a double mind, a war mind as regards steamships and a peace mind as regards wooden ships.
The experiment of the Government in public ownership was disastrous, and was an utter national catastrophe in regard to railways, and we should not make the same mistake with shipbuilding. The Minister of Marine says that if we have the ships and the railways working together we will have different results and possibly a surplus. The deficits that are creeping up in the Merchant Marine are liable to become as great as the deficits in the administration of the railways. Some day in the future the Minister of Marine will say that it is all right, we have deficits in the railways and in the Merchant Marine, but that is because there is a missing link, and we should build aeroplanes to run in connection with the ships and the railways. When Sir Vincent Meredith, Sir Herbert Ames, and the newspapers supporting the Government condemned these policies, it was about time to stop. I would urge that the Rt. Hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce should advise his colleagues that further discussion should be postponed.

I have not had the pleasure of sitting the seance through to-night, but I recall old times when I have seen daylight streaming through the window. My hon. friend from St. James (Mr. Rinfret), has appealed to me to ask members on this side of the House to agree to rise and report progress. In order to report progress, we will have to show that some item has been passed which would

indicate that we have made some progress. The item before the House is one for the fulfillment of contracts already let. I am informed that not a single contract for which this money is being asked has been let since the last session of Parliament. These contracts were in conformity to a policy which had been supported and received an affirmative vote in the House, and the contracts were let in the line of a policy which had been determined upon in the House. The contracts having been let and the work having gone on, they must be proceeded with and the contractors must be paid, and the money necessary to complete the vessels must be voted, so as to bring them upon the water, where they can produce returns. Is it reasonable under the circumstances to refuse the vote for the completion of this Work? We have our differences as to policy in this House, but Parliament can never proceed with its work unless the majority rules. The previous vote received the approbation of the House and the money was voted. Is it supposable now that the Government is going to back up, and that no money should be voted to complete the work? That is impossible. If that were done the Government could not retain its self-respect, and could not function. The Government must give such information as can properly be given. I venture to say that no new matter has been introduced during the debate and the subject is worn thread-bare. If the Government is to function they must have the money to carry on the established policy.

My right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce has made a brief speech on this subject, but he suffers very great difficulty in not having heard the discussion during the night. If he had heard that discussion he would not have ventured on one of the arguments that he used^ and certainly would not have ventured on the guess that he has made as to what has been going on. He says that if progress had been made he would willingly accede to the request to report progress. That is an endeavour on his part to get round what is ordinary parliamentary formula. He has frequently taken part in the reporting of progress when no item had been voted. I will try to show him that progress has been made during the time he has been enjoying a much-needed rest. His argument is based exclusively on the fact that this $8,000,000, equal to one-fifth of the total expenditure, roughly speaking, of this whole Dominion at the time my right hon. friend ended his

period as financial adviser of the previous Conservative administration, is to complete a contract. In this shipbuilding scheme the Government has not shown any very great respect for contracts. They had a contract in connection with this very scheme with the Dominion Iron and Steel Company of Nova Scotia, a contract in good faith I presume, to take 250,000 tons of steel from the Dominion Iron and Steel Company for this shipbuilding project. Only 40,000 tons have been delivered, and this Government who, my hon. friend says, must observe the sacredness of contract in connection with building ships has cancelled the steel contract and arbitration proceedings are going on now to settle their account with the Dominion Iron and Steel Company.
My right hon. friend also ventured upon the guess that no new matter came out during the night. I may say that a great deal of new matter came out during the night, and I will deal with the new matter in referring to the short speech which the Minister of Railways made just now, of which I did not hear the whole, but which I venture to refer to in regard to the part which I did hear.
He was saying, when I had to leave the House a few minutes ago, that this government building of ships was primarily a war measure. Now, I venture to take direct issue with my hon. friend, if he means that it was a war measure undertaken, of necessity, by the Government. We elicited very important information in regard to that during the night-very important, as far as I was concerned, during the period since twelve o'clock which my hon. friend, the Minister of Marine said a few minutes ago had practically been wasted. That hon. minister himself told us that when this shipbuilding scheme of this Government was taken up, the Imperial Munitions Board had been for some time engaged at fourteen different points in Canada, marshalling all the forces that Canada could spare of men and material for shipbuilding; had been doing all that Canada could do in addition to her almost superhuman efforts in the field. I take the ground that the hon. Minister of Railways could not have known all about this scheme or he would not have claimed that this was undertaken in the first instance as a war measure. It was transferred from the Imperial Munitions Board, who were doing the work splendidly, and who would have had this very great advantage in the doing of
the work, that they would have been able to stop it at the end of the war,-transferred not the better to attend to the war, but transferred to the Dominion Government with this idea in the back of the hon. Minister's head-and I take it with this idea also in the Government's head-that the busines might be undertaken [DOT] as a Canadian work, and the benefits presumably passed into the pockets of Canadians; so, I say, the defence that this was a war measure falls to the ground. The Minister of Railways has used the argument in this House-and we have heard it during the night, we heard it last evening-that the shipping scheme of the Government is a necessary complement of the National Railways. Well, now, the thing that we cannot get over in that connection is this: This Dominion is very short of money at the present time, all railroad extensions within Canada have had to cease, and I commend the Government for their firmness in that connection. We have had a report in connection with the Canadian railways which, to say the least, of it, ought to make every member of this House, whether on the Government or on the Opposition side, anxious about the financial condition of these roads and the financial condition of the whole country. The duty of the Opposition comes in at this point to find out exactly what is going to be done with the vote of $8,000,000 and what the Government hope for. Now, if we are to regard the shipping scheme as the complement of the railway scheme, and if we could have the assurance that the shipping scheme was going to be such a success in the next few years, that it will help the railways out of the hole, we on this side of the House should be satisfied. Will the Minister of Trade and Commerce say he has any hope that this shipping scheme will help the railroad scheme?
Certainly.

My hon. friend says " Certainly," then he must prove to us how two deficits will mhke a surplus. That is the financial difficulty that is bothering the humble individuals on this side of the House. I do not know who it was who interrupted me with that confident adverb, " Certainly." Whoever used it is omniscient in railroad and shipping matters. If he believes that this shipbuilding scheme, this building of ships at a time when ships are a drug, not only in the Canadian market, but in the markets of the world, is

justified economically and will help in the railway situation, to meet the deficits on the railways of forty millions last year and seventy millions, this year,-well, we cannot see how two deficits are going to make a surplus, and how a small deficit is going to help to meet a bigger one. I want to get to very close quarters with this scheme, and I want to tell the right hon. the Prime Minister and the Government exactly what is troubling him, and to give my right hon. friend, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, some information that we have received during the night. I wonder if my right hon. friend has any idea how many of these ships are in Halifax harbour at the present time. I do not think he know's. Well, we have been here all night, and we have the information. There are fifteen of them. I do not think they are two years old. And what are they doing in Halifax harbour? The Halifax Herald, a journal which generally supports this Government with might and main says they are tied up to the wharves and doing nothing. We heard during the night from the minister that they were being overhauled. Well, the overhauling of fifteen ships within two years of being turned out by this Government is a pretty serious operation for the people of this country. And what else is going on at Halifax? Will he (Sir George Foster) believe that, with these fifteen ships tied up in the Halifax harbour and their counterparts sailing over the seven seas seeking cargoes in Scandinavian and other ports, and not finding them; with their capital value cut in the middle

there are now two new ships being built in Halifax harbour? Does he not think this is a work of supererogation and that there is danger of financial disaster if this policy is continued? Does my right hon. friend wonder that we, on this side of the House, are anxious and that we do not want this work to go further without the country being fully apprised of the facts and understanding the situation of the shipping scheme at the present moment? Why, I ventured to indulge in a flight of imagination during the night. I wondered if a man from Mars, if he were intelligent, who came to Halifax harbour for the first time and looked over it with one of the Government supporters and saw the condition of affairs-I wondered what he would think of the inhabitants of this planet and especially of this country and the members of the Dominion Government. He would naturally say, " Well, what are these 
fifteen ships doing here idle? They look to be pretty new. The paint is hardly off them." He would have to be informed, " They are getting overhauled. They have been for two years pulling us out of our railroad deficit, and they have now come into this harbour to be overhauled." Now, if he were of an inquisitive turn of mind he would take the Government supporter to where the two new ships were being built and ask: " What are these ships for?" " Oh, these are new ships to join the company of the idle ships that are getting overhauled." Then what would he say? If, as I have presumed to imagine Mars is inhabited by intelligent people he would say " Get me an aeroplane, and let me go back to the planet Mars where there are intelligent people, for I cannot find any intelligence in the Dominion Government." He would be compelled to say that if he were intelligent, which I have presumed to imagine.
I had sworn to myself I would not say any more about the merits of this scheme. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine will tell the House I have occupied very little time during the night. Indeed for the last four or five hours the men who have been debating the merits of this scheme have been growing so strong that I could not get a word in edgeways except to promote walking in the paths of peace. I have been endeavouring in the last four or five hours to get the Minister of Marine to listen to reason, and as I am on my feet I will tell my right hon. friend (Sir George Foster) the advice I have been giving him. I have pointed out to him that this scheme is doubtfully popular, that the Government's hold in this House is a slender one, that their tenure of the country is still more doubtful, and that it would have been the part of wisdom to use the legal regular machinery for terminating this debate. I fully concede-my right hon. friend knows I concede it before I say so, and as I have said before on critical occasions this session-a government is constitutionally a government as long as it has a majority of the House behind it. But my right hon. friend knows	his	Shakespeare:	"It is excellent to have a	giant's	strength, but itis tyrannous	to	use it	like	a giant,"and what	I	tried	to	impress
upon the immature and inexperienced parliamentary mind of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was that it would be a wise thing to let the few of us who feel very keenly on this sub-

ject go home some hours ago and then he could meet the House later and put his estimate through by the legalized procedure of the closure. What are we going to gain by sitting here hour after hour? I do not know what the proper machinery will be for bringing this seance, as my right hon. friend has called it, to a close. I am not very well up on how the guillotine is operated in this country, but I understand that notice is needed. In any case I refer this matter to my right hon. friend in a conciliatory spirit, which the Minister of Marine will admit I have displayed again and again at this sitting-I said hours ago that as far as I was concerned I did not believe in the policies of force. I have only a distant connection with my hon. friends to the right; I was only supported by one member of the Progressive group for hours; so that I could not do more than suggest a certain line of conduct. We have arrived at an impasse in which physical force is being used. Now the closure is physical force, but it is physical force reinforced by reason, and carried out in a reasonable way. And I say to my right hon. friend, (Sir George Foster) who is now leading the House, that he should consider that aspect of the case. We cannot refuse the estimate; the Government is in power, and we cannot refuse it. But we can surely take two nights to discuss it, and if the night runs into the morning, then it is an obstinate minister that is to blame and not an inquisitive Opposition. May I show my right hon. friend the reasonableness of what I am saying by reminding him that ten years ago he himself took a leading part in holding up estimates, in holding up the House of Commons against the beneficent measure of reciprocity, most of which he himself has since helped to carry, and he did that not for two nights only, but for days and days, and weeks and weeks, and almost months, until he forced the Liberal Government to go to the country. Now there is no power in an Opposition to do that now, because my right hon. friend has the closure as every civilized country in the world has been compelled to have it, so it is only a question of following properly arranged and legalized machinery, instead of methods which are perfectly natural to a strong-minded and decided character who has spent his life in business, like my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, but are utterly foreign alike to the nature and experience of my right hon. friend who leads the
House. I pray the Minister of Marine to postpone his eagerness to get his estimate through, and to consider the new matter we have brought out during the night in as favourable a light as he can, and to meet me half way, and seize the olive branch which I offer on behalf of the recalcitrant group to my right.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I rise to endorse the appeal made to the Government by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) that they may consent to adjourn and report progress.
I heard a moment ago the hon. Minister of Commerce (Sir George Foster) who had just re-entered the House and upon whom we counted to induce his colleagues to show themselves amenable to common sense, say that it was difficult to report progress as no progress had been made. It seems to me on the contrary that we have accomplished much. The members of this Parliament who opposed this item of eight million dollars have spent the night here defending the interests of the country and trying to obtain information which, unfortunately, were denied them by the Minister of Marine. The only information we obtained-I heard the hon. member for Red Deer mention it a moment ago-is that at the present moment there are fifteen vessels lying idle in the port of Halifax. It is most astonishing that the Minister of Marine should come before this House and ask for a vote of eight million dollars for boats when we already have more boats than what we know what to do with.
The hon. Minister of Commerce pretended that it is a matter of abiding by a contract. I am much astonished at hearing members of the Government speak of abiding by a contract. I remember many contracts which the Government repudiated; many times when their word had been given they broke their word. I find them now strangely ticklish on the point of honour and of abiding by their word. They have not accustomed us to this.
Eight millions is an enormous sum while we only vote four millions for the Department of Agriculture. Do you not think it would be more to the point to vote eight millions for model farms, for the improvement of means of communication in the rural districts? It seems to me that eight millions given for the development of agriculture would be the very best investment at present.
We are opposed to the merchant fleet because we believe we don't need it. I heard

members of the Government tell us, "But you, of the Liberal party, have you not favoured a marine, have you not advocated a marine?" Quite so, Mr. Chairman, but to-day circumstances are altogether different. We are no longer in pre-war times, when the German danger was abroad. It seems to me that now every dollar should be used for reconstruction and for the promotion of agriculture, and not for building boats, which is throwing money away. I now ask of the Government not to force us to sit day and night until they have their gag ready. I humbly invite them to be willing to abide by common-sense, in order to allow the members of this House to go and rest. It seems to me that it should not be necessary to talk to them for days and nights in order to make them understand that an expenditure of eight millions for boats at the present time is an extravagance which we, on this side of the House, cannot allow to pass. If the Government want absolutely this item to be adopted, there is no use in our sitting here any longer, let them have the courage to rise, let the right hon. Minister of Commerce, who is now leading the House (Sir George Foster) rise boldly and put on the gag, the machine which they invented and patented in order to silence us. We shall leave the matter to the electors of the country for them to pronounce between the two parties. We shall submit to the gag here, confident as we are that they will understand that we have acted as we have through love of duty and care for their interests.
You know it, Mr. Chairman, the Government no longer possesses the confidence of the country. The Government have no mandate and the electors would be much surprised if we did not oppose this expenditure. I say that this expenditure is not necessary, first because the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) is at a loss for taxes to meet the interest on our war debt. From January to December he racks his brain to find means for meeting our liabilities. Then, why this expenditure which, in my judgment, is quite useless? I heard a few days ago the right hon. Prime Minister say that owing to the financial situation, he had decided to reduce by 25 per cent the bonus for the civil servants. The Government have no money to pay the civil service, and they ask us to vote eight millions to build ships which we don't need, probably with the object of benefiting political friends.

Mr. Chairman, why does the Minister of Marine seem to take offence? I heard him say, about six o'clock this morning: "The hon. members of the Opposition have spent the whole night reading newspaper extracts and repeating the same thing over and over again." Why, are we not justified in taking every possible means to prevent the adoption of this item? And since the hon. ministers will not yield to common sense and to the arguments submitted by us, is it not our right and our duty to resort to the constitutional means at our disposal, in order to check this expenditure? As I said a moment ago, since the Government is unwilling to supply any information or to pay any heed to our arguments, let them have no hesitation in resorting to force. As a general rule, they are not afraid to do so. Why should they spend all this time uselessly? Why not apply the gag right away?
I do not think Parliament would be justified in voting this item. I say, again, that when we are bound to burden ourselves with such sacrifice, when the ratepayers of this country have to disburse such enormous amounts in the shape of taxes, when the Minister of Finance keeps imposing tax over tax, it is unreasonable on the part of the Government to have us vote items amounting to eight millions, without even supplying the information that all the members of this House have a right to get.	.
The Minister of Marine seems to become extravagant, or rather has he always been so.
