I understand that a man, used as he is to handle millions, may be unable to fancy that we would reduce the amount of the vote he is asking; but he must remember that all the rate-payers and citizens of this country have not had, like himself, the good fortune to belong to all kinds of companies paying big dividends and having paid still larger dividends, during the war, on account of the war. We, citizens of this country, who are sitting on this side of the House, belong to the people, and we ask, in the name of the people, that the members of the Government should return to the right path and yield to our legitimate demand. Should the Government wish to go on with the debate in this style, let them be assured of our strength, of our resolution, of our earnest desire to do our duty to the extent of sitting here as long as they may like us to. We are ready, however, to adjourn; but let not the Government or the Minister of Marine fancy that they are going to wear us out. Perhaps we are not the majority, but we have the

courage and we know that we are performing our duty. We are not so numerous as is the other side of the House, but I may well say, Mr. Chairman, that we have the satisfaction to know that we are doing our duty by sticking to the position we did take, and, thank God, the members of the Opposition will keep doing their duty to the last minute. Useless is it for the Government to think or to fancy that they will wear us out. We are going to follow them up and I do not think they should resist any longer. Let them use the gag, the weapon which they are so fond of, the public is in expectation of that, after all. Here is what my electors have kept telling me for a long time: "Doctor, you hold a seat in the House, you allow to pass all manner of expenditure to the amount of millions, we are driven to wretchedness, the city is filled with unemployed people, the shops are closed, we shall soon have to depend on public assistance to save our citizens from starving." Meanwhile, the magnates of the Government, the millionaires, the presidents of the big companies will force us to sit during the whole night because they wish to get more millions and to keep on piling up money for themselves and their political friends. How is that?
I think I voice the wish of my electors in rising to speak at this hour of the day, and I am sure they will give me credit for it. It is my candid opinion that the Government is wrong and should not persist in its pertinacity, it being admitted that pertinacity is an ill-adviser. I am surprised to see that the hon. Minister of Commerce, who has so much experience, who has grown old in politics, does not make his colleague, the Minister of Marine, listen to reason. I understand that the Minister of Marine may be liable to stubbornness as he is younger, more fiery, more enthusiastic, and as he has been a minister for just a couple of years, but the Minister of Commerce, an old man who has spent fifty years of his life in politics, should not listen to this ill-adviser called stubbornness, he should rather bring the members of the Government back to reason and say to them: "Since the Opposition is eager to obtain further information, since they will not let this item pass before they have been supplied with sufficient information, all right, we will adjourn and give them the information they want."
Moreover, the members of the Government and more particularly the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, know this by experience. It was not my privilege to
occupy a seat in this House at the time of the reciprocity measure, but I have been told that the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce had led obstructionist tactics against that measure for months. That shows once more that a stubborn man never wants woe. A few years ago, the members of the Government, who were then in Opposition, fought against that policy which was to bring happiness to every farmer of this country; to-day you may see them ready to run to Washington asking for favours and willing to accept anything. Why should we not make the most of past experience and why, glancing backwards, seeing that ten years ago he committed serious blunders to the detriment of the country, does not the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce listen to reason and acknowledge for once at least that we are right and should have every needed information? For, after all, when it is a matter of spending the people's money, Mr. Chairman, if you only knew how conscientious, how timorous I am. Had the hon. Minister of Marine himself to pay the eight millions, I can assure you he would not be so much in a hurry and would willingly grant the wish of those who surround him and who want some explanations. Unfortunately the money belongs to [DOT]the people and they do not care when spending other people's money.
Mr. Chairman, I beg the hon. Minister of Marine to think the matter over. It seems to me that his political training would have caused him to act otherwise, but I realize that his connection with the hon. members on the other side of the House has quite altered his nature. Formerly, when he was president of the Montreal Harbour Commissioners, the hon. Minister of Marine would not have had that Tory tendency towards compelling people to vote millions of dollars without even supplying them with the necessary information. It hurts me to see that he has agreed to sit on the other side of the House where, coming in touch with such sinners, he has become a greater sinner than them. Once more, I believe it is useless for the Government to hold on. Were they to compel us to sit until three o'clock in the afternoon, their situation would not be any fairer nor any better.
Besides, the whole press of this country, save those papers that are paid to stand by the Government, the fairly independent press that ponders is against that expenditure for the marine; the press that often

sides with the Government is opposed to all this expenditure. What is the reason of that stubborn determination to build a fleet, in spite of the members of this House, were they free to act according to their convictions; for, could we read what is in the heart of every member on the other side, we would see that, like us, they are against that expenditure. However, the rod brings them into submission and besides they fear the elections. These gentlemen know very well that were they by a mishap to compel the Government to go before the people, they would never come back here. I am afraid interest is the prime mover in their actions, I apprehend we will not have a free and independent jury in this House so as to do justice to the people, because they are too selfish.
It seems to me that persons having as much experience as the members of the Government have should halt a moment, think the matter over and realize they are going astray. They may by such an expedient, thanks to their majority, hold on to power until next year, until the elections, but they must know that by such a behaviour, by ignoring the voice of the people, by gagging the House, they are doing unpopular acts which the electorate will be well able to judge at the proper time. I am not here to offer any advice to the Government-God forbid such a pretension on my part-but it seems to me they ought to reflect. Sometimes a fair word does no harm, no matter where it comes from, be it from the most humble being, from the most unassuming workingman. Before resuming my seat, I say once more to the members of the Government to think it over, to see in what situation they are placing themselves before the country and the electorate. From my own viewpoint, they might above all let the committee report progress because, after all, the farther they go along that path, the more they harm themselves in the eyes of the electorate, so for us on this side who are raising objections, we deem that in doing so we are doing our duty, that in acting in that way we are keeping our trust as the representatives of the people. At this time, when we have no money, when industries have had to close, when the people are in distress, it seems to me that it is a most unpardonable -extravagance to ask us to vote a million dollars, especially when this money is to be voted without serious thought being given to it, without the necessary information. I think the members of Parliament have certain

rights. I understand that we are not entitled to such privileges as are enjoyed by members of the Government, I admit that we are very modest, very humble, that we do not, as does the hon. Minister of Marine, belong to powerful companies, yet, I think that we are entitled to fair play, and that the Government are wrong in refusing to give the information that we have been asking for. Besides, has not every member the right to obtain full information? What would our electors say should we vote millions of dollars without requiring that the Government render us a detailed and conscientious account of such expenses as have been made?
Mr. Chairman, it is most important that the members of the Opposition fulfil their duty, and let me say so, we shall read with pride and satisfaction, in the papers, that we have fought bravely all night through, so as to bring the Government to its senses.
I would like to say one word more before I resume my seat. I notice that the hon. Minister of Marine is not in his seat, but I hope that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid') or the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce will stand up and declare that they are ready to give, in to our fair request, and as they are not well informed and they are not sufficiently acquainted with all the items, since it is because of ignorance on their part that we cannot obtain any information, let us grant them the benefit of the doubt:	I hope they
will soon adjourn so as to allow them to secure this information, which they can afterwards impart to us.
In behalf of the country, in behalf of those whom I have the honour to represent, I beseech the Government to do justice to our claim, to do right by our country, and I ask all the members of the Opposition to stand firm in their rights so that the Government shall surrender.

(Translation.) I wish to ask my hon. friend a question concerning the ships which are in the harbours of St. John and Halifax. It appears that there are at the present moment fifteen ships at Halifax:	Does my hon. friend know how
many of those ships which are now in St. John's harbour belong to the Department of Marine?
I believe that the Government ships which are at present in the St. John's Harbour are absolutely idle.

Mr. Chairman, members
on the other side of the House have been accusing those on this side of obstructing,

stating that we had formed plans and schemes to obstruct the Government; but as one of the members who have been sitting here all night I wish to assure the hon. minister that that has not been" my purpose. It is not a matter of pleasure or a matter of satisfaction to sit here all night; I am here to get information on both sides, as far as possible. I wish to hear the arguments for and against. I have heard a good deal of sound argument showing why this marine should not have been undertaken. Our friends on this side of the House have been asking for information, and I am very sorry to say they got but little. The least the minister of this department, or the minister of any other department, in bringing estimates before the House and asking to have them voted, could do would be to come forward with all the necessary information possible. Suppose this marine were undertaken by private corporation, and the general manager of the corporation at a general meeting came before the directors, and they asked him a lot of questions, and he said "Oh no, I do not feel like giving you this information," do you think they would tolerate that kind of thing from their manager or president or any other officer? It appears, we have constructed some 47 vessels and put them afloat. I believe we should have the date that every vessel was launched and a statement of the cargoes they carried, and what money they made or lost, separately. Then when we had this information as to the prospects or outlook for those vessels as a paying investment, we would probably have more courage to go on and vote more money to complete the project, but I have sat here all night trying to obtain information. I have not voted either on this question or any other question without information, and I do not propose to vote on this question until I get all the information possible, so that I may form a sound and as well-reasoned judgment as I can as to whether this project was a wise or foolish one.
After listening to the argument and the information given, from what little knowledge I have of the shipping business I concluded that it was the height of foolishness for this Government to undertake to build vessels at all. During the war no doubt everybody was doing everything possible in the way of building ships and making munitions; and all this kind of thing, for the purpose of winning the war. Every manufacturer in this country was busily engaged in making munitions of war. But
when the war was over we stopped, immediately shut up the shops and ceased making munitions. Why did they not do the same thing with shipbuilding? But they say, "These contracts were let." Was it wisdom on the part of the Government to let contracts which would not be completed for three years? Why did they not let the contract for the building of one or two or three vessels, but not more than could be finished within six months, and when that one was completed, if the war was still continuing, and we needed more vessels, let the contract to build another? But the letting of contracts by the Government for the building of some 63 or 64 vessels at a cost of some $60,000,000 to $70,000,000, and coming to the House and saying they were built for war purposes, is worse than nonsense-it was foolishness.
Ever since I came to the House, I have questioned the wisdom-or the foolishness- of constructing so many railways. Indeed,, the consensus of opinion on both sides is that too many railways have been built. But the Government have said: "Oh, yes, but it was your party which commenced these railways, and we had to finish them." In 1911, when the then Opposition appealed to the electors for support, their cry in the Eastern Townships was that the then Government, of which the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier was the leader, were not business men, and hon. gentlemen then stated to the people that if they were returned to power they would adopt and apply business principles. Well, if they had carried out their undertaking, the very very first thing they would have done upon taking office would be to carry out an investigation of the railway projects and of any projects involving the considerable expenditure of public money with a view to seeing whether the expenditure was wise or unwise. Then, as business men, they should have caused any projects found to be unwise and uncalled for to be discontinued right then and there. But my hon. friends did not do that; yet they come to us now and say: We "were simply completing what you people commenced. The least we would expect from intelligent men-and I think there are some intelligent men on that side of the House- is that they would profit by the mistakes made in connection with the building of railways. If experience is worth anything, was not the building of transcontinental lines, for which there is no traffic, not a simple reason for caution before any programme of building vessels was undertaken? There is some justification for the



building of railways, even if traffic is not offering for them at the moment; there is the possibility of developing our natural resources and of encouraging settlement. But the building of ships is quite a different matter; a ship built at Halifax can sail any sea and call at any port. Before the war shipping was not a paying proposition; for years men who had put their money in ships were not making money. Now, I have done a little shipping and in the particular line of goods with which I have to do, the pre-war rate from the ports of Canada-* Montreal, Quebec, Halifax, St. John-to the ports of England or Scotland was anywhere from thirteen to sixteen cents a hundred. The rate during the war from and to the same ports was anywhere from $1.60 to $1.80. In other words, the rate went up more than twelve times. And the Government launch out on a ship-building programme. When this question came up last session, the minister made the argument that the operation of thd Government -ships was a paying proposition. Well, I would like to know why it would not be a paying proposition, in view of the tremendous increase in rates. But when you have regard to all the information-such information as we have got-it is very doubtful whether the operations were really on a paying basis. It is said that a net profit of some 2.35 per cent was realized. Is that a good profit, having regard to the fact that rates were about twelve times what they were in pre-war days? To-day the rate on the same class of goods is about 55 cents a hundred, or more than three times the rates under normal conditions. But with fifteen of these vessels already tied up, unable to get cargoes, nothing to do, and the rates dropping every day, what do you think of the chances of vessels constructed at a cost of $192 a ton? The ordinary cost of constructing vessels in normal times was about $50 a ton, or one-quarter of what it cost the Government to build its ships. The Government ships then, built at a cost of about $200 a ton, are going out to compete with vessels built at $50 a ton? Do you think they have any chance of success? Absolutely none. I venture to say that even if these fifteen vessels' that are tied up could get cargoes, they would make a smaller loss by remaining at anchor, because I doubt very much if they would get rates that would pay the cost of operation, to say nothing about profit.
Mr. Chairman, I surely will not he accused of obstructing because this is the first time that I have been on my feet to 
address the House or the committee since the session opened. I should not rise to take up the time of the committee now had I not wished to express my opinion that this is one of the rankest, most foolish, most unjustifiable expenditures that the Government has ever made on railways or on anything else. There is some justification, as I have said, for building new railroads into new territories to develop new sections of the country, but no argument of this kind can possibly apply to the carrying out of an extensive shipbuilding programme. If we had large surpluses at our disposal, there might then be some justification for experimentation in shipbuilding and the carrying out of a large shipbuilding programme. But we have $70,000,000 of a deficit in railway operations alone; in fact, if the Minister of Railways brought down a correct statement, making a fair allowance for depreciation of rolling stock, roadbed, and everything else, the deficit would be nearly twice $70,000,000.

The minister shakes his head, but I want to tell him that the depreciation on rolling stock, ties, rails, and on everything else pertaining to a railway would run into a tremendously large sum. I do not find that he has made any allowance for this depreciation, nor has he, sc far as I can see, made any allowance for capital invested.

What allowance has the Minister made for the capital invested in these roads? What allowance for depreciation of rolling stock, road-bed, and everything else? No, I am not fond of talking: in fact, I would rather avoid it. But I did not sit up all night on this occasion simply for the love of sitting up; I have passed that stage. But I think I owe something to the constituency I represent, and besides, I try to represent the people of Canada, so far as my ability goes. I consider that I would be far from doing my duty if I sat quiet and allowed this vote to go through without making a strong protest. So far as I am concerned, I propose to remain here until this item is withdrawn, or until it is put through by closure.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I wish to join with the brave phalanx of the Opposition and prevent the

Government from committing such an act as they would be blamed for by the people. Together with the electors I have the honour to represent I object to this vote or $8,000,000 for the Canadian merchant marine. I do not think that the reasons given by the Minister of Marine, at the beginning of the debate, can in anyway whatever justify the Government in.voting such large sums as this for the continuation of a useless undertaking.
I was in my seat when the hon. Minister of Marine rose to speak in favour of the building of a merchant marine. He told us that his reasons were these: Firstly, because it bad been a war undertaking and therefore must be continued; secondly, because the country owned the railways, and our transportation facilities must be co-ordinated; we must add to our railways a fleet of merchant ships; thirdly, he said Canada must carry out her treaties with foreign countries, and this is required to complete our transportation system. Let us take his reasons one by one. After having considered each of these reasons, I feel justified in objecting to vote this sum. In fact, if the merchant marine has been altogether a war undertaking, we should, now that the war is finished since several years, discontinue all works undertaken because of the war. That which is most important to-day, for the country, is to forget the war: when Canadian finances were involved to such an extent as will bear not only on the present generation but also on several generations to come. After the armistice had been signed, Cabinet ministers and especially the Minister of Finance told us that we had entered upon a new era that we must give up expending such large sums as we had been obliged to do during the years of great sacrifices; what we must now do was to practise economy and encourage production.
The period of reconstruction is beginning; let us turn our efforts towards a new era of economy and production. On this condition only Canada may be able to meet its obligations and to look into the future with confidence.
Now, the second reason invoked by the hon. Minister of Marine is that we must build this merchant marine in order to complete our transportation system. For several sessions we have been told of the nefarious work of the Government in nationalizing the railways. We have the proof now that the country is involved in enormous expenditure, in yearly deficits which reach over fifty millions and will still increase; we have the proof, I say, that there was no necessity for the Government to acquire those railways. We have indulged in an undertaking the consequence of which is to pile on taxes which will burden the country for ever. Now, why should the present Government want to add to this enormous liability incurred by the acquisition of the railways, almost as large an indebtedness for the construction of a merchant marine. If the railways, as has been several times stated, are too huge for the present population of the country, if a vast immigration policy is needed to give these railways the employment they now lack, why tack to this railway system a merchant fleet which will have no employment either? This second reason advanced by the Minister of Marine does not hold good. It only shows more plainly the utter uselessness of this policy.
Thirdly, he said, we must seek commercial treaties with foreign countries, and to that end it is necessary to have mercantile ships. I understood that it is in the country's interest to seek commercial treaties with the neighbouring republic. I understood that, from generation to generation, the policy of the government-whether Liberal or Conservative-has always been to secure commercial treaties with our neighbours; I understood that even in spite of the absence of treaties, Canada has no better ally than the United States and that it would continue to deal with the Americans. Whatever have been the barriers raised between the two countries, whatever have been the customs duties imposed on the exchange of our commercial products, they have not prevented Canada from dealing with the United States far more than with any other country in the world. Therefore what is the use of building ships to go and beg for commercial treaties with the West Indies or some unknown country of South America, when we have by our side the American republic which is interested in dealing with us, and when it is our constant interest to deal with it? Besides is not the present Government rather inclined to secure commercial treaties with the United States? It is surely the policy of the Opposition ; it is certainly the policy which was adopted at the great convention held here in 1919. I for one would see with the utmost-satisfaction new treaties on the basis of reciprocity which we fought for in 1911, and which allowed the producers of this country to carry on a profitable commerce with the neighbouring republic.

The two principal reasons which induced me to rise and oppose this enormous vote of eight millions are the following: First, the debts and the liabilities of the country do not allow us to embark upon such considerable expenditure. Mr. Chairman, I would not at this moment put before the committee the lamentable picture of the enormous debt with which the country is encumbered, and which reached two billions; of the yearly liabilities which Canada has to meet; of the interest upon the debt; of the expenditure involved in our participation in the war; of the war pensions which amount to an annual disbursement of over fifty millions; and moreover, of the lamentable liabilities incurred for the acquisition of the railways and for the building of the merchant marine. Ministers have told us that the country has annually to face deficits on account of their railway policy, deficits which amount to more than fifty millions, and which will next year probably reach one hundred millions. We also know that on account of this merchant marine building policy, the country will again face annual deficits. These are only incipient and will, of course, grow annually, all these obligations which to-day burden our Canadian Budget will, not allow us to think of such a stupendous undertaking as this one.
In order to meet these yearly deficits of our Canadian finances, the Government has been forced to have recourse to this abominable system of taxes. No doubt, it is necessary, to meet the war expenditures, that taxes be levied whatever may be the cause of their assessment, however, it is not less true that in their results they are odious, when they are levied on the income and specially when their consequence is to bring misery in the Canadian homes, and to-day the taxes levied on the ratepapers are more odious than any of those that may have been imposed in the past. They are levied upon the income of the humblest, upon the head of families that have to support their children and are forced to borrow to meet this tax.
But this is not the only consequence of this disastrous policy of unlimited expenditure brought on by the Government. Another which glares at us in this Capital, has been the extraordinary treatment meted out to the Civil Service. For instance, but a few days ago we saw in the press and even heard, I believe, through the official channel of the Government's representatives, that the civil employees of the Dominion Government will have to put up

with a curtailment in their bonus. Are you aware, Mr. Chairman, of what a curtailment in the bonus means at the presenl time? Are you aware what a curtailment of bonus means to this large number of civil employees who support a family, many of whom have sacrified their career to give their country the best part of their life, do you realize what this means in the year 1921? They had come to look upon, for the last few years, this bonus as an integral part of their salary, and the Government were obliged to admit that it was absolutely necessary to permit them to exist. In reality, if there is a bonus which can be considered as an integral part of the salary which a civil employee receives, it is certainly that bonus which was given to them since these years of war, since the high cost of living. I would like to see the name of bonus disappear and the employees, who after all would not be drawing such a high salary owing to the maintenance of the high cost of living, receive to-day as a permanent salary, his present one plus the bonus received for the last few years. Instead of fully considering this question as it should be, that is judiciously, we find the Government depriving the civil employees of part of their income at a time when the high cost of living has not decreased. Rents, for instance, far from going down, are on the upward trend, and the cost of living maintains itself at a high level and if anything threatens to rise. Therefore no justification exists for the Government to lower the salary and particularly the bonus which the civil employee receives. They will put forward as a reason that the expenditures are heavy, that Canada's obligations are numerous and that they must economize and clip the salaries of the civil employees in order to continue to administer the coun-[DOT] try's business. But what contradictions do we not find in the Government's attitude, on the one hand cutting down the civil employee's bonus and on the other trying to force a vote to-day for $8,000,000 for its merchant marine building policy, when this undertaking is not justified, the war being over, when we should enter on a period of reconstruction, when we should economize the most and when, lastly, instead of spending uselessly as the Government wishes to do, we should busy ourselves with reconstruction work.
It was justly pointed out during this debate, that the Government want this enormous sum to be voted so as to continue the construction of ships, when they have but small amounts placed to the credit of agri-

culture and other important departments of the Administration. There is but $4,000,000 placed to the credit of agriculture and yet they wish to pass a vote, for this year, of over $8,000,000 for the building of ships. It would be wiser to increase, if the country's finances will permit it, the subsidies to agriculture than to continue to vote money for these merchant ships. There are many openings in our dear Canada where the Government could well spend money to help the agricultural interest. They have told us that in the future they would encourage the establishing of experimental farms. There are many places, and I could indicate some in our province and in my . county, where the Government might well encourage agriculture by establishing some of these experimental farms.
As it was remarked a few days ago, there is a movement towards agriculture and all eyes are turned to the host of farmers who are the important producers of this country. We see the reason why the Government, in order to beget a little popularity, has promised to expand that policy of establishing experimental farms; however we are still waiting. I do not see any in my section, and certainly it is a place where one should exist, in that colonizing territory. No doubt, it is important that these farms should be established in the more settled parts of the country, in the St. Lawrence valley and in the different parts of the other provinces, but if there are places where these agricultural subsidies would have the best results, it would certainly be in those colonizing parts, such as Labelle where in the midst of the Lau-rentian hills a new region of cultivable land is being opened under beautiful blue skies and amongst evergreen hills where is to be found a very energetic population, forming to-day one of the important centres of the province. It is in those places where experimental farms should be established, and instead of spending money for the building up of a navy, it is in encouraging agriculture, if there is money to spend, that this money would be better placed. The second reason I invoke to oppose the vote of this amount, is that to-day this merchant marine is absolutely useless. Indeed, it is in this debate that the fact came out. Certainly, the number of ships built or acquired by the Government up to date, is too large. Of what use are these ships? Are they employed on trips from which we derive some returns such as to transport our products to countries with which we have commercial treaties
for the exchange of produets or are they not awaiting in some port or another the cargo that luck will bring their way? It was shown in this very sitting of the House, that there are in the port of Halifax fifteen of these ships which are at anchor for the last few days. No one knows when they will obtain a cargo. This brings out the uselessness of our merchant ships and the futility of the Government's policy on that question.
Instead of spending money to acquire new ships would it not be wiser, now that the Government is in possession of almost all our railways with the exception of the Canadian Pacific, to see that not only in one particular province but that in all of them necessary branches be built to complete their system?
Would it not be wiser for the Government, who wish to complete our transportation system, instead of acquiring new merchant ships when the number we own is already too great and when it is shown that these ships are absolutely useless, would it not be better to complete our railway system? Does not the country now know that the construction of the Transcontinental, for instance, was certainly justified by the fact that in going through these unknown regions of the northern provinces of Ontario and Quebec, it opened up to colonization a vast territory? The glory certainly is to the credit of our Canadian statesman, it is to the honour of Sir Wilfrid Laurier who foresaw the development of this beautiful region of Abitibi, where to the north of the Laurentides, is thrown open a domain almost as extensive as that of the St. Lawrence valley and where the sons of that old province have ventured in great numbers to open up important and prosperous centres. It would be advisable to complete this system of railways inasmuch as our finances will permit. Before spending millions in the shipbuilding enterprise it would be more appropriate for instance to connect Montreal with the Transcontinental by means of that projected road of a few years ago, by the "North Railway Company," and thus by this extension connect the Metropolis of Canada, the large city of Montreal with the Transcontinental by skirting the counties of Argenteuil and Labelle and through this vast region situated to the north of these counties. This is an enterprise which by its own merit commends itself to the Government. Since we have millions to spend for useless enterprises, I take it upon myself to draw the attention, for the are the most urgent. mB.Oydcvmome m

I see the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) looking at me. I am sure he thinks it strange that the persuasive appeal which he made a few moments ago to members on this side of the House, to allow the minister (Mr. Ballantyne) to report progress, after voting the amount under discussion, has	hqd	no effect.	If his appealcould affect	the	mind	and	heart of onemember on	this	side	of the House, heknows it is	the	mind	and	heart of the
member for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon).
However, I deem it my duty on this occasion to express, as briefly as I possibly can, my views on the great question of the Merchant Marine of Canada, a question, the discussion of which I had left to my hon. friends from Nova Scotia . and other provinces who are more competent to discuss it with the authority derived from practical experience in the pursuit of their own business. The Minister of Trade and Commerce no doubt remembers that every session during the war I rose in this House and implored him and the Government of which he is a member to begin at once the construction of merchant vessels to help the Allies in carrying not only munitions but provisions to Great Britain in her stress, when it was taking every ton that a vessel could, carry to maintain the millions of soldiers who were fighting for democracy and for the salvation of Canada.
The time came when the United States felt that she had to join the Allies in the war, and she found herself pretty much in the position of Canada-without a navy able to transport the millions of soldiers which she was determined to send to help the Allies. During that period, I for one, and others on this side of the House, appealed to the Right Hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and to the other members of the Government, to give help to Great Britain in the matter of transporting the American soldiers who were so badly needed to put an end to the struggle in which the Allies were engaged.
There was no attempt on the part of the Government to build a ship. I will not refer to the time of the naval debate in 1911, when we on this side of the House placed on the statutes of the country an Act for the construction of a naval service, which would have been so useful during the war, and so remunerative to Canada after the war, because we would have had those vessels ready for the transportation
of our commerce from this time forward. But my hon. friends on the other side remained silent at that time and did nothing at all. The press of the country could never persuade any member of the Government to undertake the construction of a vessel, either for the navy or the merchant marine. At last in 1917, when my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce came into the Government, he announced to this House that he had a naval programme ready to submit to us. War was still going on. I remember, when speaking on the Budget, that I congratulated him upon the project he had enunciated. But he had remained silent for three years, and they were only commencing to construct the navy at that time. But still, as I thought, it was time then to begin. But war ceased almost as soon as the Government commenced the construction of marine vessels. We asked them to halt, because we knew that Great Britain had all those vessels which she had used for the transportation of munitions and soldiers, not only from Canada but from the United" States, and there were more ships on the ocean than could possibly be used for business. They had commenced too late, but, late as it was, they were determined to go on. There was certainly no constructive or wise policy adopted in this matter-no policy that would be carried out by any business concern in Canada, or in any place the world over. They knew that freight had risen high-twelve hundred per cent from the pre-war rate up till that time. They knew that with the cessation of the war, and the cessation of the transport of munitions and soldiers, with an immense fleet at the disposal of the countries interested, those freight rates would necessarily come down as rapidly as they had risen during the war, and that, therefore, the new vessels they were building were bound to be a loss to the country. But no appeal could be effective upon the mind of my right hon. friend and his colleagues in the Council.
When I came into this Chamber about nine o'clock this morning, the hon. gentleman from St. James (Mr. Rinfret) was addressing the House,. He stated that they had been accused by the hon. members on the other side of the House of having had an understanding that they should continue this debate during the night, and stop the vote from being effective. In contradiction of this statement, I will tell my hon. friend that I left this House last night, contrary to mv habit, a few minutes before twelve.

thinking that, on a private members' day, [DOT] the Government had simply taken the vote merely to finish the day, and that in a few minutes my hon. colleagues would be following my example and going home. When I came here this .morning and heard that statement made, I desired to register a [DOT]denial of the statement that there was any such understanding. My hon. friend will give me credit for this-that had I known there was to be any such protracted sitting I would have been here all night, the same as the rest of my colleagues. When we appeal to the Government to stop the waste of money upon the building of ships which cannot be used, they tell us that they have a contract, and, having a contract, they had to carry on. I always thought, from my experience in business of the departments of government of the country for the last twenty-five years, that every contract the Government made with a firm or private individual contained a clause that the contract would be terminated on the Government giving notice within a certain time specified in the contract. No contract has ever been made by any Government of Canada without such a provision. They gave a contract to the Dominion Iron and Steel Company in Nova Scotia for 250,000 tons of plate, and, after they had received about 25 or 30 per cent, they stopped the contract and advised them they could use no more. They could have exercised the same privilege with the shipbuilders in the different shipyards of the country. But they were not always so timid when they wanted to cancel a contract or stop shipbuilding in this country. Great Britain has been building ships for a year or two in our shipyards in Canada through the Munitions Board. They had work going on all the time. They had been building ships which they thought they might need in the future. They were not so sensitive at that time about contracts. They practically told the Munitions Board to vacate the shipyards of Canada, and that they themselves would build these ships, instead of the Munitions Board which represented the Government of Great Britain. This 1 consider most criminal. If this had been done by the poor member from Gloucester, or Sir Wilfrid Laurier when he was at the head of the Government, and if he had said to the Government of Great Britain: " I will discontinue your work here and I will take your place," such action would have been condemned very strongly. It was certainly not only audacious, but it was against the friendly

intercourse between the Government of Great Britain and one of her Dominion under the British flag. Why not allow Great Britain to go on with the project if they desired to do so? When the war was over, Great Britain having so many ships that she did not need them all, could have sold to Canada any number of vessels which we might have required for that ocean traffic. But they have built those ships now, and we are told by the Government that fifteen of them are to do in the port of Halifax a certain traffic. I do not wish to mingle the question of railroads with this question of marine to-day, as I do not intend to occupy the attention of the committee very long. I do not say that we have too many railways. I always took the ground that if our railways are not paying what they should pay to-day, and do not give the service they should give, it is not because we have too many railways, but because we do not give to the Canadian railways the traffic Which is there for them, but which is diverted from Port Arthur-seventy per cent of it-every year to Buffalo and New York. And I say again in regard to the relations between the railways and the merchant marine, that all the import trade that is coming back from New York, Philadelphia and Boston comes also through those ports, and, therefore, our own marine is deprived of the ocean trade going and coming. My hon. friends on the other side have said that the Transcontinental was a useless expenditure, but I say that it was the most patriotic and beneficial expenditure in railroads that Canada ever made. I am sure that that view will be expressed by future historians, to the great shame of those who have opposed the building of this road.
I do most earnestly appeal to the Government to take this matter into further consideration and see whether they can determine upon a policy more in line with the interests of the people. Why do my hon. friends, in view of the enormous financial burdens of the country, insist upon proceeding with this ship-building programme? The minister has endeavoured to Show a surplus on operating account in connection with his Government ships, but I am afraid that this does not disclose the real condition, and that next year he will come to the House with an even more unsatisfactory result. Sir, wherever the Canadian may set foot upon his native land there he finds rich natural resources. Why, then, not take such steps as are necessary to make full use of this great Transcontinental

railway,-built to compete with railroads leading to the ports of New York; built to suit Canada's condition; built to carry the produce of the western farmer through Canadian ports to its destination across the sea; built to carry,a tonnage which no other railroad in America could possibly handle. Sir, all these considerations were had in mind by these who projected this great system. The road is so constructed that trains of from sixty to ninety cars can be hauled with a single engine, over a road-bed as smooth as the floor of this House. Only by developing to the full by every means at our disposal the traffic handled by these lines can we hope to get rid of the deficits which the railways of Canada have experienced during the last two or three years. I am not opposed to the management of railroads by the Government. When some people in despair cry out: Give back the Government-owned railroads to their former owners, or hand them over to a private concern, I say, let us do the best we can; let us develop these roads which have been constructed to make short our great distances and to make more direct and convenient the transport of our produce from the field to the point of export.
Mr. Speaker, my right hon. friend who leads the House may question my judgment, but he will not doubt my sincerity. I appeal to him in all earnestness, not as the member for Gloucester, but as one who is trying to reflect the opinion of the people of Canada generally, to take such steps as will prevent this wasteful expenditure. Let the Government do this in their own interests, if for no other reason, because if they reconsider their action the people will say: They have taken the right course; we will support them. If we proceed as we are doing we shall only have to struggle with new deficits year after year. We have to look forward to a deficit again next year and as long as that is the case why should we not stop the construction of useless vessels? I am appealing to the Government in the exercise of their duty- their duty, not to the Opposition but to the people of Canada-to stop this expenditure, and I still trust that my right hon. friend who now leads the House will consider what I say and will consent to report progress and in the meantime to consider the matter, and when we come back again tomorrow or next week he can present a programme upon which we on this side of the House, will perhaps be responsive to his appeal.

Mr. Chairman, I
would be the last person in this House to doubt the sincerity of my hon. friend for whom I have now, as I always have had, a very high esteem. But after listening to his remarks in reference to the Transcontinental project, I trust he will not think I am using harsh or disrespectful language if I say I^have certain doubts as to his judgment. I agree with the hon. gentleman that we have too many railroads in this country; that is a fact which has been pretty well impressed upon us from one end of Canada to the other, about which, I think, there is perhaps no real difference of opinion. But it just strikes me that it will be well if hon. gentlemen who sit on the other side of the House would look over the pages of the history, going back a few years, and measure the extent of their responsibility for the fact that Canada has too many railroads to-day. It might be well if they, in all fairness, in considering the question, should estimate what portion or parts of the Government railways of Canada are most responsible for the $70,000,000 deficit which we have to-day and, if they will seriously and honestly give consideration to that question they will admit the responsibility for such a huge deficit is very largely, I might say, almost entirely theirs.
But, sir, I have not risen for the purpose of discussing the railway situation, I want to say a very few words in regard to this particular matter which is covered by the vote before u$. Might I be permitted to call attention, very briefly, to one or two facts:	The original shipbuilding programme, of which this is a continuation and a part, was launched on April 4, 1918, at which time $20,000,000, I believe, was asked for and voted. I think I am right in saying that the shipbuilding policy was pretty generally accepted by both sides of the House at that time, and that there was no objection to voting the $20,000,000. If I am right in that statement, then those who consented to the shipbuilding policy inaugurated in 1918; who gave their consent and raised no objection to the vote must, in all fairness, assume their fair share of responsibility for the inauguration of the policy and for the voting, at least, of that $20,000,000. We proceed next to the following year. Then, I think, some $30,000,000 was asked for in May, 1919. On that occasion, I believe the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux), or as he was referred to the other night, seeing that he sits for the constituency of Maisonneuve also, the hon.

member for Graspy-commended the Government very strongly for its shipbuilding policy, for keeping the wheels of industry going in this country. Now that was in May, 1919, and I think I am right in stating that the distinguished member for Marquette, the leader of the progressive party, was in May, 1919', a member of the Government and therefore-

That is perhaps the
reason he left, he did not agree with them.

That is perhaps so,
no doubt the hon. gentleman can state the reasons why he left, but I am stating the fact; and I do not think my hon. friend will question the reasonableness of my statement, when I say that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Crerar) cannot reasonably get away from his responsibility in voting that money and in the endorsation of that policy. In regard to those hon. gentlemen sitting around him now, and who occupied seats on this side of the House at that time, and who at that time voted the same way that hon. member voted, they are in the same position, and cannot escape their full share of responsibility for the second vote of $30,000,000 and for their endorsation of the shipbuilding policy. Now, that places the responsibility for a total of $50,000,000. I come now to last session when I believe $20,000,000 was asked for and was voted, and with regard to that vote I believe that some hon. gentleman who gave their support to the shipbuilding programme when it was inaugurated in 1918 and again gave their support to that programme when the $30,000,000 was voted in 1919, did not give their support. In all fairness I want to state that fact. But the item was voted. This Parliament, rightly or wrongly, did vote $20,000,000 last year. Now let us see how much it is proposed to add to that amount. True, a vote of $8,000,000 is asked for by this item. But I ask hon. gentlemen in all fairness to consider this fact, that of the $20,000,000 that, rightly or wrongly, was voted last session, only $15,334,000 was actually expended, so that of the $8,000,000 which is asked for now, $4,664,000 is a revote of money which was voted by Parliament last year, and in reality the further money which this Parliament is asked to vote now is $3,334,000. That completes the shipbuilding programme.
Let me go back to the question of responsibility for the building of the ships.
I say that there are hon. gentlemen sitting across from me who gave their support not only to the shipbuilding pro-[Mr. Edwards.}
gramme in 1918-that was unanimously approved-but who gave their support to the shipbuilding policy in 1919 and to the vote of the $30,000,000, and many of them took a less hostile attitude, at all events, last session in regard to the $20,000,000 than they are taking at the present time. I want to call attention to this further fact The $30,000,000 voed in 1919 was voted at a time when the hon. member for Marquette was a member of the Government, and when most of the hon. gentlemen sitting across the floor to my immediate right were sitting on this side of the House and giving their support to the Government, and therefore supporting that $30,000,000 vote. I claim that, whatever that vote enabled the Government to do in the way of building ships or carrying out their programme, any man in this House who voted for that $30,000,000 must share responsibility for the work that the Government did and that they were enabled to do because that money was voted. That vote of May, 1919, carried the programme through not only to the end of 1919, but to the end of the fiscal year, that is to March 31, 1920. I claim, therefore, that hon. gentlemen like my hon. friend for Marquette, who was in the House and a member of the Government when this money was voted, must share responsibility for whatever work was carried on up to the end of that fiscal year in so far as shipbuilding was concerned. There were not any new contracts let for vessels after December, 1919. Therefore, if I am wrong in backing the Government up in this programme, it appears to me that certain hon. gentlemen opposite who have expressed their opposition to this programme are just as far wrong as I was wrong. They gave their adherence to the policy of the building of ships just as much and as far as I did. And, after December, 1919, no further contracts were entered into, and the contracts entered into in December, 1919, would not have been entered into if this House had not consented to the vote of $30,000,000, to which vote hon. gentlemen opposite gave their approval just as much as I did.
My understanding is that contracts were entered into as late as May, 1920.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There have been no contracts entered into since 1919.

That was my understanding when I made the statement. I will concede at once that if the hon. member for Marquette or any other hon. gentle-

man who sat on this side of the House at that time and gave his approval to the vote of $30,000,000 can show that contracts were entered into after the expiration of that fiscal year, that is, after the 1st of April, 1920, he is absolved from all responsibility in that regard; but in so far as anything was done by this Government on their shipbuilding programme in the year 1919, it was only done, and could only be done, because this Parliament voted $30,000,000 for that purpose. In voting that $30,000,000 for that purpose we told the Government to go ahead with their shipbuilding programme and enter into contracts.
What other conclusion could you come to? No contracts were entered into after December, 1919. Therefore, if I was wrong in regard to the vote that enabled and encouraged the Government to proceed with their shipbuilding programme, some hon. gentlemen who are trying to get out from under now were just as far wrong as I was. It is all right for some of these hon. gentlemen to bring this matter up now in the way they have done, for the purpose of achieving what is patent to everybody here. Since this matter has come up, it has afforded an opportunity to some hon. gentlemen to make speeches and deliver orations, in order to try and impress their constituents with the fact that they are great for economy; that is the whole purpose. Of course, the opportunity afforded by this vote has been followed up by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) to present, as usual, some more of his free trade fallacies, of which he has always a stock on hand. It has given him that opportunity, of whicn he avails himself no matter what item comes up for discussion. It has given some other hon. gentlemen the opportunity to say " Oh yes, we agreed to your shipbuilding programme in 1918, but the war was on then, and we did so as a war measure." Mr. Chairman, I will freely accept that as a reason from an hon. member like my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Tur-geon), but should I accept it as a reason from the hon. member from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), for instance? I cannot accept such a reason from any hon. member who assumed the attitude which that hon. member did at a time when our soldiers were asking for reinforcements. He did what he could to prevent them from getting there. That hon. gentleman had a use for his ships at that time, and it was not in the interests of the Allies, but to take men away out to sea so that they could not
report for service. So, when my hon. friend states as a reason why he supported the policy of 1918 that it was a war measure, I say that he has got to bring up another story to convince me.
I do not think the hon. gentleman's record is such as to substantiate any such assertion on his part. Now, the House sat all night debating this question, and I think we may look at it for a moment.
Are you in a position to say whether any of those contracts for ships could have been cancelled?
Most frankly, I am not in a position to say; the Minister of Marine must answer that question.
Certain railway contracts have been cancelled, and I do not see any reason why the same procedure could not have been taken in regard to the ships.

I am not in a position to give my hon. friend an answer. Speaking from my own personal knowledge, I know that in the city of Kingston, where there is a small shipbuilding plant, the Collingwood Company, there was an anxious request the winter before last for a contract for a new vessel. I know also that in December, 1919, out in Vancouver they pleaded with the Government very strenuously for one or two orders to relieve the unemployment situation, because the soldiers were coming back in great numbers and there was considerable unrest. Unemployment was staring the people in the face in various parts of the country, and something had to be done. To what extent the Government was influenced, in giving orders for ships, by conditions that then arose and the urgent appeals that were made, I can frankly say I am not in a position to state. But so far as I am concerned, I am willing to take my share of responsibility for voting this additional $3,300,000, which is really all that we are asked to vote, to complete a shipbuilding programme which was in the first place unanimously agreed to. The first vote of $20,000,000 passed without objection; the second vote of $30,000,000 passed, if not without objection, at least with compliments from certain prominent gentlemen opposite; and as regards this final amount, I for one am willing to assume my share of responsibility. What does it amount to after all?

Is there any , more reason why this programme should be com-

pleted than there is why other programmes in regard to other national projects should be carried out?
Yes, I think there is. I do not blame my hon. friend for keeping constantly in mind the building of the Hudson Bay Railway.
I did not mention it.

Well, I do not profess to be a mind reader, but I will bet a horse to a hen that I am not very far wrong. If I represented the constituency represented by my hon. friend, I think that probably .1 should have done what he did the other day. I would have made a speech in the House which I could send to my constituents to show them that I was putting up a vigorous fight on their behalf for the building of this railway. Now, that is playing the game, and I have no objection at all to that course. But I do think, without going into the details, that some reasons might be advanced for carrying out contracts entered into in the shipping programme of the Government, while reasons equally cogent could be given for not completing the Hudson Bay Railway at this juncture. I may say, however, speaking for myself, I hope the day is not very far distant when the line in which my hon. friend is deeply interested will be completed. I sincerely hope that.
But you will not vote for it.

Not this year; if it comes up this year I will not vote for it.
Mr. -CAMPBELL: And I will not vote for this item this year.

I do not think you will, and that brings me exactly to the point I was coming to. My hon. friend will give reasons, as others did last night and yesterday afternoon, why he will not support this proposal. That is within the rights of hon. members. But having done that, what is the use of taking up further time? The Government must assume responsibility for this vote, and eventually we will put it through. The hon. gentleman opposite, having placed their views before the country and stated their opposition to this vote, having maintained that opposition throughout the whole night, must be satisfied that the country will be fully aware of their attitude towards this subject.	That
being the case, what is the sense of spending further time discussing the 
question? If there are any hon. gentlemen opposite who have not put themselves on record as being opposed to it, for Heaven's sake let them get up and express themselves. But having done that, what more is there for them to do? For my part, I am prepared, for reasons I have given, to support the Government in this matter; and hon. gentlemen opposite are equally prepared, for reasons they have advanced -I will not enter on the question of their sincerity-to vote against the item. Very well, having put themselves on record, they should see the futlity of further opposition. That is all I desire to say now. I do object to certain hon. gentlemen trying to lay the blame, if blame there is, on the Government for its shipbuilding policy that received their support in its initial stages, when they voted the great bulk of the money that has so far been expended on this programme.

The members of this House generally, and more particularly the members of the Opposition, are extremely grateful to my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) for having accorded them the privilege of expressing their views on this subject. I trust, however, he will be good enough to concede that the members of all sections of the Opposition are aware of this privilege, and are prepared to exercise their rights on this question. The fact that they have stood here in the front line trenches, many of them all night, in defence of their views on the policy of the Government, shows that they not only know their privileges, but are ready to assert them. The member for Frontenac has taken to task very seriously the member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), Who precipitated this discussion. He has referred to the war record of that hon. member, and while I cannot see that that has anything whatever to do with the discussion now in progress, I think that the war record of the member for Lunenburg will compare favourably indeed with that of the hon. gentleman.
A good deal better.

My hon. friend has said that the Opposition did not object to this vote ,last year. If the hon. member will read " Hansard " covering the Estimates when that vote was under consideration last year, he will find that many of the members, including the member for Lunenburg, raised strenuous objection to that vote.

I would remind my
hon. friend that I did not say anything of the kind.

If I have not understood the hon. member for Frontenac, I am sorry; but I am still of the opinion that that was the impression left on the House. We are not here to-day to wave the flag.
I think that the members on this side of the House can claim equal honour with the members on the Government side in regard to war work and war activities, and there is no need for any references of that kind. That sort of thing is ancient history, and has nothing to do with the subject we are dealing with to-day.
Some hon. members on this side of the House did in 1918, 1919, and even in 1920, support this shipbuilding proposition; but it is quite evident that they have a seen the error of their way in that regard, in which respect they differ from the members on the Government side of the House.
The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) claims that in view of the fact that this project was favoured at one time, and in spite of the admitted fact that it is a losing game, we should continue spending $192 per ton in building ships that are worth only $35 to $42 per ton today. Is that good business? I ask you Mr. Chairman, I ask the Minister of Railways whether this is good business, and I would like the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to get up and say now, if he will, that it is good business. It is suggested that as the Government have entered into the contract, it is sacred matter; but it is a well known fact that contracts which were entered into during the war by the Government, by manufacturers, by importers, and by business men the world over, are not now regarded in that sacred light. In many cases those contracts were cancelled, and a readjustment was made on a fair basis. I know of many instances in which manufacturers and importers were allowed that privilege and where an adjustment was made satisfactory to both parties to the transaction. The Government, during the period that has ensued since the Armistice was signed, have exercised that right, and have cancelled munition contracts, adjusting the matter satisfactorily with the parties concerned. Why not exercise the same right in regard to building vessels that are not needed, vessels that would simply lie idle alongside the 16 other vessels that are now lying idle in the harbour of Halifax? The Government have exercised their right to cancel war contracts for textile materials, and I know that in these instances they have paid bonuses amounting to three-quarters of a million dollars, for the cancellation of those contracts. I think it was good business on the part of the Government to make an adjustment of that kind.
I was delighted to see the Minister of Trade and Commerce come in so bright and fresh this morning after his night's rest when others had been labouring all night and had, as he says, produced nothing. He immediately took hold of the situation and suggested that we pass the item without further discussion. It was quite evident to him that the Committee had reached a stage where it was impossible to make progress without the application of the rules of the House. He could gather from the temper of the Opposition and from the tenor of their remarks that we were determined that this item, $8,330,000, shall not pass unless the Government take the only course open to them and apply the closure. I am very much of the same opinion as the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) in regard to that matter. I detest the word " closure," but as he points out it is a method that has been adopted by all the governments of the civilized world. If it is clear-and I am sure it must be clear to the Government-that this Opposition is determined that this item shall not pass unless we are forced to pass it by the only means in the hands of the Government, they should in all reason and in all decency listen to the appeal made by the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) and repeated by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon), the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea), and others. This item is only one installment of the amount required by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
I have been figuring while this discussion has been going on, that there is a balance of 114,470 tonnage still to be constructed, and at $192 per ton this will cost the sum of $22,978,240. If this item of $8,000,000 is passed for the purpose of doing this work, it is only an instalment on the amount required to complete the work-about one-third of the amount actually needed. So that we are committing ourselves to a proposition that is really like a will-o-the-wisp. We are getting nowhere. It would have been better if the Minister of Marine had

exercised the privilege granted in all contracts entered into during the war, and have cancelled the contracts for the ships, the construction of which had not been commenced. That would have been the sensible course. The attitude of the minister is worse than nonsense. It is unbusinesslike to go on spending $192 for $35 worth of service. The hon. member for Sherbrooke says it is worse than nonsense-it is foolishness. I go further and say it is worse than lunacy. No sane business man would adopt such a course in his own affairs. The Government can only force this item through by closure, and I would ask them to consider the possibility, the advisability and the desirability of cancelling the contracts, in order to see if a reasonable adjustment cannot be made with-the firms who have these contracts in hand. Comparing the result of the railway operations in the past year, with the operations of the Government Merchant Marine, it seems to me that the Minister of Railways and Canals and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries have been running a race with each other to see which would pile up the biggest deficit. The Minister of Railways presents the result of the operation of the railways during the past year and shows a deficit of some $70,000,000, and he says " There it is, boys, go to it; what will you do with it?" The Minister of Marine and Fisheries does not come up quite to that point, but, according to the estimate made by a man experienced in shipping, the hon. member for Lunenburg, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries piles up a loss on the year's operation of not less than $59,000,000. That statement has been made on the floor of the House and I have not heard it successfully contradicted. The figures submitted by the hon. member for Lunenburg are very convincing, and no one could seriously dispute them. The Minister of Trade and Commerce made the assertion, or possibly the guess, that no new idea had been advanced during the whole night's discussion and nothing had been achieved, and intimated that the Opposition were simply marking time. As a member of the Opposition, I am willing to continue marking time until we obtain satisfactory information from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and we have been asking for information all night. There is one item here which I think cannot be explained by the Minister of Finance. I refer to the discrepancy $148,175.86-I am now quoting the figures from the minister's own statement, page 1334 of Unrevised " Hansard." I

find under operating account, 1920, an item deducted for depreciation of $067,665.46. In a subsequent statement also presented to the House by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries I find an item for depreciation the total of which is given $815,842.32. That is an item transferred in the balance sheet by the minister submitting the annual net result for the year. That shows a discrepancy of $148,175.86, between the two diiferent accounts. We should have an explanation of this discrepancy. It is a large amount to the ordinary citizen, but may seem only trifling here. I think it is large enough to warrant the Opposition in holding up the item until we receive a satisfactory explanation of it. We have been asking all night about the earnings of the different ships, and we have been told by the hon. member for Lunenburg that a great many of these vessels have been parading up and down the coast of North America with mud ballast. It would have been better if these vessels had been left in Halifax harbour or some other harbour. We were told that these were built for the purpose of assisting the export trade of Canada, but these vessels have been engaged in coast trade in the Mediterranean sea, taking cargoes from one point in the Mediterranean to some point in Europe. In view of the fact that the Government have to go out to all ports of the world to look for trade to keep these vessels going, it seems to me it is not reasonable that they should continue building vessels presumably to help the trade of Canada, and send them out	to foreign ports to be used
in this way. All this is being accomplished at the expense of the taxpayers of this country. The Minister of Railways some time ago volunteered the information, when asked the question, that one of these vessels was being used in the trade between Canada and South Africa, he was asked what class of merchandise was brought by that vessel from South Africa to Canada, and he was entirely ignorant as to the commodity handled by vessels on that route. We would like to know what proportion of the $8,000,000 is going to be used in overhauling the vessels laid up in Halifax harbour. I understand that most of these vessels have not been in use for more than two years. It is preposterous that a vessel from which the first coat of paint is hardly worn should have to be laid up for repairs.
I have urged the reasonableness of my request that these contracts be cancelled. The Government saw fit to cancel various

contracts for munitions, textiles, and steel plates; the railway companies, I understand, have cancelled large contracts let during the war and the period of reconstruction. The Government having exercised its right to cancel many other contracts since the termination of the war, I appeal to them to consider seriously the advisability of cancelling the contracts for the remainder of the ships under construction, and thus save an enormous amount to the taxpayers of Canada. I wish to voice my opposition to the continuance of these contracts. These contracts are being carried on without any probability of effecting good objects so far as the public are concerned. A few individual contractors and labourers might be benefited by their continuance, but the people generally would be penalized. It would be in the interests of the country in the long run if some compromise between the contractors and the Government was arrived at with a view to the cancellation of these contracts. Possibly the vessels actually under construction might be completed and disposed of, but we should be recreant in our duty if we permitted the Government, without protesting on our part, their right to go ahead with the building of vessels for use in Canadian trade. I have much pleasure in associating my protest with that of other hon. members on this side-and I am glad that all hon. members sitting on this side of the House, including those to my extreme left, are included in this oppositiqn. The Government may rest assured that this vote will not be carried without the adoption of the strongest measures that it is in their power to employ.
Mr. ROCH LANCTOT (Laprairie and Napierville). (Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I think the Minister of Marine will not complain that I am making any obstruction regarding this amount of eight millions, as this is the first time that I rise to discuss this mercantile marine scheme launched by the Government some three years ago. I want to know why we should persist in this insane policy, why we should spend more and more millions when past experience proves that all this Government's undertakings have caused some awful losses to the people of this country? I agree with you, Mr. Chairman, that we have to deal with a most unlucky Government. They have taken over most of the railways in this country and thus bringing about heavy deficits. They have undertaken shipbuilding, then the cost of construction fell about 80 per 100 and the Government is still paying the same price, that is $192 a ton, though the. price should not be more than $40 or $45. I want to know why the minister did give such long term contracts when he could have followed the exemple of other countries and cancelled those contracts whenever there occurred a change in prices, or else, grant contracts from year to year, so as not to pay in 1920 and 1921 prices which are three times what they were when the contracts were given.
Now, we are charged with having coun-. tenanced this mercantile marine policy. So far as I am concerned, Mr. Chairman, I may say that I never did countenance any undertaking of this Government. If some of my hon. friends from this side of the House saw fit to aid the Minister of Marine in this shipbuilding policy, that is their business and I have nothing to do with it. However, I was ef opinion at that time that they were mistaken in helping out this Government and you will admit with me, Mr. Chairman, that I never supported the Government in anything they did since 1914 and, particularly since 1917 till this day, and that I do not propose to do so in future.
This shipbuilding policy, if I understand what has been said in this House within the last few days and especially by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), will probably cost the country as much as our national railways. Not only will the Government pay the construction of these ships four times what it is worth, but they will also be called upon to pay a handsome amount to the Dominion Steel people for their cancelled contract. Is it not a fact, Mr. Chairman, that in the United States such cases had been provided for and that the Government had a right to cancel a contract at any time? But, in this country, our Government, always generous towards the big corporations, and loath to displease them, have put no such clause in our contracts and we are now at the mercy of the Dominion Steel, who, after the elections or even before, will send an account which Jean Baptiste will have to settle. I wonder if we merchants, we farmers, could not [DOT] strike such bargains as those made by the Minister of Marine? I wonder if a Western farmer could have, three years ago, sold his wheat for three years to come at $3 a bushel, and kept up this price for three years?
I also wonder if I could have sold my hay, three years ago, for $30 a ton and

insist on this price being paid for three years to come? Under such conditions I do not think that any serious-minded man would want to do business with me or with the Western farmer, but our Government, though posing as a serious Government, make contracts with shipbuilders for two or three years, always at the same price and even when those prices fall to $40 or $45 they must still pay $192.
I often hear the railway question discussed in this House. True it constitutes a white elephant on the hands of our people, but I am always surprised to hear the hon. members on the Government side. They look as if they wanted the people to believe that the Liberal party is responsible for this state of affairs. If I remember correctly, the Conservatives are in power since 1911, and before 1911 the Government of the day had given the Canadian Northern 35 millions to build their road from Prince Arthur to Montreal, but this building was not carried through till after the hon. gentlemen opposite came into power.
