Thus, they had a perfect right, once the elections were over, to stop this undertaking and take over the road from Mackenzie & Mann as they have done some years latter, but too late. If they had been business men they should have dispossessed Mackenzie & Mann after the 1911 elections, they should have taken over all the western branch lines so as to provide feeders for the National Transcontinental.
Moreover they had completed the Transcontinental as projected under the administration of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and as stipulated under the contract with the Grand Trunk, we would have had the finest railway of the country and we would now have had two 'transcontinentals to maintain instead of three. The Government now say that they made no greater mistake than we have. They carried on the construction of the Canadian Northern railway as far as Vancouver on the Pacific coast, after the year 1911. Why? To help the McBride policy which had it been allowed to prevail would have dragged the province of British Columbia into bankruptcy. I ask you, is it their work or ours? I say it is the doings of this Government, since 1911.
I have a certain knowledge of this railway policy. It is always the same thing. Mackenzie and Mann having obtained, in 1911, $35,000,000 from the Liberal government, must have contributed to the Conservative party's funds, three or four million dollars to carry the elections of 1911. They now put the plea that we did not protest against 
the merchant marine. Did the Conservatives protest, in 1911, against the grant of $35,000,000 to Mackenzie and Mann? They did not cast their vote against this railway policy because they had the certainty of getting a good share of those $35,000,000 in order to defeat Laurier. "Anything to beat Laurier." Let them not throw the stone, because they are the most open to criticism.
This disastrous policy must change. On this subject I wish to remark that I entirely approve of the principle adopted by my hon. friends of the Agrarian party, that each side will have to look to the re-election of its own candidates. Mr. Chairman, if to-day we have to put up with such enormous debts, the fault can be found in our election, it is due to election organization, to the buying up wholesale of newspapers to favour a party's politics, because for these things money is needed and who are those who put it up. They are the magnates, the railway companies, the banks and the large manufacturers. Have you any doubt that these gentlemen in return expect to retrieve their losses, as the saying goes? This is what ruins a country. We should act with Parliament as is done with a municipal council of a parish when it makes a mistake with regard to public works within its limits. Those interested would not allow the cost of such work to be 400 per cent higher than if it was done by a contractor at the cost price of the market. If however such a thing should happen, and if a council paid exorbitant prices, those interested could have recourse to a court of justice and would certainly be upheld in their contentions, for the municipal councils can be called upon to give an account of their act before the courts and be convicted as the case may be; but this House is the highest court of justice in this country, there is no higher tribunal and that allows it to adopt the most senseless and the most expensive enterprises which the people have to pay.
When one speaks in this House, no matter on what subject, it always ends on war topics. My hon. friend from Frontenac cannot to-day say one word on the merchant marine without bringing in the war, without mentioning what such and such a member has done and what he has not done. Well, Mr. Chairman, for my part, I have done what I should have done, and I fear no reproach, but I would like to see things cease and that the House betakes itself to business. Mr. Chairman, you have often heard that Sir Wilfrid Laurier's

Transcontinental as it is called, was to cost but $13,000,000, and often have I noticed when these figures of $13,000,000 were mentioned, they were greeted with prolonged applause on the Government side. The right hon. member from King's (Sir Robert Borden) has many times mentioned to us those figures, $13,000,000 to construct 1,800 miles of railway! I never took it for granted that the ex-Prime Minister was serious when he used to throw this bomb of $13,000,000 for an 1,800 mile railway. I never paid much attention to it and I also noticed, up to now, my hon. friends on this side of the House never passed any remarks about it. I think the proper time has come for me to take up this assertion. If I am not mistaken, the Laurier government who conceived this transcontinental project, declared that the railway after completion, would be handed over to the Grand Trunk who would undertake the operation of it for seven years without paying any interest to the Government which would mean to the country an expenditure of $15,000,000 of unpaid interest. At the expiration of the seven years, the Government was to rent the railway to the Grand Trunk for forty-nine years, the latter paying an annual interest of three per cent on the total cost of the road. That is what I understood. If the ex-Premier wishes to visit my county and there declare before my constituents that the transcontinental built by Sir Wilfrid Laurier was to only cost $13,000,000, I am certain that my electors would not take him seriously. It is simply a political bluff. I consider myself a practical man, I know the value of a dollar, I have laboured and handled the plough, I am not always an easy mark for the politician's bluff. I would like to see a change in this state of things; that business be taken up seriously in this House. Is. it possible for a Government like the present one to administer railways and a merchant marine? Mr. Chairman, I say it is not, because I know but too well the members of the Government. No returns can be expected from what they do. First, I give them no credit for ability unless it is that of furthering their aims through politics. These gentlemen are directors or are shareholders in large companies and they have more at heart the companies' interests than those of the public. So far I have not seen this Government do anything for the welfare of the country. What is however, evident to me, is that they have not followed our example, for the Liberal party after having held power for fifteen 124
years, had to retire as poor as it was in; 1896; in contrast to the Liberal party, which was always opposed to the nationalization of public utilities, the present Government thus reasoned: we shall take possession of the whole public service; not only shall we have control of the civil employees, but we shall have all the employees of the state-owned railways and of our merchant marine. In this way we shall control the country, cost what it may, we shall succeed nevertheless. I foresee that it will place a great number of electors at their beckoning, but on the other hand, I believe, that the latter will not all vote for them and besides there is the people who pay for these ruinous enterprises, who have an inkling of what transpires behind the curtains and who will dismiss them at the next general elections. I do not wish to ramble away from the question. Why this great hurry to vote $8,000,000 for the merchant marine? We cannot afford it this year; then why not place that amount on next year's estimates? The hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Campbell) complained only yesterday of the Hudson Bay Railway for which $21,000,000 have been spent. I believe it is more important to complete that railway, the cost of which has been more than reimbursed by the sale of lands which skirt this road, than to continue the building of ships when we have not sufficient freight for the ships we already own, not mentioning the enormous deficit we are accumulating. If it is wise, in order to economise, to delay the construction of the Hudson Bay Railway for one, two or three years, how much wiser would it not be for the Minister of Marine to postpone his own project to next year or later if need be. He would simply have to complete the ships already in building, not to start any others and leave things as they are. For as the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) remarked the ocean freight rates will fall in the proportion of 90 per cent. I have some experience of what took place before the war. I was an exporter of hay to Europe and pre-war times we could export hay through the port of Montreal tc Liverpool from the opening of navigation up to July at a price of 12 shillings and at times for 15 to 17^ shillings to Glasgow. You are well aware that for the last few years we could not export a ton of hay to England for less than $20 and $30 a ton.
Now, if the Minister of Marine has been somewhat encouraged by the fact that the number of ships built in 1919, were re-



munerative, he cannot pin his faith to the belief that the rates will be maintained at those high levels, because all the countries of the world have now larger merchant fleets than previous to the war and taking into consideration that the European countries are ruined, and buy very little, there exists very little water transportation. He stated last year that he could have sold his ships, at a profit. I am afraid that he has lost the occasion of reimbursing the people of this country, the money invested in that enterprise. Still, it was the advice that was given to him by many members of this side of the House, people of great experience, such as my hon. friend of Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) and Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), who knew better than the Minister of Marine and better than myself what ought to be done and the things that relate to the merchant marine. It is not perhaps too late: it is still better, when the market conditions are unsteady to sell at once and not to put off. When a man has netted 75 or 80 per cent, he sleeps in peace, whereas when he keeps his stock, he gets sick. I am surprised that the hon. minister is not ill on account of the appalling cost of his merchant marine. As a matter of fact, it is not he who pays, but the country, and so he may sleep quietly. Many hon. members on this side of the House know more about that matter than myself, and I trust they will continue the discussion, but I may refer to it again this afternoon should it be necessary.

In reading over the Hansard of March 29, 1921, page 1329, I find there the most interesting statement of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries:
When we are in Committee of Supply I will, to the very best of my ability, and with the greatest pleasure, give the fullest information to hon. members regarding the operations of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.
Taking the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to be a man of his word I should like to ask him a number of questions. I am sorry he is not in the House, but if the hon. gentleman who is now leading the House can tell me whether he will be in a position to answer them, I will put them to him. Will the hon. gentleman who leads the House tell me whether he is in a position to answer?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I am not a mind reader. I have not heard what the hon. member wishes to be answered.

On page 1331 of unrevised Hansard, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries gives a list of the vessels which compose the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, and which when built will complete the programme of the Government. I am glad to see the excellent deputy minister of Marine and Fisheries enter the House. I assure him that it is with great pleasure that a large number of the members of this House and the people generally heard that he had returned to the department which he had graced with his presence for a long time. We, and I imagine the business people of this country, are somewhat at a loss to know how the Department of Marine and Fisheries could be carried on in his absence. With the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) we all agree that he has had large experience in matters connected with the department.
I am glad to see the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) also in his seat again. I was just pointing out that in his statement it is set forth that 114,470 tons have yet to be completed. At $190 per ton this would amount to twenty odd million dollars. We are now being called upon to vote $8,000,000. Would the minister be kind enough to tell me whether this is the only instalment, or whether we may expect to vote other items later?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am sorry that the hon. member for Quebec South was not present last evening as he would have heard this question answered. But I have no objection to answering it again. The vote we are asking for now, $4,000,000, is a re-vote for last year, and is to complete the Government's shipbuilding programme. All the ships are so far advanced that by the end of the month of June, and not later than the month of July, all the ships will be finished. Possibly, it may be some little time before I have the honour to ask hon. members to vote money again, but you never can tell.
Really then, we have only $3,000,000 of a new vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Over how many ships is this $3,000,000 to be spread?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Sixteen.

Would the hon. minister be kind enough to give me the names of the ships? I hope they will be christened with proper names. If as my hon. friend the member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff)

has pointed out, the Government are entering into the spirit trade, I hope the ships will be properly named. I would suggest to the minister that he enter into a conference with his friends from Ontario, who are disturbing the electorate of Ontario with the presence of " Pussyfoot " Johnson and others, to have proper names attached to those ships, so that this country and other countries will know the kind of business that this Government has entered upon. I would like to know the names of those ships and the places where they are being built. It is important to know that. It has already been pointed out that when large public undertakings are being carried on in any constituency, it is extremely difficult for a member to ask for a public accounting. Such being the case, it would be well to know in what constituencies these ships are being constructed. I imagine that one is being constructed in a constituency close to my own, but I am prepared to oppose the vote in spite of that.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have not got one called the " Canadian Power," but if I had thought of it sooner, there would have been.

It would be a mighty
good ship.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The steamers are the Traveller, the Cruiser, the Constructor, the Reefer, the Thresher, the Pathfinder, the Leader, the Logger, the Skirmisher, the Coaster, the Challenger, the Harvester, and the Transporter. The Traveller is being built at the Harbour Marine Works, Victoria, and the Cruiser and Constructor at Halifax. On the Cruiser and the Constructor a little over a million dollars each has been spent, and on the Traveller about a million and a half.
How much more remains to be spent on the Traveller?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know.
Surely you are in a position to tell us what you expect to pay for these boats.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The contract price on the Traveller was $1,673,000. We expect to have the Cruiser and the Constructor finished in July.

It might not interest members of this House, but it would interest business men engaged in shipping to know how the Government's programme is being carried out. It would be well for us to
take our loss generally on the whole marine and let it sell for what it can. If we stopped building now, what would be our loss approximately, as compared with the loss we should sustain if we completed the boats and sold them below cost? I do not ask these questions in order to annoy the minister; nothing is further from my thoughts. How much more remains to be expended?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We will find out and let you know during the next hour.
What about the next boat?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If you want full information regarding the minor details of every boat I shall have to send to the office and get it. You want to know exactly how far advanced these boats are, how many more plates are to go on, what decks, and everything like that?
It might be interesting.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: And all about the piping, and so forth. We will try to get it for you.
And particularly the amount which is still to be expended on each. The minister can give that now.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: [DOT] I have not got it.
Give me the contract price for each ship, and approximately how much has been expended on each.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot tell you that, but I will get all the information I can, down to the smallest screw, if you will give me time.

I am only too glad to give you time. The members on this side want complete information in order to form a reasonable judgment on the whole question. I am sure that if we had full information some of us who are prejudiced against the scheme might become staunch supporters of it. I at present have a prejudice against the minister's policy but if I got all the information I require that prejudice might be removed. I do not believe in government control of ships or railways, or, for that matter, of anything else-not that I have no confidence in hon. gentlemen opposite, but I have no confidence in tne operation of public utilities and even if we were sitting opposite I should hold the same view. I do not know that the minister attaches very much value to the conversion of a new recruit, but if he does I would be only toe glad to be converted to his view, and cal.

his attention to the old saying of the joy in Heaven over the conversion of one sinner. It is Heaven to be in the minister's place just at the present moment, but there-might be joy in that portion of the Chamber if he could obtain one or more converts. I would like to ask the minister whether he has taken seriously into consideration the suggestion which was made in the House by the Minister of Railways last week, that we should take these boats and place them on the inland coasting trade and use them for carrying coal from the Sydneys to Montreal. Have representations been made to him with respect to this, and by whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not only have representations been made, but the company have decided to put those vessels on the coal trade. A large number of them are in Halifax just now, having a certain amount of overhaul, and then they are going to be put on the route.
Is that what the sixteen vessels are doing?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The number has varied. I would not want to make a guess, but I will wire and find out.
How many boats does the minister intend to place on the route?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is not arranged by the minister: it is done by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.
How does the minister know there was such an intention?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Because I was told so by the management.
Is the minister given all the information?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Oh, certainly.
Has he anything to do with influencing the decision?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not at all.
Is the management convinced this will be a paying route?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know what the management's views are.
If not, why does he think the management is going to run the boats from Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is the arrangement we have with them.

That is the arrangement the minister has with the management?
fMr Power]

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is very old news to my hon. friend, that the management of the merchant marine is entirely free from Government interference, and that Mr. Hanna, and his experienced steamship men, manage the boats and put them on whatever route they see fit.
Is Mr. Hanna a steamship man?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Mr. Teakle, of the Allan line, is the experienced man.
And all matters of policy such as these are entirely in the hands of the Canadian Merchant Marine?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: As far as the management of the ships is concerned.

Questions of policy as to where those boats are to sail would, I presume, be in the hands of this company. So that when the hon. minister takes credit for extending the trade of Canada to such and such ports, the minister was really not responsible for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I gave the management full credit for the great showing of the Merchant Marine as to the carrying of Canadian products and the profits. I do not take any credit.
The hon. minister is not responsible for the opening of new trade routes, in any part of the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
If any credit is to be given, it is to be given to the management company?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

If the minister became convinced that certain sailings were not paying, that certain services-such as the service to Newfoundland for instance-were not paying, could the minister, under his arrangement with the Merchant Marine, make representations to the Merchant Marine?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Surely.
If the House becomes convinced of this, would the decision of the House have any weight with the Merchant Marine?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The decision of the majority of the House always has influence with the minister.
It always has?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

I am glad to hear that. Therefore, should it be shown that the policy of establishing a service to certain countries, at the same time subsidizing the concern to run the steamship service, were in its nature apparently an absurb policy, a bad system to be followed, could the minister, after listening to representations on the part of shipping men, such as the hon. member from Lunenburg and others, make such a representation to the Company as would induce them to change?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am quite sure that if the member for Lunenburg makes representations to my colleague the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce that he is entitled to a subsidy on his fishing smacks, it will receive careful consideration of the Government.
I do not know that he has asked for any subsidy on fishing smacks, but I think it rather unfair for the minister to say

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I thought I heard him mention the hqn. gentleman's (Mr. Duff's) name.

I said he had made certain representations that it was a bad business to subsidize boats to go to a certain - country or to certain parts, and at the same time to send our own mercantile marine there, often at a loss, and I asked the minister. If he were convinced that these representations of the member for Lunenburg were just and reasonable, could he have any influence on the Merchant Marine Company and ask them to change this policy?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Again, I am sorry my hqn. friend was not with us last night. The Government ships are freight ships- the hon. gentleman from Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) describes them as tramp ships; I do not call them that. None of them are passenger ships, and, therefore, none of them are subsidized. The ships that are subsidized to Newfoundland, to the West Indies and Australia, are passenger ships subsidized by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
It is not a reflection to call vessels " tramp ships."

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I understand that.

Is there any possibility of the minister influencing the decision of the Merchant Marine Company?
I would like the minister to lay down the principle because I wish to make some representations on behalf of my constituents. Is it worth while making representations to the minister with regard to any question of policy as effecting the Merchant Marine?
Is my hon. friend in favour of the Government operating these ships?
I am not.
If not in favour of operating them, is he in favour of having them operated by a private company?
I am in favour of getting rid of the whole thing, lock, stock and barrel.
Is the hon. member aware of the amount of trade from the west coast of Africa that is now coming to Canada?
No.
Is the hon. member aware how much trade from the coast of Africa is going to the United States?
No.
Would the hon. gentleman think it advisable to have a transport service between here and the west coast of Africa?
Now, I will put that question to the minister. Will he please give me an answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am not the Minister of Trade and Commerce;-he will be here in a few moments.

Then I give that answer to my hon. friend from Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer). Then, may I again ask for an answer to my question whether the minister can influence the management of the Merchant Marine to change or to amend its policy if the proper representations are made?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am a modest man and would not like to claim too much. If, however, my hon. friend will tell me what he wants I will try to get the influence that he thinks I ought to have.

I have recently been asked by a number of people in Quebec and Montreal to place before the minister the suggestion that he ask the Merchant Marine to arrange their services so as to facilitate
19&6

the shipment of horses to the Old Country. I understand that that would be a very profitable trade, and that if we could get the boats, American horsemen would be only too glad to come to Canada and carry on their shipments from Montreal or Quebec. I have also been told that the Merchant Marine boats have been discriminating against the port of Quebec. They obtain cargoes, say, in the East Indies and carry them through to Montreal, refusing, unless the cargoes are very large, to discharge at Quebec, with the result that shipment has to be made by rail back to Quebec. This involves considerable expense and inconvenience on the part of Quebec merchants and consumers, and it would seem to be only fair that these cargoes should be discharged at Quebec. I would like the minister to take these matters into consideration. If we have him with us this afternoon I hope to read to him some letters with reference to the trade in horses with the United Kingdom.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, it is much to be regretted that the Government saw fit to force the Opposition to spend so much time in trying to make them agree to what common sense should have caused them to accept from the start. The difference between the Opposition and the members of the other side of the House is now to be seen clearly, because when some members of the other side suggests some practical measure, dictated by common sense, we of this side are always anxious to accept it. For many years the Government has proven that, on account of our bad financial conditions, it is necessary to practice economy. Now it is in the name of that very economy that the Opposition feel it is their duty to oppose these extravagant Estimates. Mr. Chairman, we cannot possibly agree to the votes asked for, under the present circumstances, for many reasons. First of all, it has not yet been shown to us that the carrying of this naval policy of the hon. Minister of Marine was obligatory, necessary and beneficial. We refuse to vote such enormous sums of money when we know that they will serve to convey once more that same man Crosby from Halifax to Hudson bay where he goes with food for some Eskimos who do not exist there. We refuse to vote any amount in order to allow that man or others to carry to Chesterfield some wire with which to fence 10,000 square miles of land, so that cariboos that never pass

there may breed. We refuse to vote those Estimates because we know that, on the shores of the Richelieu river the minister puts to dry many a vessel that could be used somewhere else. We then refuse these Estimates because we know that at Port Nelson a number of boats do not serve any purpose. There is amongst others a steamer called the Neophyte which is idle on the shore. There are four other barges there. There is* that precious dredge which for the last fifteen days has not been used. For all those reasons, Mr. Chairman, we object to the shipping Estimates at the present time.
We know that the selection of Port Nelson as a seaport is altogether ridiculous, that the natural port of that district was Port Churchill. But the Minister of Marine saw fit to remove the natural port of the Hudson bay from Port Churchill to Port Nelson, which is at the further end of the Hudson bay and where the boats of Crosby cannot reach but at a distance of 25 miles when year after year they carry on shipments of supplies for people who do not exist. And that is the reason why they have transferred there that notorious dredge, in order that they might dig a channel through which ships could more easily reach the port when all the time it was demonstrated that the Nelson carries alluvia which destroys year after year the work accomplished during previous years.
We are asked to grant those sums of money for the building of ships. It was shown lately in this House the present boats of the Government had wandered about the seven seas in quest of cargoes. We have sufficient proof of that.
Now that the war is over and this question of patriotism seems to have been settled for the time being while exports have been reduced to normal, it is understood that we do not need more ships. Moreover, if we wish to help the expansion of shipping, we may, in imitation of the Montreal Vickers', go to work and build ships for Norway and other countries. Why build ships if we have no cargoes to carry? Such a departure might prove most dangerous to our young nation. True it is that we hold this famous title of nation, having bound ourselves to respect the conditions of the League of Nations. Now, as far as Canada is concerned, what does that League of Nations mean? The right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and the former president of the Privy Council (Hon. Mr. Rowell) told us wonderful things in this

connection, things of such a nature as to exalt the patriotism of a young nation to the utmost. On the other hand, their utterances in Europe were dreadful, so much so that, at a certain moment, Europe felt itself shaken and, surely, the nicident would have been most ingracious had not the former president of the Privy Council thought fit to deny his own words.
By clause 10 of the covenant of the league, we bind ourselves to carry, in war time, our human cargo overseas; and by that same clause, we also bind ourselves to carry the victuals necessary to feed about fifty nations. Surely, this famous League of Nations does not rank very high in my estimation, it rather constitutes a snare, a screen behind which Europe may pull its wires at the expense of the smaller nations.
I beg leave to quote an instance of this before I proceed further. When the last war between Russia and Poland took place, Poland and thirty-three other nations had signed the Peace Treaty according to which, in the case of war, those nations were to help Poland to have the integrity of her territory respected, and were to come to her rescue. Well what happened? Poland, in that war with Russia, was abandoned and found herself alone. The nations which had assumed the obligation to defend the integrity of her territory and to use their influence in her favour in the council of the League of Nations, did nothing of the kind. What, then, does that League of Nations amount to? It is apparently a mere means of calling the smaller nations to the rescue of the bigger. Supposing a war was declared in India, in Egypt or elsewhere and we had a navy which was available, our ships would be at the disposal of those nations which had signed the Peace Treaty.
I shall oppose, with all my might, the votes intended to develop the naval scheme of the hon. minister, because a scandalous misuse was made of our ships in the past. No later than three years ago, when the people of this country were put on short allowance in the restaurants and in the hotels, the Government's ships were carrying bacon over to the Esquimaux, who eat nothing hut raw meat, and that merchandise, which would have been so useful to our white people, the officials at Port Nelson were ohliged to deliver it to the Esquimaux, who made candles with it.
We have met with the railway disaster; we have run into a debt of $650,000,000 in connection with the Canadian Northern; we have to conclude the purchase of the Grand Trunk by which we shall incur a debt of
$900,000,000. The railway deficit is a real disaster, and yet, we find, on the Government side, no less a man than the hon. member for Lambton East (Mr. Armstrong) who would like to see the present Government marine operated under similar conditions.
It is claimed in certain quarters that, at a time of enforced idleness, when so many people are out of work, it would be most important for the Government to let contracts and to operate and develop the marine. I think that' reason is groundless. When the last Norwegian ship was launched at Montreal a statement was made during the banquet which followed, to the effect that it was the intention to close the Vickers shipyards within a month or more from that date. I have said, just a few days ago, that we had, in this country, an industrial policy which was surely not unfamiliar to the Government, and that this policy was no more nor less than a policy of protection beyond measure. It is desired that the question of salaries should be settled, and there you have the reason why the president of the company stated at that banquet, that work would cease at the Vickers' shipyards, at Montreal, although there was no lack of contracts.
We also oppose the present votes for economy's sake, because the burden of taxes on the ratepayers' shoulders is already heavy enough. Our marine is bringing us a deficit, our railways have brought us one likewise. It is probable that the Budget will reveal still higher taxes. I find it altogether unreasonable to favour a programme which in the past has brought about deficits and which, on account of its present uselessness, will entail deficits still larger. With a debt of over two billions, we can say that the Government cannot afford to spend such sums for an undertaking which at best can only be a matter of chance.
I heard a short time ago, "The two parties cannot throw stones at each other in the matter of the national railways; the Liberal party have a great share of responsibility, and so have the Government party." There is, however, a slight difference to be considered. Under the Laurier regime it could be allowable for a government to spend something to foster the progress of the country; but at a time when Canada's debt reaches two billions, I think the blame we can level against the present Government is much more serious. We are often told that the resources of the country

must be developed. True, if you have the wherewithal to do so. Our credit is wretched; we have a formidable debt which demands at all cost the strictest economy, and our resources are but hypothetical at the present time. We cannot believe in the reason invoked by the Government that they want to give work to people in shipyards, no more than we could believe them when they talked of a programme of workmen's lodgings. They were to give employment to ail the trades, they were to keep from the working class the danger of unemployment. They had an underlying design. They meant to impose such impossible conditions that no one would accept the offers, and they were refused everywhere.
I admit that under the present circumstances, we should follow the advice of the Government who urge us to practise economy; but we do not want to be the only, ones to do so; they must do likewise; they must put an end to the development of its merchant marine programme; they must stop their expenditure on the Welland canal to make a seaport of Toronto; when we know that the Welland canal can only be of use to the coast trade. Under present circumstances, they ought to undertake to strike out the fifty millions intended for the Welland canal, and the hundred millions voted to continue the development of the port of Toronto which will never be anything but a port for tourists.
I therefore beseech the Government to practise that which they preach, to content themselves with the strictest economy in the matter of shipbuilding. And I hope they will recognize the good faith of the Opposition and the duty which is now imposed upon us to oppose most energetically votes for which there is certainly no excuse, and which can only result in heavier taxes being imposed upon our fellow-citizens.

The minister has gone
far afield for justification of his merchant marine policy citing legislation existing in Cromwell's time. He may be	Cromwellian	to	that	extent,	buthe	is mistaken	if he	thinks	the
Canadian people are behind this proposition. Leading Canadian journals on both sides of politics have been quoted indicating clearly that the people generally and the business interests are altogether opposed to it, but the Minister apparently intends to carry it through with the assistance of his supporters. Let me quote from the Toronto Saturday Night, the leading financial

journal in Ontario, which has supported the Government in practically all its legislation. The last issue of that journal says:
When the war was at its height and when the deadly submarine was getting in its best work, the thought was very general that it would be years before-there was again sufficient shipping to meet the public demand. But see what has really happened? There are to-day tied up at the docks or swinging at anchor more idle vessels than ever before known. An authoritative statement is to the effect that there are five million dead weight tons of shipping laid up in Britain, America and Scandinavia, a total of 1,278 ships. It is not a case of there being too many vessels, provided world conditions were normal is place of being utterly demoralized as they now are. It is safe to state that there are not less than two hundred million people over in Europe who would only be too glad to see these ships now motionless sailing into their ports carrying from this continent the necessities of life. But, alas, they have nothing with which to pay, so they must go without.
Much of this idle shipping can now be purchased at far less than original cost, the owners being only too glad to get out from under. A prominent Canadian ship broker informed the writer the other day that first-class vessels could now be purchased at well under $10 0 per ton,'whereas these same vessels cost $200 or upward per ton to construct.
This is one of the foremost journals in Ontario and has been a sympathetic supporter of the Government and particularly of the Minister, and what I have just read indicate one of the storm signals in that province.
On Thursday last, April 7, the Evening Telegram of Toronto, which has been a Government supporter ever since it was founded, opposed this scheme in a very vigorous editorial headed " Concealment Can't Help." The editorial reads:
The financial showing of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine is quite as good as was to be expected. But the Minister of Marine might well have been a little more frank with the public. The merchant fleet was started under the stress of war. The building was continued under popular demand that no Government would have dared to deny. The operation has been, so far, as can be seen, businesslike and economical.
But what was to be gained by attempting to conceal the fact that a great deal of the wartime cost will have to be written off? What profiteth it the Government to give a false impression that the fleet showed a surplus when the capital charges must necessarily be taken into account? The fact still remains that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine has a deficit of $1,500,000, a statement such as any business man would give serious consideration when the actual depreciation in shipping values is increased by many millions.
Hon. Mr. Ballantyne may be playing politics, but playing politics won't pay deficits. These are serious financial times in the country's history, and nothing is to be gained by misleading statements that will have to be amended at an early date.

The significant point is this, the minister says:
I wish to point out that these net earnings are before providing for interest, and the above amount of net earnings, $781,460.09 is equal to 2.35 per cent interest on notes given to the Government for the full cost of the ships.
Now, the depreciation in any asset is the difference between its actual cost and its replacement value. The replacement value of ships to-day is shown by the many authorities which have been cited to the House to have been cut in two, and yet the hon. minister assumes to cut off by way of depreciation only the 5 per cent which is the annual depreciation outside of any which comes by reason of the condition of the world's markets and the absence of business for shipping. If a loss of 50 per cent had been caused to the merchant marine by tempest, or in any other way, that would be the present depreciation. Loss has been caused, not by tempest, but by reason of certain conditions existing. So that the proper course for the minister to take would have been to carry on his books the shipping at its actual cost, to write off the depreciation, and to take his loss as any business house would do. I submit that the hon. minister has confused the principles of depreciation, because 5 per cent is depreciation which continues outside of any other consideration, no matter what happens. That is the basis which is generally accepted in the matter of depreciation. But in addition to that, there is the depreciation which results from other causes, such as tempest, fire, or anything else that involves the laying up or destruction of the ships. For such depreciation the minister should have, made allowance in his figures, and had he done so, as the " Telegram " points out, the loss would amount to something like $1,500,000.
The minister should revise his figures in order that the exact situation may be understood, and should adopt the principle that depreciation is the difference between the actual cost and the present replacement value. That is the principle which has been adopted in all the courts. The position is more serious in view of the fact that every dollar taken from business in taxes reduces by $1 the possibilities of business expansion. If it was necessary to keep returned men employed, it would have been well for the Government to cancel its orders when it found that shipping was no longer needed, and adopt some scheme along the line of housing, or establish some fund in e<>
ordination with the funds of the provinces to keep the returned men engaged. By doing so, they would have kept the men busy establishing homes instead of building a vast fleet of ships which is resulting in loss day by day, and the outcome of which we are unable to ascertain.
Every village and every town is opposed to the scheme, and every paper that is printed has something to say in criticism of it. The confidence of the public is shaken, and there is a widespread feeling that the Government should immediately get rid of a scheme which is not paying and which is adding to the burden of this country day by day.
There may be, and there is, a reason why we cannot get rid of our difficulties in connection with railway construction, because railways are necessary to maintain communication between the various parts of the country. Cities, towns and villages would be cut off, and great loss would be entailed in trade and business if we did not carry on the railways even at a loss. But that is an entirely different situation from the shipping; it is entirely different from carrying on trade (between negro ports in Africa and Canada, or carrying whiskey to Cuba and Jamaica, and so on, as is being done, at a loss.
I submit, therefore, that we should not pass the estimates which the minister has submitted to the House, as it is simply throwing money away on a scheme which has not been well considered, and which will entail greater loss as time goes on.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I
have often heard people of all conditions say that we should expect anything from the present Government; and I don't doubt but my colleagues on this side of the House have also heard the same opinion expressed;

but there are limits to all things, and that is why we could not foresee that, last night, between eleven o'clock and midnight, after a day especially allotted to the private members, the Government would bring forth this item of eight millions for the consideration of the House, especially under the unfortunate circumstances known to all, circumstances which necessitated the absence of a number of members either already in Montreal or on their way there. I say that the Government must necessarily have known of those regrettable circumstances, and that it took a good deal of audacity on their part to ask the House, under such circumstances, to deal with a matter of such importance. Evidently, had we been able to foresee that the Government would bring forth this matter last night, there is no doubt, as was stated with as much sincerity as valiance by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon), that most of the members would have spent the night here to take part in the debate.
There is no doubt but that the Government counted upon the absence of many of us; but if they had hoped thus to pass this item without difficulty, they must have found themselves much out in their calculations. The Opposition is still hale and hearty, and ready to fight day and night, the whole week if need be, until the Government bring into operation the means at their disposal to close our mouths, and apply foreclosure.
Mr. Chairman, like all those who have spoken before me I am opposed to this Government marine policy, and I also, am decided to adopt all possible means to oppose it. The Opposition have been blamed for having passed the time, during the night, in reading paper extracts. Has not the Opposition a right to do so? Have they not the full right to do so? The duty of the Opposition here is to express the opinion of the public, the opinion of the electorate throughout the country. And what is the best way to do that? Is it not by quoting such comments as are made by the Canadian press? Although it may displease the Government, or perhaps the hon. Minister of Marine, I beg forgiveness for giving myself the pleasure of reading an extract -and especially of reading it in English- of an article published by the Citizen of Ottawa, in December, 1920. I do not know whether this article has ever been read; in any case, it may be well to read it again.
Too Many Ships.
While our Government is taking much credit to itself for its extensive and costly shipbuild-

ing programme, which goes on apace, there is developing a world situation in tonnage which is becoming of serious import to all maritime nations. This relates to the glut of tonnage from which the European and American continent is suffering. Writing in the New York Evening Post, Mr. Allan Nevins calls attention to the fact that the United States shipping ' board has tied up seven steel vessels since the end of September and now announces that eight more, all large ships, have been withdrawn. A noted American authority on maritime affairs is quoted to the effect that hardly half the world's available ocean tonnage is being employed at this time and that a general fall in shipping securities in the United'States and Britain marks the general situation. Companies here and abroad have resorted to special devices to keep their tonnage moving. Five lines plying from Liverpool to Oriental ports-the Cunard, Ellerman, Moss and others -have offered rebates to shippers who will promise to restrict themselves to their vessels. Steamship agents in New York and other American ports are making vigorous efforts to obtain parcel freight in default of full cargo shipments. A fortnight ago the American shipping board announced that American lines carrying freight to the four chief ports of Germany, Holland, Belgium and France, would be allowed to fix their own rates. This means a price-cutting war in competition with European lines.
The chief causes for the present situation are given as too much tonnage and a heavy decline in freight shipping. According to Lloyd's Register the world had, in June, 1914, a gross tonnage of about 45% million tons of shipping. In June of this year it had almost 54 million tons. In addition to this there is building some seven or eight million more tons. In the United States the shipping board has attempted in vain to sell some of the 1,000 steel ships under its control to private parties, but the knowledge that the world is in for a protracted spell of sharp competition and of freight rates that spell disaster to lines lacking in efficiency and very heavy capital has proved too strong for the board to do business.
For this reason and for several others, we are strongly opposed to this naval policy, but the chief reason is that the country cannot afford this expense, as many an hon. member has repeatedly said before me, but in such a struggle as we have been going through, since last night, I think repetitions are necessary, and there cannot be too many of them.
Some time ago, I heard the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals state before this committee that for several years no railway would be built by the Government. The same thing has been said for the Public Works Department. There is a pressing need of certain works which we have asked for, for many a year, such as an extension of the wharf at Chicoutimi, for this wharf is too small, and the development of our district is consequently delayed. We are invariably told: "We cannot do anything for you, the Government has no

money." It has been the same for everything we have asked. I have always received the same answer to all that I have asked for, for several years: "We have no money, and the proof is that we do not undertake any work." That is why thirty-one engineering offices have been closed in the country; the Government have closed sixteen of these offices in the Department of Public Works. We are told that the Government have decided not to undertake any public works because of the need for economy. These offices have been closed; yet, I hear that the employees have been kept on, that they have been transferred to other departments. As I have already said on many another occasion, the county of Chicoutimi is certainly a beautiful one. I believe that on the other side of the House, there is not one member who has any idea of the extent of the district of Chicoutimi-Saguenay, and even on this side of the House, I am sure that some would be surprised were I to tell them that in order to go from one end of my county to the other, one has to travel eight hundred miles. It is perhaps larger than the rest of the province of Quebec. The Dominion Government owns large properties in the lake St. John district and also in the Chicoutimi district, and all along the northern coast to Labrador. I do not think I am exaggerating when I say that the Government has built in my district, in the lake St. John district, and along the Saguenay, about sixty wharves which will certainly fall to pieces, now that the engineer's office is to be closed.
I do not know whether this engineer has left his office; at any rate, the closing of the office is a foregone conclusion; the engineer will leave Chicoutimi and come and live in Quebec; and the Government property-some sixty wharves-will continue to deteriorate. Besides, the Government has had dredges made; they spent several thousand dollars in the dredging of the Saguenay river; but there are absolutely urgent works to be attended to, for the district is going to develop at an unexpected rate within the next few years. However the Government seem to put obstacles in the way and impede progress. Why refuse in all the counties of the country the carrying out of absolutely necessary works, and spend some ten millions for an altogether useless marine? When we confer about such matters with well informed people, people of second judgment and free from political entanglement, they cannot imagine that a government should
take the responsibility of so nefarious a policy: of spending ten millions for an absolutely useless marine while refusing to carry out positively urgent works in all parts of the country.
Well, as I had occasion to say yesterday, the Government under a pretense of economy, has suppressed a small grant which the Laurier government had allowed for 12 or 15 years, as soon as the Price firm ceased to carry on its industry at St. Catherine's bay. For several years Sir Wilfrid Laurier's government granted a supply of $3,500 to a very interesting population, that of the north shore. It is not a mere fishing community; they have large industries, they own fine farms, numerous, flourishing parishes. Now, under the pretence of economizing a few cents, this population is deprived of an absolutely necessary service. The Minister of Commerce gives as a reason for it that this service is a "ferry service". I had always understood that a ferry service was carried on between the two shores of a river. This subsidy granted by the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier was to allow a boat to go from Tadoussac, on the north shore of the St. Lawrence, to St. Catherine's bay, which is not on the Saguenay river but on the St. Lawrence. Therefore it seems to me that this cannot be a "ferry service". When a boat leaves Tadoussac she has to go to the St. Lawrence and come back to St. Catherine's bay. For 12 years this subsidy was granted; everybody found it absolutely'necessary, and now, in order to save a few dollars a whole population of about fifteen thousand souls are deprived of all communication during the long winter months.
I say that, for all those reasons, no confidence can be placed in ministers, who thus carry on the business of the country, and I oppose the vote of eight millions which the Minister of Marine is asking for.
