(Translation.) Last night a bomb exploded in the House of Commons. A credit of $8,330,000 was asked for the Merchant Marine. The House was taken by surprise. No one expected that such a demand would be made last night. The debate started vigorously. The siting lasted all night; it will last probably all day and perhaps the whole week. The members on your left, Mr. Chairman, are convinced they have an imperious duty to fulfil, and want to protect with all their might against this policy, which is condemned by the electors from one end of the country to the other.
We were given, last week, a statement on' the operation of the Government railways, acknowledging a deficit of seventy
million dollars, and I believe that if the auditing of the accounts of the administration of the National Railways was conscientiously and properly made, it would not be seventy millions we would have to deplore, but more likely one hundred millions and perhaps more, as stated by many newspapers, including those favourable to the Government. It is therefore found, Mr. Chairman, that the Government operation of the National Railways is disastrous, to the utmost, altogether ruinous, and calculated to bankrupt the country, unless the Government be driven from office by the wrath and indignation of the people, and unless competent people having the interest of Canada at heart, should take the direction of national affairs. After having had a deficit of 120 millions in two years with the railways, the hon. Minister of Marine asks us to continue the building of a Merchant Marine as a means of giving employment to returned soldiers. This aim would be most praiseworthy, and if it had been faithfully carried out there would have been nothing but congratulation to offered to the Government. But, as in all the programmes introduced by the Government, this one has been brought down as a mean of maintaining themselves in power, ontwithstanding the will of the people. Favouritism has been shown to friends of the Government in the giving of contracts, and a bid made for popularity.
I asked the hon. Minister of Marine a short time ago if he had received requests from different parts of the province and from the district of Quebec for shipbuilding contracts. The hon. minister does not recollect having received numerous requests from this district. I know that he speaks in good faith when he says his memory fails him, but to my personal knowledge the most urgent requests have been made to the Government by firms of the highest standing for some of these contracts for Quebec, the cradle of shipbuilding in Canada, in order that work might be given there, as elsewhere to the brave soldiers who distinguised themselves at the front, and who asked the Government an opportunity to earn the bread for their families. If the Department of Marine wishes to make the necessary search it will be found that the Quebec firm of Quinlan and Robertson, offered to construct steel vessels at that place, but there have been no contracts for shipbuilding given to Quebec. There is neither work nor patronnage of any kind for that city, because it is hostile to this Government. I

have myself pleaded with the Government; I have forwarded petitions. Formerly I had the honour to be mayor of the city of Quebec ant it was in that capacity that I took these steps. The Quebec Chamber of Commerce also applied to the Government with the same objection in view, but we received merely acknowlegements of our petitions, and the contracts were given elsewhere, some times without tenders, to the friends of the Government. Enormous contracts were given, and Quebec was rerefused even the slightest consideration for the returned soldier who wanted bread for his family. Apart from the firm of Quinlan and Robertson, the Davie Shipbuilding Co. of Levis, one of the best organized firms in the country also applied for contracts. The hon. minister answered one of my questions just now by saying that the firm of Davie, of Levis, had built two vessels, and had given full and entire satisfaction. A lay number people from the city of Quebec worked in the Davie Shipyards, and Levis as well as Quebec tried to obtain contracts, but the citizens of Levis were no luckier than those of Quebec, and after the building of the two boats, no other contract was given. The great majority of the labourers who worked at Levis were deturned soldiers, as I know from having Government places for most of them, and they are now thrown out of work.
I listened with much interest to the judicious remarks of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) an the subject of shipbuilding, and I congratulate the hon. member upon the valuable and interesting information he has given to the country. The same applies also to the hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair).
Because of the disastrous Gouvernment Merchant Marine policy, and the administration of the National railways, the people of the country are to be bled white to replenish the public treasury to which they willingly contribute since they know that the Government during the war contracted very heavy debts which, whether wise or not, have to be paid. The public is obliged to make the greatest sacrifices, even the humble labourer who earns barely enough to keep his family, must contribute a certain percentage of the wages he earns by hard work, to pay the debts contracted by this Government. And where does this money go? Can the tax-payers at least have the satisfaction of being able to say that their money serves to decrease

the National debt? No, Mr. Chairman, I am well informed? I believe that the Income tax brought about 28 millions to the public Treasury last year. Has any part of these 28 millions been used to reduce the national debt? On the contrary, these amounts contribute only iil a small degree to pay off the disastrous administration of the national railways and merchant! marine, which are running the country to ruin and will prove more costly to the people than the war.
I was proud and rather satisfied to notice lately that the city of Quebec for the year 1919, had contributed to the public treasury through the income tax, the amount of $2,-
800,000.	It has therefore the right to claim her share in the distribution of government grants. Each time, however, Quebec has asked for some favour; what has been the Government's reply? Only of late, I petitioned the hon. Minister of Public Works, asking for the rebuilding of a breast wall, the property of the Government, which had been destroyed during the flood of 1918 and which supported the Saint Gregoire de Montmorency road, in the beautiful county that I have the honour to represent in this House. It was refused, they even declined to do anything, whatsoever, even to repair this property which was their own. My predecessor asked the Government who had even promised to relieve the situation by the construction of a bridge on the island of Orleans connecting the mainland with seven of the most flourishing parishes of the Quebec district, comprising deserving farmers, who. are isolated on that island during a certain period of the year, when they cannot sell their products to the city and neither ship them, not even can they dispose of their fish which become a loss, Mr. Chairman, at a time when we are pre-occupied in lowering the cost of living. Subsidies were once granted them but they have since been cancelled. For many years we have insisted that the Government put to execution this important project, and which will be done, you may rest assured, when the Government of this country will be under the administration of persons having a sense of justice and wish to be equitable to the population of this country without distinction of race or religion.
When we shall have at the head of the Government men of the stamp that I have just mentioned, the bridge of the island of Orleans will be built and it will be an act of justice and an important improvement.

We have requested, Mr. Chairman, that the Government instead of throwing away their money in enterprises like the merchant marine, in order to favour their friends, I might also add the city of Quebec has also made the request, that this Government, its Premier its ministers, the entire Cabinet, fulfil the contract and keep their pledges. While the right hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) is in his seat, I shall recall his words pronounced in 1913 at the Chateau Frontenac on the occasion of a large banquet given to him by the citizens of Quebec. He then declared to the citizens of Quebec that he wished to do them justice and that he had come to Quebec to see that these large enterprises were to be continued without any interruption and completed. Where are those pledges, those contracts signed1 by the Government for which the city of Quebec has made enormous sacrifices to obtain the development of railways, to obtain the transportation of the western wheat which had been promised to them and which was to the advantage of the whole country? The promises, the contracts, the solemn pledges and the declarations made by ex-Premier of Canada before many hundreds of persons at the Chateau Frontenac, in Quebec, where are they? All these pledges have become a dead letter. They always answered us:	"Gentlemen,
your demands are reasonable, but we cannot for a moment think, during war time, to execute any work, we cannot think of spending any money." Nevertheless, we voted millions after millions and the Government spent that money in the building of ships and they refused to the citizens of the Quebec district, improvements which would have benefited the whole country. They continued to ship the western grain through the American ports, at a 'cost of 34 to 35 cents per bushel, when by shipping it by the St. Lawrence river and Quebec, route, having given us the wharves and the elevators promised, we could have shipped the Winnipeg wheat at a cost of about 16 or 17 cents per bushel, this is to say 50 per cent cheaper and at the same time utilize our national railways and shortten the route by 214 miles, from Quebec to Winnipeg. This is the way that the Quebec province has been treated by the Government since 1911. And to-day when they wish to bring on closer relations with Quebec, when they want to shake hands on the eve of federal elections, is it not time, Sir, for the citizens of the province of Quebec to
consider how shamefully they have been treated by the Government. You may be sure, Mr. Chairman, that the people of the city of Quebec and of the whole province do remember and will not forget; such is their motto. Can this Government, which has only three members from Quebec in its ranks, after having denied all its pledges and if I may be allowed to use the expression-boycott the province of Quebec, can this Government expect in the next general election any other result than that which it obtained in 1917? The representatives who will be sent to this House by the province of Quebec will be just as united as they are to-day.
There has been another injustice towards the city of Quebec to which I would like also to refer. Quebec has a very well organized exhibition, whose board always relied on the $50,000 allowed by the Dominion Government. When our turn came to apply for the grant, we were told that the Government could not give it because they had to economize during the war. It is always the same answer as regards the province of Quebec. After the war, we sent our request to which they replied: "We are not giving any more grants; we have done it two or three times for other provinces; Quebec never got it, but, now we have stopped these grants."
I wanted to draw the attention to that injustice on the part of the Government towards the city of Quebec, because if you want to have god farm products and to encourage young people to remain on the land in order to cultivate it and to provide cargoes for the Government ships, it seems to me that it would be an excellent policy to give a little encouragement to the good farmers of the Quebec district, as it has been done elsewhere, and to give to Quebec the grant which it did not get, although entitled to it. The Board of Harbour Commissioners did not meet with greater success, when they asked for the construction of a cold storage plant, which would allow to ship through Quebec the butter and cheese which we are forced to ship through Montreal, because we have no cold storage plant in Quebec. I do not know that any of the members of the Government who are present in this House can say that the province and especially the city of Quebec actually received a share of the grants.
Allow me, Mr. Chairman, to say a few words about the government-owned railways and the service which we have in Quebec. I believe it is the duty of the

people to patronize the national roads as much as possible and when I am not in too great a hurry to reach Quebec or Ottawa, I travel on the Canadian Northern. Do you know what kind of service we get between Quebec and Montreal, for instance? The Canadian Pacific runs three good trains daily which cover the distance in five hours; the Canadian Northern has pretty good coaches, it is a fairly good train but it takes seven hours to go from Quebec to Montreal. When taking the Ocean Limited from Montreal to Quebec, you would think that they would make use of the Quebec bridge and take the passengers right through to the city, however they do nothing of the kind. The Ocean Limited, when not late, reaches Levis at five minutes past twelve at night, and there is a boat to take the passengers over to Quebec city; but unfortunately it happens sometimes that the train is late-it is a habit with the government-owned railways -and as it reaches Levis at 2 or 3 o'clock in the morning, passengers have to wait on the wharf for ferry boat. Travellers coming from Quebec to take the Ocean Limited, who number sometimes 50 or 60 and perhaps a 100, cross over with the ferry boat which leaves at 11.30 p.m. and if the train is late, they have to wait in the open air until 2 or 3 o'clock in the morning. That is how the national railways are being operated. It would be much better to have a train leaving from the Pacific station, which would go over the Quebec bridge and connect with the Ocean Limited, for the convenience of the passengers bound for Montreal, and those bound for Quebec could be taken right through to the city. When a request to that effect was made by the council and the Chamber of Commerce of Quebec, the Government replied that it would involve too great an expense. The administration of our national railways is the same throughout the country.
The operation of the road is about the same elsewhere-I have had occasion to travel a little between Quebec and Winnipeg, for instance. When I passed by way of Toronto, I found magnificent coaches, very large, very well appointed; but if I pass via Cochrane, it is another story between that place and Quebec. It is as if one would say, It will always be good enough for Quebec-I would like the Minister of Railways to see for himself; I am sure he is ignorant of the state of things, and I would be most happy if he could realize what kind of service is given from [Mir. Da vigueur. ]
Cochrane to Quebec. It is one that could not be compared with that to be had between Toronto to Winnipeg.
These are some of the grievances of the citizens of Quebec. For my part, I am absolutely opposed to the policy of the Government Merchant Marine, which is nothing less than a duplicate of the disastrous National Railways policy, and had I an advice to give the Government, I would tell them to give up the whole scheme at all cost, immediatetly if possible, to get rid of this load which is breaking the country's back, and which together with the national railways, spells the ruin of the nation.
I said a moment ago that we had solicited contracts for the firm Quinlan & Robertson. It comes to my memory now that we also asked for contracts for a company of shipbuilders of Saint Laurent, on the Isle of Orleans, which employ a large number of workmen there and elsewhere. This request was no more heeded by the Government than the others. So that when I say that the distribution of contracts was marked by favouritism, I believe that it will be admitted that I am absolutely justified.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman I shall vote against the item of $8,338,000, and I will ask the Government before indulging in useless expenditure, before sinking millions as they do, to give a little more consideration to the citizens of Quebec, who pay their taxes like everybody else. I will ask them again to continue the work on the St. Charles river, at Quebec, and I will not weary asking this. The Government have already sunk $1,600,000 in these works; moreover they have cancelled the contract which they had with the contractors and acquired the whole plant, and if I am well informed this plant was valued at about five of six -hundred thousand dollars. Without any reason, the Government, some day, decided to discontinue the work in spite of engagements taken and in spite of their contracts. Notwithstanding many solicitations from the citizens of Quebec, the Government have refused to resume the work, and the matter will no doubt go no further, like the rest. It seems to me this would have secured a fine port for the Government marine.
I will vote against this item of $8,000,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the committee has been sitting for about eighteen hours continuously. The item under discussion was before the committee on a previous day from about 4.30 until six

o'clock, and again from eight o'clock in the evening until 12.30 the next morning. Certain hon. gentlemen opposite have formed the opinion that they should block this item, for what purpose I am unable to conceive, and for what purpose I modestly suggest they do not quite understand themselves.
The history of the item under review is very briefly this:	During the progress of
the war, indeed at a period which turned out to be fairly near the end, having in mind the total amount of construction, the Government did undertake a shipbuilding programme of certain dimensions. Toward the undertaking of that programme they had been repeatedly urged by the hon. members of this House, and from the entire Dominion pressing requests came that this country should commence the task of establishing a mercantile marine, requests that were all the more pressing because of the all too-imminent necessity of the hour.
That policy was embarked upon, if I am correctly informed, with the unanimous approval of this House in the first place. That was in the spring of the year 1918. In the spring of the year 1919, after the armistice had been signed, but before, I believe, peace was formally established, the policy was continued with certain limitations. A vote of this House was taken for its continuance, amounting to $30,000,000, and my recollection is that that vote was unanimous, some objection being taken (but no vote being called for) on the part, not of the official Opposition, but of one or two hon. gentlemen who now are among the Farmer group. However, the policy that the Government had ventured upon received the unanimous, or almost the unanimous endorsation of this Parliament some six months or more after the armistice had been signed, with the limitations set up in the vote of that day. That constituted endorsation of the programme which the vote embodied, and to which the vote should be applied. Following out the mandate of Parliament, the Government let certain contracts, and the decision to let the last contract was come to in the month of December, 1919, now almost a year and a half ago.
Towards the end of the year 1919, the unemployment situation in Canada was becoming more and more acute; not that we suffered as other countries did, but undoubtedly in December, 1919, and during the early months of 1920 there was very considerable distress due to unemployment
in various parts of the country. The Government was importuned, as only a Government can be importuned, to relieve that distress. The importunity was particularly strong because so great a degree of the distress was suffered by men who had returned from the war, and the chief pressure came from those men, and from those who represented them and pressed for consideration on their behalf. That was a factor of considerable magnitude in relation to the letting of the last two or three vessels or more, all of which had been authorized by this Parliament.
Now, I say again, the last decision was arrived at in that month. Efforts were made to keep the price down to the lowest possible point, thus delaying the final Order in Council approving of the contract until the month of March, 1920. Since that date no new engagement of any kind has been entered upon, none whatever; all that the Government has done, all that was left to do, has been to carry out the obligations into which this country had entered by the authority of this Parliament, by virtually the unanimous authority of this Parliament and which had been pressed upon us from all sides.
To complete that work, to carry out the contracts into which we had solemnly entered by the authority of Parliament, a vote was taken last year. It was stated in that vote last year that more would be required, that probably it would be impossible to complete the ships within the then present year, and that something more would be later requested. The vote that is now before the House, a vote of $8,000,000, is to cover $4,665,000 that was included in last year's $20,000,000 vote, and the balance for that completion which it was plainly stated last year would be required as the work would necessarily continue into this year. The Government then is merely engaged in asking for a revote of about three-fifths of this amount and of the other two-fifths for the completion of work which this Government was authorized to perform by this House.
The position of the Opposition, if I am able to put it into words, seems to be this: They are entirely with us in authorizing expenditure at a time when it is popular, where the work is being done, but after the work is nearly done and it is time to pay, then they are altogether against us. They quite agree that the country should enter into solemn engage-

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
ments, but they are entirely opposed to the country carrying them out.
Just a few days ago, one hon. gentleman stated that because certain moneys were not paid in London, England* he hung his head in shame at the spectacle of Canada repudiating her obligations. Canada has repudiated no obligation to which Canada was bound, but the party of which he is a member now believes that this House should be held between heaven and earth, stagnant, sterile, doing nothing, for days for fear that Canada may comply with her obligations to people of this country. There are contracts to pay for that have been entered into, and there are also contracts to complete. Are hon. gentlemen taking the position that we are perfectly right in laying down the hull of a vessel, but wholly wrong in completing the vessel?-that it is perfectly proper to build a ship, but wholly wrong to put the engines in that ship? Do they say that it is wholly wrong to complete that which it was wholly right to commence? Because they believe that just at this time when the operation of shipping the world over is suffering by reason of reversal, in which suffering we bear our part, do they say this is the time- for the Opposition to stand here and say, " When the sun shines everything is all right and we approve of it, but when the clouds come we go back on everything we have said and we want to sit back and do nothing?" I was surprised that the hon. gentlemen of the agrarian party should have allowed themselves to be lured by plausible phrasing on the part of the official Opposition into the position they have got themselves in. Are they aware that the leader of the agrarian Opposition (Mr. Crerar) was a member of the Government when the whole work was undertaken and when the last ship was ordered?

I am quite sure my right hon. friend the Prime Minister does not willingly misrepresent me. I left the Government early in June, 1919, and I have here Hansard, containing a question asked by my hon. friend, the member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) -

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon; he is right, I know the point he is making.

Mr. Chairman, my right hon. friend made the statement definitely and very explicitly that I was in the Government when the last contract was made.

I left the Government early in June, 1919, and I want to tell my right hon. friend, and my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that according to the information brought down in reply to the question by my hon. friend from Lunenburg in this House, and answered on March 4th, of this year, the last contract for these ships, two in number, was let on the 7tli April, 1920, ten months after I left the Government. Now, I do not wish to take up the time of my right hon. friend the leader of the Government, but this simply illustrates all that he knows, and all that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows, about his own business. When my right, hon. friend the leader of the Government makes such sweeping statements in order to score a point, he wants to be very certain that his facts are correct before he repeats them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I was quite ready the moment the hon. gentleman called attention to the date. I knew then I was wrong in that statement, and I accepted the hon. gentleman's statement-the hon. gentleman's resignation was in the June previous -and for that error I am quite prepared to make amends to the hon. gentleman. I have no desire to misstate the position of anyone. But the fact that the hon. gentleman was not a member of the Government at the time the contract for these two ships was let, does not alter the fact that he was a member of the Government when the estimate was prepared and brought into this House and that he supported the entire shipbuilding policy when it was thus undertaken.
Might I ask my right hon. friend another question? If his statement just now is correct, does he mean to say that that commits me indefinitely to the building of ships by the Government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It commits the hon. gentleman to the support of the programme which was then undertaken. That is the point. We are not taking a policy, we are not continuing a policy but only completing an authorized programme which he supported. We undertook a certain task which we are carrying out. It is true, the contract for two ships were let after the hon. gentleman resigned, but that is not a reversal of policy, it is an execution of policy -
Almost one-third of the contracts for building ships were let after I left the Government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Let me say that if 1 understand the situation aright, the position of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) at least has the greatest resemblance to consistency of that of any hon. gentleman opposite. He takes the position that we should not have undertaken the building of ships at all, the building of ships being peculiarly the commercial prerogative of the United Kingdom, they being able to build them much more cheaply than we, and that consequently we should leave to them the work of supplying the carrying needs of this country. While it might be such a difficult task for us that it may not be wise for us ordinarily to enter into competition of that nature, at the time this was done there were very special circumstances which made it our duty to build them, even at great cost; special circumstances which made it our duty to build ships in this country because they were required, and had to be built wherever the ships could be constructed. These are the circumstances under which this programme was undertaken. The hon. gentleman went through a performance similar to that in which he has been engaged during the last twenty-four hours some years ago. In 1913 I remember he delivered then a long series of speeches, taking the ground that instead of ordering any ships for war purposes in England, we ought to build two fleet units in this country, no matter what they cost, that we ought to build ships on the Atlantic , and on the Pacific, at a time wben the cost of building in this country would have been easily double the cost in England and at a time when emergency called for them being built with the least possible delay. The hon. gentleman held this Parliament up, or was instrumental in doing so for weeks in an effort to compel the building of ships in Canada for purposes of war, on the Atlantic and on the Pacific, at a cost of probably fifty million dollars to this-country. At a time when the ships had to be built we undertook the building of seventy million dollars' worth of ships to this country.
But hon. gentlemen opposite are evidently tired of the task they have undertaken on this occasion. One after the other they have pleaded that this debate be brought to a close, that they do not want to continue the performance that has been going on for some thirty hours. Well, I do not think we could wish clearer evidence of the purpose of that performance. The hon. member for Red Deer, the hon. member for St. James, Montreal, the hon. member for Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, and the hon. mem-
125i
ber for Westmoreland all have pleaded for the Government to intervene and have the closure applied in this committee. Well, if that be so, it is'pretty good evidence of the purpose of their talk. It is the best evidence that the debate was conducted only in order that it would have to be stopped. Under the circumstances, I feel that it is the duty of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House to accede to their request. The Estimates were brought down in this House on the 8th of last month. I believe the debate on the Address was finished only on the 3rd. I do not know of any previous occasion when the Estimates were brought down so early after the conclusion of the debate on the Address. Commencing, I think, on the 15th, or earlier, on each and every day when the House reached Government Orders, we have moved the House into Committee of Supply. As yet merely fractional items have gone through. The progress this House has made has been infinitesimal compared with the work the House has to do, and if this is to go on, then Parliament will cease to be the High Court of the nation. It will arrive at a status in the public eye that I, for one, would not like to contemplate. I, therefore, feel it my duty to take the first step to bring to an end this performance, and I move that the further consideration of this item be postponed.
Under the rules this motion is not debatable.

The minister does not quite catch the point I want to make. Generally, there are in the Department of Justice different lawyers looking after special cases; but when it comes to a matter of pleading cases before the Exchequer Court 6r Supreme Court or a local court, the department generally retains the services of lawyers in the different localities where the cases are to be pleaded. speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
