Coming back to the matter to which I invited the attention of the committee a few moments ago and referring to this transaction between the Government and the Gulf of St. Lawrence Navigation Company re the sale and disposal of the steamer Champlain. The minister told us that a contract was signed on a certain date, but he did not tell us who signed that contract. Of course, the Government was one party, but who were the parties of the other part?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Gulf of St. Lawrence Shipping and Trading Company, Mr. H. de S. Bosse signed on behalf of that company.
Did any other person connected with the company sign?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
As far as our
knowledge goes it was Mr. Bosse alone.

Would it be possible for the minister to obtain the contract from his two valuable assistants who are helping the committee in disposing of these items? I would like to have a more positive answer in regard to the parties who- signed on behalf of the company. I am informed on good authority that the person who was supposed to. have a controlling interest in the company, who, as we say in French was the bailieur de fonds, was a prominent lawyer in the city of Montreal, Mr. Barnard. I would not say that he went so far as to give a bond or guarantee for the transaction, but I think there is something in the information tendered to me. Would the minister refer to the contract and let us see it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend does not expect me to send it across the floor of the House at this moment?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not got the contract, but I will be very pleased to forward it to the hon. gentleman.

If the contract was made and signed by Mr. Bosse on behalf of this company, and if notes for the balance were also signed by him on behalf of the company and endorsed by one Thomas Harling, how is it that afterwards this new company, the Gulp Pulp and Paper Company, which was not a party to the contract, endorsed the notes? At whose suggestion did the new company endorse or guarantee the notes, and why?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: These gentlemen were interested in establishing this service with Clarke's harbour.
Do I understand that the steamer Champlain is to run between Quebec and Clarke's harbour, and that it has been transferred to these people?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I could not
answer that.

I understand the Government had in its possession the contract signed by the party who is buying the steamer, and that notes were also given by the company, one for $12,000 and another for $11,000 odd; later a new company came in and endorsed the notes. I would like to know why the Government thought it necessary to require that further endorsation if the company and Mr. Harling were considered sufficiently responsible in the first place?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I know my hon. friend will find no fault with the vigilant officers of the department getting all the endorsements they possibly could in the public interest. That is just what they did. They would have obtained more endorsements had that been possible.
Were these two notes that the minister has been speaking of the first notes, or renewals?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The first notes.

Are they overdue
now?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: One of them has been paid, as I told my hon. friend a few moments ago. The others have not been met, and that is the reason we are referring the matter to the Department of Justice.
What is the amount of the two notes that have not been met?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Twelve thousand dollars each.
Has the Gulf of St. Lawrence Navigation Company, through the liquidator, refused payment of those notes?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
On what ground?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The usual ground -that they did not have the money.
Did the Government have recourse to the endorser, Mr. Har-ling, for payment?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The department protested the notes and we are holding Mr. Harling liable along with the Gulf Pulp and Paper Company.
When were the initial protest proceedings taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In the language that legal gentlemen generally use, the notes were duly protested. I cannot give the exact date.
Did the minister ask the Gulf Pulp and Paper Company Limited for payment of those notes?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The notes were put in the bank and they were not met. Thereupon they were protested in the usual way.

A few moments age the minister told us that it was good policy to obtain as many endorsements as possible in connection with these notes; that not only had we the signature of the gulf of St. Lawrence Navigation Company, but also the endorsement of Mr. Harling; then, to obtain further security the department got the Guly Pulp and Paper Company to endorse the notes. Now the minister has taken proceedings against this company. I would like to have some enlightenment from the minister as to the financial backing and capacity to pay of this Gulf Pulp and Paper Company Limited.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: From what information I have been able to give my hon. friend and the fact that we have a mortgage on the ship, I do not think we need worry about the Government getting the full price. My hon. friend knows very well that the Gulf Pulp and Paper Company is owned by Lord Northcliffe and is thoroughly sound; he also knows that Thomas Harling is fairly good; and with a mortgage on the ship besides that, why should any one worry?

It is all very well to have the names of such big companies as

the Gulf Pulp and Paper Company, controlled by Lord Northcliffe, and Clark Brothers, but I have known many big corporations that were reputed to be very strong financially, but which sooner or later we discovered were far from being what they were supposed to be. The minister tells us that we have a mortgage on the ship, but this ship is in the hands of other persons to-day, and therefore the Government has no control over it, and should the ship meet with disaster no one knows what position the Government would be in in regard to their security. If the Gulf Pulp and Paper Company is so good and is controlled by Lord Northcliffe, I would sooner that the minister would apply immediately to that company and to the Clark Company for payment of these notes.
I want to refer again to the "Druid, Mr. Chairman. Have any tenders been asked for the expenditure of $46,000 in repairs on that particular shiv

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Such work as was not done by our own workmen was carried out by tender.
Where was the work performed and how long did it take the department to spend $46,000 on that ship?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The work was
done by the Davies, but I cannot tell my hon. friend the number of days or hours that they took.

Does the hon. minister
know how much was done by tender and how much without tender?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I cannot inform
the hon. gentleman just how much was done by the department and how much by tender. I shall have to get the information for him.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will allow me, the Department of Marine and Fisheries has not treated him quite so badly as all that. The information has just been handed to me that the depart-

ment instructed Captain Bloise of the Stanley to pick out four men to go to the assistance of the Marie-Lydia which is reported off the Magdalen Islands. It does not give the hours at which she pas-Captain Dumont, the owner, has been so advised. So my hon. friend will admit, I think, that the department has paid the attention we always do pay in such cases.
I am glad to get that information from the hon. minister. When was that done? This letter is dated March 1.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
To-day, at 11
o'clock.

Well, I hope that
those people have been rescued and have received assistance from the department. But I would point out that a long time has elapsed since I received the letter.

Before the item carries, I would like to call the minister's attention to something that has occurred in the past few months in the city of Quebec. Now, in accordance with the consideration which the Minister of Marine always gives to the labouring classes, and particularly to the unemployed labouring classes, the statement has been made that these ships were constructed in accordance with a programme which was simply carried out in order to afford employment, in view of the serious unemployment situation in Quebec, I applied to the minister to carry on the repairs of ships early in the beginning of the winter in order that the unemployment situation, which is undoubtedly very acute at that season of the year, might be relieved, and in order that the work would not have to be carried on late in the spring, thus delaying navigation. In that connection I wrote to the minister calling attention to the fact that the unemployment situation was acute in Quebec, and that the department had a large number of vessels which it intended to winter in Quebec, and asking that if possible orders should be given for the repairs to be carried on during the early part of the winter. I suggested that by taking this course, employment would be given to a large number of workmen at a period when work was difficult to obtain. This was on November 30, 1920. I thought it was a reasonable request to make of the minister. If ever there was an emergency in a small way, it was during that period, and had the minister acceded to my request it would not have involved the expenditure of one single extra cent to the department, the 
money would simply have been expended at a period of the year when it would have done the most good. I might say that at the present time these repairs are not made and that for well over a week, or I might say two weeks, or perhaps three weeks, navigation has been opened from the port of Quebec. I not only wrote to the minister on November 30, but I wrote him again. In answer to my letter of November 30, I received a letter on December 13, the minister, I might say, is apparently a very busy man, and takes a long time to answer letters, when he answers them at all. In his reply he stated that as soon as these ships were placed in winter quarters, they would be gone over in order to ascertain what repairs were required. On December 17, I again called his attention to the fact that the ships were in their winter quarters and that the repairs would give employment to 70 or 100 men for some six weeks, at a period of the year when it would be of very great assistance to the workman. To this the minister did not reply. On Dececmber 24 I received a letter from the secretary of the department acknowledging the receipt of my letter and stating that reports were expected from the inspectors. At that time a large number of people in Quebec city were literally starving, being unable to obtain employment. I corresponded with the inspector and was told that the inspection was completed, and that the ships were ready to have the repairs undertaken. At the same time a mass meeting of unemployed was held in Quebec, at which resolutions were passed stating that
Whereas it is the announced policy of the Government to in as far as possible carry on Public Works in order to alleviate the present acute unemployment situation;
Whereas There are in the Port of Quebec a large number of Government vessels which need overhauling and repairing;	.
Be it resolved that this meeting requests the Right Honourable Arthur Meighen, Prime Minister, and the Honourable C. C. Ballantyne, Minister of Marine and Fisheries, to immediately proceed with the work of refitting and repairing these vessels as a Government undertaking and not by contract;
That the work be begun at once in order that insofar as possible the worst season of the year, which is the present, may be passed over without undue suffering or hardship to the labouring classes of the City.
Copies of these resolutions were sent to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the members representing the districts surrounding Quebec. But no answer was received. On January 10,

not having received any answer to these representations, I telegraphed to the minister:
With reference to previous correspondence, department vessels wintering in Quebec. Important that decision to carry out repairs be carried out at once. Kindly reply.
Charles G. Power, M.P.
To this the minister replied:
Our inpectors are now working on specifications, for repairs to vessels wintering Louise Basin, and will arrange put work in hand as soon as possible.
That was a month and a half afterwards. On January 26, having been given to understand from the Fisheries Department that preparations were completed, I wired to the minister as follows:
Re repairs to vessels Louise Basin. Understand all preparations made but no authority received here to employ labour. Could this not be given at once?
On the same day, January 26, the deputy minister replied:
Agent has been authorized to take on extra men required for repairs to vessel Louise Basin.
I might say that these extra men were three men and one boy. I stated in another telegram on January 27:
Authority given departement to employ labour for only one vessel. What about other vessels?
I received a reply that repairs were being carried out by the department, and that any additional help necessary would be taken on. I carried on this correspondence for a week or ten days, and the situation in Quebec became more and more acute. The vessels were lying there, all preparations apparently had been made for the repairs, and yet, for no reason I have been able to fathom, the repairs had not been undertaken. I sent numerous telegrams to which I received no answer until on February 3, I received a telegram from the minister's private secretary:
Your telegram February second received and will he submitted to hon. Mr. Ballantyne on his return to city next week.
Now, Sir, I have carried on correspondence with the deputy minister and with the minister, and one or the other invariably answered. But this time the private secretary refused to answer and stated that the minister would not return "until the next week." That, I may say, was during the famous Peterborough election. I suspected that the minister was busy, and I sent the following telegram to the minister's secretary:
Your telegram of February third-why not relay mine to the minister?
That would have been the logical thing for the secretary to do. I have no doubt, even if the minister were engrossed in his electoral labours, he could have had time to answer the telegram and to give instructions to have this work done. Anyway, the sum and substance of it all is this: That I repeatedly, as representative of an important constituency in the city of Quebec,
[DOT]-called upon the minister to do this work, asked him to do something which would not involve the expenditure of one single extra cent to the country, which, on the contrary, would possibly have saved some money to the Government,-which would have been a considerable utility to my constituency and the city of Quebec and the district in general,-which would have been a charitable act on the part of the Government since a large number of those who were seeking work had not been able to obtain employment since navigation closed; yet, in spite of all these appeals, and appeals made by the mayor and other people of the city, almost nothing was done during the whole winter. The work is now being carried on when a large number of people can find employment elsewhere, and it is not so necessary. I have called the minister's attention to this, because I am under the impression-and I warn him now, because next winter will be probably as hard as last winter and perhaps more so-that it will be a matter of policy for his department to have these repairs carried out at a season of the year when the workingmen need help from the Government in the worst way. It was the announced policy of the Government last autumn to carry on public works so far as possible, in order to relieve the situation. I would ask the minister, not only to make a promise and announce a policy, but as a matter of fact, to carry out that policy, and next winter, when the same situation or a worse situation arises, to take care that these necessary works shall be carried on?

May I ask the hon.
minister why an increase of $450,000 has been made in these Estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That increase is
principally for fuel labour, and repairs to ships.

May I ask what
proportion of that amount is supposed to be spent in actual repairs?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The following
ships will be repaired at Quebec:	The

Druid, the Lady Grey, the Montcalm, and the Rouville.
What is the amount of repairs on those ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The repairs to
hulls and engine of the Druid are estimated at $25,800; the Lady Grey $30,000; Montcalm $40,000 and Rouville $15,000.

I understand the
Government boat gives a service from the Island to Quebec during the period of non-navigation-that is after the close of navigation. Can- the hon. minister tell me if that is correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Our icebreaker
runs to the island of Orleans and also to Quebec bridge.

I would remind the hon. minister that every year there appears to be^ great difficulty in making the service, and it is only after a few days or weeks that we can manage to get the boat to make the service. I would like to have the department arrange for a service at the close of navigation next autumn, so as to give those people on the island communication with the city.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We have now been
over an hour-
Carried, carried.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think that the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent) showed the proper appreciation when he expressed the view that it was time this item was disposed of. We have been over an hour on the item. I think it is no reflection on the hon. gentleman to say that the course of the discussion indicates that there is no very important question which ought to be raised now, and, even if we postpone now, or propose to move the further consideration of this question, if there is anything really important there will be, within the rules, an opportunity to bring it up. I beg to move that the further consideration-
Carried, carried.
We are not wasting our time in getting this information. The hour was well spent. This is a large item,-million and three-quarters,-and when we remember that this department has increased enormously-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Either the item is carried or not carried; if it is not carried my motion before the Chair is not debatable; 
so that in either event the hon. gentleman is out of order.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Investigation into wrecks, $12,300.

I suppose this item is debatable. I wish to make my position clear. Although I was quite willing, as far as I was concerned, to let the other item be carried, I do not think we deserved the lecture given us by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), as to having spent too much time on the two preceding items. Those items were very important, asking for a large amount of money, and it was certainly the right of the Opposition to discuss them, and we have not trespassed upon our right in taking one hour to discuss it, and ask for information in regard to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not say too much I said enough.

Might I ask the hon.
minister how many minutes we will be allowed on this item?
One hour.

Will the hon. minister say how many investigations into wrecks have taken place in the last year? I want to know all the names of the ships in regard to which investigations were held, and by whom the investigations were made.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend
will not make much headway by asking all the names and that sort of thing. I am only too willing to give the information, but I think we ought to try to get along with the business in a friendly way, instead of hon. members endeavouring to embarrass the minister by asking him to read out a number of unnecessary' names.
I do not think I can be charged with asking unnecessary questions. On another item I wanted to discuss some matters, but I was prevented by the Minister of Justice by a motion which he moved.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have given the hon. gentleman the information that there were 34 wrecks, and while I am perfectly willing to give the names, I cannot see what useful purpose would be served by doing so.

My object in asking by whom the investigations were held is that it has come to my knowledge that some of the parties in charge of the investigations

cannot understand the French language, and when they had to try captains and pilots, these men were not in a position to give the evidence they wanted because they did not understand English. I call the matter to the attention of the minister, so that steps may be taken to have those who sit on these tribunals understand both languages, in order that justice may be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Can the hon. member cite one case in which the wreck commissioner or his assistants did not understand French?
If they do understand French, that settles the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Mr. Demers is the name of the wreck commissioner.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Expenses of schools of navigation, $8,000.
Where are the schools of navigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Halifax, Yarmouth, North Sydney, St. John, N.B., Quebec, Kingston, Collingwood and Vancouver.
How long has the school at Quebec been established?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: About eight years.
Who is in charge?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Captain Napoleon Lachance.
Is he a pilot?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He used to be.

This looks like a very small item to carry on all the navigation schools in the Dominion of Canada. There has been for a few years an application for a navigation school at Canso, and my hon. friend has not yet taken any steps in that direction. I would like to place the matter before him again, because this is, as he knows, an important point. It is the greatest fishing point in the Dominion, and a large number of young sailors are brought up there. Some years ago something was done by the department in the way of establishing a navigation school at Canso but the project was abandoned and nothing has been done of late. It looks as if we are going to be a maritime country, and if we are to be able to navigate even my hon. friend's ships, we must pay a little more attention to the training of sailors and officers, and $8,000 for this purpose for the whole of Canada seems a very small amount when such large
amounts are spent in other directions. The education of our seamen is very important, and I should like the minister to take note of the fact that this application of Canso is especially important for my constituency.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall be glad to look into the matter.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Removal of obstructions in navigable waters, $18,000.
(Guysborough) : What is the reason for increasing this item by $13,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: A serious wreck occurred at Port Weller, the entrance to the new Welland canal, and it has to be removed.

In this connection I
should like to call the minister's attention to a wreck at the entrance to what is called Collins' bay. Several years ago I took this matter up with- the Hon. Mr. Hazen, and I regret to say that I did not make much progress. This is a case of an old vessel that was brought up from Kingston, and the owner of it apparently thought that was a very good place to drop it and leave it. It was left there as an old derelict, and some persons set fire to it. It was burned down to the water's edge, and the rest of it has remained there ever since, although the owner, Captain Donnelly, has been asked on several occasions to remove it. This wreck lies just a few inches below the surface of the water, and I know of one case where a pleasure yacht running into the bay ran up on this wreck. Inasmuch as the water in this bay is deep and vessels are apt, in case of a sudden storm arising, to run in there for shelter and this wreck is right at the entrance, steps should be taken to remove it or to compel Captain Donnelly, who, by the way, is manager and owner of the Donnelly Wrecking Company, to remove his old wreck out of this bay. I have taken this matter up with the Department of Public Works, and I am drawing it to the attention of the minister (Mr. Ballantyne) because it seems to come properly under this item. The order that was given by Mr. Hazen to remove the wreck should have been put into effect, and Captain Donnelly should have been made to remove it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is the first
time that I have heard of the matter. I am glad that the hon. member has brought it to my attention, and one of my assistants has made a note of it.

A few minutes ago the minister referred to the fact that the greater part of this appropriation was for the removal of a wreck at the entrance of the Welland canal. Is this a steamer, and by whom is it owned?

Would it not be well for
the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) as well as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) to look a little further into the law of marine insurance and see if the marine insurance company is not the one which should remove the wreck?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In answer to the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) I might say that the Muriel W. is the name of the vessel, and it is owned by Senator Webster, of Montreal. It is one of those large wooden hull ships.

Was she engaged in
private business, or was she chartered by the Government at the time of the wreck?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Private business.
She was caught in a storm and became wrecked.

As I understand the law, if a ship sinks and obstructs navigation, the duty of removing the wreck is not necessarily that of the Government, but that of the owner. Have any further efforts been made to get the owner of the wreck to remove this obstruction?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. member is quite right. The owner of the ship should see to it that this wreck is removed. We are taking the matter up and intend to charge the owner for whatever expense may be incurred in connection with the removal.
I hope there is no question but that the private owner of this wreck will be made to reimburse the Government for the cost of removing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, we will do the best we can.
The minister says he will do the best he can, but I am not satisfied with that statement. I want an assurance that the hon. Senator Webster will be made to pay the cost of removing that wreck.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My colleague, the Minister of Justice, advises me that we have a good legal claim against the owner, and therefore we will see that he does pay the cost.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.

To continue subsidies for wrecking plants- Quebec and British Columbia-$35,000

We
ought to have some explanation of this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is an old item that has been voted every year while I have been Minister of Marine. The amount of subsidy paid to the Quebec Salvage & Wrecking Company, Limited is $25,000, and to the Pacific Salvage Company, Limited, $10,000. As far as the former company is concerned I notice that the contractors are required to pay to the Government fifty per cent of the amount of such excess which is over the rate of interest at 51 per cent on a capital of $150,000.

The committee would like to know whether the Quebec Salvage & Wrecking Company rendered any service during the past year for the $25,000 they received. These subsidies are very apt to be continued from year to year without any investigation as to whether the company receiving the money are rendering service or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will be very glad to get a statement -for the hon. member. I do not recall any serious wrecks in the river St. Lawrence, down the Gulf, or on the Pacific Coast, but in the interest of navigation the Government has always thought it wise to have these wrecking plants available. I will take a note and have the information which the hon. gentlemen or placed in his hands to-morrow.
Is there any return from these companies showing the service they performed during the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, there is an annual return. I will see that the return for the past year is mailed to the hon. gentleman or placed in his hands to-morrow.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Life saving Service including rewards for saving life-$90,000

Does this vote deal
with the life saving stations?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. The life
saving stations have now been transferred from the naval service to the Department of Marine and Fisheries.

I notice that the minister has closed several of these stations. I want to know where those that have

survived his destructive tendencies are located?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In the province of Nova Scotia-Baker's Cove, Bay View, -Blanche, Canso, Clark's Harbour, Devil's Island, Duncan Cove, Herring Cove, Sea-tari, Seal Island, and Westport; and the cost to the Government is $18,000. I have given orders to close up as many of these life saving stations as could be closed without running any risk of jeopardizing human life.

I am not going to discuss this question at all. I merely wish to say that I have had correspondence with the minister with regard to the Cheti-camp station which was opened in 1911. It was unworthy of the minister and of his department to have closed that station, because it is the only contribution to the fishing industry in my constituency that I can credit the minister with. The only thing I wish to say now is that Ii am going to ask the minister to he good enough to leave the buildings there and not to sell them. I am sure the minister is convinced by this time that we are going to have a change of Government, and just as soon as that change comes we will see that this station is restored to its former status-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not for a while yet.
-and that the minister's destructive operations will be corrected by the successors of the present Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am not in a combative mood this afternoon, and therefore the only thing I will say to my hon. friend is, that he will have to wait for quite a few years before his hopes are realized.

We will see; the
people will decide that question.

In
former years there was a life-saving station at Whitehead in the county of Guysborough. Has it been closed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That has been closed also, I think. I may say, quite frankly, that when I became minister I found that a great many of these stations were really political life-saving stations and nothing more. I therefore felt it to be my duty in the public interest to close them up.

I want to say to my hon. friend that Whitehead is a very dangerous point on the coast where a good many wrecks occur. The station that was located there was doing very good work, and on very many occasions not only vessels but human lives have been saved by the efforts of the crew. Now as far as politics is concerned the moment my hon. friends opposite got into power they dismissed the crew. The men had been trained for some years in their duties, and had done good work; but within two or three weeks after the election of 1911 the crew were all dismissed, and a man who was not residing at Whitehead, but lived at the time in the town of New Glasgow, although he was a former Whitehead resident, was made captain of the crew.
That was not politics, though.

That is what happened. The new crew, of course, were not as good as the former men. I wish the minister would take note of the fact as to whether that station at Whitehead has been done away with, because, as I say, it is a very important point on the coast, and the station ought to have been continued.

I would like to ask if the minister has received any request for the establishment of a life-saving station on the islands called Main Ducks, in the lower end of lake Ontario near Kingston, and if so, whether, the matter has received any consideration from his department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The matter is
now receiving the attention of the department.
Is it the intention of the department to re-open the life saving station at Richibucto?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am sorry that I cannot give any encouragement to my hon. friend that it will be re-opened.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
River St. Lawrence ship channel-Maintenance and operating dredging fleet, 5528,000.
Will the minister explain the reason for the increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The $50,000 increase is largely due to repairs to the dredging fleet.
Are all the dredges employed on that part of the river the property of the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Are any contracts given at all to private individuals?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: None.

Between what points
was the main part of the money spent?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Principally in the Cap a la Roche region between Montreal and Quebec, and also in the North Channel, below Quebec.

Last year when these Estimates were before the committee I asked the minister about certain dredging that ought to be done in the county of Charlevoix at Riviere St. Francois in the Baie St. Paul district. The approaches to the land are not very good, there being many rocks which make it very inconvenient to the people who travel from Quebec and Murray Bay to the various ports in that locality. If the Government would send one of their dredges to that district for a few days it would help the people a good deal. Last year the hon. minister promised to take the matter under consideration, but nothing has been done.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It has not been done by the Department of Marine simply because the matter comes under the control of my colleague, the Minister of Public Works.
Can the minister give the committee a statement as to the depth of the channel at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have a 30-foot channel, at low water, as my hon. friend probably knows, from Montreal to the sea. Some of the curves are 500 feet in width, and others as much as 1,100 feet. The dreding, of course, is going on constantly, but where prior to the war we had nine dredges operating, now we have only three. If I can get enough money from my colleague the Minister of Finance we may possibly put on another dredge.
Was there not a time when the channel even so far as Three Rivers was 35 feet deep? Since then that depth has been gradually reduced to the extent just stated by my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: So far as I know the channel has not yet been dredged to a depth of 35 feet.
Is the river getting any deeper on account of this dredging?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am quite sure my hon. friend has travelled between Montreal and Quebec and from Quebec to the sea. The channel is so well lighted and buoyed that one might think one was going down a city street.
The White Way of Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We are almost
free of wrecks. When the dredging is done the channel does not refill, but it is a big contract to keep it open to the depth and width we think it ought to be. I suppose the dredging will go on as long as we live.
Does it re-fill?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
I do not think the minister quite understood my question. Are we simply dredging out the mud that comes in during the year, or are we deepening the channel year by year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, the channel is getting deeper and wider every year.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
For the maintenance and improvements of the Sorel shipyard, shops and offices as well as operating expenses, $75,000.
Will the minister explain the ^increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: , The $10,000 increase is for the maintenance of the shipyard wherever it has become in a bad state of repair.
Is that the yard where the minister repairs his dredges and so forth?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
To provide an icebreaker to be used in St. Lawrence river, including maintenance of same (revote), $2,000,000.
Will the minister explain?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This was voted
last session, but when my department called for public tenders I was surprised and disappointed to find the lowest tender was $2,220,000.
Wherefrom?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
From the Wallace Shipbuilding company, of North Vancouver.

199S
Come east-the tenders will be lower.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That tender was
more than double the cost of a similar icebreaker called the J. D. Hazen, built in 1912 and 1913 for less than $1,000,000. I did not think I was justified in letting a contract for more than double that amount. Therefore we rejected all the tenders. I am asking for a re-vote, and now that material and labour are coming down I hope we may be able to get tenders somewhat closer to 1912 prices. I am sure all hon. gentlemen, especially those from the province of Quebec, will recognize how necessary it is to have a very powerful icebreaker. Both the Montcalm and the Lady Grey are very old icebreakers. In 1919 the Canadian Spinner and the Canadian Recruit were both caught in the ice, and had the department an icebreaker similar to the one intended to be covered by this re-vote we would have had no difficulty at all in releasing both those vessels. It is of the highest importance in the interest of navigation that we should have an icebreaker of this type, as she will enable us to keep the channel open later in the winter and to clear it earlier in the spring.

With such a powerful
vessel, has the minister in mind to keep navigation open all the year round from Quebec to the sea?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I would not like
to be so ambitious as that, but we will be able to keep the channel open later in the winter and clear it earlier in the spring. If any ship should be caught in the ice, we will be able, with such a powerful icebreaker, to release her.

What was the original
cost of the Champlain? I see that she was sold last year for $61,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The cost was

I find that during the
year the department spent $46,000 on repairs to tha^ icebreaker. Was that amount spent after the sale had been made to the Gulf Pulp and Paper Company, owned by Lord Northcliffe?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, I have just been informed by my deputy that no money was spent on the repairs of the Champlain by us. I do not know what the company did after purchasing the ship, which was very old. The Government has not
used her for a number of years, and we think that the price we got was a very good one.

According to the minister, it was a fairly good price, that is, if he obtains payment. I understand that the minister has received one payment on account of this icebreaker, the Champlain, and also holds two notes that have been endorsed by a firm which is considered excellent security for the amounts of those notes. But the notes have been protested. I would like to know, if I am in order, why it is that these notes, endorsed by a good endorser, have not been collected by the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am afraid that my hon. friend is a little out of order. I do not know whether he was in the House when the hon. member for Charlevoix-Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) and the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent) discussed this matter for half an hour or so. We are now on an entirely different item, to provide an icebreaker for the St. Lawrence river. The Champlain item was passed some time ago.

I appreciate* that position, but we are discussing the purchase of a new icebreaker. My first question was as to why the Government was buying this new icebreaker and selling the old one. The question follows as to the disposition of the icebreaker. If I am not in order, I would like to know.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I fear that the hon. member is not in order. The Chairman has always endeavoured to allow the widest possible discussion on any item, but believes such discussion should be limited to the most appropriate item. In this particular instance, the matter has already been discussed for some time, as was pointed out by the hon. minister. It relates to item 205, and not to the item now under consideration. By a series of questions my hon. friend could lead up to the formation of the company which signed the notes, and that would certainly not be in order.
Would the minister inform me how long the period of navigation from Quebec, and also from Montreal, extends?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That depends altogether on the weather conditions. For instance, the opening of navigation this year from the port of Montreal was tka



earliest for some fifty odd years, the first river boat having arrived at the port of Montreal somewhere around March 28 or 29. Below Quebec, owing to the very mild and favourable winter, navigation is quite open also. But as a general rule navigation closes at the port of Montreal about November 25 or 26, and opens anywhere from April 25 to 30. As the port of Montreal opens and closes, so does the port of Quebec.
To what extent would this period be extended by the operation of the icebreaker which the hon. minister is proposing to build?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We hope to keep navigation open two weeks longer. We have not an icebreaker that can go through any considerable thickness of ice, and it is very necessary to have such an icebreaker. But I want hon. members to understand that unless we get a tender much lower than the one for $2,000,000 I shall not place the order.

I think that if the hon. minister had been frank he would have told the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) that the port of Quebec is generally open about fifteen days earlier than the port of Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Quite so.
And in that connection, if he had used the ships which are lying idle at Halifax, and sent them to Quebec we would have been doing business fifteen days earlier. .

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: When I made the statement in reply to the hon. member for Marquette, I meant ships bound to Montreal only. I quite realize that the port of Quebec is open nearly all the year round.
So is the port of Murray Bay.

As this is the only
item I see for the construction of new icebreakers, I think I am in order if I again draw the attention of the minister to the desirability of the department having a better equipment ,for dealing with the occasional closing of the harbours on the south coast of Nova Scotia. I do not mean that there should be a two-million-dollar icebreaker for that purpose. But occasionally, in very sharp weather, some of the largest harbours are closed, and it has been found necessary to have some equipment to open them. I must do the minister the just-
[Mr. Ballantvne. 1
ice of saying that in every instance when the matter has been brought to the notice of the department, he has made the best use possible of the available ships, and has met the difficulty as best he could. But in other instances, we have found an inadequate equipment for that purpose. I do not propose that a powerful, expensive icebreaker should be equipped, but some vessel adapted for general service should be made sufficiently powerful to be used in that service in the winter, a vessel that would not be laid up in the summer, but would be useful all the year round, and would have sufficient power for that service when the occasional closing of those harbours occurred. I would ask the minister to keep that in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I would be only
too happy to do so. We were able to open the harbour of Shelburne twice this spring with the Lady Laurier, and we hope to be able to do so next spring.
I would like to be assured by the minister that when this contract is let, public tenders will be called for.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Oh, yes; I mentioned just a few moments ago that public tenders had been called for, and I thought my hon. friend was arising to compliment me upon not placing the order with the lowest tenderer because the department considered the price too high. I can assure my hon. friend that not only will tenders be called for, but that unless they are very much below $2,000,000, the Government would not feel justified in placing the contract.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Lighthouse and coast service-agencies, rents and contingencies, $215,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The increase of
$17,000 is explained solely by an increase in the salaries granted by the Civil Service Commission.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Salaries and allowances to lighthouse keepers, $650,000.

I would like to draw the
attention of the Government again to the remuneration of the lightkeepers. At the last session of Parliament I called the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to the matter, particularly to the nemuneration paid to part time employees, and we were told at that time that the $60,000, then being voted, was to increase

the salaries. I understand that their salaries have been increased to the extent of from $10 to $20 per annum, which is a very small increase. The range of salaries under the present Civil Service classification is from $210 to $270. The lightkeeper who was paid $250 in 1919 has had his salary increased by $20, which makes his salary for 1920,	$270.
In some other classes there have been larger increases of salary and in view of the fact that the salaries of these men are very low, that there has only been an increase of from $10 to $30 since 1911 whereas the cost of living has increased in that time 150 per cent, and that the judges required an increase in salary by reason of the increase in the cost of living there is cause ' for protest on the part of these men. In this particular instance, we have a large class of public servants, who perform duties for which they are deserving of great credit, and on their behalf, from a reasonable point of view, I do appeal to the Government to be more considerate towards these public servants, and to allow these hard-working employees sufficient compensation to provide properly for the support of their families. I therefore hope that this question will be taken into consideration by the Government and that justice will be done to the lighthouse keepers of Canada by increasing their salaries to such an extent that will be able to make a living, anyway, for the time for which they are employed.

We have not very many lighthouse keepers in my part of the country, but there are a few, and I have felt for a long time that these men have not received the consideration that is due them in the matter of salary. I merely rise to give general endorsation to the remarks of my hon. friend who has just taken his seat.
Mr. J. E. S. E. D'ANJOU (Rimouski) : (Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words in support of the request which my hon. friend from Kent (Mr. Leger) has just made. The hon. Minister of Marine has referred to an increase of this item, an increase which is due to the re-classification of the Civil Service, and I desire to call the minister's attention to the necessity of an increase of salary for lighthouse-keepers.
. Mr. Chairman, there is not in the Civil Service, a class which, in my opinion, is so poorly paid than that of the lighthouse-keepers. Such increases as have been
126J
granted by this department have not been adequate to the present high cost of living. Most of the lighthouse-keepers could not make a living, were it not for their large families, for their sons who are able to work and support them. I hope, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of Marine will take my request into consideration and that he will make sure that these lighthouse-keepers are not ignored.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I wish to second the request made by the hon. member from Rimouski (Mr. d'Anjou) as to an increase of salary for the lighthouse-keepers. There are several in the country of Charlevoix-Montmorency. I do not think the Government should hesitate in granting a small increase of salary to those poor lighthouse-keepers who have so much to suffer during the winter and spring seasons.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Marine to do something for this part of my county which is known as the river St. Francis. I have asked him to place an icebreaker there so that there would be an easier access to the port. This place is situated in a bay which explains the difficulty of reaching it. They are also obliged to keep lights at a high cost during the fall and the spring. I would ask the Government if it would not be possible to place a lighthouse there. If this were done, and it would not cost much, I think it might prove satisfactory to the Government.
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to make any opposition, this is not the time, but I say that if the Government would accede to my request, I am sure that they would do well in erecting this lighthouse, it would be of such advantage to the county of Charlevoix-Montmorency which I have the honour to represent.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have listened very sympathetically to what hon. members have said about the low salaries that are paid to lighthouse keepers. The matter of the reclassification of lighthouse keepers, is in the hands of the Civil Service Commission, and I see that a sum of $40,000 has been added to the Estimates for the year 1920-21. That is all we will be able to do this year, but I am heartily in sympathy with what hon. members have said about the inadequacy of the remuneration to these lighthouse keepers. In regard to the light that my hon. friends wants, I will not put the "light in the window"

for him, but I will do my very best to see that it is placed on the wharf, and I hope it will guide him in the right direction.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Maintenance and repairs to lighthouse. $800,000.
Might I ask if this item includes repairs and light?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, it does; this is for all the lighthouses and all the lightships and the amount is just the same as last year.
Might I ask how many lights belonging to the St. Lawrence South [DOT]district were repaired during the last winter, and where they were repaired?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There were four repaired at Quebec and one at Halifax.

Were any repaired at
Sorel?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, none.
Might I ask how much of this item is for maintenance and how much for repairs?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend will recognize that that would be pretty difficult to answer, depending altogether on the wear and tear and the condition that the lighthouses would be in. One year the maintenance might be more and another year the repairs might be Idss. It is rather too difficult a question to answer.
What destinction does the minister make between " maintenance" and " repairs?"

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: About half and half.
Really, the " maintenance" is " repairs."

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
What actual expenditure is covered by the "maintenance?"

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The principal
charge is for oil, for fuel and for light.
Where is the oil purchased?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have a War Purchasing Commission, and they make the purchase.
Does not the minister at Ottawa have his engineer make a report to him as to what repairs are necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes.
[Mr. BaManytna.)
The minister made his general answer, " half and half."

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not the engineer's report, but of course, before this amount is placed in the Estimates we will have a more detailed report.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Construction of Lights and Aids to Navigation, including regulation of traffic in the Detroit river and such other places as may be neces-' sary, $400,000.
May I ask the hon. minister to whom aids to navigation have been granted? Are they to private companies or individuals?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This item is for lights and buoys. ,
And aids to navigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is the same thing.
Where are the lights and buoys constructed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am informed
these buoys are constructed at different points in the Dominion of Canada, depending on where they are going to be placed, and who is the lowest tenderer,
Where are the buoys desired to be placed on the Atlantic coast constructed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Most of them are made by the Robb Engineering Company, at Amherst, and some are made at Sorel.
By whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: By the Government shipyards.
There was a lightship at Barrington passage which outlived its usefulness. What is the minister doing about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have placed a gas buoy tnere.
It is not intended to renew the lightship.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not at the present time.
What is meant by "regulation of traffic in the Detroit river?"

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is an international channel in the Detroit river, and the Canadian Government has an agreement with the American Government. We take care of one side of the channel and the

American Government takes care of the other.
This is for the construction of new lights and lighthouses?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

The last two years
I have been endeavouring to get the Government to build a small range light at Grande Etang. They assured me that this would be attended to., and I have some correspondence in my room where the officers of the Department inform me the work was to be undertaken "immediately." Well, "immediately" is quite a distance away.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We would have
put that light there before, but the department has been hard-up the last year or two. Our expenditures have been cut, but, as my hon. friend thinks we have not done what we should, I shall make a special inquiry about it and see what we can do.
_ Mr. CHISHOLM:	The hon. gentleman
is very kind. I got the same promise last year. My difficulty is this. I am always anxious to protect the Government. I told my people that such work was going to be undertaken, that the Government has provided the necessary money, and I gave them the assurance that it would be undertaken.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I assure my hon.
friend in all seriousness that we will put the light there if we can. Note has been taken of it, and it will come before the Lighthouse Board, and afterwards before me.

I find
an item in the report of the Auditor General that a considerable sum of money out of this vote was paid to D. D. Swan, of Montreal, for services as consulting engineer, Victoria Harbour, B.C. This gentleman received payment at the rate of $75 a day. It struck me as a large figure to pay for consultations which appeared to last for fifty-five days. I should like to know the necessity for this large payment out of this fund. It does not seem strictly connected with the maintenance of lights.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Well, it comes
under the vote, Lighthouse and Coast Service. What we really employed Mr. Swan for was to send him out to Vancouver and look over the situation and make a complete detailed recommendation to the Department of Marine as to what developments should be provided for that most important port; and, not having any vote that we could
charge it to, we thought it very properly came under Lighthouse and Coast Service, as expansion and development of navigation.
Is that a usual charge?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is the usual
charge for a marine engineer of Mr. Swan's type. He is the best harbour and marine engineer we have in this country. The Montreal Harbour Commissioners Board brought him out from England ten or twelve years ago to carry out the large improvements that were undertaken at that time at the Port of Montreal, and I understand it is the usual charge for a man of his ability and skill.
At Six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at Eight o'clock.
lighthouse and coast service-single service, $75,000.
Will the minister explain the increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This increase of $10,000 is principally to cover increased telephone charges.
What is comprised in this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Signal service
stations have been established to report movements of ships by means of wireless telegraphy, telegraph and telephone signals, the system extending from St. John, New Brunswick, to Halifax and Cape Race.
Is the minister having new telephone lines put up along the coast, and, if so, where?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Department of Marine have a contract with the Bell Telephone Company who have put the rates up. This $10,000 covers the increased rates for the current year.
The money goes to the Bell Telephone Company?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Is there a signal station at Westport, Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
It has been alleged that some change has been made in that respect of late, and that the old signal station has been taken down and removed to another place.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It has been removed from the old point down to the lighthouse, at the request of the shipping interests.

Is it generally assumed that the change is beneficial? It has been alleged* that the change is by no means suitable to the place, and that the station is not convenient to shipping, but I do not like to make the statement too positively.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The storm signal will remain where it is, but the signal service station has been moved down to the lighthouse, as I have said, at the request of the shipping interests.
What does the term "shipping interests" mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Ocean liners and steamship companies, principally the Canadian Shipping Federation of Montreal.
The records, if necessary, will show that the change was made at their request; is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Quite correct.

What
are the places on the coast of Nova Scotia where storm signals are operated.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is the signal service. Storm signals come under the appropriation for meteorological service.
What is this for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: As soon as a ship passes a signal station, the person in charge telephones to the next station giving the name of the ship and the time at which it passes the station, so that if my non. friend were coming from Liverpool to Montreal, his friends in Montreal would know at what time the ship would reach Montreal, supposing she reached Sorel at such and such a time, and Three Rivers at such and such a time.
Are there any such stations on the coast of Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Partridge island,
Camper down and Westport.
Does this item cover salaries to men in charge of the service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Are there increases in salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There has been an increase in salaries to the extent of $2,000.
I understood the additional $10,000 was for extra allowance in connection with the telephone signal service.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Telegraph and
telephone, both.

I notice in the Auditor General's report of last year that $14,157.10 was paid to the Bell Telephone Company for these services. The total amount for this service after deducting provisional allowance, cost of living bonus, was only $59,000. If there is only $2,000 extra to be allowed for telephone service, I can hardly see the reason for the minister asking for an increase of $10,000 when the expenditure was only $59,000 last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The increase in salaries is not $2,000 but $4,000; the telegraph charges are $4,000 more and the telephone charges are $4,000 more.
Who keeps up the private telephone line between Montreal and Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Bell Telephone Company.
They construct and keep it in repair?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Then this amount is to pay the operators along the line of this service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
What is the necessity for this private telephone line between Quebec and Montreal? Would it not be possible to get the same information by Marconi or otherwise?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is the
promptest and most efficient service that the Department of Marine and Fisheries could possibly get. Wireless would not suit. If my hon. friend were on a ship, he would notice that the signal stations signal by flag as well as by telephone.

speechtext:
The telephone
service is just from Montreal to Quebec, and the wireless from Quebec to cape Race.

The most important reports are those that come from'below Quebec when a ship is approaching Canada. Why then should we have, for the sake of reporting movements between Quebec and Montreal, a special telephone line when we already have a Marconi service? Are there special reasons?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is not a new vote; it is one that has been made for a great many years. It is necessary for the ships to get this telephone service when they are passing each other in the river, and there are many special reasons for it.

Administration of Pilotage, ?250,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: A few years ago the pilotage district of Halifax and St. John was administered by a local pilotage commission. The department have taken those districts over and, like the districts of Montreal and Quebec, they are now under the Marine and Fisheries Department. The general superintendent of pilots stationed at the marine office here, I refer to Captain Robertson, has supervision of the pilotage districts of Montreal. Has the minister received any communications from the Shipping Federation suggesting a decrease in the number of pilots for the district of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Well, I have not seen the communications myself but my deputy tells me they have been received, and that the Shipping Federation are under the impression there are too many pilots.

Upon what grounds do the Shipping Federation base that opinion? For years the pilots have given good service in the country but now it appears the Shipping Federation are asking for a reduction in their number, and suggesting that no more apprentice pilots be admitted. I think the minister should give further information as to the recommendations of the Shipping Federation and the grounds upon which they are based.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will be very glad to tell my hon. friend that the Government and the Minister of Marine have to stand as impartial judges between the demands of the pilots on the one hand, and the demands of the shipping people on the other. Ever since I have been Minister of

Marine the shipping interests have claimed there are too many pilots in the districts of Montreal and Quebec and they have urged me very strongly to reduce the number. So far the department have not done so. Furthermore the shipping people think the pilotage charges are too high, whereas the pilots themselves consider they are too low. The shipping people think there are too many pilots, and the pilots consider there are enough. That, briefly, is the situation.
How many pilots do the Shipping Federation think would be necessary for the service?

speechtext: There are sixty pilots below Quebec and the Shipping Federation think there should only be fifty.

Yes.
Would my hon. friend suggest cutting the number down to forty.
I am not a minister.
No, but you are making a lot of noise.

When
this matter was up last year we drew the attention of the minister to the fact that while the pilots of the St.- Lawrence are pensioned, the pilots in other ports of Canada draw no pension. I would like the minister to define what a " decayed " pilot is?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext:
Is there not a system
of pensions in the case of some of the other pilots? Who appoints the pilots in Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The pilots of
Quebec, like the pilots of other districts, serve an apprenticeship; then on passing the prescribed examinations, they are made branch pilots, and as vacancies occur they are taken on the strength.
Do they get their papers from the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Then, if there are too many pilots, the trouble can be very easily corrected by the department restricting appointments. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is an oldstanding difficulty, and is one of the reasons why my predecessor, Mr. Brodeur, agreed to give the pilots at Quebec a pension of $300 a year, providing that their number was reduced from 75 to 65, and that is gradually being done. On the other hand, it is rather hard to say to a young man after he has served seven years as an apprentice pilot and is ready to become a branch pilot that he cannot become one. We

are meeting the difficulty by not taking on any more apprentice pilots.

Did I understand the
minister to say that the corporation of Quebec pilots is now entirely under the control of the department? If so, when did that'corporation effectively disappear?

speechtext:
An Act was put

Is the minister aware

and Halifax under the direction of the minister during last year ending March 31?
