speechtext:
I think, Mr. Chairman, it is practically impossible to carry a resolution of this character except by common

consent of the House. I would be glad to know whether my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) is prepared to receive the suggestions which we offered the other day in what I think was a friendly spirit. If it be that the suggestions then made are not to receive any consideration, why, of course, we must take advantage of whatever the rules of the House will permit. I do not think it is wise for my hon. friend to try to get this motion otherwise than by that common consent which has accompanied such motions in times past.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I entirely agree with the hon. gentleman that this is a matter which ought to be covered by consent. I would go further -I would entirely agree with him that the consent which ought to be now given should be characterized by the same terms and in the same manner as the consents which at his requests were so frequently given during the many years he was Minister of Finance.
A suggestion was made when this matter was first under discussion that salaries should be paid and that other accounts should be stopped. I think it went further than that afterwards-to the extent that essentials should be paid. But we do not intend to pay anything except what is essential and is required to be paid. We certainly did not intend to launch out into expenditures in connection with undertakings which' we are not bound to discharge when we have not got a sufficient vote to carry them through. But my position is exactly the same as the position of my hon. friend on many occasions; it is extremely hard to say in advance what is exactly necessary and what is not. On a former occasion when the same question was put my hon. friend said that he would like to know just exactly what items the Opposition were objecting to when he would consider the matter. We have not, of course, that information as yet.
I would like to point out very briefly some of the difficulties, because I think all hon. gentlemen will realize them. Suppose you take the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment. Of course, you have the salaries of your officials, but you have also your pay and allowances to the veterans who are receiving treatment or education; you have your unemployment relief; you have your operating expenses, consisting of cash advances for disbursements to meet current expenses, and so on; you have your vocational expenses, payments for supplies
[Mr. Fielding.)
in connection with vocational training, tuition fees and the like; you also have your vocational loans which are being made to returned soldiers under certain circumstances.
The truth of the matter is that the country's business is a pretty big one, perhaps entirely too big a business, but it is impossible to stop it. Take for example your immigration; are we to stop all the work in connection with the Immigration Department, with the exception of payments for salaries and bills already approved? You have your rent of offices all over the country. You have the travelling expenses of agents. I suppose they would have to be stopped. You have your expenses in connection with the deportation of undesirables which has been going on all the time. You have your telegraph and telephone expenses and the necessary alterations to buildings which ought to be done this year. These alterations should be started very soon if we are going to properly look after immigration. You have your running expenses at border points of entry on the international boundary. You have all your expenses in connection with the detention and feeding of immigrants at these border points. Then in regard to the Health Department you are exactly in the same position. Going through all the departments, where there is any work to be done, this simply provides for salaries. If the money is not voted, it means for one thing that you might just as well discharge your employees, because unless these things can be looked after, unless they have something to work with and for, you are getting nothing for your salaries.
The position this year, it seems to me, is exactly the same as in any other year. There have been a great number of these votes. I have already pointed out to the House that English authority states that interim supply is an integral and necessary part of parliamentary and national finance.
I have given already one authority for it; but if there is any doubt in the mind of anybody that what is asked here is not what is necessary, I am going to fortify it with another authority. I will now read from May's Parliamentary Practice, 12th edition, page 448. May says:
Owing to our financial system, and the conditions of parliamentary business, the presentation of estimates for grants in advance upon the estimated departmental expenditure of the year, before a complete sanction has been given to that expenditure, is an annual necessity. These grants are known as "votes on account." It was hoped that the vote of the committee of

supply would be taken upon the bulk of the annual estimates during the earlier portion of each session, as the financial year closes on the 31st March, and begins on the 1st April. The futliity of a hope centred on the 1st April is the experience of every session. When that day comes round, session after session, very slender provision has been made for the requirements of the new financial year. Moreover, as every grant Of supply is limited to the service of the financial year for which it is made, the grant lapses, if it has not been utilized before the 31st March; and under the provisions of the Exchequer and Audit Departments Act, 1866, all unexpended sums in the hands of the departments are surrendered to the exchequer. Thus, obviously, during the first quarter of each calendar year, a vote on account must be demanded ; for if no grant in advance has been made upon the 31st March, the maintenance of the public service in the early part of the new financial year will be wholly unprovided for.
It seems to me it is unnecessary to refer to further authority. The matter is one which is well within the recollection and knowledge of any member of this House who has sat here any length of time. It is certainly well within the memory and recollection of my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance. Something was said the other day that conditions were entirely different, that at the present time there were large deficits, while, when previous interim supplies were voted, there were large surpluses. I am looking now at the Public Accounts, page 63, which gives the tabulated statement of surpluses and deficits. While I do not think the question of surpluses or deficits has anything to do with it, nevertheless I notice that in the year 1911 there was a net deficit between receipts and ex-penditues of $3,773,505.70.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: A net deficit in 1911?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: It is only by adding the capital expenditure that the hon. gentleman can make that statement.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
The hon gentleman's point is well taken, just as well taken as was the statement made by the hon. gentleman from Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) because if we deal with the matter in the way suggested by hon. gentlemen, then of course there was a surplus. Going back to the year 1911 again, if you forget all about capital there was a surplus of $30,000,000. Let us treat this year in the same way as the hon. gentleman thinks the matter should be treated. Treating it in the same way for 1920, there is a surplus of $45,900,000. For the present year the surplus is a great deal larger than that.
If we are going to talk about surpluses, we have at least to get on common ground. We have no surpluses when we look at our capital account. We have large surpluses on our ordinary expenses and on our ordinary receipts. The hon. gentleman had surpluses on his ordinary expenditure and on his ordinary receipts. The only difference is that ours is much larger in so far as those items of the account are concerned. On the other hand, our capital expenditures are also much larger. As I was pointing out, there was a deficit in 1911 of three million odd; a deficit in 1910 of $12,338,000; a deficit in 1909, in times of peace with no war debt, of $45,969,000; and a deficit in 1908 of $14,000,000. Let us see now about interim Supplies. Take the year of the big deficit $45,969,000, that occurred in 1909. In that year the interim Supply was allowed to go, not for a sixth, but for a quarter. It seems to me the thing is too plain really to require further elaboration. If it was necessary to carry on the business of the country during the year that I am referring to, during the years my hon. friend moved interim Supply in proper conformity with Canadian practice and with British practice, if it was necessary to decently carry on public business, it is just as necessary in order to decently carry on public business now. If it was necessary to pay Canada's commitments, to observe good faith to carry on our obligations, it is just as necessary to-day. My hon. friend says it should foe done by consent. I entirely agree him, and I hope this matter will be carried through by consent, as indeed, it ought to be.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: I think some hon. gentlemen on this side of the House made some references to surpluses which perhaps justified the hon. gentleman's comment. I did not, however, and so I pass from that. I pause only to say that, if I am not mistaken, my successor in office came down to this House and announced a very handsome surplus and did not find it necessary to draw the line that my hon. friend draws now. However, there is no difference between us in substance in that respect. I am going to suggest to my hon. friend that when he is spending his time pouring over the pages of history he should not deal so much with what the late Minister of Finance said. It would be exceedingly interesting if he told us what the Prime Minister of to-day, and the late Prime Minister and what another hon. gentleman sitting on that side of the House, said at this time. It might be as interesting as

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
I gentlemen opposite in efforts which they are making to distinguish between conditions that obtain this year and those that have obtained for many
years gone by in relation to this vote. The distinction was put on one basis last week; it is put on a wholly different basis to-day. Last week we were told: "We could not agree to interim Supply this year because, when interim Supply was voted under a former Government, there were surpluses, whereas now there are large deficits." The facts fell from under that contention, so the contention was abandoned. The facts were the contrary. The surpluses as calculated by hon. gentlemen are much greater now than they were then.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
Yes, the difference between ordinary expenditure and revenue is much greater to-day than it has ever been before, and hon. gentlemen opposite have asked and obtained interim Supply when there was no surplus at all, but a huge deficit amounting to a large proportion of the whole annual revenue. The facts fell from under that contention, so the whole footing was shifted to-night. To-night we are told: "It cannot be agreed to, because there is so much money needed;" or to put the matter in other words: The necessities are so great, the reason for objecting is all the greater. In Great Britain there is interim Supply voted where the necessities are ten times as great as ours, and I have not heard of any hon. gentleman in the British House of Commons putting forward that ground for refusing interim Supply, nor do I know of any interim Supply being refused anywhere or any time upon grounds such as suggested by hon. members opposite to-night. I have looked the records back over many years to find whenever conditions were such in this, or any other House, and I know of no such case.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have shifted their grounds in other respects very materially. The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), read what he said on April 7, to- the effect that he was not so very much opposed to interim Supply to the extent that the public service be paid. But when he spoke in this House on March 15, that was not the position he took; he did not hold open any door then, so far as I could see. If any hon. gentleman can see any hole or opening in this door, his mental eyesight is better than mine. This is the ultimatum that the leader of the Opposition gave to the House when the question was up on March 15:
This delay on the part of the Government is the less excusable inasmuch as the matter was
to be absolutely ne time.
sympathise with ho: the rather awkwan

expressly brought to its attention on two or three occasions during our last session.
He goes on to show that, the session before, he had told us there could be no more interim Supply:
When we were discussing Supplementary Estimates on June 7 last I took occasion to speak to the hon. Minister ot Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) as follows :
I want to say, not by way of threat but simply that hon. gentlemen opposite will understand the position of the Opposition, that if the government of the day should by any possibility be in office next year we shall not be willing to make these advances.
I was referring then-and I think the Government would do well to consider this particular feature at the moment-to the practice which my hon. friend asked us to adopt of voting a portion of the Supply en bloc at the end of the fiscal year before there had been any opportunity of considering the Estimates.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Does the hon. gentlemen say that he meant there that we had asked Supply en bloc last year before any Estimates had been considered? That was not the fact. He meant that he would object this year to any vote en bloc; that is interim Supply.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Without consideration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Nobody is asking him to vote this without consideration. We have given him time for consideration since last Thursday; in fact, we notified him first on Tuesday night, so that he has had a week for consideration now and he can have still longer. There will be an hour or so to-night, or, perhaps, still more, for consideration to be given to the matter. His statement, quoting what he said on June 7, is that he would not be willing to vote interim Supply this year. That was the ultimatum which he gave to the House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: En bloc, yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Is this not en bloc?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
One-sixth
without consideration would be en bloc.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
Who is talking about no consideration; we have never refused consideration, never suggested such a thing. This is an interim Supply vote which is a vote en bloc, which he told us on March 15, supplementing what he said on June 7 of last year, he would not agree to vote. Now he complains because we did not go to him and beg him to recede from his position. If the hon. gentleman had not made that statement, it would have been our duty to

approach him; but he notified us twice from his place in the House that he would not grant interim Supply. Now he complains that we have taken him at his word. Such is the first shift. Then when this came up on the seventh it was suggested by hon. gentlemen opposite that they were not ready to vote interim Supply, but they would vote to pay the public servants. That was as far as they were ready to go then. That is to say they were ready to pay wages and salaries to the civil servants of this country as long as the civil servants did not work-as long as we could not supply them with the material to work with. They would, for example, pay the nurses and the doctors, and other employees in the hospitals under the Department of the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment but they would not buy medicines for the patients, they would not heat the buildings, and they would not pay the rent. They would vote the money to pay the salaries of engineers on irrigation works but they would not vote them supplies to go on their trips. In a word they would pay civil servants money for their services as long as they gave no value therefor. That was the position hon. gentlemen took on the seventh. But to-day they go further: They say we will vote the salaries of the civil servants but nothing else except what is necessary to be voted in order to carry on the public service. But they want to surround even such a vote of interim Supply with some conditions. I ask why surround with conditions this year when conditions were never suggested before? Is it because the amount is larger? Is it because we have to pay $15,000,000 a year on the war debt? Is that the reason for surrounding interim Supplies with conditions? Is it because we have to maintain hospitals for our soldiers at an expenditure of twenty millions or more a year? Is that a reason for surrounding interim Supplies with conditions? Is it because we have to have from forty to fifty million dollars for the land settlement of our soldiers? Is that a reason why there should be conditions? Is it because we spend thirty millions a year or more for pensions? Is that another reason? I hope hon. gentlemen opposite realize in that regard how formidable was their position on the seventh when they were ready to pay the pension commissioners, and all the officers of the commission, but they were not ready to pay any pensions.
Now what is it in the Estimates that hon. gentlemen think should be held up? What is there in those Estimates that is

not necessary for the public service? If hon. gentlemen to-night-and there is yet time

will go through the Estimates and lay their finger on something that they think can profitably wait for a month or two months we are ready to consider it. But they have had plenty of time to do that. Since a week ago they have known that interim Supply would be introduced. I venture to say that never since interim Supply was first asked in this House has it been left as long-in order to enable supplies to be voted in the regular way, if possible-as it has been done in this case. We are now twelve days past the end of the fiscal year and no interim Supply has been voted. We are one week past the time when notice was given that a motion for interim Supply would be introduced. My hon. friends have had all that time to search out an item of some nature-I do not know what it could be-that is in the Estimates to which they want to take exception. We will give them a little longer time, and if there is such that it can, without any injustice at all to the public service, be omitted I have no desire to go on therewith. But we must have interim Supply or there will be paralysis of the public service of this country, and it is interim Supply that we have been notified by the leader of the Opposition officially, on two occasions, that will be denied. Consequently I ask hon. gentlemen from every side of the House what it is that has occurred that justifies an attitude never before assumed in Parliament, that justifies defiance-frank defiance first, modified defiance next, and conditional defiance now-of a practice essential to the business of Parliament. We ask only for the rights that every Government has had in other times; and while we have a majority in this House-while we have a majority ready to support us in that position-we are prepared to give all reasonable time for consideration of every reasonable suggestion, but that done we intend that the majority ' shall rule.	,

If the Prime Minister intends to secure interim Supply, he has, I submit, adopted the wrong tone and the wrong language for securing it. Personally, I do not intend to have my position misrepresented by the right hon. gentleman, any more than the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) permitted him to misrepresent his position. The right hon. gentleman spoke of facts having dropped from under the position taken by hon. gentlemen on this side. Well,
Sir, if anything dropped from under anybody, the ground dropped from under the right hon. gentleman this afternoon when he made an accusation against my hon. friend from Marquette, an accusation that was refuted by that hon. gentleman's reference to Hansard and by his quoting words that fell from a member of the present Government.
Now I would have thought that the generous offer that was made from this side of the House with regard to securing interim Supply by a conference, and subsequently by unanimous consent, would have been met in a very different spirit from that displayed by the Prime Minister. He has endeavoured to ridicule the language used by the leader of the Opposition by twisting the words that the latter hon. gentleman used when he referred to his statement that he would decline to grant interim Supply. Without question the words used by my hon. friend (Mr. King) on that occasion referred to the fact that he would not grant interim Supply for any of the Estimates which had not been considered and the Prime Minister, I submit, must have so understood him. In any event that is the way in which we on this side of the House understood the statement. Personally, I repeat that language and, speaking for myself, and for myself only, I decline to be a party to granting interim Supply for any item in these Estimates which, up to the present time, we have not considered. Now analogies have been sought to be drawn between conditions that exist now and those that existed in times past; and the hon. gentleman who now occupies the position of Finance Minister undertook to re-write the bookkeeping of this country for the last ten years and to make it appear to-night in this House for the first time that there were deficits in years past in which the Finance Minister occupying the position he does, and belonging to the same party that he does, declared that there were surpluses. One notable example of that was referred to by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), who quoted what was said by the minister who occupied that position in the Borden Government in 1912 when, speaking in this House in the spring of that year, he announced a surplus of thirty odd millions and, in a spirit of playfulness, said he would give credit for one-half of it to the Laurier Administration and credit for the other half to the new administration. I refer to that only by

the way. But this is the kind of argument that is used, and this is the spirit in which the generous offer from this side of the House is met.
As I mentioned a moment ago, attempts have been made to prove that conditions now differ in no respect from conditions in the past when interim Supply was asked and granted. Mr. Chairman, conditions differ vastly now from those which prevailed in times past. Generally, conditions differ to the extent which has been alluded to by the two hon. gentlemen who have preceded me in this debate. But there is another important difference which I wish to bring to the attention of the committee, and in regard to which I wish to define my own position whether any other hon. gentleman on this side agrees with me or not. The proposal has been made to pay the salaries of the civil servants. So far as I am concerned I want to qualify that. In as much as it may be regarded as expressing my personal agreement I want to qualify it to this extent-that I will not agree to vote any interim Supply which covers salaries for any of the six hundred and ninety-two new positions which are set forth in these Estimates; I will not be a party to that.

The point of order raised by the hon. member for Queen's and Shelburne (Mr. Fielding) is that the Estimates which appear in the printed volume for the current year cannot be bulked together for the purpose of voting en bloc on account a certain proportion of the said Estimates. The hon. members who have spoken on the point of order have referred to the rule of the House, but none of the members has cited the rule. As a matter of fact, there is no rule of the House of Commons of Canada relating to the manner in which the Estimates shall be submitted to the House. There is however, a general rule, rule 1, which says:
In all cases not provided for hereinafter or by Sessional or other Orders, the rules, usages and forms of proceeding of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland in force on the first day of July, 1867, shall be followed.

Referring to Bourinot and May in order to find the precedents and the customs then in force, I find that my hon. friend the member for Quebec East did not, in citing Bourinot, cite the strongest statement in Bourinot in support of his contention. Bourinot at page 425 says:
When the House goes into committee of supply, the Speaker will call on the chairman of committees, or in his absence, on an experienced member, to take the chair of the committee. The rules that obtain in other committees prevail also in this. Each resolution will be formally proposed from the Chair, and amendments may be made thereto. Each member is provided with a printed copy of the estimates, and the Chairman reads the vote at length frpm a written set of resolutions, each of v/hich he signs when it has been adopted by the committee. As in other committees, each resolution must be proposed and discussed as a distinct question, and when it has been formally carried, no reference can be made again thereto. Neither i3 it regular to discuss any resolution before it has been formally proposed from the Chair. Each vote or resolution is necessarily a question in itself to be proposed, amended and put as any motion or Bill in the House.
That would make it quite clear that the Government would not have the right to vote en bloc the total Estimates for any one year. But provision has been made for an interim vote, and if hon. members will turn to page 450 of Bourinot they will see there the following statement:
"It is an established rule," says a high authority, "that a vote on account should Involve no new principle, but should merely provide for the continuation of services which had been sanctioned in the previous year; and it is the practice not to take more than two or three months' Supply, except in certain particular cases of public emergency, so that the committee in agreeing to vote on account are not pledged to the Estimates for the year in anticipation of the opportunity to be afterwards afforded of voting them in detail."
That is not very clear, but by referring to the 12th edition of Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice, at page 479, hon. members will find the following:
The motion by which a grant on account is proposed follows the customary form. The motion states the total sum required; and the various amounts needed for each department, which compose that sum, are stated in a schedule appended to the resolution^ The question proposed thereon from the Chair follows the terms of the resolution, and places the total sum, the aggregate grant, before the committee for its decision; and upon that question amendments can be moved for the reduction of the whole grant, or for the reduction or omission of the items whereof the grant is composed.
I certainly must follow the precedent just cited and rule that the resolution is quite in order.

speechtext:
I understood from the Prime Minister's argument that he thought as this interim Supply had been granted in times vpast, it should, without question, be granted now, and in connection with his argument the Prime Minister endeavoured to make out that the financial condition of this country was not a serious one. He endeavoured to convey to the House the impression that we had on ordinary account a very large surplus of revenue over expenditure. I cannot think that the Prime Minister, with the sense of responsibility which that position entails, would wish to convey to this House and this country anything but the real fact, that the country's financial condition merits the serious attention of every patriotic Canadian citizen. What has been done in the past is not a precedent as to what should be done at this time, because our financial condition is so different from what it was in days gone by.
I think that perhaps members of the House may be interested in a every brief consideration of the following figures: the total expenditure of Canada for the fiscal year in which Confederation took place, 1867-68, amounted to just under thirteen and a-half millions on ordinary and on capital account. If you estimate the population of Canada at that time as three and a-half millions-and I think that is a fair computation for the purpose of my argument-you will find that the expenditure per head during that year, both on capital and ordinary account, was $3.84. Ten years afterwards, our expenditures had gone up to twenty-three and a-half millions. Our population had gone up to about four and a-half millions, and the

per head expenditure amounted to $5.43. In 1887-88 our expenditure had risen to almost thirty-seven, millions. The population was then over four and three-quarter millions, and the per capita expenditure- and those figures always relate to capital as well as ordinary account-amounted to $7.63. In 1897-98 the expenditure amounted to thirty-nine millions and the average per capita expenditure to $7.24 and at the end of the next decennial period, 1907-8 it had risen to just over seventy-six and a-half millions. Our population was estimated then at about seven and a-quar-ter millions and the per head expenditure to $10.63. In 1910-11 the former Prime Minister of this country stated that an expenditure of just over eighty-seven and three-quarter millions was a fair indication or prima facie evidence, if I remember his terms correctly, of corruption. Our population was then about seven and a-quarter millions, and the yearly expenditure amounted to $12.18 per capita. In the last year before the war the total expenditure on capital and ordinary account amounted to about one hundred and twenty-seven and a-quarter millions, and, estimating our population at seven and a-quarter million, we find an annual per head expenditure of $17.68. Last year our per head expenditure was just about $74.20, and it will be just as high this year. It is true, as the Prime Minister said, that money is badly needed; but is it not even more true that reduction in the Estimates is required, and that we must cut down the expenditures of this country?
I know that complaint against extravagance of governments by Oppositions is not a new note to be sounded in legislative halls, but the Minister of Finance has asked us to point to some expenditures to which we object, and as regards which we do not wish to take the responsibility of voting even one-sixth. I would like the representatives of business on the other side of the House, who, I trust, have some feeling of responsibility for the financial condition of the country, to do me the honour of following me in what I say and, if necessary, to turn over the Estimates and look at the figures to which I very respectfully invite their attention. On page 37 of the Estimates, I find a new dry-dock at Esquimalt, B.C., amount $300,000. Is that a necessary expenditure? I should like to enlist, if I could, on my side the Minister of Finance whose responsibility is very great in the premises at the present
time. I would ask him whether he believes a new drydock at Esquimalt, at a cost of $300,000, is a proper expenditure in the present condition of the country's finances.
I said $300,000; I was wrong; I should have said $1,300,000. It is just one million times worse than I thought it was. Then we find Toronto harbour improvements, amount $1,000,000. I have put upon the Order Paper a request for a return of the quantity of tonnage which comes into and goes out of every port in Canada, and I say that the tonnage that comes into and goes out of Toronto harbour cannot justify for one moment an expenditure of $1,000,000. The expenditure there is a great scheme of civic improvement to give a fine marine driveway or lake driveway for the people of Toronto. It is not in any degree an expenditure for the purpose of bettering the shipping of Canada. One million seven. hundred thousand dollars was spent on this last year, and we are asked to- spend $1,000,000 this year. I would ask hon. members who are interested in this question, which is, after all, the most important question that we have in Canada to-day- the bread and butter question, the question of expenditures of the Government-to look at page 44 of the Estimates where they will find it is proposed to spend $20,000 more on the National Gallery of Canada. No doubt it is a splendid thing to develop art and the artistic qualities and perceptions of our people; but, after all, the first thing that Canadians have to do at the present time is to cut down expenditures.
I would ask hon. members to 1 10 p.m. refer to page 61 of the
Estimates where they will find this item: Civil aviation, $700,000. During the war, I understand that one-half of the British Air Force was manned by Canadians and that they made a grand name for themselves on the western front in air operations. With the advantage of a number of young men who have qualified themselves for work in the air, it should not have been necessary for the Government to propose to spend this amount on civil aviation, and it is a mistake to propose to spend this money because the question is not a pressing one. Then we have a Canadian air force at an amount of $825,000, and again I object to such an item. I cannot pretend to be exhaustive in this discussion; I am only picking out items here and there. I pick out this item on page 63: The Canadian Press, Ltd., $50,000. I have on previous occasions criticised this item, and it is a great mis-

take, for the sake of the Government and the press of this country, that one should be under any obligation to the other. The press of Canada should stand on its own feet, pay its own expenses, and look to no Government, no matter what political complexion that Government may have, for any aid. In days gone by, in the time of Queen Anne, the Grub street scribblers used to be retained by one party or the other in order to help themselves to remain in power or to get into power, I am utterly opposed to this subsidizing of the press by the Government.
I have tried to answer very briefly the challenge of the Prime Minister to indicate in the Estimates anything that fault could be found with. I cannot think, having the pleasure of the personal acquaintance of hon. gentlemen opposite, that they are altogether lost to a sense of responsibility; but may I say, in all seriousness, that the financial condition which confronts our country is of the most serious nature, and economy must be not only preached, but practised.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
May I be permitted
to say just one word in reference to a statement made a short time ago by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy), regarding the apparent increase in the number of employees in the Department of Militia and Defence? When the Estimates were tabled about a month ago, there was some comment in the press and in the corridors of this House, because there was a large apparent increase in the number of officials in the department. But if hon. members had read the Estimates as prepared on page 8, they would have received notice, by means of an asterisk, that the votes now submitted, and the votes previously submitted for the same purpose, differ in this respect, that in former years during the war, those who held many of the positions now tabulated under the Militia Department, were paid, not out of the funds of the Militia Department, but out of the War Vote and the Demobilization Vote which were granted from year to year. As a matter of fact, there has been, during the past year, a tremendous decrease in the employment of the Militia Department. It might well be expected that since the end of the war, employment in that department would rapidly decrease, and such being the case, a short table of figures shows the employment in that department during the war. I give these figures now to correct any misapprehension that may have arisen on the part of 'Mr. McMaster.]
hon. members who hastily read the Estimates as printed.
The total number of civilian employees, temporary and permanent, at Ottawa, and in the various military districts throughout Canada for the war years, was as follows:
1914		 558
1915		 1,231
1916		 2,875
1917		 4,092
1918		 5,201
1919		 8,105
1920		 5,900
At the present date, there are 1,386 both at headquarters and throughout the eleven military districts of Canada. When I assumed office in this department a little over a year ago, there were approximately 5,900 employees. To-day at Ottawa and throughout the districts, there is a total of 1,386. In Ottawa we have still temporary employees to the number of 805. We propose, through the Civil Service Commission, to have a list for some years to come of permanent employees to the number of 339, not 441, as printed in the Estimates. This arises for this reason: Many of these positions, which have arisen only since the war, will have to become permanent for a number of years yet to come. We shall have to maintain a staff in our record office of approximately 74 additional permanent clerks; in our separation allowance and assigned pay branch, of 50 additional permanent clerks; in the central registry, of 43 additional permanent clerks, and in other branches, of 92 additional permanent clerks. Just how long the services of these permanent clerks will be necessary one cannot more than surmise, but I should fancy for a few years, perhaps five, or in extreme cases, seven or eight years. These clerks have not been employed this year for the first time; they have been carried throughout the war. We have reduced the number now to what we believe is a minimum number for future years; but for the first time we propose to .pay those clerks this year out of Militia Department vote while, during former war years, they were paid directly out of War Appropriation and Demobilization votes. The Demobilization vote this year has been reduced to some $6,000,000 or $7,000,000; last year the House will remember that it was $38,000,000. I think the explanation which I have now given will be satisfactory to the committee. I merely wanted to demonstrate that there has been no increase, but a tremendous decrease; in fact, at the present moment in the city of

Ottawa, we have only 805 temporary employees; we propose to have 399, which will make a total of 1,204, and our total in the districts outside of Ottawa will be 184 temporary employees, making a total of 1,386, which we have to-day as against the total of 5,200 which we had fourteen months ago.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, would

Resolution read by the Chairman.

I would like you to
permit me, Mr. Chairman, and I bow to your ruling, to say that the ruling of the Deputy Speaker was in the words of May. He read the words from May and upon that he based his decision.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
I suppose we have a
right to ask questions in regard to any item
in the Estimates? There is an item, number 325, asking for a vote of $80,442, to provide for salaries and contingencies for a purchasing commission. If I remember well, a Bill was introduced two years ago to create a purchasing commission but the Government had to withdraw it owing tc. the opposition it evoked, especially from their own supplies. Last session the Bill was again introduced for the purpose of creating a purchasing commission. Once more strong opposition to that Bill was expressed on both sides and the measure was not pressed to a vote. However we all read in the press, some time after the session was through, that an Order in Council had been passed creating such a commission. I now desire to know if the vote which is covered by this item is to pay the expenses of that purchasing commission created by OrdeT in Council, and I would like to have all the details and particulars surrounding the creation of that body.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: It ik quite true that there was a Bill before the House last year looking to the creation of a statutory purchasing commission with authority conferred upon it to do certain things in virtue of the provisions of that measure. However the proposed Bill did not pass and did not become law. Nevertheless, last session Parliament voted money to provide for the expenses of a purchasing commission to be constituted by the Government. That purchasing commission was constituted by Order in Council, but the Order in Council did not purport to confer upon the commission so named any qualities, functions, or powers special to itself as a distinct and independent body. It was a commission appointed by the Governor in Council -who had the general responsibility for the supervision and direction of the purchasing to be done by the different departments-to exercise, under the authority of the Governor in Council, powers of supervision and direction. For a commission of that kind money was voted at the last session of Parliament and the present item, as 1 understand it, is to provide for the expenses of a commission of that nature-a body quite distinct from what had been proposed to be created under statutory authority with independent powers of its own.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Then this commission does not exist under any statutory authority?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
There is no specific
statute creating that body but, as I have endeavoured to point out, the Government has the responsibility for all the purchasing that is done. Having that responsibility it has the power to direct and the power to supervise, and it has constituted the body which I have just mentioned to exercise these powers of supervision and direction under the authority of the Governor in Council.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: But the will of Parliament-as expressed last year and in the preceding year by members on both sides of the House-was that the purchasing ought to be done as formerly for every department. I would like to know from the minister what is the difference between this purchasing commission, appointed by Order in Council against the will of Parliament, and the commission that it was proposed to create under the Bill that was withdrawn last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
talks about a commission being appointed against the will of Parliament. He completely ignores what I have twice stated, and what he will find to be the fact if he refers to the Estimates of last year and to the Hansard reports of the discussion on the item which provided for the expenses of a purchasing commission. That item was adopted by Parliament after it was quite clear that the Bill was not being proceeded with. It was voted after an explanation which-as nearly as one can affirm when speaking from memory-was identical with the explanation I have given now. It was not a vote to provide for a statutory commission, because there had been no statute, but it was explained to the House what was sought to be done.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: What I am anxious to know is the difference between the functions and the work of this commission and the one whose appointment Parliament refused to sanction?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
The difference is in the powers and authority to be exercised. The commission which it was proposed to create by statute was one upon which Parliament if the statute had been passed -would have conferred directly the power of doing the purchasing, to be exercised independently of authority from the Government; whereas the body that is now constituted is delegated by the Governor in Council to carry out its duties of super-
[Mr. Lapointe. 1
vising and directing the purchasing, and has no independent authority derived from Parliament.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Who are the present members of the purchasing commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: The commission as at present constituted, is composed of the Minister of Interior, Mr. Howard, and Colonel Affleck.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Who is the Minister of Interior?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Sir James Lougheed.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
Would it not have
been better, Mr. Chairman, when Parliament had expressed itself so emphatically against the formation of one sort of body -I hope the minister will not be impatient with me because I am always very good natured, respectful and polite towards him-

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Do not lay it on too thick now.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
I will endeavour to be nothing less than courteous and polite to the Minister of Justice, and I hope that equal courtesy and politeness will be shown by hon. members opposite. The point I wish to make is this: We had a debate upon the purchasing commission last year, and I think the session before, and we all remember the eloquent and businesslike speech made by the member for Lanark (Mr. Stewart) upon the subject. Now the Minister of Justice says this purchasing commission is, in some way or another, different from the purchasing commission which it was proposed to create by the Bill of last session, and if I mistake not by the Bill of the session before. Well, as I understand it, a purchasing commission must of necessity be a commission having to do with purchasing or buying, whether created by a Bill or by an Order in Council. The question I would like to put to the minister with all respect is this: Would it not have been well when Parliament declined to authorize it not to have endeavoured to introduce this purchasing commission-even though it differs somewhat from its predecessor-through a side door by way of Order in Council rather than through the front door by way of a Bill in this House?
' Mr. DOHERTY: That must be done by a Bill, but Parliament having intimated that it did not desire the appointment of this statutory commission, the idea was aban-

doned. Parliament then said by its vote: We do authorize you to create a commission acting under the authority of the Governor in Council, and we are so satisfied you should do it that we vote you some $80,000 for the purpose. Could there be any clearer expression of the will of Parliament? They are two perfectly different things, Parliament realized that, and consequently while Parliament did not want a statutory commission, it did vote to the Government the money to provide this supervisory body to assist it in the performance of the duty that lies upon it to see that the purchasing is done to the best advantage, subject of course to any statutory rules there may he with regard to it which we have hot sought to interfere with.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Would the minister explain the modus operandi followed by this new and alleged unobjectionable purchasing commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: I am not in a position to give the details of their operations, but in substance their functions are supervisory, if I may so express it, and advisory to the different bodies connected with each of the departments. I may say, as being that branch of it which comes most under my cognizance, that the purchasing in my own department proceeds in this way. The officers, say, in charge of the penitentiaries make requisitions for what they require, and those requisitions go in the first instance to the superintendent of the penitentiary. If he approves then they go to the purchasing agent of the Department of Justice.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: The requisitions are made out by whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: By the warden of the penitentiary. He requires certain things, and he forwards his requisitions to the superintendent. Each requisition is sent to him for his approval or criticism. From him it goes to the purchasing agent, who also goes over it and-

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Is that purchasing agent an officer of the commission or of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
He is an officer of the Department of Justice. If my memory serves me right, there is a distinction in amount, and where the amount involved is under $500 the requisition goes to the deputy minister, and if he approves, it is returned to the superintendent. It is then submitted by the purchasing agent to the supervision of this purchasing commission,
and the calling for tenders and so forth is done under and by the advice of that commission. When the tenders come in they are opened by one or the other purchasing agents of the department or the commission, hut both are present or are represented. That, so far as I understand it is the modus operandi.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: As so many shifts are made are not the papers likely to be lost?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: We are not anxious about the papers getting lost, but we are anxious to provide every possible check to see that we have our purchasing made with as close an eye to the public interest as is possible. If the hon. gentleman would reflect for a moment I think he would see the utility of having the co-operation of a body which comes into contact with all the purchasing of all the departments and with the individual officers of those departments. By this means you put at the service of all departments the united knowledge of all the transactions and you get the whole experience derived from the purchasing for all of the departments put at the service of each of them. Surely that is a very substantial advantage; at least it seems so to the Government. When Parliament authorized the Government to provide that additional protection for the public purse the Government felt it was doing nothing but its duty in providing it.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: As far as I have followed the minister I understand the modus operandi to be this. For instance, the warden of the penitentiary wants, say, twenty beds. He writes out his requisition, which would amount to less than $500 I presume. Then he submits that first of all to the superintendent of the penitentiary; the superintendent sends the requisition along to the department's purchasing agent, and as it is under $500 it goes to the deputy minister, and is finally returned to the superintendent. Am I right?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: It is returned to him for the purpose of reaching the commission. That is the machinery.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Then does it go to the purchasing commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
I am not in a position to say whether the purchasing agent carries the document there or not, but it gets to the purchasing commission. The purchasing agent proceeds then under the direction of and with the cooperation of the purchasing commission. Let me point

out that perhaps for our purposes I have begun too far back. There are two substantial things to be decided; in the first place, should these articles be bought; in the second place, if they are to be bought, what is the most advantageous way of buying them.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that you have created a body which would not be needed at all if the departments were administered as they should be with honesty and efficiency. I do not see why we should spend $90,000 a year to create an outside body from the various departments to control those departments. I have had some experience in the administration of public affairs as the head of a large spending department, and I know it was not necessary to have an outside body to judge whether or not the expenditure proposed in that department was needed. In those days they proceeded in this way. Suppose in the Post Office Department paper or ink or stamping machines or letter boxes were required, these were looked after by the officer in the department itself in charge of equipment. The requisition was made by that officer to the deputy minister, and the deputy minister presented it to the minister. If relatively a small amount not over $5,000, it was not necessary that the minister should bring the requisition before his colleagues in council; if over that amount he would have to get an Order in Council. It is the same in all departments. In the Public Works Department, for instance, you cannot go over that amount of $5,000 unless you get special authority in the Estimates or from Council.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Except in the Marine Department.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
Except in emergency cases, and then we know how the Audit Act provides: So I do not see the reason why the Government when it had a number of officers trained in the service since confederation, should consider it necessary to spend this large sum of $90,000 on that outside body particularly when the House on two occasions declined to permit the creation of such a body. Even on the other side of the House I remember hon. gentlemen objected very strenuously to its creation. In spite of that the Government, after being refused that authority last session, created a purchasing commission. Now during the period of the war as ex-
penditure was due, when there was really an emergency and you had no time to consider very much the prices, for time was the essence of all the contracts, I am ready to admit that under those conditions it was a good thing to have such a commission. I have already said that, as to the personnel of that commission during the war, certainly I found no fault, but the war being over, and departments having resumed their natural functions, the various departments came within the normal conditions, as we all did, and it was the duty of the Government to do away with any such expenditure. Such was the desire of Parliament, because on two occasions the then President of the Privy Council was very insistent that this vote should carry, and that this authority be given to this new body. Parliament refused. The members on this side of the House fought as strenuously as we did those on the other side of the House. I say, then, this lack of confidence is in their own followers, but I would place the lack of Confidence above the followers. It is a lack of confidence in the authority of Parliament that has been shown in the present instance by the Government, and I have no hesitation in proposing to do away with that expenditure.
I would, therefore, move that that item be struck out.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: I would like to point out that a motion to strike out would not be in order.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: For what reason? The Deputy Speaker has ruled, quoting May, that a sheet and schedule should be annexed to the resolution, specifying every amount and each amount from each department. That would carry with it permission for the committee to discuss any of these special items mentioned in the list that should be annexed to the resolution, and if we grant to the committee the right of discussing each item included in the list that should be annexed, then it goes without argument that we have the right equally to move for a reduction, of the striking out, of such an item in that list. I think that my hon. friend the member for Maisonneuve, has a perfect right, and that it is in keeping with the ruling of the Deputy Speaker to move that one-sixth of the amount in the main Estimates for the purchasing commission should be struck out. I would like to have your ruling upon that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
A motion of that nature is purely a negative motion which,

under the rules of the House, is never in order.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: I would like to discuss the point of order before you give a ruling. I quite understand that if we were moving to strike out the whole resolution it would be a purely negative motion, but that is not what my hon. friend for Maisonneuve is doing. The resolution is general. It asks to us to vote $70,000,000 en bloc, and my hon. friend for Maisonneuve asks that out of this amount of $70,000,000 an amount of $80,000 be struck out. Surely this is not a motion to negative the whole resolution, and the chairman specifically stated in his ruling that we would have to move to strike out any of the items forming the whole resolution.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman is not quite right as to what is before the committee. In order to get a clear appreciation of it, let us understand what the real practice is, what we are talking about, what we are voting on and what flows from that. In the first instance, we do not, by this vote, either challenge, approve or endorse a single item in the Estimates. The whole of them are left open absolutely. I will take what has been the practice of this House. At page 5595 of the Hansard of 1903 the then Finance Minister said:
I propose that the House give us a vote of credit for one-fifth of the total sum. The effect of this will be to give us a Supply for about two months. All the matters that can be discussed in connection with these votes will, of course, still remain before the House, and we will have to take these up item by item for the purpose of obtaining the remaining four-fifths of the Estimates. So that the course we now propose does not in any way restrict the fullest and freest discussion. It simply facilitates the granting of a partial supply which will be very much needed before the end of the present month.
And the then leader of the Opposition said:
The only question which suggests itself to me is as to the effect of the proposed resolution upon items which there might be a motion to strike out, or upon items which eventually might be dropped.
That is the furthest the hon. gentleman ever went. The Minister of Finance said:
I admit that would be a proper criticism; and if any particular item were indicated as likely to be the subject of debate I would strike it out of the present motion, but if such a motion should be presented later it would apply to the four-fifths.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: That is all based on understanding.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: To this effect: that every item is open to the fullest discussion.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: What are we here for?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: To enable business to be carried on; to try to get money to continue to do business here. There has been ten times more discussion this year than there has ever been before.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend
allow me to say that if he were debating this point with the decision of the Chairman in his mind he would probably alter his judgment. What I am asking now of this committee is that a certain specified amount be omitted from the schedule which is supposed to he annexed to the motion which was made by my hon. friend a moment ago. Suppose that my motion is ruled out, my hon. friend will realize that one-sixth of an item which I want completely omitted will be voted upon. Is that logical? I am against this whole amount which gives life to a commission and a body, the existence of which was refused on two previous occasions by this Parliament, and if we now vote one-sixth of the $80,000 the principle is admitted, and later on it will he absolutely illogical for me to comment and propose its omission. But my friend, as I submit with all due courtesy, has not lived up to the decision of the Chair. The Chairman quoted from May at page 479 as follows:
The motion by which a grant on account is proposed follows the customary form. speechtext:
This amount is largely for salaries of clerks and officials of this commission, so-called. Two weeks have already passed since the beginning of the fiscal year and there is no money to pay them for the two weeks. This institution is carrying on business. By this amendment, if it carries, we refuse Supply for amounts already in a sense ex-
11 p.m. pended, and so close this institution right up. When I say "already expended" I mean that services have been rendered to the country by these officials and nothing has been paid. So much for that part of the matter. I hesitate to delay the committee, but I am a member who is wholly in favour of this purchasing department, and I will give one or two simple illustrations of its value. I have not, under my hand, information that I had on a former occasion. Take, for instance, the question of purchasing of bedding. I understand some of my hon. friends say that they do not want a general discussion of this item, but in view of the opposition made to it, I have a right to express my views in support of it. I am opposed to the striking out of this item for the reasons already mentioned, and this additional reason, that this commission has given good service and has saved a good deal of money to the country, and that if the item were under proper consideration, we might have full information to that effect. Before the committee passes upon this item, we ought to have before us full information as to the value of the services of the commission.. For those reasons I support the passing of this one-sixth vote to pay the expenses of the commission up to the present time and to continue it until the item is under consideration.

speechtext:
My hon. friend says
that he is in favour of this body called the purchasing commission. I respect his views; but unfortunately, he was in a minority, and the Government chose to ignore the will of Parliament expressed during two different sessions. My hon. friend says: "The poor officers of that body are awaiting their salaries." I have much sympathy for them, but the responsible party is the Government. Why did the Government, in spite of Parliament, in spite of the expression of opinion on both sides of the House, immediately after the session was over, ignore the will of Parliament and create that body? Parliament is supreme. The hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Butts), said a moment ago that Parliament was omnipotent. I do not like that expression, but let us say that it is the true expression. Parliament has not been omnipotent in the present instance; the will of Parliament has been disregarded.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: The Government assumed to itself the will of Parliament and created that body. I have much sympathy for the officers of the commission, who, as my hon. friend says, are awaiting their salaries, but the country is entitled to be respected. Members on both sides represent the electors of this country, we have been sent here to check the expenditures of the Government, and not a cent can be spent by this Government without its being voted by Parliament. Parliament has refused on two occasions to vote that amount, to create that body.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: A vote was passed last year.

speechtext: But the vote was to meet a condition to be created by Parliament. An amount was put in the Estimates, but along with this amount a Bill was introduced, and that Bill was combatted by both sides of the House and was finally withdrawn. Yet as soon as Parliament prorogued and the members dispersed, the Government took upon itself to create that body, ignoring the will of this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member would not want to mislead intentionally. Parliament voted that amount of money, after Parliament knew that no Act was going to be passed, for the purpose of providing for the totally different body which, I have pointed out, was explained at the

time and has been explained since. When the hon. gentleman persists and will persist in saying that this commission was created against the will of Parliament, he persists in absolutely confusing two totally different things, one thing which Parliament said it would not have, and another thing which Parliament said it was willing to provide for, one thing that took the absolute control out of the hands of the executive Government to put it into the hands of a body created by statute, and a totally different thing which, leaving the control and the responsibility in the hands of the executive Government, provided for their having suitable agents to aid in the carrying out of that business. Whatever may be right or may be wrong about the principle of the commission, when Parliament comes to deal with the other five-sixths, it will have that principle before it to deal with. What is it that the hon. members' amendment asks us to do? It asks us to say that these clerks and employees, who are engaged in a presently existing service, as regards which it is not anticipated that we may for some time reach the consideration of the item as a whole providing for that expenditure, and who will necessarily go on working in the interval, shall work for two months for nothing. Parliament will be in a position to decide upon the entire principle when we come to deal with the five-sixths. It does not commend itself to my judgment to suggest that, before we come to deal with the entire principle and to determine it, we should take off that two months' pay from those persons whose operations will go on in the meantime. Let us get down to common sense and realize what it is that is before us, however we may technically discuss this matter. One thing is beyond peradventure, that the worst that can happen in regard to anyone of these items is that two months expenditure could be made even though Parliament should ultimately determine not to carry on the operation at all. And when it is the case, as in this particular instance, that the worst thing that can happen is that two months' pay will go to officers who will have done two months' work-even if Parliament finally decided not to carry on this work for the future-I do sumbit to the common-sense judgment of the House that the right time to settle the principle is when you are dealing with the great and substantial vote, and when you can deal with it and settle it once and for all, and not endeavour to do so when it is merely 
a question of voting two months' pay for all these employees.

I do not misunderstand them and I am young enough to have a good memory. I tell my hon. friend that during the period of the war a commission was instituted by the Government with a view to the purchase of the various equipments that were necessary, and in order to review some of the war contracts. That was the commission presided over by Sir Hermisdas Laporte. After the commission had completed its work, and after the war was over, it made a report asking the Government to make it a permanent body, representing that it would be an excellent idea if there was a permanent purchasing commission. That idea was embodied in a Bill which was introduced two years ago by the then President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell). It was combatted with much vigor by gentlemen on both sides and the measure was withdrawn. Last year it was decided to re-introduce the Bill embodying the exact principles cited a moment ago by my hon. friend and, under the assumption that Parliament this time would not oppose the legislation, an amount was plated in the Estimates for the purpose of creating the organization. But Parliament-with a persistence that I can only admire-again made its opposition felt, and again members on both sides stood firm in their objections. I see my hon. friend from Dufferin (Mr. Best) shaking his head but he was one of those who continued to oppose the Bill-in fact there were many on the Government side who took that course. Have not the various ministers in the Government the necessary authority to control the expenditures in their departments, and have they not enough confidence in their own personal honesty to exercise, that control? Why should they have such an external body as this to purchase the supplies needed by their departments and to supervise the acts of their employees? There is in every department the necessary machinery

to supervise the purchasing of supplies and the purchasing of equipment, and there is no need for such a body as this. Mr. Chairman, we cannot understand how the Minister of Justice can so explain this item, in view of the withdrawal of the Bill referred to, as to make it clear, in his own way,, that it is a totally different body from the one contemplated last year and the year before. I see hon. gentlemen opposite me who expressed opposition to this proposal, and I trust their memory and their honour in this matter. Is not this item regarded as a way out of the impasse in which the former President of the Privy Council found himself after the experience of the last two sessions of Parliament? He could not succeed in passing the legislation because it was opposed as much by members on the Government side as by members on this side. And yet the Government now comes forward with this proposal. They have ignored and disregarded the opinion of Parliament, but they now come here and say "You must pass this item because we have decided by Order-in-Council to create this body in spite of your opposition." I have more regard for the authority of Parliament than to expect that such a proposition will be successful. I say that Parliament is the supreme master in this question, and we have the right to say now if we approve of the principle involved. I say further that if we now vote one-sixth of the Estimate we are committed to the principle which Parliament last year, and the year before, opposed. Therefore, let us reduce this item by one-sixth, and Parliament will then have expressed its opinion as to the necessity of having such an external body foisted on the country when the country is simply hungry for economy and still more economy. My right hon. friend may think I am lacking in sincerity, but I hope not, because from what is happening outside and from what news he may receive-not only from Canada but from Great Britain-he must realize that this great country of ours is in very serious , difficulties at this very moment. Why, Mr. Chairman, is it not a time not only to speak of economy but to practise it? There is a payment due and overdue in London-

the arbitration now going on. Yet the shareholders of that company are denied their payments-a payment guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada. People say that there is no money in the Exchequer to meet the obligation of Canada. I do not believe that but at all events, be that as it may, in view of that circumstance, and in view of many others, is it not time for us not only to speak of economy but to practise it? The Minister of Finance should not only practise economy in the ordinary sense of the term but he should adopt a policy of cheese-paring. We are living in a fool's paradise. We have been so accustomed to speak of millions, and even billions, during the last few years that we have lost all sense of proportion, and the country is facing a very heavy bill of taxation. If you do not cut down the expenditure wl^en it is useless expenditure, as in the present instance, how can you ask the people of this country to tax themselves to the limit as they are doing? They have taxed themselves last year and they are ready to do it again provided there is adequate justification. But who is there in the Government who is practising economy, instead of merely preaching it? Look at the volume of the Estimates with whicn Parliament is now called upon to deal- the figures are simply appalling. We are spending our time looking at each other and deprecating the huge financial commitments of the country and yet no one applies the pruning knife. Why not begin by applying the pruning knife to this very unnecessary appendage to the various departments of the Government?

Hon. members opposite have said that we cannot consistently move to reduce a single item if we pass this one-sixth to-night. But I would remind hon. gentlemen that on June 30, last, as will be seen by a reference to page 4549 of last year's Hansard, the leader of the Opposition, when the Committee of Supply were considering an item of $6,500,000 for the Permanent Force in the Estimate of the Department

of Militia, moved to reduce the item by $1,000,000. Was he within his rights in doing so or was he not? Without presuming to give an opinion as to what the parliamentary practice is, I submit that common-sense would suggest that the hon. gentleman was within his rights and yet interim Supply had previously been voted on this item as well as on all other items. I think, if my memory serves me right, without referring to the records, the leader of the Opposition, subsequent to that date last year, voted to reduce several other items in the Estimates. I presume he will do the same this year; it will be his right to do so. There are items in the Estimates which hon. members may wish to scrutinize, and even to criticise, and they can only do that when the minister in charge of the department, with his officials, is here to explain why the vote is being asked and what work is being accomplished in connection with the expenditures for which authority is sought. Again I say that if the contention is sound that we cannot reduce or change any item because of voting this interim Supply of one-sixth, then the committee might just as well vote the one-sixth and go home, because there is no use discussing the Estimates in any shape or form.

Perhaps I could give some information which I know the hon member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) would be glad to get. He says that we are ignoring our responsibilities in the English money market. We want to be able to discharge them. He has expressed great anxiety that Canada's fair name is suffering in England. I may tell him and the committee that as a matter of fact payments there will become due within two days, and this interim Supply is to enable those payments to be discharged.

speechtext: Will the minister tell us what construction has been done this year on the Welland ship canal?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Four contractors have been working for the last two or three years.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Were the contracts given by tender, and what were the amounts?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: The original contracts were given by tender, but shortly after the war broke out those contracts were cancelled. Last year the officials of the department did not think that it was in the public interest to call for tenders on account of the very high cost of labour and materials, and contracts were given on a cost plus basis, terminable at any time and not to extend longer than December 31, last. At that time we again extended the contract for 1921 on the same basis. When we decided to do that last January we believed it would be far better if we could let the work by public tender. Accordingly the officials of the department were instructed to prepare plans and call for tenders at the earliest possible date. Plans were ready for section five and three tenders were received last Thursday.

subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext: Did the minister say there were five sections or four?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: RESOLUTION FOR ONE-SIXTH OF AMOUNT REQUIRED FOR NEXT FISCAL YEAR
speechtext:
No. There are nine sections altogether, but prior to the war ten-



ders were called for and contracts let for sections 1, 2, 3 and 5, which were cancelled later as I have stated, and the contractors were allowed to continue on a cost plus basis. We received tenders for section 5 last Thursday, and an Order in Council will be passed to-morrow or next day awarding the contract. The other three sections on which work is continuing, on the cost plus basis, will be let by tender within a very short time just as soon as the officers of the department can get the specifications ready.

If the hon. gentleman will pardon me for interrupting. It has
been suggested to me that we had a fairly long session last night we should not unduly prolong the sitting this afternoon. However, before moving that the committee rise, I desire Mr. Chairman, to give the following notice:
That at the next sitting of the Committee of Supply I shall move that the further consideration of Resolution No. 218 as printed at page 49 of the Estimates for the current fiscal year and the further consideration of the resolution proposed this day for interim Supply, shall be the first order of business of the committee and shall not further be postponed.
Progress reported.
On motion of Right Hon. Mr. Doherty the House adjourned at 11.45 p.m.
